failure_type: relevance/noise; Paper B additionally covers consistency/conflict (counterfactual noise)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor for both; Paper B constructs an explicit three-way noise mixture (relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual), Paper A focuses on naturally noisy retrieval plus distractor passages
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts); Paper B: generator prompting or training only (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise classification head)
metric_target: answer correctness (F1/EM) for both
action_policy: Paper A: filter then answer (NLI-driven fallback to no-retrieval); Paper B: answer (no explicit abstain/filter); action policies are reported but not aligned
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RALMs for ODQA and train generators to better tolerate imperfect retrieval, with NQ as a shared dataset. However, the failure-type scope differs: Yoran et al. concentrate on irrelevant/distracting passages, while RAAT explicitly partitions noise into relevant, irrelevant, and counterfactual, with the counterfactual case crossing into consistency/conflict territory. The interventions also occupy different points in the pipeline (NLI-based context filtering plus fine-tuning vs. adversarial training with a noise-aware auxiliary task), and the action policies diverge (Yoran can drop retrieval entirely; RAAT always answers from the augmented context). Because of these mismatches and only partial benchmark overlap (5 ODQA incl. multi-hop vs. RAG-Bench's 3 single-hop datasets with constructed noise mixtures), the two should be discussed as complementary mechanisms rather than ranked head-to-head.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-run both methods on a unified benchmark that includes all three noise categories and at least one multi-hop set, with identical base LLM (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), identical retriever and top-k, identical noise-injection protocol, and identical F1/EM normalization. Report an explicit action policy for each system (answer vs. abstain vs. fall-back-to-no-retrieval) and evaluate NLI-filter and RAAT both independently and stacked, so that intervention point and action policy are controlled rather than confounded with method identity.
notes: Pair is the canonical 'related but not directly rankable' case in noise-robustness: clearly the same problem family, but different noise taxonomy, different intervention surface, and different action semantics.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); rgb2023 additionally covers sufficiency (negative rejection) and consistency/conflict (counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: irrelevantContext2023: benign retrieval error from real ODQA retrievers, plus training-time mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts. rgb2023: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents.
intervention_point: irrelevantContext2023: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (fine-tune on mixed contexts). rgb2023: evaluation artifact (benchmark only; no model-side intervention proposed).
metric_target: irrelevantContext2023: answer correctness on 5 ODQA datasets. rgb2023: answer correctness + rejection rate + accuracy under counterfactual + integration accuracy across 4 testbeds.
action_policy: irrelevantContext2023: answer (with filter acting as an implicit abstain-from-context but not a reported abstain action). rgb2023: answer and abstain (explicitly scored via negative rejection).
rationale: Both papers address robustness of RAG to noisy retrieved context, so the topical area genuinely overlaps. However, irrelevantContext2023 is a method paper proposing NLI filtering and robustness fine-tuning evaluated on naturally retrieved ODQA passages with answer correctness as the sole metric, while rgb2023 is a benchmark artifact with four separate testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness), controlled noise ratios, and explicit abstain scoring. The intervention points (model-side mitigation vs. evaluation construction) and action policies (answer-only vs. answer + explicit abstain) do not align, so they cannot be ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard. They are best treated as complementary - rgb2023's noise-robustness testbed could in principle measure the methods from irrelevantContext2023, but as published, only partial comparison is justified.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the NLI-filter and robust-fine-tuned generator from irrelevantContext2023 on RGB's noise-robustness, negative-rejection, and counterfactual testbeds with identical retriever/generator backbones; report the same metric family (accuracy, rejection rate) and an explicit, evaluated action policy (answer vs. abstain) so both works are scored on the same axes. Conversely, irrelevantContext2023 would need to add abstain scoring and counterfactual stressors matched to RGB's construction.
notes: A method-paper vs. benchmark-paper pair: leaderboard-style ranking is structurally inappropriate, but the two are not in incompatible problem settings, hence partial rather than invalid.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (raat2024); evaluation artifact (rgb2023)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (rgb2023 negative rejection only)
action_policy: answer (raat2024); answer + abstain (rgb2023 negative rejection); otherwise unreported
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs and share a counterfactual-noise sub-problem, and both rely on benchmark-constructed retrieval stressors. However, raat2024 is a training-based intervention (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise classification on LLaMA-2 7B) evaluated on its own RAG-Bench with F1/EM under noise mixtures and an answer-only action policy, while rgb2023 is purely an evaluation artifact (bilingual benchmark) that decomposes RAG into four abilities including negative rejection (an abstain action) and counterfactual robustness, evaluated zero-shot on off-the-shelf LLMs. The intervention point, evaluation protocol, and action policy set therefore diverge: one produces a method to rank, the other produces testbeds and diagnostics with abstain semantics that raat2024 never measures. They are complementary (one could in principle evaluate RAAT on RGB), but cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as alternative methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT and reasonable baselines on the RGB testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) using RGB's noise-ratio protocol and accuracy/rejection-rate metrics, and conversely evaluate the LLMs scored in rgb2023 on RAG-Bench with matched retriever, noise construction, and an explicit action policy (answer vs abstain). Reporting must include the same generator backbones, retriever, noise-ratio sweep, and per-ability metrics including rejection accuracy.
notes: Asymmetric pair: method paper vs benchmark paper; partial is appropriate because the failure-type overlap is real but intervention and action-policy axes are structurally different.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error, benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (CON note-taking + abstain); context assembly/compression (NLI filter) and generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning) (Yoran et al.)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage and rejection rate (CON only)
action_policy: answer + abstain (CON, explicitly evaluated via rejection rate on RealTimeQA); filter + answer (Yoran et al., NLI-based passage filtering); no abstain mechanism reported in Paper B
rationale: Both papers target the same failure type—generator distraction by irrelevant retrieved passages in open-domain QA under benign retrieval errors—and both report answer-correctness gains, so they sit in the same problem family. However, the intervention points differ substantively: Chain-of-Note modifies generator reasoning with per-document reading notes and an explicit 'unknown' abstain output, whereas Yoran et al. either filter passages upstream via an NLI entailment check or fine-tune the generator on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts. The action policies are also different—CON evaluates an abstain/rejection-rate metric (selective risk), while Yoran et al. evaluate filter+answer behavior and add multi-hop reasoning as a key axis that CON does not test. These are complementary mitigations that could even be stacked, so a direct leaderboard ranking would mislead; the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A common evaluation harness with the same retriever, generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 fine-tuned), shared single-hop AND multi-hop ODQA benchmarks, and aligned noise constructions; report both answer accuracy and an abstain/coverage curve so CON's rejection behavior and Yoran et al.'s filter behavior are scored on the same selective-prediction metric; include an ablation that decouples the NLI filter from fine-tuning and CON's note step from its abstain head; and either disable CON's abstain or add an equivalent abstain policy to the Yoran et al. system so action policies match.
notes: Action policies are explicit in both papers but are not the same policy; this is the strongest break, with intervention-point divergence reinforcing the 'partial' call.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, verifier, system-control policy, retriever
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, citation faithfulness
action_policy: abstain, answer, re-retrieve
rationale: Both papers tackle quality issues in RAG by introducing some form of adaptive/reflective decision-making, and both share a broad concern with hallucination caused by unhelpful retrieved context. However, Sufficient Context is an inference-time diagnostic + selective-generation method whose action policy is explicit abstain-vs-answer gated on a sufficiency autorater and self-confidence, while Self-RAG is a training-time framework that teaches the LM to emit reflection tokens governing on-demand retrieval and self-critique, with the action being retrieve/continue/select-best rather than abstain. The intervention points (post-hoc verifier + selective policy vs. end-to-end generator training with reflection tokens and adaptive retriever calls), the action policies (abstention vs. on-demand retrieval + critique), and the headline metrics (selective accuracy/hallucination rate among answered queries vs. citation faithfulness and task accuracy across six tasks) diverge enough that a direct leaderboard ranking would conflate orthogonal contributions. They are better discussed as complementary mechanisms operating at different stages of the RAG pipeline, hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared QA benchmark suite with (i) the same retriever and base generator, (ii) a common action-policy interface that lets each system either abstain, answer, or trigger re-retrieval, (iii) a unified metric set covering selective accuracy at matched coverage, hallucination rate, and citation faithfulness, and (iv) controlled evaluation on instances stratified by sufficiency so Self-RAG's adaptive retrieval and Sufficient Context's selective abstention can be compared on the same operating points.
notes: Both are plausibly cited together in RAG-quality surveys, but the comparison is mechanism-vs-policy rather than head-to-head.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence); Self-RAG: relevance/noise + sufficiency (indiscriminate retrieval, ungrounded generation)
evidence_assumption: Both: benign retrieval error / standard non-adversarial setting; no threat model specified in either paper
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker + context assembly (forecasting function f(t,q,d) used for selection) with calibration training signal; Self-RAG: generator training (reflection tokens) + system-control policy (on-demand retrieve decision)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness for decision-making; Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer (with calibrated confidence) — no abstain/escalate evaluated; Self-RAG: re-retrieve (adaptive) + verify (self-critique) + answer
rationale: Both papers aim to improve RAG reliability, but they target different failure modes via different mechanisms. CalibRAG addresses calibration of decision confidence by training a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) and is evaluated primarily with calibration metrics in a decision-making setting, while Self-RAG addresses indiscriminate retrieval and ungroundedness by training an LM with reflection tokens for adaptive retrieval and self-critique, evaluated on factuality and citation accuracy. Their intervention points (reranker/selection-time calibration vs. generator training + on-demand retrieval control) and their action policies (passive answer-with-confidence vs. adaptive re-retrieve/verify) differ substantially, and the primary metric families barely overlap. They are best framed as complementary modules in a reliable-RAG stack rather than as substitutable methods on the same leaderboard, so partial is appropriate rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark with (i) the same retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; (ii) joint reporting of calibration (ECE/Brier/decision-correctness calibration), task accuracy, and citation/grounding faithfulness; (iii) a common, explicit action policy space (e.g., answer/abstain/re-retrieve) evaluated under matched thresholds; and (iv) either applying CalibRAG's forecasting function on top of Self-RAG's adaptive-retrieval outputs or adding calibration metrics to Self-RAG (and citation faithfulness to CalibRAG) so both systems are scored on the same metric family for the same operating regime.
notes: Both works are non-adversarial; threat-model coordinates not applicable. The asymmetry is mostly in metric target and action policy rather than evidence assumption.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (FaithfulRAG) vs integrity/adversarial corruption (PoisonedRAG)
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge (FaithfulRAG) vs attacker-created evidence (PoisonedRAG: corpus write access = yes, query control = knows target questions, retriever visibility = black-box and white-box, generator access = black-box, insertion budget = ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer)
intervention_point: generator prompting/training and context assembly (FaithfulRAG: self-fact mining, alignment, self-think) vs corpus/index (PoisonedRAG: malicious text injection into the knowledge database)
metric_target: answer correctness / faithfulness (FaithfulRAG) vs attack success rate (PoisonedRAG)
action_policy: answer with conflict reconciliation (FaithfulRAG) vs unreported defender policy; PoisonedRAG only measures attacker-induced answers and does not evaluate any defender action policy
rationale: Both papers touch on RAG behavior under problematic retrieved content, but that is where the overlap ends. FaithfulRAG treats naturally arising parametric-vs-context conflict and intervenes at the generator with a fact-level reconciliation module, evaluated by answer correctness and faithfulness on standard QA. PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that assumes an adversary with corpus write access and a small injection budget, intervenes at the corpus, and reports attack success rate against a defenseless RAG. The failure type (benign conflict vs adversarial corruption), evidence assumption (natural vs attacker-crafted), intervention side (defense vs offense), and metric family (accuracy vs ASR) all diverge, so leaderboard-style ranking would be category-error misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe as a defense-vs-attack evaluation rather than alternative methods: deploy FaithfulRAG (and a matched baseline RAG) as the target system, instantiate PoisonedRAG with a fixed threat model (same corpus, retriever, generator, insertion budget, target question set), and report a common metric pair such as attack success rate and clean-task accuracy under identical action policies (answer/abstain). Only then can the two be placed in the same comparison, and only as defense vs attack, not as substitutable robust-RAG methods.
notes: PoisonedRAG is fundamentally an attack contribution and FaithfulRAG a generator-side conflict-resolution contribution; they belong on orthogonal axes of the robust-RAG space.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption shared; Astute RAG also covers relevance/noise and consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model (corpus write access yes, query control yes, retriever visibility both black-box and white-box, generator access varied, insertion budget ~5 texts per target question into a corpus of millions, attack objective induce attacker-chosen target answer). Astute RAG: mixed benign retrieval error, benchmark-constructed stressor, and some attacker-created evidence in worst-case RGB, without a specified threat model.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free source-aware consolidation). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious text injection); defenses only surveyed.
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness including worst-case accuracy. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate, plus retrieval recall of malicious texts.
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer with implicit verify/consolidate over source-tagged candidates (reported). PoisonedRAG: unreported on the defender side; attacker objective is to force answer equal to target.
rationale: Both papers concern integrity and adversarial-corruption failure modes in RAG, so they share a problem area, but one is a defense (Astute RAG) and the other is an attack (PoisonedRAG). Their intervention points differ (generator-side consolidation vs. corpus-side injection), their headline metrics differ (answer correctness vs. attack success rate), and their evidence assumptions are not aligned because PoisonedRAG specifies a concrete threat model while Astute RAG mixes generic noise, benchmark stressors, and unspecified malicious content. They are complementary modules in an attack-defense cycle rather than substitutable methods on the same leaderboard, so the comparison is partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate Astute RAG and competing defenses directly against PoisonedRAG attacks under a single declared threat model (fixed insertion budget, retriever visibility, query control, generator access), using the same corpus, retriever, generator, target questions, and report both ASR and answer correctness with explicit action policies (answer, abstain, expose conflict). Symmetrically, run PoisonedRAG attacks with Astute RAG as a defender baseline alongside other robustness methods.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pairing; partial is the appropriate verdict since they map to opposite sides of the same threat surface but are not directly rankable.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence in both; PoisonedRAG threat model = corpus write access (inject ~5 malicious passages per target question), no query control needed, both black-box and white-box retriever visibility evaluated, no generator access required, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer; RobustRAG threat model = bounded number k' of corrupted retrieved passages, adaptive attacker with full knowledge of defense, attack objective abstracted (any response degradation)
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG, attacker-side injection); context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG, defender-side isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG ASR); answer correctness with certified lower bound under bounded corruption (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported / not applicable on attacker side (PoisonedRAG); answer via aggregated keyword/decoding output with implicit abstain branch ('I don't know') (RobustRAG)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, role (attack vs defense)
rationale: Both papers share the same failure type (adversarial retrieval corruption) and assume attacker-created evidence in the corpus, so they live in the same threat ecosystem. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack paper whose intervention is corpus injection and whose metric is attack success rate against undefended or weakly defended RAG, while RobustRAG is a defense paper whose intervention is context assembly via isolate-then-aggregate and whose metric is certified answer correctness under a bounded corruption budget. Their action policies are categorically different (induce target answer vs. produce a robust answer through aggregation), and they sit on opposite sides of the security pipeline. Placing them on a single leaderboard would conflate attacker capability with defender robustness, which is a category error; the correct relationship is composition (use PoisonedRAG as the threat against which RobustRAG is evaluated), not ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require both artifacts to be the same kind of method. Either (a) compare PoisonedRAG against other attacks (e.g., GCG-style, Phantom, corpus poisoning baselines) on a shared defended RAG stack using a common ASR/utility metric, or (b) compare RobustRAG against other defenses (e.g., majority voting, perplexity filtering, retrieval re-ranking) under a shared attack such as PoisonedRAG with fixed k', the same retriever, generator, knowledge base, and an agreed accuracy/certified-bound metric and explicit action policy (answer/abstain). Without this, the two papers should be reported as complementary—attack vs. defense—rather than ranked.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pairing; even though both target retrieval corruption, the comparability question collapses because they are not alternative methods for the same task.

failure_type: sufficiency, consistency/conflict, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (RAGTruth: naturally generated LLM hallucinations over standard RAG contexts); benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: deliberately injected noise documents and counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally exercises verifier (hallucination detection methods, fine-tuned detector)
metric_target: citation faithfulness, evidence support (RAGTruth: span-level hallucination detection P/R/F1); answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (RGB: accuracy, rejection rate, error detection rate)
action_policy: unreported (RAGTruth — detection is post-hoc, no abstain/expose-conflict evaluated); abstain, expose conflict (RGB — negative rejection and counterfactual identification are explicit)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation artifacts addressing trustworthiness of LLM outputs given retrieved context, and both touch consistency and sufficiency failures. However, RAGTruth is a corpus of naturally generated LLM responses annotated at the word level for hallucination, evaluated via span-level detection metrics and used to train detectors; RGB instead constructs targeted stressors (varying noise ratios, all-noise contexts, counterfactual passages) and scores LLMs on end-task accuracy plus an explicit abstain/rejection behavior across four distinct abilities. The evidence assumption (naturally occurring vs. benchmark-constructed), the metric family (detection F1 over annotated spans vs. answer accuracy and rejection rate), and the action policy (none vs. explicit abstain/expose-conflict) all diverge, so a number reported on one benchmark cannot be ranked against a number reported on the other. The two are best framed as complementary diagnostics — hallucination detectability vs. ability-decomposed accuracy under stressors — rather than alternatives on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) re-run RGB-stressed contexts through the same generators and have annotators produce RAGTruth-style word-level hallucination labels, then report span-level detection F1 and answer correctness jointly on a shared set; or (b) define a common task (e.g., abstain-or-answer with grounded support) with matched generators, matched retriever/contexts, a single noise/counterfactual construction protocol, and a single metric family (e.g., faithfulness + selective accuracy + rejection rate). Both benchmarks would also need to declare the same action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict) and the same evidence-construction regime (natural vs. constructed) so that scores measure the same quantity.
notes: Both are 'evaluation_benchmark' in surface category, but the unit of evaluation (annotated span vs. ability testbed) and the required system behavior (silent generation graded post-hoc vs. explicit rejection) differ enough that direct ranking would mislead.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise (RGB also covers consistency/conflict via counterfactual testbed and an information-integration ability not present in Sufficient Context)
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents; Sufficient Context: naturally occurring retrieval (Wikipedia/HotPotQA/Musique/FreshQA) labeled by an LLM autorater - i.e., observed sufficiency rather than synthesized
intervention_point: RGB: evaluation artifact only (benchmark + four testbeds); Sufficient Context: evaluation artifact (autorater) + verifier (sufficiency classifier) + generator prompting (selective generation combining sufficiency and self-confidence)
metric_target: Both: answer correctness and an abstention-related quantity. RGB reports accuracy, rejection rate, error detection rate and integration accuracy across separate testbeds; Sufficient Context reports correct/abstain/hallucinate stratified by sufficiency plus selective risk/coverage trade-offs
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention/negative rejection rather than just default QA answering)
rationale: Both papers are RAG-evaluation contributions that explicitly score answer-vs-abstain behavior when retrieved context is noisy or insufficient, so the failure type and action policy genuinely overlap. However, RGB is a fixed bilingual benchmark with four orthogonal synthetic testbeds (noise ratio, all-noise rejection, integration, counterfactual), whereas Sufficient Context defines a property over (Q,C) pairs, builds an LLM autorater to label naturally retrieved contexts, and adds a selective-generation intervention on top - so the intervention points and evidence assumptions diverge, and the metric families (per-testbed accuracy/rejection vs. sufficiency-stratified correct/abstain/hallucinate and selective risk-coverage) are not directly commensurable. The two should be reported as complementary lenses (controlled stressor benchmark vs. sufficiency-stratified analysis + selective generation), not ranked on a single leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both systems on a common dataset where each instance carries (a) RGB-style controlled noise/counterfactual conditions and (b) Sufficient Context autorater labels, using the same retriever and generator(s); report a shared metric set including accuracy, abstention rate, hallucination rate and selective risk-coverage curves, and align RGB's 'negative rejection' with Sufficient Context's 'abstain when insufficient' so both papers' action policies are scored on identical (Q,C) pairs.
notes: Both papers do satisfy the action-policy requirement (abstention is explicitly evaluated), so the break is not action_policy but the intervention/metric/evidence axes.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (both); RAGTruth also covers relevance/noise and sufficiency as hallucination categories
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error and naturally occurring conflict in standard RAG outputs; FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring parametric-vs-retrieved conflict (no adversarial threat model in either)
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) plus verifier (detection methods benchmarked on it); FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining + self-think) with context assembly/compression (chunk alignment)
metric_target: RAGTruth: span-level hallucination detection performance (evidence support / citation faithfulness as detector F1); FaithfulRAG: answer correctness on knowledge-conflict QA
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (detect hallucinated spans, no answer policy); FaithfulRAG: answer (after self-think reconciliation); neither evaluates abstention or escalation
rationale: Both papers target unfaithfulness in RAG, but they are different categories of contribution rather than alternative methods. RAGTruth is an evaluation corpus with word-level hallucination annotations used to benchmark detection approaches (evaluation artifact + verifier intervention, with detector F1 as the metric and a 'verify' action). FaithfulRAG is a generation-time method that mines parametric self-facts, aligns them with retrieved chunks, and runs a self-think module to reconcile conflicts before producing an answer (generator-prompting intervention, answer correctness metric, 'answer' action). The failure-type overlap is only partial: RAGTruth spans general hallucination categories across QA/summarization/data-to-text, while FaithfulRAG narrowly targets parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflict in QA. They are complementary (FaithfulRAG could be evaluated on RAGTruth) but cannot be ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG end-to-end on RAGTruth's QA subset (and ideally summarization/data-to-text) using identical retriever/generator stacks, and either (a) evaluate FaithfulRAG outputs with RAGTruth-style span-level hallucination annotation/detection to report the same evidence-support metric, or (b) build/adopt a shared knowledge-conflict QA benchmark with matched answer-correctness and faithfulness metrics on which RAGTruth-fine-tuned detectors are operationalized into a verify-then-answer pipeline. The two systems must also share an explicit action policy (answer vs verify vs abstain) so that detection F1 and answer correctness become directly relatable.
notes: Classic benchmark-vs-method mismatch within the same broad topic; partial rather than invalid because the artifacts are interoperable and the failure type genuinely overlaps on consistency/conflict.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B counterfactual noise only)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (naturally retrieved irrelevant passages via Google/SerpAPI-style retrieval over Wikipedia/web); Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAG-Bench synthetically injects relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual noise on top of DPR retrieval over Wikipedia)
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI entailment filter) + generator prompting/training (fine-tune on mixed contexts); Paper B: generator prompting/training only (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-type classification head)
metric_target: answer correctness (both; EM/F1 on ODQA)
action_policy: Paper A: filter (drop non-entailing passages, fall back to closed-book answer) — explicitly evaluated; Paper B: answer — no explicit abstention, filtering, or recovery action reported
rationale: Both papers tackle noise robustness for RALMs on open-domain QA and even share NQ as an evaluation set, so the high-level failure family (retrieved noise hurting answer accuracy) overlaps. However, Paper B explicitly enlarges the noise taxonomy to include counterfactual/conflicting passages (a consistency failure), whereas Paper A targets only irrelevance/distraction; the noise is also constructed differently (naturally retrieved vs. benchmark-synthesized over DPR top-k). The interventions sit at different points in the pipeline — Paper A combines an NLI context filter with mixed-context fine-tuning and explicitly evaluates a filter-then-fallback action policy, while Paper B is a pure training-time adversarial method that just answers without any filter/abstain action at inference. Different retrievers (web search vs. DPR), different base LLMs, and different action policies mean a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate noise-type coverage, pipeline interventions, and inference policies. The pair is therefore complementary/partial rather than directly comparable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold the retriever (e.g., DPR over Wikipedia) and base generator constant; evaluate both methods on a common noise suite that covers irrelevant AND counterfactual passages with matched injection budgets; report each system both with and without the NLI filter so the filtering intervention is ablated separately from the training objective; explicitly define and evaluate a common action-policy set (answer vs. filter+fallback vs. abstain) with the same metric family (EM/F1 plus a conflict-handling/abstention metric); include multi-hop as well as single-hop conditions so Paper A's scope is matched.
notes: Paper B cites Paper A as prior work but does not reproduce A's NLI-filter pipeline or A's multi-hop setting, so the published numbers cannot be lined up directly.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); sufficiency and consistency/conflict (Paper B only via negative rejection and counterfactual testbeds)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real open-domain retrievers over Wikipedia/Web corpora across 5 ODQA benchmarks. Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios, plus injected counterfactuals; sources are recent news articles processed via ChatGPT-assisted construction.
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) and generator prompting or training (fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts). Paper B: evaluation artifact only (no intervention, just diagnostic testbeds across 6 LLMs).
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness (EM/F1 on ODQA, including multi-hop). Paper B: answer correctness plus rejection rate and counterfactual identification accuracy across four ability-specific metrics.
action_policy: Paper A: answer (with implicit filter step); abstention not evaluated as an outcome. Paper B: answer plus abstain (negative rejection is explicitly scored). Mismatch in evaluated action set.
rationale: Both papers center on noise robustness in RAG and share the failure type of irrelevant retrieved context. However, Paper A is a method paper that proposes NLI filtering and robust fine-tuning evaluated against naturally occurring retriever noise on ODQA benchmarks, while Paper B is a diagnostic benchmark that synthetically varies noise ratios and additionally probes negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness across off-the-shelf LLMs with no proposed intervention. The evidence construction (real retrieval errors vs. controlled synthetic insertion), the intervention point (filter+training vs. none/benchmark), and the evaluated action set (answer-only vs. answer+abstain) all differ. They are complementary—Paper B could plausibly serve as one evaluation surface for Paper A's methods—but cannot be ranked head-to-head as alternative systems, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI filter and fine-tuned generator on Paper B's four RGB testbeds (matched LLM backbones, identical noise-ratio sweeps, identical rejection and counterfactual-identification metrics), and conversely report Paper B's accuracy/rejection/identification metrics for Paper A's ODQA settings under the same retriever. Both papers must also fix and report the same retriever, top-k, corpus snapshot, and a common abstention policy so that answer correctness and rejection rate are jointly observable.
notes: Asymmetry of paper types (method vs benchmark) is the dominant reason direct leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful here, even though the noise-robustness framings overlap heavily.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (RGB only via negative rejection)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer + abstain (RGB negative rejection testbed)
rationale: Both papers address noise robustness in RAG, and both construct controlled stressors with categorized noise types (irrelevant/counterfactual etc.), so the failure-type overlap is real. However, RAAT is a training intervention (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B) evaluated on a self-constructed RAG-Bench from NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ using DPR with the constraint of ≥2 golden contexts, while RGB is a diagnostic benchmark built from fresh news + search-engine documents that decomposes RAG into four abilities including negative rejection (explicit abstention) and information integration. The intervention point differs (training method vs. evaluation artifact), the action policy differs (RAAT only answers; RGB explicitly scores abstention), the metric families diverge (F1/EM only vs. accuracy + rejection rate + error-detection rate), and the corpus construction protocols are not aligned. They are complementary—one could plausibly evaluate RAAT on RGB—but they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as alternative methods to the same task.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and a matched non-RAAT baseline) on the RGB testbeds with RGB's noise-ratio protocol, news corpus, and the full metric suite (accuracy, rejection rate, error-detection rate) for both English and Chinese; or alternatively, port RGB's negative-rejection and counterfactual testbeds onto RAG-Bench's NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ setup with identical retriever (DPR), identical generator backbone, identical noise-construction recipe, and explicit abstain labels. Both papers would additionally need to report an explicit action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. flag conflict) under matched query/retriever conditions.
notes: Asymmetry of contribution types (method vs. benchmark) is the dominant reason a direct ranking is not meaningful, even though the topical scope overlaps.

failure_type: relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error, benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (CoN: reading-notes prompting + LLaMA-2 fine-tuning); context assembly/compression + generator training (Yoran: NLI-based passage filtering + mixed relevant/irrelevant fine-tuning)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage and calibration error (CoN rejection rate on RealTimeQA only)
action_policy: answer, abstain (CoN: explicit 'unknown' response); answer, filter (Yoran: NLI filter then answer with vanilla LLM)
rationale: Both papers target the same failure type — generator distraction by irrelevant retrieved passages in open-domain QA — and use benign retrieval noise (with some benchmark-constructed stressors) on overlapping ODQA datasets, so they belong to the same problem family. However, they intervene at different points and commit to different action policies: Chain-of-Note inserts a per-document note-taking reasoning step inside the generator and explicitly evaluates an abstain ('unknown') action with a rejection-rate metric, whereas Yoran et al. add an NLI-based passage filter upstream of the generator (falling back to a no-retrieval answer) and additionally fine-tune on mixed contexts, measuring only answer correctness. Yoran also emphasizes multi-hop QA, which CoN does not target. These differences in intervention point, action policy, and metric coverage mean leaderboard-style ranking would conflate a filter+robust-training pipeline with a reasoning+abstention generator; they are better framed as complementary modules, hence partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods with a shared retriever (e.g., DPR), shared generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), and a common evaluation suite that includes (i) single-hop and multi-hop ODQA, (ii) controlled relevant/irrelevant/adversarial-distractor mixes, and (iii) a unified metric panel covering answer EM/F1, abstention/rejection rate, and accuracy-on-attempted (selective risk). Both systems must be evaluated under matched action-policy options (answer-only, answer+abstain, answer+filter+abstain) so that CoN's abstention and Yoran's filtering are scored on the same axes. Reporting must also disclose whether NLI filtering is applied before CoN, and whether CoN's training data overlaps Yoran's 1K mixed-context training set.
notes: Both papers are explicit enough about their action policies that this is a confident partial; the gap is mechanism/policy, not under-specification.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: Paper A: evaluation artifact (sufficiency autorater) + generator prompting (selective generation at decode time); Paper B: generator prompting or training (reflection-token fine-tuning) + retriever (adaptive on-demand retrieval)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (hallucination vs abstention rate); Paper B: answer correctness, citation faithfulness
action_policy: Paper A: answer, abstain (explicit selective generation); Paper B: re-retrieve, filter, answer (reflection-driven on-demand retrieval and passage filtering)
rationale: Both papers target robust RAG behavior under imperfect retrieval and overlap on the failure types of sufficiency and noisy/irrelevant context with benign retrieval as the evidence assumption. However, they intervene at very different pipeline points: Sufficient Context is a post-hoc autorater plus decode-time selective generation that takes the retrieval as given, while Self-RAG retrains the generator with reflection tokens to decide when to retrieve, filter passages, and critique its own output. The action policies they actually evaluate are different (answer/abstain vs. re-retrieve/filter/answer), and the headline metrics diverge (selective risk and hallucination-among-answered for A vs. citation faithfulness and factuality across long-form tasks for B). They are better framed as complementary modules at different operating points of a robust-RAG stack than as direct leaderboard substitutes, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold the retriever, corpus, and benchmark suite constant (e.g., PopQA + HotpotQA + a long-form factuality task), instantiate both methods over the same base LM, and report a common metric family that covers (i) answer correctness, (ii) abstention/selective-risk curves, and (iii) citation/grounding faithfulness. Additionally, both systems must expose the same action-policy interface (allow Self-RAG to abstain, or wrap Sufficient Context with an explicit re-retrieve branch) so that selective-generation trade-offs are measured under matched action options and matched retrieval budgets.
notes: Self-RAG's training-time intervention vs. Sufficient Context's inference-time selective generation makes cost/latency and base-LM dependence non-comparable without normalization.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise and sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; no adversarial or stressor construction in either paper
intervention_point: reranker plus evaluation artifact (CalibRAG forecasting function f(t,q,d)); generator prompting/training plus retriever (Self-RAG reflection tokens and on-demand retrieval)
metric_target: calibration error and answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: unreported (CalibRAG does not evaluate abstain/selective-answer thresholds despite producing confidence); re-retrieve and filter (Self-RAG evaluates adaptive retrieval and IsRel-based filtering via reflection tokens)
rationale: Both papers extend vanilla RAG with a control mechanism, but they target fundamentally different failure modes and operating points. CalibRAG addresses miscalibration in decision support by training a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) and using it to rerank and to expose calibrated confidence; its headline metrics are calibration error and accuracy, and it does not evaluate an explicit abstain or selective-answer policy from that confidence. Self-RAG addresses indiscriminate retrieval and ungrounded generation by training reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval, relevance filtering, and grounding critique; its headline metrics are factuality and citation accuracy, with explicit re-retrieve and filter actions. Because the intervention point, primary metric family, and evaluated action policy all diverge, the two should be discussed as complementary controls (probability calibration vs adaptive retrieval and self-grounding), not ranked as substitutable methods on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Common retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; a shared evaluation suite that reports both calibration metrics (ECE/Brier, selective accuracy at coverage) and factuality/citation metrics (e.g., FActScore, citation precision/recall); explicit action-policy evaluation for both systems (abstention thresholds for CalibRAG; calibration of IsSup/IsUse confidences for Self-RAG); and ablations isolating the reranker-vs-generator-training contributions so the comparison is not confounded by intervention-point differences.
notes: Both are 'control' style but on orthogonal axes; partial rather than invalid because a downstream-accuracy slice could be reported jointly, and rather than under-specified because each paper is internally clear about its own targets.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (benign parametric vs retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict / benchmark-constructed stressor (no adversary); PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, no query control (attacker chooses target questions in advance), black-box and white-box retriever visibility, black-box generator access, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, contextual alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive insertion, not a defense)
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support (faithfulness); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (with internal reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported / not applicable (attack paper does not specify generator-side action policy)
rationale: Both papers concern situations where retrieved RAG evidence is unreliable, but they sit on opposite sides of the pipeline and assume incompatible threat models. FaithfulRAG is a defense-side generator-time method targeting benign parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflict, optimized for answer correctness and faithfulness; PoisonedRAG is an offensive corpus-poisoning attack that assumes an adversary with corpus write access and prior choice of target questions, optimized for attack success rate. Every coordinate diverges: failure type (benign conflict vs adversarial corruption), evidence assumption (natural conflict vs attacker-created passages), intervention point (generator vs corpus/index), metric target (accuracy vs ASR), and action policy (answer with self-think vs not reported, because it is an attack). Placing them on a shared leaderboard as alternative robust-RAG methods would conflate an attacker and a defender and is therefore invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: These two papers cannot be made directly comparable as alternative methods. A meaningful interaction would be a separate robustness study: run FaithfulRAG (and matched baselines) as the defender against PoisonedRAG-style corpus injections under a shared retriever, generator, corpus, insertion budget, and threat model, and report defense metrics (ASR reduction, answer accuracy on clean+poisoned splits, abstention/quarantine behavior, citation faithfulness). Direct head-to-head ranking would still be inappropriate; only an attack-vs-defense evaluation pairing them is sensible.
notes: Classic attack-paper vs defense-paper mismatch within the conflict-security area; the surface-level overlap on 'evidence reliability' does not justify leaderboard-style comparison.

failure_type: AstuteRAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict (with weak mention of malicious); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: AstuteRAG: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor + naturally occurring conflict; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model (corpus write access=yes, query control=targets specific questions, retriever visibility=both black-box and white-box, generator access=both, insertion budget=5 malicious texts/question, attack objective=induce attacker-chosen target answer)
intervention_point: AstuteRAG: generator prompting + context assembly/compression; PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attack injection point)
metric_target: AstuteRAG: answer correctness (defense-oriented); PoisonedRAG: attack success (offense-oriented)
action_policy: AstuteRAG: answer (after source-aware reliability comparison); PoisonedRAG: unreported from a defender perspective (the action is the attacker inducing target answer generation)
rationale: Both papers concern RAG robustness, but they occupy opposite roles in the attack/defense ecosystem rather than being substitutable methods. AstuteRAG is a generator-side, training-free defense that consolidates internal and external knowledge under imperfect retrieval and reports answer correctness; its 'worst-case' evaluation on RGB does not instantiate PoisonedRAG's formal optimization-based corpus injection threat model. PoisonedRAG intervenes at the corpus/index, formalizes an attacker with corpus write access and a 5-text insertion budget under both black- and white-box settings, and reports attack success rate against undefended RAG. Because the intervention points (generator vs corpus), metric targets (accuracy vs ASR), and evidence assumptions (benign/benchmark noise vs attacker-crafted poisoning) are categorically misaligned, a leaderboard-style head-to-head ranking would be category-confused and misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make these comparable, one would have to either (a) recast both as defenses on the same task by evaluating AstuteRAG against the PoisonedRAG attack distribution (fixed retriever, generator, target-question set, k=5 injected malicious passages, both black- and white-box variants), reporting attack success rate alongside answer correctness and any abstain/escalate action policy; or (b) include a PoisonedRAG-style stressor as one of AstuteRAG's noise conditions with the same insertion budget and threat model. Without sharing corpus, retriever, attack budget, threat model and a common metric (e.g., ASR on attacked queries plus clean accuracy), the two cannot be ranked.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense category mismatch; even though AstuteRAG briefly mentions 'malicious' content, it never instantiates PoisonedRAG's threat model or reports ASR.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG assumes corpus write access with ~5-text insertion budget per target question, black-box and white-box retriever visibility, attacker-chosen target Q/A pairs (targeted attack objective); RobustRAG assumes a bounded number of injected malicious passages and an adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious text injection); RobustRAG: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (isolate-then-aggregate with keyword/decoding aggregation)
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success (ASR on target questions); RobustRAG: answer correctness plus certified robustness lower bounds against bounded corruption
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: answer (victim system answers; no defensive action evaluated); RobustRAG: answer or abstain ('I don't know' branch in keyword aggregation) — explicitly evaluated
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat space (integrity/adversarial corruption of RAG via attacker-created passages injected into the corpus) and even reference compatible threat models (bounded insertion budget, adaptive adversary). However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive method whose intervention is at the corpus and whose metric is attack success rate on attacker-chosen target questions, whereas RobustRAG is a defensive method whose intervention is at context assembly/aggregation and whose metrics are clean accuracy and a certified robustness lower bound, with an explicit abstain action. Because one paper's success metric (high ASR) is the other paper's failure metric (low certified accuracy), they cannot occupy the same leaderboard as substitutable methods; they are instead natural complements in an attack–defense evaluation. Therefore the comparability is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head leaderboard would require both papers to play the same role. Two viable framings: (1) Defense leaderboard — re-instantiate PoisonedRAG only as the attack instance and compare RobustRAG against other defenses (e.g., perplexity filtering, paraphrasing, majority vote) under matched retriever, generator, corpus, insertion budget k, target question set, and shared metrics (clean accuracy, attacked accuracy, certified accuracy, abstention rate). (2) Attack leaderboard — compare PoisonedRAG against other corruption attacks (GCG-text, Phantom, etc.) under matched victim RAG stack, retriever budget, and reported ASR plus stealth/quality metrics. The current pair is better written up as an attack–defense pairing (run RobustRAG vs PoisonedRAG with matched k and report certified/empirical robustness), not a ranking.
notes: Confidence is 4 rather than 5 because a strict panel could argue 'invalid' on the grounds that attack and defense papers are categorically incomparable; I prefer 'partial' since the threat model and failure type are genuinely shared and the two are routinely co-evaluated.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict (RAGTruth: spans annotated on real LLM outputs from standard RAG pipelines); benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactuals, all-noise rejection sets)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth also enables verifier training
metric_target: evidence support, citation faithfulness, answer correctness (RAGTruth: span-level hallucination detection F1 / hallucination frequency); answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (RGB: accuracy, rejection rate, error-detection rate, correction rate)
action_policy: unreported (RAGTruth does not evaluate generator action policy; it scores post-hoc detectors); abstain + answer (RGB explicitly tests negative rejection alongside answering)
rationale: Both are RAG trustworthiness benchmarks, and both touch hallucination/conflict-style failures, but they instantiate fundamentally different evaluation paradigms. RAGTruth collects ~18K naturally generated LLM responses and supplies word-level hallucination spans to benchmark detector models (and fine-tune them), with no controlled stressor design and no generator-side action policy under test. RGB, by contrast, programmatically constructs four separate testbeds (noise ratio, all-noise rejection, multi-doc integration, injected counterfactuals) to score the LLM itself on four abilities, explicitly including an abstain action via negative rejection. Because evidence construction (natural vs. constructed), measured object (external detector quality vs. in-context LLM behavior), metric families (span-level detection F1 vs. ability-specific accuracy/rejection/correction rates), and action policies differ, leaderboard-style ranking would conflate incompatible tasks. They are best framed as complementary evaluation lenses rather than substitutable benchmarks.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the same generator(s) on a shared task formulation where both span-level hallucination (RAGTruth style) and ability-specific scores (RGB style) are measured on identical inputs; align evidence construction (e.g., apply RGB's controlled noise/counterfactual perturbations to RAGTruth source passages, or annotate RGB-style LLM outputs at the span level); and declare a common action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. flag) so detection F1 and negative-rejection rate can be reported on the same items with the same reference answers.
notes: Partial rather than invalid because the counterfactual-robustness slice of RGB and the 'evident conflict' category of RAGTruth share a conceptual target, but operationalizations diverge enough that direct ranking is misleading.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents from search-engine results around news articles); Sufficient Context: naturally occurring (uses existing QA datasets stratified post-hoc by an LLM autorater for sufficiency)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); system-control policy (Sufficient Context adds selective generation combining sufficiency signal with self-rated confidence)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context), abstention/rejection accuracy
action_policy: answer, abstain (both explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via negative rejection testbed; Sufficient Context via selective generation)
rationale: Both papers diagnose RAG behavior when retrieved context is imperfect, and both explicitly evaluate an answer/abstain action policy, so the conceptual overlap (especially RGB's 'negative rejection' vs Sufficient Context's 'insufficient context' analysis) is real. However, the evidence assumption differs sharply: RGB constructs stressors with controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactuals from news+search, while Sufficient Context labels naturally retrieved contexts via an LLM autorater on existing QA sets. The intervention point also differs—RGB is purely an evaluation benchmark across four ability testbeds, while Sufficient Context also proposes a selective generation method on top of its autorater. Metric decomposition is incommensurate (per-ability accuracy/rejection rates vs sufficiency-stratified hallucination/abstention/correct rates and selective risk). They function as complementary diagnostic lenses rather than substitutable methods on a single leaderboard, so partial is the right call.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both diagnostics on a shared corpus and retriever with the same generator family: (a) apply Sufficient Context's autorater to RGB's four testbeds to verify whether RGB's noise/negative-rejection/counterfactual splits correspond to insufficient/conflicting context labels; (b) report the same metric family (correct/abstain/hallucinate rates plus selective risk-coverage curves) under both stressor-constructed (RGB) and natural-retrieval (Sufficient Context) regimes; (c) make the action policy explicit and identical (answer vs abstain with a shared abstention prompt). Without this shared substrate, the two papers cannot be directly ranked.
notes: Sufficient Context is partly a method paper (selective generation) while RGB is purely a benchmark; even if metrics aligned, the unit of comparison would still differ.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (both); sufficiency and relevance/noise (RAGTruth additionally)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations from LLM outputs over standard RAG corpora; FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring or benchmark-constructed parametric-vs-context conflict scenarios
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) plus verifier (fine-tuned hallucination detector); FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining + self-think module before generation)
metric_target: RAGTruth: span/response-level hallucination detection performance (precision/recall/F1 against annotated spans); FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and faithfulness to retrieved context
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify/flag hallucinated spans (post-hoc detection); FaithfulRAG: answer after fact-level reconciliation; neither evaluates abstain/expose-conflict/re-retrieve as a graded action
rationale: Both papers nominally address RAG faithfulness and overlap on the consistency/conflict failure type—RAGTruth includes 'Evident Conflict' as one annotation category, and FaithfulRAG centers on parametric-vs-context conflict. However, they occupy fundamentally different pipeline positions: RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact plus a post-hoc detector (verifier intervention) scored on hallucination-span detection, while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention scored on answer correctness/faithfulness on QA benchmarks. The metric families (detection P/R/F1 vs. answer accuracy) and effective action policies (flag spans vs. produce reconciled answer) do not align, so they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as alternative methods. They are best framed as complementary—FaithfulRAG could be evaluated on RAGTruth—rather than directly ranked, which makes the comparison partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) evaluate FaithfulRAG (and the prompt/decoding baselines RAGTruth-style detectors flag) on the same RAGTruth test split with both (i) downstream answer faithfulness/correctness metrics and (ii) hallucination-span/response-level detection metrics, and report a shared action policy (e.g., answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict); or (b) restrict the comparison to a common knowledge-conflict subset using identical retriever, generator, conflict construction, and metric definitions. Without a shared task formulation, shared evaluation corpus, and explicit action labels, direct ranking is not meaningful.
notes: RAGTruth is primarily a benchmark/detection contribution; FaithfulRAG is a generation-side conflict-resolution method. The asymmetry in contribution type is the main reason for partial rather than invalid.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B counterfactual only)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); Paper B's counterfactual subset borders on naturally occurring conflict but is synthetically injected, not attacker-created
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (both); context assembly/compression (Paper A NLI filter only)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, EM/F1)
action_policy: unreported (both default to answer; neither paper evaluates abstain, re-retrieve, expose-conflict, or selective risk policies)
breaking_coordinates: failure_type (scope mismatch on counterfactual), intervention_point (filtering vs. training-only), action_policy (unreported in both)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA, share answer-correctness (EM/F1) as the metric, and both use benchmark-constructed noise stressors with overlapping datasets (e.g., NQ); Paper B even builds on Yoran et al. Comparability breaks on three coordinates: (i) failure-type scope—Paper A treats only irrelevant/distracting context, while Paper B additionally targets counterfactual (conflicting) passages, a different failure family; (ii) intervention scope—Paper A combines an NLI filter at context assembly with fine-tuning, while Paper B is a training-only adaptive adversarial scheme with multi-task noise classification; (iii) action policy is unreported in both—neither evaluates abstain, re-retrieve, or selective coverage, so a leaderboard ranking would silently equate two methods that may behave very differently under uncertainty. They are best discussed as complementary noise-robustness recipes rather than as ranked substitutes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever (e.g., DPR) and generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B); evaluate both methods on a shared noise taxonomy split (irrelevant-only subset for apples-to-apples, plus counterfactual subset reported separately); report EM/F1 alongside an explicit action-policy axis (answer vs. abstain vs. re-retrieve) with coverage/selective-risk curves; control for training-data size and disclose whether the NLI filter is applied at inference for both systems.
notes: From a trustworthy-ML lens, the missing action policy and absence of calibration/abstention metrics are the most consequential gap; both papers implicitly force-answer, which masks how each method fails under counterfactual noise.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); rgb2023 also covers consistency/conflict and sufficiency
evidence_assumption: irrelevantContext2023: benign retrieval error (real top-k retrieval errors on ODQA); rgb2023: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: irrelevantContext2023: reranker/filter (NLI) + generator prompting/training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts); rgb2023: evaluation artifact (benchmark, no system intervention)
metric_target: irrelevantContext2023: answer correctness; rgb2023: answer correctness + (implicitly) selective risk via negative-rejection rate and counterfactual-rejection rate
action_policy: irrelevantContext2023: filter (explicit NLI gating) then answer; rgb2023: abstain is explicitly evaluated as 'negative rejection' alongside answer
rationale: Both papers concern LLM behavior under noisy retrieval and overlap on the 'noise robustness' failure type, but they occupy fundamentally different roles in the stack: irrelevantContext2023 is a method paper proposing NLI filtering plus fine-tuning interventions and is evaluated almost exclusively on answer correctness across 5 ODQA datasets with a filter action policy, while rgb2023 is an evaluation artifact that constructs four distinct testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and explicitly elicits and measures abstention behavior. The intervention point (system modification vs. benchmark), evidence assumption (organic retrieval errors vs. controlled-ratio stressors and counterfactual injections), and action policy (filter-then-answer vs. answer-or-abstain) all diverge, and rgb2023's selective-risk/abstention measurement has no counterpart in irrelevantContext2023. They are best framed as complementary—rgb2023 could serve as a probe for the methods in irrelevantContext2023—rather than as substitutable entries on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate irrelevantContext2023's NLI-filter and fine-tuned model on rgb2023's noise-robustness testbed at matched noise ratios, using the same LLM backbone, and report both answer correctness AND rejection/abstention rate (selective risk and coverage). Conversely, evaluate a baseline RALM matching rgb2023's setup on the same 5 ODQA benchmarks used in irrelevantContext2023 with a declared abstention policy. Without harmonized evidence construction, common backbone, shared action labels (answer vs. abstain vs. filter), and a shared metric family covering both correctness and selective-risk, leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful.
notes: Method-vs-benchmark pairing; the abstention/selective-risk axis is central to rgb2023 but absent from irrelevantContext2023, which is the most consequential coordinate break from a trustworthy-ML perspective.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor, benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (RGB only, via negative rejection rate)
action_policy: answer (RAAT, no abstention reported); answer, abstain (RGB, explicit negative rejection testbed)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in retrieval-augmented LLMs and both construct stressor-based test settings that include relevant, irrelevant, and counterfactual-like contexts. However, RAAT is a training-side intervention paper (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B) evaluated only on answer correctness (F1/EM) under an answer-only action policy, while RGB is a diagnostic benchmark that decomposes RAG into four distinct abilities — including negative rejection, which explicitly evaluates an abstention action and a selective-risk-style metric. The intervention point, action policy, dataset construction (NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ with DPR vs. bilingual news with search-engine retrieval), and the metric scope therefore diverge meaningfully. The two works are complementary — RGB could in principle diagnose a RAAT-trained model — but they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as alternative methods for the same problem.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT-trained and RAAT-untrained baselines on the RGB testbeds (all four abilities, both English and Chinese) using RGB's noise-ratio protocol, and conversely evaluate the LLMs RGB tested on RAAT's RAG-Bench using the same noise typology. Critically, both sides must report a consistent action policy — i.e., explicitly evaluate abstention/negative rejection with a shared rejection-rate or selective-risk metric in addition to F1/EM — and use a shared retriever, generator family, and noise-construction recipe so that answer correctness and abstention behavior are jointly measured.
notes: Asymmetry in action policy (answer-only vs. answer+abstain) is the most decisive break from a selective-risk/calibration perspective; this alone precludes a 'valid' verdict even though the failure-type taxonomies look superficially aligned.

failure_type: relevance/noise; CoN additionally evaluates sufficiency and uncertainty/OOD via 'unknown' real-time questions
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (imperfect DPR/retriever returns off-topic passages); no adversarial threat model in either paper
intervention_point: CoN: generator prompting/training (note-taking step). Paper B: reranker/filter (NLI entailment) plus generator training on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts.
metric_target: CoN: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (rejection rate on real-time/unknown). Paper B: answer correctness (EM/F1) only.
action_policy: CoN: answer or abstain ('unknown'). Paper B: filter (drop non-entailing passages, fall back to closed-book answer) + answer; no explicit abstention.
rationale: Both papers tackle RALM brittleness to irrelevant retrieved context under benign retrieval error, so the failure type (relevance/noise) and threat assumptions overlap. However, Chain-of-Note intervenes inside generator reasoning with sequential note-taking and explicitly evaluates an abstain action via a rejection-rate metric on unanswerable/real-time questions, while Yoran et al. intervene with an NLI-based passage filter plus mixed-context fine-tuning and report only answer correctness with no abstention head. The action policies (abstain vs filter+closed-book fallback) and metric families (selective risk/coverage vs accuracy only) are not aligned, so a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate genuinely different operating points. The two methods are best framed as complementary modules (a pre-generator filter vs an in-generator abstaining reader) rather than direct substitutes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold retriever, generator backbone, and QA benchmarks constant; evaluate both systems on a shared correctness + selective-risk rubric (e.g., correct/abstain/wrong with a rejection metric on an unanswerable or noise-only slice); report both methods on the same noise-injected and clean splits; and ideally include a stacked ablation (NLI filter -> CoN reader) to disentangle the filtering vs note-taking contributions.
notes: Abstention asymmetry is the decisive break for a trustworthy-ML reader: comparing a selectively-abstaining system to a forced-answer system on accuracy alone would mis-rank them.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, uncertainty/OOD
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, evaluation artifact, retriever
metric_target: selective risk/coverage, answer correctness, citation faithfulness, calibration error
action_policy: abstain (Paper A), re-retrieve and verify (Paper B)
rationale: Both papers address robustness of RAG when retrieved evidence may be unhelpful or insufficient, but they tackle different stages and outcomes. Sufficient Context intervenes at the evaluation/generator-prompting layer by building an autorater for (Q,C) sufficiency and combining it with self-confidence for selective abstention, with selective risk/coverage and hallucination reduction as the primary metric target. Self-RAG instead retrains the generator (and changes inference) to emit reflection tokens that drive on-demand re-retrieval, relevance filtering, and citation critique, with answer correctness and citation faithfulness as the primary metric target. Because the intervention points (prompted selective generation vs. trained reflection-token model), the action policies (abstain vs. re-retrieve/verify), and the headline metrics differ, direct leaderboard ranking would conflate methods that occupy different operating regions; they are better framed as complementary modules.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold retriever and base generator fixed across both methods; evaluate on the same QA datasets with a shared action-policy protocol (force both methods to report risk–coverage curves with explicit abstention, plus citation-faithfulness when an answer is produced); align metrics to a common family (selective accuracy at matched coverage, AURC, calibration error, and supported-answer rate); and report whether Self-RAG's reflection-driven 'no answer' state is treated as abstention comparable to Sufficient Context's selective generation.
notes: Selective-risk lens highlights that the two methods are operating on different axes (when-to-answer vs. when-to-retrieve-and-critique); aggregating them on a single accuracy number would hide the abstention/coverage trade-off.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence); Self-RAG: relevance/noise + sufficiency (when retrieval helps, what is relevant/supported)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval errors; neither targets adversarial corpus poisoning or staleness. No security threat model on either side.
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker (forecasting function f(t,q,d)) + generator prompting with calibrated confidence; Self-RAG: generator training with reflection tokens + retriever (on-demand)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness (decision accuracy); Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence score (no explicit abstain reported); Self-RAG: re-retrieve on demand + verify/critique via reflection tokens. Non-overlapping action policies.
rationale: Both papers fall under the broad 'control' umbrella for RAG reliability, but they target distinct failure modes and use disjoint mechanisms. CalibRAG addresses uncertainty/miscalibration by training a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) to predict decision correctness and rerank/expose a calibrated confidence; its headline metrics are calibration error and decision accuracy. Self-RAG addresses relevance/sufficiency by training reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and critique whether output is supported; its headline metrics are factuality and citation accuracy. The intervention points (reranker + confidence head vs. on-demand retrieval + self-critique tokens) and action policies (calibrated answer vs. retrieve/verify) do not align, so a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate calibration quality with adaptive-retrieval quality. They are better discussed as complementary modules than as substitutable systems.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold the retriever, generator backbone, and evaluation datasets fixed; report a common metric battery including both calibration (ECE, Brier, selective risk/coverage curve) and grounding (citation faithfulness, evidence support, answer EM/F1); fix an explicit action policy (e.g., selective prediction with shared abstention threshold, or fixed retrieval budget); and, ideally, ablate whether Self-RAG's reflection tokens produce calibrated confidence and whether CalibRAG's forecaster can drive on-demand retrieval decisions. Only then can the two be ranked rather than treated as complementary.
notes: From a trustworthy-ML lens, Self-RAG's reflection tokens are not validated as calibrated probabilities, and CalibRAG does not evaluate on-demand retrieval or abstention coverage, so any single-number leaderboard ranking would be misleading.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (FaithfulRAG) vs integrity/adversarial corruption (PoisonedRAG)
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge (FaithfulRAG) vs attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, small insertion budget (~5 texts), black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, and targeted-answer attack objective (PoisonedRAG)
intervention_point: generator prompting/reasoning (FaithfulRAG) vs corpus/index attack with no proposed defense (PoisonedRAG); evaluation artifact also differs
metric_target: answer correctness / evidence support / citation faithfulness (FaithfulRAG) vs attack success rate (PoisonedRAG)
action_policy: answer after self-think reconciliation (FaithfulRAG) vs unreported / no defender action (PoisonedRAG is an attack paper)
rationale: Both papers concern the trustworthiness of retrieved evidence in RAG, but they live on opposite sides of the threat-model boundary. FaithfulRAG addresses naturally occurring parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflicts and intervenes at the generator via fact-level reconciliation, reporting answer correctness/faithfulness. PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that assumes corpus write access, a small insertion budget, and a targeted-answer objective, reporting attack success rate with no defender action policy. The failure type, evidence assumption, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all break: FaithfulRAG is never evaluated under adversarial corpus poisoning, and PoisonedRAG never measures faithfulness or conflict resolution, so any direct leaderboard ranking would conflate a defense for benign conflicts with an attack benchmark.
