what_valid_comparison_requires: To be directly comparable, one would need to evaluate FaithfulRAG as a defense on the PoisonedRAG benchmark (same retriever, generator, target Q/A set, 5-text insertion budget, both black- and white-box settings) and report ASR reduction and selective-risk/abstention behavior; conversely, PoisonedRAG would need a defender baseline operating in the same conflict-resolution regime that FaithfulRAG targets. A shared threat model (corpus access, insertion budget, query control), shared evaluation set, and an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine) with matched metrics (answer correctness AND attack success) are required.
notes: From a selective-risk perspective, neither paper reports abstention or coverage under contaminated contexts, which is exactly the operating point that would bridge them; without that, leaderboard-style comparison is misleading.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption shared; Astute RAG also covers relevance/noise and consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG assumes benign retrieval error, benchmark-constructed stressor, and naturally occurring conflict; PoisonedRAG assumes attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, query control over target questions, retriever visibility in both black-box and white-box settings, no generator access required, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts per target question, and attack objective of inducing attacker-chosen target answers
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free source-aware consolidation); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (poisoning attack, not a defense)
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness under worst-case retrieval; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR)
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer based on reliability comparison (selective integration, no explicit abstain); PoisonedRAG: unreported (no defender action policy, it is an attack paper)
rationale: PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that injects malicious texts into the corpus to induce attacker-chosen answers, measured by ASR, with an explicit adversarial threat model (corpus write access, ~5 injected texts per query). Astute RAG is a defense/robustness method operating at the generator stage via source-aware consolidation, evaluated on answer correctness under imperfect retrieval and worst-case RGB scenarios that are not specifically PoisonedRAG-style attacks. The two papers sit on opposite sides of the attacker/defender boundary: one constructs adversarial evidence and reports ASR, the other modifies generation behavior and reports accuracy. Without a shared evaluation where Astute RAG is tested against PoisonedRAG injections (or PoisonedRAG is run against Astute RAG as a defense), they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate Astute RAG as a defense against PoisonedRAG-injected corpora using identical retrievers, generators, datasets (e.g., NQ/HotpotQA), insertion budgets, and threat-model settings (black-box and white-box). Report both ASR and answer correctness, and define a shared action policy (answer vs abstain vs filter/quarantine) so that defender-side robustness can be ranked against the attack on the same axis.
notes: Attack paper vs defense paper; comparability requires explicit attack-defense pairing rather than direct leaderboard ranking.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume corpus write access with bounded insertion budget (PoisonedRAG: ~5 malicious texts per target query; RobustRAG: bounded m' corrupted passages); PoisonedRAG attacker has query control over targets and operates in black/white-box retriever visibility; RobustRAG considers adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense; attack objective is targeted answer manipulation in both cases
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack) vs. context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate defense)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG) vs. answer correctness with certified lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported for PoisonedRAG (attack-side, not evaluated); abstain + aggregated answer for RobustRAG (explicit 'I don't know' branch and keyword/decoding aggregation)
rationale: Both papers operate inside the same threat surface—integrity/adversarial corruption of the RAG corpus by an attacker who inserts a bounded number of malicious passages—so the failure type and evidence assumption are aligned. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack paper whose intervention is the corpus and whose metric is attack success rate against an undefended pipeline, while RobustRAG is a defense paper whose intervention is at context assembly/generator (isolate-then-aggregate with explicit abstention) and whose metric is certifiable answer quality under bounded corruption. An attack and a defense cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as alternative methods; they are complementary components of the same threat model. The natural relationship is evaluative pairing (does RobustRAG's certified bound hold against PoisonedRAG-style insertions?), not ranking, so the comparison is partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, one must fix a role: either (a) compare PoisonedRAG against other corruption attacks (e.g., Phantom, GASLITE, corpus poisoning baselines) under an identical defended pipeline with matched retriever, generator, k, and budget m', reporting ASR and any abstention rates; or (b) compare RobustRAG against other defenses (e.g., perplexity filtering, majority voting, instruction-tuned robustness) under an identical attack including PoisonedRAG with matched corpus, budget, query set, and an explicit action-policy report (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict). Cross-role comparison should instead be reported as an attack-defense evaluation matrix, not a ranking.
notes: Verdict could slide toward 'invalid' under a strict reading because attack and defense have orthogonal objectives, but 'partial' better captures that they share the integrity threat model and are routinely co-evaluated in the literature.

failure_type: RAGTruth: consistency/conflict and sufficiency at word/span level (hallucination against retrieved context). RGB: relevance/noise, sufficiency (negative rejection), consistency/conflict (counterfactual), and multi-doc integration as separate testbeds.
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict / benign retrieval-then-generation errors, no adversary, no insertion budget. RGB: benchmark-constructed stressors (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents), corpus assembled by benchmark authors, no real attacker model.
intervention_point: Both are evaluation artifact. RAGTruth additionally enables generator-side fine-tuning of a detector; RGB is purely a diagnostic evaluation of off-the-shelf LLMs.
metric_target: RAGTruth: citation faithfulness / evidence support measured via span-level hallucination detection F1. RGB: answer correctness plus a selective-risk-like negative-rejection rate, integration accuracy, and counterfactual identification rate.
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported as a system action (the benchmark scores detection of hallucinated spans, not answer/abstain decisions). RGB: explicitly evaluates abstain (negative rejection) and answer.
rationale: Both papers are RAG reliability benchmarks and share concern with LLMs producing unsupported content given retrieved context, but they instrument different failure modes with non-overlapping metric families. RAGTruth provides word-level hallucination annotations over naturally generated RAG outputs (QA, data-to-text, summarization) and scores span-level detection; it does not evaluate abstention or controlled noise ratios. RGB constructs synthetic testbeds for four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness), scoring answer correctness and an explicit abstention rate rather than span-level faithfulness. Because the evidence assumptions (natural vs. constructed stressors), metric targets (span detection vs. answer/abstain accuracy), and action policies (detection vs. answer/abstain) differ, a direct leaderboard ranking would conflate detector quality with generator behaviour and is misleading. They are best presented as complementary diagnostics, hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the same set of LLMs on (a) RAGTruth's span-level hallucination detection and (b) RGB's four ability testbeds, and report results per coordinate rather than ranking. To collapse to a single comparison, both benchmarks would need a shared failure taxonomy (e.g., both annotating word-level support AND noise-injection conditions), a common action policy (answer/abstain decisions evaluated alongside faithfulness), aligned metric families (e.g., joint correctness, abstention, and span-faithfulness scores on shared items), and matched stressor construction so naturally occurring and synthesized errors are comparable.
notes: From a selective-risk/abstention perspective, only RGB makes the answer/abstain decision explicit; RAGTruth leaves the action policy implicit, which is itself a substantive coordinate gap.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: RGB uses benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactuals, all-noise rejection sets); Sufficient Context uses naturally occurring retrieval over existing QA corpora (HotPotQA, Musique, etc.) with an autorater labeling (Q,C) sufficiency
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); Sufficient Context additionally targets generator prompting and system-control policy via its selective generation method
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, calibration error (Sufficient Context); answer correctness, rejection rate, counterfactual robustness (RGB)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via 'negative rejection', Sufficient Context via stratified %Correct/%Abstain/%Hallucinate and a selective generation policy)
rationale: Both papers diagnose RAG behavior when retrieved context is noisy or insufficient, and both explicitly score abstention as a first-class outcome (RGB's negative rejection; Sufficient Context's hallucinate-vs-abstain stratification), so the action-policy coordinate is genuinely shared. However, RGB is a constructed stressor benchmark with fixed noise ratios and synthetic counterfactuals reported as four ability scores, while Sufficient Context defines a (Q,C) sufficiency property over naturally retrieved contexts via an LLM autorater and additionally proposes a selective-generation method with selective-risk style metrics. The stressor construction, the unit of analysis (ability-per-testbed vs. stratified-by-sufficiency), and the inclusion of a method intervention break direct leaderboard comparability. They are best treated as complementary lenses on the same robustness/abstention problem rather than substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both systems on a shared retrieval pool with (a) the Sufficient Context autorater labeling each RGB testbed instance for sufficiency, (b) common selective-risk and abstention metrics (e.g., %Correct | answered, coverage, calibration error) computed identically, (c) the same generator(s) and prompting protocol, and (d) explicit reporting of action-policy outcomes (answer/abstain/hallucinate) on both benchmark-constructed and naturally retrieved contexts so that the sufficiency stratification and RGB's ability decomposition can be aligned on the same axes.
notes: Action policy is unusually well-specified for both papers, which is why this is partial rather than under-specified; the breakdown is on stressor construction and metric framing.

failure_type: consistency/conflict for FaithfulRAG; broader hallucination including relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict for RAGTruth
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict for FaithfulRAG (parametric vs retrieved); benign retrieval error plus naturally occurring conflict captured as naturally generated LLM outputs for RAGTruth
intervention_point: evaluation artifact plus verifier/detector fine-tuning for RAGTruth; generator prompting (self-think) for FaithfulRAG
metric_target: evidence support and detection performance over span-level hallucinations for RAGTruth; answer correctness and contextual faithfulness on QA for FaithfulRAG
action_policy: unreported in both; RAGTruth produces span labels post-hoc, FaithfulRAG always answers after reconciling with no abstain or escalate evaluation
rationale: Both papers concern faithfulness in RAG, but they operate at fundamentally different stages of the pipeline and pursue different objectives. RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact: it ships a word-level hallucination corpus across QA, data-to-text, and summarization, and benchmarks (and fine-tunes) post-hoc hallucination detectors, with span-level detection performance as the metric. FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention (self-fact mining, context alignment, self-think) that specifically targets parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflicts on QA, measured by downstream answer correctness and faithfulness. Because the intervention point (evaluation artifact/verifier vs generator prompting), the metric family (span-level detection vs end-task QA accuracy), and the failure scope (broad hallucination vs narrow knowledge conflict) diverge, and neither paper evaluates a common action policy, direct leaderboard ranking would be misleading; the works are complementary rather than substitutable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, one would need to evaluate FaithfulRAG's generator outputs on the RAGTruth corpus using its span-level hallucination annotations (or, conversely, evaluate RAGTruth-fine-tuned detectors as a verifier wrapped around a vanilla RAG generator on FaithfulRAG's knowledge-conflict QA benchmarks), holding retriever, generator backbone, and context construction fixed, reporting both span-level hallucination metrics and end-task QA accuracy, and declaring an explicit action policy (answer vs abstain vs flag) so the two systems are evaluated on the same operating decision.
notes: These are best framed as complementary layers (detector/benchmark vs generation-time conflict resolver) in a faithful-RAG stack, not as competing systems on one leaderboard.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B counterfactual noise only)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper A); benchmark-constructed stressor including counterfactual/adversarial passages (Paper B). Not a security threat model; no corpus write attacker, no insertion budget — both rely on synthetic noise constructions rather than an adversary writing into a real corpus.
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (both); context assembly/filter via NLI (Paper A additionally)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1 in both)
action_policy: answer (both); Paper A additionally evaluates a filter action via NLI; abstention/escalation not evaluated by either
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA, share NQ as an evaluation set, and both train the generator to better tolerate noisy contexts. However, Paper A scopes noise as irrelevant/distracting retrievals and offers two distinct interventions (NLI filtering at context-assembly time, plus fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts), while Paper B expands the noise typology to include counterfactual (conflicting) passages and uses adaptive adversarial training plus a noise-aware multi-task classifier. The intervention points overlap only partially (Paper A also acts pre-generator), the failure-type coverage diverges (Paper B adds consistency/conflict), and the noise-construction protocols and base models differ, so headline EM/F1 numbers cannot be placed on a single leaderboard without confounds. The works are best framed as complementary noise-robustness mechanisms with overlapping but non-identical operating regions.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold base model, retriever (DPR with same top-k), and benchmark constant; evaluate both methods on a unified noise mixture covering irrelevant, relevant-but-distracting, and counterfactual passages; report EM/F1 per noise type plus a filter/abstain action where applicable; ablate Paper A's NLI filter and Paper B's noise-type classifier separately so the generator-training contribution is isolated; and explicitly state the action policy (answer vs filter vs abstain) used at inference.
notes: No adversarial threat model in the security sense; corpus write access and attacker query control are not in scope for either paper.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers consistency/conflict via counterfactual robustness and sufficiency via negative rejection testbed
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real retrievers over ODQA; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (noise ratios, counterfactual documents, all-noise sets). Neither is an attacker-controlled corpus write scenario; counterfactual documents in RGB are author-injected but framed as evaluation perturbations rather than an adversarial threat model with insertion budget, query control, or retriever visibility constraints.
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (robust fine-tuning). Paper B: evaluation artifact (benchmark only, no proposed defense).
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness on ODQA. Paper B: answer correctness plus rejection rate, integration accuracy, and counterfactual error/identification rate across four separate testbeds.
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (abstention not evaluated as a measured action). Paper B: explicitly evaluates abstain (negative rejection) and expose conflict (counterfactual identification) in addition to answer.
rationale: Both papers care about robustness of RAG to noisy retrieved context, so the failure-type families overlap on relevance/noise. However, Paper A is a method paper that intervenes via NLI filtering and fine-tuning and reports answer-correctness gains on ODQA, while Paper B is an evaluation benchmark (RGB) covering four distinct abilities—noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness—and proposes no defense. Crucially, Paper B explicitly measures abstain and conflict-exposure action policies (rejection rate, counterfactual identification) that Paper A neither implements nor evaluates, and Paper B's counterfactual testbed touches a different failure type (consistency/conflict) than Paper A's irrelevance setting. They are best treated as complementary—Paper A is a candidate system that could be scored on a subset of Paper B's RGB testbeds—rather than as two entries on the same leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI filter and robust fine-tuned generator on Paper B's RGB noise-robustness testbed using the same retriever-free oracle-passage protocol, and additionally report rejection rate on the negative-rejection testbed and counterfactual identification on the counterfactual testbed. Alternatively, restrict comparison to a shared metric (e.g., exact-match under controlled noise ratio) with a fixed action policy (answer-only, no abstain) and matched generator backbones. Without this, the two papers operate at different intervention points and action policies and cannot be ranked directly.
notes: Not a security pair in the strict attacker sense; RGB's counterfactual documents are benchmark-injected, not modeled as a write-access adversary with insertion budget.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); RAAT samples noise from DPR top-k on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ with relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual categories; RGB synthesizes noise from news articles + search engine snippets with controlled noise ratios. Neither posits an attacker with corpus write access, query control, or insertion budget; both are benign/benchmark stressors rather than adversarial integrity threats.
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, via EM/F1 or accuracy); RGB additionally measures rejection rate, integration accuracy, and counterfactual robustness/error-detection rate
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer + abstain (RGB's negative rejection testbed explicitly evaluates refusal)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, evidence_assumption (noise construction differs)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RAG and explicitly treat counterfactual/misleading retrieved passages as a core failure mode, so they share the same failure-type family. However, RAAT is a training-time defense (adaptive adversarial training + noise-type multi-task head) evaluated on its own DPR-built RAG-Bench over NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ with answer-only action policy, while RGB is a diagnostic benchmark with no proposed defense, constructed from news + search-engine snippets in English and Chinese, and explicitly scores abstention (negative rejection) and information integration in addition to noise robustness. Because the intervention point (method vs. evaluation artifact), the action policy (answer-only vs. answer+abstain), and the noise-construction pipeline differ, they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitutable methods, but they are clearly complementary along the noise-robustness axis—hence partial rather than invalid or under-specified.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and a matched non-RAAT baseline) on the RGB testbeds in both English and Chinese, reporting noise robustness accuracy, negative-rejection rate, information-integration accuracy, and counterfactual error-detection rate; conversely, evaluate the LLMs benchmarked by RGB on RAAT's RAG-Bench with the same DPR retriever, identical noise-type splits (relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual), the same answer-vs-abstain action labels, and shared EM/F1 metrics, so that intervention, evidence construction, action policy, and metric family are aligned.
notes: Security-coordinate analysis is largely moot here: neither paper assumes attacker-created evidence, corpus write access, or an insertion budget, so the gap is between a defense method and a diagnostic benchmark over benign/synthetic noise, not between two threat models.

failure_type: relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error; both rely on naturally occurring retriever noise (DPR / Google retrieval) over ODQA corpora, no adversarial corpus write access, no attacker model
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (Chain-of-Note); context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (NLI filter + fine-tuning in Yoran et al.)
metric_target: answer correctness; CoN additionally reports rejection/abstention rate, Yoran et al. additionally reports robustness deltas with/without retrieval on multi-hop
action_policy: answer + abstain (CoN explicitly evaluates 'unknown' responses); filter + answer with no-context fallback (Yoran et al. explicitly bypasses retrieval when NLI says contradiction/neutral)
rationale: Both papers target the same failure mode — RALM distraction by irrelevant retrieved passages on open-domain QA — under benign (non-adversarial) retrieval assumptions, and both intervene partly via generator fine-tuning, so they live in the same problem area. However, Chain-of-Note couples a note-taking reasoning chain with an explicit abstain ('unknown') action and reports rejection rate, whereas Yoran et al. couple an NLI-based context-assembly filter with a no-retrieval fallback and emphasize multi-hop robustness without an abstain channel. The action policies are concretely different (abstain vs filter+fallback), the intervention points only partly overlap, and the headline metrics emphasize different things (EM+rejection vs accuracy delta with/without retrieval, including multi-hop). They should therefore be discussed as complementary mechanisms rather than ranked head-to-head, i.e., partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-run both methods with a shared retriever, base generator (e.g., Llama-2 7B), and a common benchmark suite covering single-hop (NQ/TriviaQA) and multi-hop (StrategyQA/2WikiMQA); report a unified action protocol that includes both abstention and filter behaviors (e.g., accuracy, EM on answered subset, abstention/filter rate, accuracy delta vs no-retrieval baseline) under matched noise conditions (both naturally retrieved and synthetically injected irrelevant passages), so that gains attributable to filtering, reasoning-chain notes, and abstain policy are separable.
notes: Not a security pair; attacker capability coordinates (write access, query control, insertion budget) are not applicable since both assume benign retrieval error rather than adversarial corpus injection.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error; both assume non-adversarial corpora, no attacker-created evidence, no integrity threat model invoked
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (sufficiency autorater + selective generation). Paper B: generator prompting or training + retriever (end-to-end LM trained with reflection tokens for on-demand retrieval and critique)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (abstention quality). Paper B: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: Paper A: abstain (explicit selective generation). Paper B: re-retrieve + filter (adaptive on-demand retrieval, selection among parallel generations)
rationale: Both papers tackle RAG reliability when retrieved context is irrelevant or insufficient and both invoke a notion of evidence quality, so they share the failure-type space (sufficiency / noise) and assume benign retrieval. However, Sufficient Context intervenes after retrieval with an autorater plus selective generation whose explicit action is abstention, targeting hallucination/abstention trade-offs; Self-RAG instead retrains the generator with reflection tokens to control on-demand retrieval, evidence filtering, and output selection, optimizing factuality and citation accuracy. The intervention point (post-hoc autorater + abstain policy vs end-to-end trained adaptive-retrieval LM), the primary action policy (abstain vs re-retrieve/filter), and the central metric (selective risk/correct-when-answered vs citation faithfulness + factuality) all diverge. They are best framed as complementary modules on different parts of the RAG pipeline rather than alternatives rankable on a single leaderboard, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark and generator backbone where both systems are evaluated under (a) the same action-policy taxonomy with both abstention rate and citation/support metrics reported, (b) the same retrieval corpus and top-k setup, (c) a common stratification by sufficiency so that selective-generation gains can be compared to Self-RAG's reflection-token-driven retrieve/critique gains, and (d) ablations that isolate the abstention signal vs adaptive-retrieval signal so each mechanism's contribution is measured against the same hallucination and faithfulness yardstick.
notes: Control pair; no adversarial/integrity threat model in either paper, so security coordinates (write access, insertion budget, attack objective) are not applicable.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise + sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; neither addresses attacker-created evidence, integrity threats, corpus write access, or insertion budget — security threat model not in scope for either paper
intervention_point: reranker + verifier (CalibRAG forecasting function over (t,q,d)); generator prompting/training + retriever (Self-RAG reflection tokens with on-demand retrieval)
metric_target: calibration error + answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer with calibrated confidence (CalibRAG, abstention not explicitly evaluated); re-retrieve + verify via reflection tokens (Self-RAG)
rationale: Both papers fall under the broad RAG-reliability/control umbrella and both add learned components to improve RAG output trustworthiness, but they target distinct failure modes. CalibRAG attacks miscalibration of decision confidence by training a forecasting function f(t,q,d) used for reranking and confidence reporting, with calibration error as the primary metric. Self-RAG attacks indiscriminate retrieval and unsupported generations by training reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval and self-critique, with factuality and citation faithfulness as primary metrics. The intervention points (reranker/verifier vs generator training plus adaptive retrieval), metric targets (ECE-style calibration vs citation/support), and action policies (calibrated answer vs adaptive retrieve/critique) all differ, so a single leaderboard ranking would conflate calibration quality with factuality/citation quality and mislead readers. They are best framed as complementary control mechanisms.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on the same QA + long-form benchmarks with a shared retriever and generator backbone, and report a common metric bundle (ECE/Brier, exact-match/F1, citation precision/recall, and an explicit abstention/coverage curve). Define a shared action-policy contract (e.g., both must support either abstain-on-low-confidence or adaptive re-retrieval and be evaluated under it). Until both papers report calibration AND factuality/citation metrics under the same evidence assumptions, only partial overlap can be claimed.
notes: Neither paper is security-oriented; threat-model coordinates (corpus write access, insertion budget, attacker objective) are not applicable here.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge, no adversary assumed. PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access (~5 malicious texts injected per target question), targeted query control (attacker-chosen target question/answer), both black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, attack objective is targeted answer induction. Threat models are entirely incongruent.
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious text injection); no defense intervention is proposed in PoisonedRAG itself.
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR).
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (no abstain/expose-conflict evaluated). PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy evaluated).
rationale: Both papers concern tension between retrieved context and the LLM's expected answer, but they operate in incompatible regimes. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense for benign knowledge conflicts, measuring answer correctness when parametric and retrieved knowledge disagree naturally. PoisonedRAG is an offensive paper that demonstrates a corpus-poisoning attack assuming adversarial corpus write access, targeted query selection, and an insertion budget of ~5 malicious passages, measured by ASR for attacker-chosen targets. Evidence assumption (natural vs attacker-created), intervention point (generator vs corpus), metric target (correctness vs ASR), and action policy all diverge, and one paper is an attack while the other is a method. They cannot be ranked as alternative methods on the same leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe both under a shared adversarial RAG evaluation: instantiate PoisonedRAG attacks (matched corpus, retriever, LLM, insertion budget, black/white-box assumptions) and evaluate FaithfulRAG as a candidate defense against them, jointly reporting ASR, clean-task answer correctness, and an explicit action policy (answer / abstain / expose conflict / quarantine). Conversely, FaithfulRAG would need to declare a threat model permitting attacker-authored retrieved passages, and PoisonedRAG would need to include FaithfulRAG among the defenses tested under identical metrics.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense-for-different-failure-mode mismatch; only meaningful as defense-evaluation, not as leaderboard-style head-to-head.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption (shared); Astute also covers relevance/noise and consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: Astute: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict + attacker-created evidence (worst-case). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model — corpus write access = yes; query control = attacker chooses target question; retriever visibility = both black-box and white-box studied; generator access = black-box; insertion budget = ~5 malicious texts per target question; attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer. Astute does not adopt or evaluate this same threat model.
intervention_point: Astute: generator prompting (post-retrieval source-aware consolidation). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (injection). These are opposite ends of the pipeline and opposite roles.
metric_target: Astute: answer correctness under imperfect retrieval. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate. Different metric families measuring opposite-sign outcomes.
action_policy: Astute: answer (based on reliability comparison of internal vs external evidence). PoisonedRAG: unreported / not a system action — it is an attacker objective.
rationale: Astute RAG is a generator-side defense that consolidates LLM internal knowledge with retrieved passages to remain correct under noisy, conflicting, or malicious retrieval. PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that crafts and injects malicious passages into the corpus to maximize attack success rate against an undefended RAG. They share the surface concept of corpus integrity, but occupy opposite roles in the attacker–defender stack: intervention points are opposite (generator consolidation vs corpus injection), metric targets are opposite-sign (answer correctness vs ASR), and only PoisonedRAG specifies a concrete threat model (write access, 5-text budget, target-answer objective, black/white-box retriever visibility). Putting them on a single leaderboard would be category-confused and misleading; they are complementary, not substitutable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid direct comparison is not achievable because the papers play different roles. A meaningful joint evaluation would instead pit Astute RAG (as defense) against PoisonedRAG (as attack) under a fixed threat model: same datasets (e.g., NQ/HotpotQA), same retriever and generator, fixed corpus write access and insertion budget (e.g., 5 malicious texts per target question), same attacker visibility settings, and report ASR reduction plus clean-task accuracy of Astute relative to no-defense and to other defenses (e.g., RobustRAG, perplexity filtering). Only such an attack×defense matrix — not a leaderboard ranking — would make the pair comparable.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pairing; treating them as alternative methods conflates threat model with mitigation.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG: corpus write access assumed, query control by attacker (chooses target Q and target A), retriever visibility in both black-box and white-box, generator access varies, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per target question, targeted attack objective (induce specific answer); RobustRAG: assumes adaptive attacker with full knowledge of defense, bounded number k' of injected malicious passages, defends untargeted/targeted corruption, no assumption on attacker's white/black-box access to retriever
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack) vs context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate defense)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG: ASR) vs answer correctness with certifiable robustness lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported (PoisonedRAG is an attack, no defender action) vs filter/aggregate (RobustRAG isolates passages, aggregates via keyword/decoding, can abstain with 'I don't know')
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, role (attack vs defense)
rationale: Both papers address the same threat model of adversarial corruption in RAG via attacker-injected passages into the knowledge base, and both consider bounded insertion budgets with adaptive/white-box attackers. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that crafts malicious texts and measures attack success rate, while RobustRAG is a defense paper that proposes an isolate-then-aggregate architecture with certifiable robustness guarantees. They operate on opposite sides of the security game: their intervention points (corpus injection vs context-assembly defense), metric targets (ASR vs certified robust accuracy), and action policies (none vs filter/aggregate/abstain) are fundamentally non-substitutable on a single leaderboard. They are complementary—RobustRAG could be evaluated against PoisonedRAG as one of its threat instances—so the relationship is partial rather than invalid, but direct ranking comparison is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To enable direct comparison, both papers would need to be on the same side of the security game: e.g., (a) compare RobustRAG against another defense (e.g., perplexity filtering, paraphrasing defense) under PoisonedRAG attacks using shared retriever/generator/corpus/insertion budget and shared metrics (clean accuracy, robust accuracy, certified accuracy, abstention rate); or (b) compare PoisonedRAG against other corruption attacks (e.g., GCG-style, prompt injection) under shared defender configurations. A unified evaluation harness reporting both ASR and certified robust accuracy at matched k' injection budgets, with explicit action policies (answer/abstain/filter), would be required.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense asymmetry: shared threat model and failure type, but opposite roles. Useful as paired citations but not as leaderboard rivals.

failure_type: RAGTruth: consistency/conflict (hallucinations unsupported by or contradicting evidence); RGB: relevance/noise, sufficiency, and consistency/conflict (across its 4 testbeds)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict (LLM-generated hallucinations on benign retrieved passages, word-level annotated); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, all-noise contexts, injected counterfactual documents). Not security/adversarial threat-model in either case.
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally enables generator prompting/training of detectors via fine-tuning
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support and citation faithfulness operationalized as span-level hallucination detection (precision/recall/F1 over spans); RGB: answer correctness plus selective risk/coverage (rejection rate, integration accuracy, counterfactual identification)
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (only detection of hallucinated spans, no action by the RAG system is evaluated); RGB: answer and abstain explicitly evaluated (negative rejection testbed)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation artifacts addressing trustworthiness failures, but they measure fundamentally different things. RAGTruth annotates word/span-level hallucinations in naturally generated LLM responses and scores hallucination-detection systems, with no system-level action being evaluated. RGB constructs four controlled testbeds (noise ratio, all-noise, multi-doc integration, counterfactual swaps) and scores LLM answer accuracy plus an explicit abstention behavior. Because evidence construction (natural vs. injected stressor), the primary metric family (span detection F1 vs. answer accuracy / rejection rate), and the action policy (detection-only vs. answer+abstain) all diverge, models or methods cannot be ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard; they are complementary diagnostics, hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, both benchmarks would need to be projected onto a shared evaluation axis: e.g., run the same RAG generator+detector stack on both corpora and report a unified metric set covering (a) span-level faithfulness, (b) end-task answer accuracy, and (c) abstention/rejection behavior under matched noise/counterfactual stressors; in addition both must declare the same action policy (e.g., answer-or-abstain with a fixed threshold) and the same evidence construction protocol (natural plus injected) so that scores are commensurable.
notes: Both are benchmarks in the same broad space (RAG trustworthiness), but their units of analysis and what counts as a 'correct' system response differ enough that leaderboard ranking would mislead.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency, integrity/adversarial corruption (RGB counterfactual subset only)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: news + search noise + counterfactual injection; SC: QA datasets stratified by sufficiency autorater, includes naturally occurring insufficient context)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); generator prompting/verifier + system-control policy (SC adds selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (both, but operationalized very differently); SC also reports hallucination rate stratified by sufficiency
action_policy: abstain (RGB evaluates 'negative rejection' as a separate ability; SC explicitly evaluates abstention vs hallucination and proposes guided abstention via selective generation)
rationale: Both papers analyze LLM behavior under imperfect RAG retrieval and both explicitly measure abstention-like behavior, so the action-policy coordinate genuinely overlaps (RGB's 'negative rejection' and SC's 'guided abstention'). However, RGB is a four-axis diagnostic benchmark mixing noise, sufficiency, multi-doc integration, and counterfactual/adversarial robustness with per-axis accuracy and rejection-rate scores, while Sufficient Context defines a single (Q,C) sufficiency property, uses an LLM autorater to stratify errors, and proposes a selective-generation method combining sufficiency and self-confidence. The intervention points differ (benchmark vs. benchmark+verifier+selective-generation policy), the metric families are non-overlapping (4 per-ability accuracies vs. correct/abstain/hallucinate rates conditioned on sufficiency), and only a subset of failure types overlaps (noise/sufficiency), excluding RGB's counterfactual/integrity axis. They are complementary lenses on RAG robustness rather than substitutable methods on a single leaderboard, so the verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both systems on a shared evaluation harness with the same retriever, generator backbones, and dataset; report a common metric set (e.g., correct%, abstain%, hallucinate%) stratified by both RGB's noise ratio axis and SC's sufficiency label; apply SC's selective-generation policy to RGB's negative-rejection and noise-robustness subsets; and ensure both label answer/abstain actions with the same operational threshold so the abstention axis is directly comparable.
notes: No security threat model in either paper (no attacker write access or insertion budget claimed); RGB's counterfactual subset is benchmark-injected, not an adversarial attack pipeline.

failure_type: consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict; benign retrieval error (RAGTruth covers naturally generated hallucinations across QA/D2T/summarization; FaithfulRAG focuses on parametric-vs-context knowledge conflict)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (RAGTruth); generator prompting or training, context assembly/compression (FaithfulRAG)
metric_target: evidence support, citation faithfulness (RAGTruth: hallucination detection); answer correctness (FaithfulRAG)
action_policy: verify, expose conflict (RAGTruth detectors flag spans); answer (FaithfulRAG generates a reconciled response)
rationale: Both papers concern faithfulness failures in RAG outputs, and both touch consistency/conflict between generated text and evidence. However, RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact—a span-annotated hallucination corpus and detector-benchmarking effort whose action policy is post-hoc detection/flagging—while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that mines self-facts, aligns them with context, and reasons through parametric–context conflicts before producing an answer. The intervention point (evaluation artifact + verifier vs. generator prompting/context assembly), the metric target (span-level detection F1 vs. end-task answer correctness/faithfulness), and the action policy (verify/expose vs. answer) are categorically different. This makes them complementary—FaithfulRAG could in principle be evaluated on RAGTruth—but not directly rankable on a shared leaderboard, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG (and the RAGTruth-finetuned detector or prompt-based baselines) on the same task suite using a shared metric family. For example: (i) evaluate FaithfulRAG outputs on the RAGTruth QA/summarization splits using RAGTruth's span-level hallucination metrics, or (ii) build a generation-time variant of RAGTruth detectors (filter/abstain) and compare end-task answer correctness and faithfulness against FaithfulRAG on the same conflict benchmarks (e.g., ConFiQA, NQ-Swap). Both papers would also need to declare a common action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. flag) so the outputs are commensurable.
notes: Not a security pair; threat-model coordinates (corpus write access, attacker capability) are not applicable—both assume naturally occurring rather than adversarially injected evidence.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B only via counterfactual noise)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real DPR/SerpAPI retrieval; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAG-Bench with explicitly categorized relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual noise)
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning); Paper B: generator prompting or training (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-type classification)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: unreported (both default to answer; neither evaluates abstain, re-retrieve, or expose-conflict policies despite Paper B's auxiliary noise classifier)
rationale: Both papers address noise robustness in RALMs and report answer correctness on ODQA, with partial dataset overlap on NQ and a shared interest in fine-tuning models to tolerate irrelevant retrieved passages. However, the failure-type scopes diverge: Paper A treats only irrelevant context as benign retrieval error, while Paper B's RAG-Bench explicitly adds counterfactual (conflicting) noise as a constructed stressor, which is closer to a consistency/conflict failure. The intervention points also differ in kind: Paper A combines a separate NLI filter with mixed-context training on a 13B model, whereas Paper B uses adaptive adversarial training with auxiliary noise-class supervision on a 7B model with no filtering stage. Neither paper specifies or evaluates a non-trivial action policy (abstention, re-retrieval, conflict exposure), so the systems should be discussed as complementary noise-robustness mechanisms rather than ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared base model and retriever, a unified noise-construction protocol covering both irrelevant-only and counterfactual conditions (so Paper A's method is tested under counterfactual noise and Paper B's under naturally retrieved irrelevant noise), a common benchmark suite (e.g., NQ+TriviaQA+WebQ with consistent DPR pipeline), and explicit reporting of action policy per noise type (answer vs abstain vs flag-conflict) with matched metric definitions. Ablations isolating filtering vs training contributions would also be needed.
notes: Paper B cites Yoran et al. as prior work; conceptual lineage is clear but the threat surface (counterfactual) and intervention design (no filter) prevent direct ranking.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Paper B also adds sufficiency and consistency/conflict (counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error on real ODQA retrievers; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injection
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (robust fine-tuning); Paper B: evaluation artifact (RGB benchmark)
metric_target: answer correctness for both; Paper B also tracks selective risk/coverage (rejection rate)
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (explicit); Paper B: answer + abstain (negative-rejection testbed); the two papers measure different action regimes
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG and share answer correctness as a core metric, so the failure-type axis overlaps. However, Paper A is a methods contribution intervening at context assembly (NLI filtering) and generator training (mixed relevant/irrelevant fine-tuning), evaluated on five existing ODQA datasets with naturally-noisy retrieved contexts, while Paper B is an evaluation artifact (RGB) that synthetically composes noise, counterfactuals, and rejection scenarios into four separate testbeds, including abilities (counterfactual robustness, information integration, negative rejection) that Paper A does not address. Because one paper proposes mitigations while the other proposes a measurement framework, and because their evidence construction and evaluated action policies (filter+answer vs. answer+abstain) differ, they cannot sit on the same leaderboard as alternative methods. They are best treated as complementary—Paper A's interventions could be scored on Paper B's benchmark—rather than directly ranked.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robustly fine-tuned RALMs on RGB's four testbeds (especially noise robustness and negative rejection) using RGB's metric definitions, or alternatively evaluate the six LLMs studied in Paper B on Paper A's five ODQA benchmarks under matched noise-ratio definitions. In both directions, the comparison must (a) pin a common retriever and generator family, (b) align noise/conflict construction procedures, and (c) report an explicit action policy schema (answer vs. abstain vs. filter) so the same outputs can be scored across both setups.
notes: Method-vs-benchmark mismatch is the dominant break; even within shared noise-robustness scope, action policy and evidence construction diverge.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both construct noise/counterfactual passages; RAAT uses DPR over Wikipedia on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ, RGB uses news + search-engine retrievals in EN/ZH)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT) vs. evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, EM/F1 or accuracy); selective risk/coverage (RGB only, via negative rejection rate)
action_policy: answer (RAAT, no abstain mechanism reported); answer + abstain (RGB explicitly scores negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG and explicitly treat counterfactual/irrelevant passages as the stressor, so failure type and evidence assumption overlap. However, RAAT is a generator-side training intervention (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B with a multi-task noise classifier) evaluated on its own RAG-Bench built from NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ, while RGB is purely a diagnostic evaluation artifact that decomposes RAG into four abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) over news-based bilingual data and does not propose a method. They also differ in action policy: RGB explicitly measures abstention via negative rejection, whereas RAAT only optimizes and reports answer-only EM/F1. These breaks in intervention point, metric target, and action policy mean the two contributions are complementary (a method vs. a benchmark with broader ability axes) rather than rankable on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate RAAT-trained models on the RGB testbeds (or a unified noise/counterfactual benchmark) using identical retriever, base LLM, noise injection ratios, language coverage, and metric set that includes both answer correctness AND negative-rejection / abstention behavior; conversely, instantiate a baseline + RAAT-style training under RGB's four ability axes so that the answer vs. abstain action policy is measured the same way for both.
notes: Asymmetric contribution types (method+small benchmark vs. ability-decomposed benchmark) is the dominant reason for partial rather than invalid.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Chain-of-Note additionally covers uncertainty/OOD via 'unknown' responses
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor (irrelevant or distracting passages); no adversarial threat model in either paper
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting/training (sequential reading notes); Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI filtering) plus generator training on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts
metric_target: answer correctness on overlapping ODQA benchmarks; Paper A additionally reports rejection/abstention rate, Paper B does not
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain ('unknown'); Paper B: filter (drop non-entailing passages, fall back to no-context generation) + answer; abstention is not evaluated in B
rationale: Both papers tackle the same failure type—RALM brittleness to irrelevant/distracting retrieved context—on overlapping ODQA benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, etc.) with answer correctness as a shared metric, and both rely on benign-retrieval-error assumptions rather than adversarial threats. However, the intervention points differ: Chain-of-Note rewires generator reasoning via per-document notes, while Yoran et al. intervene upstream with an NLI filter plus mixed-context fine-tuning. Their action policies are also distinct and non-substitutable—CoN explicitly evaluates an abstention ('unknown') policy and reports rejection rate, whereas the irrelevant-context paper executes a filter-then-answer policy with no abstention evaluation. These mechanisms are best framed as complementary modules at different pipeline stages and operating points, so a direct leaderboard ranking would conflate intervention site with action policy; hence partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same retriever (e.g., DPR), the same base LLM, the same benchmark splits, and the same noise construction. Both methods must report under a shared action-policy protocol—either both answer-only (disable CoN's 'unknown' option) or both with calibrated abstention curves reporting accuracy, coverage, and rejection rate. Add matched-budget ablations (filter-only, notes-only, filter+notes) and identical multi-hop evaluation so that intervention point is isolated as the only varying factor. Without those controls, results cannot be ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard.
notes: Papers are clearly in the same problem family but trade off at different operating points; treating them as substitutes would mislead readers about whether gains come from filtering, reasoning, or abstention.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression + system-control policy (sufficiency autorater feeding selective generation); Paper B: retriever (on-demand) + generator prompting or training (reflection-token training)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (hallucination vs abstention rate); Paper B: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: Paper A: abstain (explicitly evaluated via selective generation); Paper B: re-retrieve, filter, answer (with citations)
rationale: Both papers target the broad problem that retrieved context is not always useful for RAG and that LLMs need a signal for when to trust or act on retrieval, so failure type (sufficiency/relevance) and evidence assumption (benign retrieval) overlap. However, Sufficient Context intervenes post-hoc with an autorater plus self-confidence to drive guided abstention, and is evaluated as a selective-generation curve trading hallucinations against coverage. Self-RAG instead trains a generator end-to-end to emit reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and judge support/utility, and is evaluated primarily on factuality and citation accuracy in long-form generation. The intervention points (control-policy/autorater vs trained generator + adaptive retriever), metric targets (selective risk vs citation faithfulness), and action policies (abstain vs re-retrieve/filter/answer-with-citations) all differ, so leaderboard-style ranking would mislead; they are better framed as complementary modules.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a single retriever, generator backbone, and benchmark suite (e.g., PopQA/TriviaQA/long-form bio); evaluate both methods under a common action-policy taxonomy (abstain vs answer, with optional re-retrieve) on the same metric family (correctness, hallucination rate, citation faithfulness, and a shared selective risk-coverage curve); ablate the sufficiency-autorater signal as a drop-in alternative to ISREL/ISSUP reflection tokens, and report identical insufficient/irrelevant context stress slices for both systems.
notes: Paper B has implicit abstention-like behavior via 'No Retrieval' / 'Irrelevant' tokens but does not evaluate calibrated abstention in Paper A's selective-generation sense, reinforcing the partial verdict.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibration causing user over-reliance); Self-RAG: relevance/noise + sufficiency (unnecessary or unhelpful retrieval, ungrounded generation)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval errors from standard corpora; no adversarial threat model. No shared stressor construction.
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker + verifier (forecasting function over (t,q,d)); Self-RAG: generator prompting/training (reflection tokens, on-demand retrieval policy baked into the LM)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + decision answer correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness, evidence support, citation faithfulness
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence (re-rank/expose uncertainty to user); Self-RAG: re-retrieve on demand + filter via reflection tokens + answer selection. Different policy families.
rationale: Both papers aim to make RAG more reliable, but they tackle distinct failure modes: CalibRAG targets miscalibrated confidence that misleads human decision-makers and intervenes by training a forecasting function that reranks documents and produces calibrated probabilities, with calibration metrics (e.g., ECE) as a primary target. Self-RAG targets indiscriminate retrieval and ungrounded generation by training reflection tokens for on-demand retrieval, relevance, and support critique, with factuality and citation faithfulness as primary targets. The intervention points (reranker/verifier vs. generator training), metric families (calibration vs. factuality/citation), and action policies (expose calibrated confidence vs. adaptive retrieve/filter/select) differ substantially. They are complementary control mechanisms rather than substitutable methods, so a leaderboard-style head-to-head ranking would mislead.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark and protocol where both systems are evaluated on the same decision-making tasks with both (a) calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, selective-risk/coverage) and (b) factuality/citation metrics under a fixed retriever and generator backbone; explicit, comparable action policies (e.g., both must either expose confidence or abstain under the same threshold) and matched training data. Ideally, ablate each method's mechanism on the other's primary metric to show whether calibration gains and factuality gains transfer.
notes: Both are 'control' broadly construed but target different coordinates of robust RAG; treating them as alternatives on one leaderboard would conflate calibration with factuality.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict / benchmark-constructed stressor with no adversary. PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target questions (query control), retriever visibility in both black-box and white-box settings, generator black-box access, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts per target, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact extraction + self-think). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (poisoning the knowledge database).
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support (faithfulness). PoisonedRAG: attack success rate.
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer after reconciling conflicting facts (implicit single action). PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy evaluated).
rationale: Both papers touch the broad surface of 'retrieved context disagreeing with what the model would otherwise say,' but they sit on opposite sides of the pipeline and address different problems. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side method that resolves benign/natural knowledge conflicts by mining self-facts and reasoning over discrepancies, measured by answer correctness and faithfulness. PoisonedRAG is a corpus-side attack that crafts malicious passages under an explicit threat model (corpus write access, attacker-chosen targets, ≈5-doc insertion budget) and is measured by attack success rate. All five coordinates diverge — failure type, evidence assumption, intervention point, metric target, and action policy — and crucially one paper produces an attack while the other produces a generation method that is never evaluated as a defense against poisoning. Direct leaderboard-style ranking would be category-confused and misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make any direct comparison meaningful, FaithfulRAG would need to be evaluated as a defense against PoisonedRAG-style injections on the same corpora (NQ/HotpotQA/MS-MARCO targets used by PoisonedRAG), using a shared threat model (same retriever, same generator, same insertion budget, same target-question set), and reporting matched metrics on both sides — attack success rate / target-answer rate AND clean-task accuracy / faithfulness — together with an explicit action policy (answer vs abstain vs quarantine). Without that joint evaluation, the two papers can at most be discussed as complementary modules (attack benchmark vs conflict-resolution generator), not as substitutable methods on one leaderboard.
notes: Attack paper vs generator-side faithfulness method; one could imagine reusing FaithfulRAG as a partial defense, but neither paper performs that evaluation, so the comparison as written is invalid rather than merely partial.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict (with some integrity/adversarial corruption in worst-case experiments); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption only
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (e.g., RGB worst-case all-negative documents). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with full corpus write access, attacker query control (chosen target Q and target A), retriever visibility in both black-box and white-box variants, generator is black-box LLM, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts per target, attack objective is targeted answer manipulation.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free post-retrieval consolidation). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious-text injection into knowledge database).
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness under imperfect/worst-case retrieval. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR) on attacker-chosen targets, plus retrieval recall of injected texts.
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (with source-aware reliability comparison); PoisonedRAG: not a defender, no defender action policy reported (defenses tested are perplexity/paraphrasing filters, not Astute-style policies).
rationale: Both papers concern the robustness of RAG to non-trustworthy retrieved content, but they occupy fundamentally different roles in the threat-model pipeline: PoisonedRAG is an attack that writes adversarial passages into the corpus and measures attack success rate on attacker-chosen targets, while Astute RAG is a generation-stage defense that consolidates internal and external knowledge and measures answer correctness (mainly under noisy/conflict conditions, with worst-case retrieval as the adversarial proxy). The intervention point (corpus vs generator), metric target (ASR vs answer accuracy), and evidence-assumption regime (attacker-crafted optimized injections with explicit write access vs benchmark-constructed worst-case retrieval) all diverge, and the two papers cannot be substituted for one another on a single leaderboard. Treating them as competing 'robust RAG' methods would conflate threat creation with threat mitigation and would mislead readers about what is being optimized. They are complementary inputs to a security evaluation, not alternative solutions to the same task.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct comparison would only be meaningful in a defense-evaluation framing where PoisonedRAG is used as the adversary and Astute RAG (alongside other defenses) is evaluated on a shared metric — e.g., end-to-end answer accuracy and targeted-ASR under matched corpus, retriever, LLM, target-question set, insertion budget (k malicious texts), and attacker visibility (black-box/white-box). Both sides would additionally need to report a defender action policy (answer/abstain/filter/verify) and report calibration/selective-risk so the leaderboard isn't dominated by clean-accuracy regressions. Without this shared protocol, any head-to-head ranking is category-incoherent.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pairing; not rescuable to 'partial' because the metric targets (ASR vs answer correctness) and roles are structurally non-substitutable for leaderboard ranking.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG threat model: corpus write access=yes, query control=knows target question, retriever visibility=black-box and white-box variants, generator access=black-box, insertion budget=~5 texts/question, attack objective=targeted misinformation forcing a chosen answer. RobustRAG threat model: defends against adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge injecting an arbitrary bounded number m of corrupted passages within the top-k.
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack injection) vs context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG) vs answer correctness with certifiable robustness lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: answer (forced target answer); RobustRAG: aggregate/abstain (keyword/decoding aggregation with explicit 'I don't know' option). The two action policies are essentially in opposing roles.
breaking_coordinates: role (attack vs defense), intervention point, metric target, action policy
rationale: Both papers operate in the adversarial RAG corpus-corruption setting and share the failure type (integrity/adversarial corruption) and assumption of attacker-created evidence. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive method that optimizes malicious text injection to maximize attack success on a chosen target answer, while RobustRAG is a defensive method that isolates passages and aggregates per-passage LLM outputs to certify a lower bound on robust answer correctness. The intervention points (corpus injection vs context assembly/decoding aggregation), metric targets (ASR vs certified robust accuracy), and action policies (force-answer vs aggregate-or-abstain) are not just different—they are in opposing roles within the same threat model. They cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitutable methods; the natural relationship is that PoisonedRAG would serve as an evaluation attack against RobustRAG, not as a competitor.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To be directly comparable, both papers would need to occupy the same role (both defenses or both attacks), operate under a matched threat model (insertion budget, corpus write access, retriever visibility, generator access, attacker objective), use the same retriever-generator stack and datasets, and report a shared metric family (e.g., certified/empirical robust accuracy at fixed m for defenses, or ASR at fixed budget against fixed defenses for attacks). The current pairing only supports a 'defense vs attack evaluation' relationship, not a leaderboard ranking.
notes: Attack-paper vs defense-paper pairings are a canonical invalid-comparability case for leaderboard-style ranking, even when threat models overlap closely.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error / naturally occurring conflict (naturally generated LLM responses under standard RAG); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally supports generator prompting/training of detectors
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection (precision/recall on annotated spans); RGB: answer correctness plus rejection rate and counterfactual identification across 4 ability testbeds
action_policy: RAGTruth: answer (post-hoc hallucination detection, no abstain channel evaluated); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection) + expose conflict (counterfactual identification)
rationale: Both papers are evaluation artifacts for trustworthy RAG and overlap on the broad concern of unsupported/conflicting generation, but they instrument fundamentally different things. RAGTruth scores word-level hallucination detection on naturally generated LLM responses across QA/summ/data-to-text, with answer-only action policy; RGB scores generator behavior on four constructed ability testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, info integration, counterfactual robustness) where abstention and conflict-flagging are explicitly part of the action space. The evidence construction (natural vs. controlled stressor), metric target (span detection F1 vs. ability-specific accuracy/rejection), and evaluated action policies diverge, so leaderboard-style ranking would conflate different constructs. They are complementary benchmarks, hence partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, one would need: (a) a shared task definition and shared evidence-construction protocol (either both natural RAG traces with annotated spans, or both constructed noise/counterfactual conditions), (b) a unified metric family covering both span-level hallucination detection and answer/abstain accuracy, (c) the same retriever/generator stack across both corpora, and (d) explicit, harmonized action-policy labels (answer/abstain/expose-conflict) scored on the same instances. Without these, the benchmarks should be reported as complementary diagnostics rather than ranked.
notes: Both are AAAI/ACL-era RAG benchmarks targeting trustworthiness but operationalize it differently; treating them as exchangeable leaderboards would mislead readers about what each measures.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: curated noise ratios and counterfactual variants); benign retrieval error (SufficientContext: standard QA datasets analyzed post-hoc)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); generator prompting (SufficientContext also proposes selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage; SufficientContext additionally reports hallucination/abstention stratified by sufficiency
action_policy: abstain (both evaluate abstention explicitly: RGB via negative rejection rate; SufficientContext via selective generation)
rationale: Both papers examine LLM RAG behavior under imperfect retrieval and both explicitly evaluate abstention as a target behavior, so action_policy is not the breaking axis here. However, RGB is a fixed diagnostic benchmark with synthetically constructed noise ratios, negative-rejection cases, and counterfactual variants, whereas SufficientContext introduces an autorater-defined property over (Q,C) pairs applied to existing QA datasets (NQ, HotPotQA, Musique) and additionally proposes a selective-generation intervention. The evidence assumption (constructed stressor vs naturally-arising retrieval outcomes), the intervention point (pure evaluation artifact vs evaluation lens + generator-level selective generation), and the metric framing (per-ability accuracy/rejection rates vs sufficiency-stratified hallucination/abstention and selective risk/coverage) are sufficiently different that leaderboard-style ranking would conflate distinct constructs. They are best discussed as complementary diagnostics rather than substitutes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run SufficientContext's autorater and selective-generation method on RGB's four testbeds with the same LLMs, and reciprocally apply RGB-style controlled noise injections to SufficientContext's datasets. Report a unified metric family — accuracy, hallucination rate, and abstention rate, plus a correctness-coverage curve — under matched retriever, generator, and noise specification. Provide explicit sufficiency labels on RGB instances so the two notions ('negative rejection' and 'insufficient context') can be aligned operationally.
notes: Both papers do report abstention, so action_policy is present in both; the breaking axes are stressor construction, intervention surface, and metric operationalization rather than missing action policy.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (RAGTruth: naturally generated RAG outputs across QA/D2T/summ); naturally occurring conflict (FaithfulRAG: parametric vs. retrieved conflict)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (RAGTruth); generator prompting or training (FaithfulRAG)
metric_target: citation faithfulness / evidence support detection (RAGTruth detector benchmarking); answer correctness with faithfulness emphasis (FaithfulRAG)
action_policy: verify / flag spans (RAGTruth detector setting); answer after self-think reconciliation (FaithfulRAG)
rationale: Both papers target faithfulness/hallucination in RAG outputs, but they occupy categorically different roles in the research pipeline. RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact—a ~18K-response word-level hallucination corpus used to benchmark detectors and fine-tune detection models—whereas FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that mines self-facts, aligns them with retrieved chunks, and runs a self-think module to reconcile parametric/contextual conflict before answering. The intervention point (evaluation artifact vs. generator prompting), metric target (hallucination-detection performance vs. answer-correctness/faithfulness), and action policy (verify/flag spans vs. answer after reasoning) are all categorically different, so a leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful. They are complementary—FaithfulRAG outputs could be scored on a RAGTruth-style corpus—so the comparison is partial rather than invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate FaithfulRAG as one of the generators scored on the RAGTruth corpus (or a comparable knowledge-conflict slice), using identical retriever, base LLM, task suite, and prompt conditions, and report both span-level hallucination rates (RAGTruth-style annotation/detection) and end-task answer correctness/faithfulness on the same inputs. Conversely, FaithfulRAG-style methods would need to fix an action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict) so detectors and reconcilers can be scored on commensurate axes.
notes: Classic benchmark-vs-method asymmetry; categorize as partial because both target faithfulness and the method could be benchmarked on the corpus, but they are not substitutable leaderboard entries.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B only via counterfactual noise)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (Paper A, naturally noisy DPR/Google retrieval) and benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper B, explicit typology with injected counterfactual passages)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression (Paper A NLI filter) and generator prompting or training (both, via robust fine-tuning / RAAT adversarial + multi-task training)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1 on ODQA)
action_policy: filter then answer (Paper A); answer with implicit noise-type classification (Paper B) — neither reports abstain/expose-conflict/verify policies
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on ODQA and report answer-correctness metrics, so the high-level failure type (relevance/noise) and metric family overlap. However, RAAT explicitly includes counterfactual (conflict-bearing) retrieval noise as a first-class category and trains adaptively against it, which crosses into consistency/conflict territory that Yoran et al. do not address; conversely, Yoran et al. add an NLI-based filtering intervention at context assembly and a 1k-example robust-training recipe, neither of which RAAT mirrors. The noise constructions, retrievers, benchmarks (5 ODQA vs. RAG-Bench's NQ/TQA/WebQ), and training data pipelines differ, and the action policies diverge (filter-then-answer vs. answer-with-noise-classification). These differences make direct leaderboard ranking misleading, but the papers are clearly complementary methods on partially overlapping noise distributions, so partial — not invalid — is the appropriate verdict.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-run both methods on a common evaluation harness: same retriever (e.g., DPR top-k), same generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), and the same set of ODQA datasets stratified by noise condition (clean / irrelevant-only / counterfactual). Either restrict RAAT's evaluation to the irrelevant-only slice or extend Yoran et al.'s training and evaluation to the counterfactual slice.
