Report EM/F1 plus, ideally, abstention/coverage to expose action-policy differences, and ablate NLI-filter vs. no-filter on top of each training recipe so the filtering intervention is on equal footing.
notes: Yoran et al. is cited as prior work in RAAT, which itself signals the authors view them as related but not directly replaceable on a single leaderboard.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency, consistency/conflict (counterfactual), and integration
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); Paper A also includes naturally occurring retrieval errors from real retrievers over ODQA corpora, Paper B uses constructed news-based corpora with controlled noise ratios and explicit counterfactual injection
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (robust fine-tuning); Paper B: evaluation artifact (no intervention proposed)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness; Paper B: answer correctness, plus rejection rate (selective risk/coverage proxy) and counterfactual error rate
action_policy: Paper A: filter then answer (abstain not evaluated as a measured outcome); Paper B: answer and abstain (negative rejection is a first-class ability)
rationale: Both papers concern LLM behavior when retrieved context contains irrelevant or misleading passages, so they share the noise/relevance failure type. However, Paper A proposes concrete interventions (NLI-based passage filtering and robust fine-tuning) and reports answer correctness on five ODQA benchmarks, whereas Paper B is a diagnostic benchmark (RGB) that decomposes RAG into four abilities and evaluates off-the-shelf LLMs without proposing any mitigation. The intervention_point is therefore mismatched (method paper vs. evaluation artifact), and action_policy diverges because Paper B explicitly scores abstention via negative rejection while Paper A treats answering as the only measured outcome. They are complementary rather than directly rankable on a single leaderboard, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robust-FT pipelines on Paper B's RGB testbeds (matching noise ratios, the same LLM backbones, and the same English/Chinese splits), and report answer accuracy plus rejection rate and counterfactual error rate. Conversely, augment Paper A's ODQA evaluations with an explicit abstain option and a sufficiency-controlled split so that both works report the same action-policy outcomes (answer vs. abstain) under matched evidence-quality regimes.
notes: Classic method-vs-benchmark mismatch within the same robustness theme; partial rather than invalid because the noise-robustness subset of RGB could in principle host Paper A's methods.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (RGB negative rejection only)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer + abstain (RGB explicitly evaluates negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG using benchmark-constructed stressors with overlapping noise typologies (RAAT's relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual vs RGB's noise robustness + counterfactual robustness). However, RAAT is a training-time intervention (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B with multi-task noise-awareness) evaluated on its own RAG-Bench, while RGB is purely an evaluation benchmark with no method contribution, run on six LLMs across four distinct abilities including negative rejection. Critically, RGB explicitly evaluates an abstain action policy (negative rejection rate) whereas RAAT only measures F1/EM on answers, so they are not assessing the same operating mode. They are best discussed as complementary contributions — RGB could serve as a yardstick for methods like RAAT — rather than ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT's trained model and a matched baseline on RGB's four testbeds (especially negative rejection and counterfactual robustness) under identical retrievers, prompts, noise ratios, and metrics; or conversely evaluate RGB-style baseline LLMs on RAAT's RAG-Bench under identical splits. Also report a shared action-policy protocol (answer vs abstain thresholds) and a common metric family (EM/F1 + rejection rate + counterfactual identification accuracy) so the two systems sit on the same axes.
notes: One paper is a method, the other is a benchmark — kind-of-contribution mismatch is the main reason a direct leaderboard ranking is not warranted, even though the problem framing overlaps substantially.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Paper A additionally covers sufficiency/uncertainty (unknown handling)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both); irrelevant passages from a standard retriever (DPR/Google) over Wikipedia/open-domain corpora
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting + generator training (note-taking reasoning chain). Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI-based passage filter) + generator training (fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness AND selective risk/coverage (rejection rate on RealTimeQA). Paper B: answer correctness only
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain ('unknown'). Paper B: filter (drop non-entailed passages) then answer; no explicit abstention evaluated
rationale: Both papers target distraction by irrelevant retrieved context in open-domain QA and treat it as a benign retrieval-error problem, so the failure type and evidence assumption overlap substantially. However, the intervention points are distinct: Chain-of-Note modifies generator reasoning via per-document notes, while Yoran et al. intervene at context assembly through an NLI filter and at training via mixed-context fine-tuning. More critically, action policies diverge — CoN explicitly evaluates an abstain ('unknown') action and reports rejection rate as a selective-risk metric, whereas the irrelevant-context paper evaluates only answer correctness after filtering, with no abstention behavior measured. These differences make the two methods better framed as complementary mechanisms (filter vs. reason-then-abstain) than as directly rankable entries on one leaderboard, hence partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared retriever (e.g., DPR) and generator backbone over the same benchmarks (overlapping NQ/TriviaQA plus a multi-hop set like StrategyQA), with a unified evaluation that reports (i) answer EM/F1 on noisy vs clean contexts, (ii) rejection/abstention rate and selective-risk curves under a common abstain protocol, and (iii) ablations isolating filtering vs reasoning-vs-training contributions. Both papers should also report the same noise-injection procedure and matched training-data budgets so intervention type, not data scale, drives differences.
notes: Pair is genuinely close on failure type; the abstention/selective-risk axis is the strongest reason to avoid a single ranking.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, retriever, evaluation artifact
metric_target: answer correctness, calibration error, selective risk/coverage, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: abstain, answer, re-retrieve, verify
rationale: Both papers target RAG quality when retrieved evidence may be unhelpful and both incorporate a model-internal signal about context usefulness, so they share the sufficiency/relevance failure type and a benign-retrieval-error evidence assumption. However, Sufficient Context intervenes post-hoc at the generator with a selective generation policy built on a sufficiency autorater plus self-confidence, with an explicitly evaluated answer/abstain action and selective-risk/coverage and hallucination-reduction metrics. Self-RAG instead trains the LM with reflection tokens to perform on-demand re-retrieval and self-critique, and its headline metrics are factuality and citation accuracy for long-form generation. Because the intervention point (post-hoc selective generation vs. end-to-end reflection-token training), action policy (abstain vs. re-retrieve + self-verify), and metric families differ, direct leaderboard ranking would conflate fundamentally different operating regions; they are better framed as complementary mechanisms.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods on a shared QA + long-form benchmark suite with the same retriever and generator backbone; report an aligned action-policy set (answer / abstain / re-retrieve) and a unified metric bundle combining correctness, abstention/coverage, hallucination rate, and citation/support faithfulness. Ideally also include ablations where Self-RAG's reflection tokens are restricted to answer/abstain, and where Sufficient Context's selector is paired with adaptive re-retrieval, so each method is tested under the other's action regime.
notes: Could be combined (sufficiency signal feeding reflection-token decisions), reinforcing complementarity rather than direct substitutability.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence); Self-RAG: sufficiency and relevance/noise (when retrieval is needed and whether passages support the claim)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval errors with no adversarial threat model; CalibRAG additionally assumes a decision-correctness signal can be forecast from (temperature, query, document); Self-RAG assumes the LM can be trained with synthetic reflection-token supervision
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker (forecasting function f(t,q,d) reranks/scores documents) plus generator calibration; Self-RAG: generator training (special reflection tokens) plus system-control policy (on-demand retrieval gating)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error and answer correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, and evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence (no explicit abstain/escalate evaluated); Self-RAG: re-retrieve and verify via reflection tokens (ISREL/ISSUP/Retrieve)
rationale: Both papers fall under the broad umbrella of 'controlling' RAG output reliability under benign retrieval, but they target distinct failure modes: CalibRAG attacks miscalibration of decision confidence and is evaluated primarily with calibration metrics (e.g., ECE) alongside accuracy, while Self-RAG attacks indiscriminate retrieval and unsupported generation, and is evaluated on factuality and citation accuracy. The intervention points differ (a learned reranker/forecaster vs. a self-reflective generator with control tokens), and the action policies are fundamentally different (calibrated answering vs. on-demand retrieve/critique). The overlap on answer correctness is genuine, but ranking them on a single leaderboard would conflate calibration quality with adaptive-retrieval quality, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both systems on a shared benchmark with (i) the same retriever, corpus, and generator backbone, (ii) a common metric suite covering both calibration (ECE/Brier, selective risk-coverage) and factuality/citation (e.g., FactScore, citation precision/recall), (iii) an explicitly defined and evaluated action policy (e.g., abstain threshold tied to confidence and a re-retrieve trigger), and (iv) matched compute/training-data budgets. Without these, the systems should be reported as complementary modules (calibrated reranking vs. adaptive self-reflection) that could even be stacked, rather than direct alternatives.
notes: Both are 'control' papers but at different layers of the RAG stack; could plausibly be combined rather than ranked.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between model parametric knowledge and benign retrieved context; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker query control, both black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce specific target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious injection) — note this is an attack, not a defense intervention
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / faithfulness; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR)
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciling conflicting facts); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attacker paper, no defender action policy evaluated)
rationale: Both papers nominally involve 'conflicting' content reaching the generator, but they sit on opposite sides of the robust-RAG problem and cannot be ranked on a shared leaderboard. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side mitigation for benign, naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflicts, measured by answer faithfulness/correctness. PoisonedRAG is an offensive method that writes adversarial passages into the corpus under an explicit threat model (attacker corpus write access, chosen target questions, ~5 inserts/question, black/white-box variants) and is measured by attack success rate. The failure type, evidence assumption, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge, and neither paper evaluates the other's object of study (FaithfulRAG does not test against adversarial corpus poisoning; PoisonedRAG does not report a defender action policy or faithfulness metric). Direct comparison would conflate an attack with a non-adversarial conflict-resolution defense and is therefore invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To even reach 'partial', one would need a shared benchmark where (a) PoisonedRAG-style adversarial passages are injected into the same corpus, (b) FaithfulRAG (and any baseline defenses) are evaluated as defenders with an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/expose conflict/quarantine), (c) both attack success rate and answer correctness/faithfulness are jointly reported under a fixed retriever, generator, insertion budget, and threat model, and (d) FaithfulRAG's conflict-resolution mechanism is explicitly tested on attacker-created evidence rather than only on naturally occurring parametric-context disagreements.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense-for-different-threat-model mismatch; the surface-level 'conflict' overlap is misleading because one conflict is benign/epistemic and the other is adversarial/corpus-level.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption (PoisonedRAG); consistency/conflict + relevance/noise + partial integrity/adversarial corruption (Astute RAG)
evidence_assumption: PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model (corpus write access: yes; query control: targets attacker-chosen questions, not user queries; retriever visibility: both black-box and white-box; generator access: black-box; insertion budget: 5 malicious texts/target question; attack objective: induce a specific target answer). Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict, with only loose mention of 'malicious' content and no formal threat model.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free post-retrieval consolidation). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (injecting malicious passages).
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness under imperfect retrieval. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (target-answer ASR), with auxiliary retrieval recall of malicious passages.
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer via source-aware consolidation (no abstain/verify/quarantine evaluated). PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action).
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, evidence_assumption (threat-model specification asymmetry)
rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior when retrieved evidence may be corrupted, so the topical territory overlaps. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution operating at the corpus/index with attack-success-rate as its target metric and a fully specified attacker model (5-text insertion budget, target-question control, black-/white-box retriever knowledge), whereas Astute RAG is a defensive generator-side method targeting answer correctness under generic 'imperfect retrieval' without formalizing an attacker. The two sit on opposite sides of an attack–defense pair with inverted metric polarities and disjoint intervention points, and Astute RAG never explicitly evaluates against PoisonedRAG-style corpus poisoning. They are complementary rather than alternative leaderboard entries, hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Cast the two in a shared attack–defense evaluation: run Astute RAG (and baselines) against PoisonedRAG-crafted corpora under matched conditions (same retriever, same generator, same target-question set, same 5-text injection budget, both black-box and white-box attacker), and report a common metric pair such as ASR-under-defense and clean-question accuracy, plus an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine). Without that shared protocol, the papers belong in different cells of a threat-model matrix and should not be ranked on a single leaderboard.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pair; the partial verdict captures legitimate scholarly co-discussion while blocking leaderboard-style ranking with inverted metrics.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume corpus write access; PoisonedRAG assumes attacker-chosen target Q/A with black-box or white-box retriever visibility and ~5 injected texts; RobustRAG assumes an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense injecting a bounded number of malicious passages; attack objective is targeted answer induction (PoisonedRAG) vs preserving correct answer or abstaining (RobustRAG)
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG injects malicious passages) vs context assembly/compression and generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate with keyword/decoding aggregation)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG ASR) vs answer correctness with certified lower bounds and selective risk/coverage (RobustRAG)
action_policy: answer (PoisonedRAG induces the target answer) vs answer plus explicit abstain ('I don't know') in RobustRAG via aggregation
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, role (attack vs defense)
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat space of RAG retrieval corruption with attacker-controlled corpus writes, but they sit on opposite sides of the problem: PoisonedRAG is an offensive method that crafts malicious passages to satisfy retrieval and generation conditions and induce a chosen target answer, while RobustRAG is a defensive framework that isolates passages into disjoint groups and securely aggregates per-group LLM responses to obtain certifiable robustness bounds. Their intervention points (corpus injection vs context assembly/aggregation), metric targets (ASR vs certified robust accuracy and abstention coverage), and action policies (forced target answer vs answer-or-abstain) are categorically distinct. A leaderboard-style ranking would conflate attacker capability with defender capability and is therefore invalid; the two should be paired in an attack-vs-defense evaluation, not ranked as alternative methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Place both papers inside a single attack-defense evaluation: run PoisonedRAG (black-box and white-box, fixed insertion budget) against RobustRAG and against baseline/no-defense RAG on the same corpora, retrievers, generators, and queries; report ASR, certified and empirical robust accuracy, clean accuracy, and abstention rate under a shared threat model with explicit attacker objective and insertion budget. Only then can the attack's potency and the defense's certified guarantee be jointly interpreted; ranking them as substitute methods is not meaningful.
notes: Attack paper and defense paper in the same threat family are complementary not substitutable; invalid for leaderboard ranking, though they belong together in an attack/defense evaluation matrix.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict (RAGTruth: naturally generated LLM responses on real retrieved passages); benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: synthetic noise ratios, counterfactual edits, no-answer corpora)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally targets verifier (hallucination detectors fine-tuned/prompted on the corpus); RGB targets generator prompting (probing built-in abilities)
metric_target: evidence support / citation faithfulness (RAGTruth: span-level hallucination detection F1, hallucination frequency); answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (RGB: accuracy, rejection rate, error-detection rate, counterfactual correction)
action_policy: verify (RAGTruth, via post-hoc span-level hallucination detection); answer + abstain (RGB, which explicitly scores negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation benchmarks concerned with grounding failures, so they share the high-level problem of measuring whether LLMs faithfully use retrieved evidence. However, RAGTruth provides word-level annotations over naturally generated responses across QA, summarization, and data-to-text, and its primary use is benchmarking hallucination detectors (a verifier-side task with detection-F1 metrics). RGB, by contrast, constructs controlled testbeds with engineered noise ratios, all-noise corpora, multi-document integration, and counterfactual passages to probe four generator abilities, scoring answer accuracy and explicit abstention/rejection. The failure types only partially overlap (consistency appears in both, but noise robustness, sufficiency-based negative rejection, and counterfactual conflict are RGB-only), the evidence assumptions diverge (natural vs synthetic stressor), and the action policies differ (post-hoc verify vs evaluated abstain). A system ranked highly on one benchmark cannot be claimed superior on the other; they are complementary diagnostic tools, hence partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a leaderboard-style comparison meaningful, one would need either (a) to evaluate the same system axis — e.g., score hallucination detectors on both RAGTruth spans and on RGB counterfactual passages with a shared detection metric; or (b) to evaluate the same generator under matched task family, identical retriever and corpus construction protocol (natural vs synthetic), aligned metrics (span-level faithfulness vs response-level accuracy/rejection), and a single explicit action-policy definition (when to answer, abstain, or flag). Without this alignment, results from the two benchmarks measure different constructs and should be reported as complementary diagnostics.
notes: Both are benchmark papers, not methods; comparability question is whether they evaluate the same construct, which they do not.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise (RGB also covers consistency/conflict via counterfactual testbed)
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, counterfactual injection); SufficientContext: benign retrieval error / naturally occurring sufficiency variation labeled by an LLM autorater
intervention_point: RGB: evaluation artifact only; SufficientContext: evaluation artifact + generator prompting (selective generation combining sufficiency signal with self-confidence)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (abstention/hallucination rates); RGB also reports rejection rate per testbed
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention vs answering)
rationale: Both papers study how RAG systems behave when retrieved context is noisy or fails to fully support the answer, and both explicitly evaluate an answer-vs-abstain action policy, so they overlap on failure type (sufficiency/noise) and on the broad metric family of correctness plus abstention. However, RGB is a pure benchmark that partitions stressors into four hand-constructed testbeds (noise ratio, all-noise negative rejection, multi-doc integration, counterfactual conflict) with no proposed intervention, whereas Sufficient Context defines sufficiency as a continuous property of (Q,C) pairs, builds an autorater to label it on naturally retrieved contexts, and proposes a selective generation intervention on top of the generator. The evidence assumption (constructed stressor with known ground truth vs. autorater-labeled natural retrieval) and intervention point (none vs. generator prompting) diverge, so leaderboard-style ranking of one against the other would conflate a benchmark-diagnostic with a method paper. They are best treated as complementary lenses on the same phenomenon rather than competing systems.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make this a valid head-to-head comparison, one would need to (a) run the Sufficient Context autorater and selective-generation method on RGB's four testbeds (especially negative rejection and noise robustness) using RGB's metrics, or (b) reconstruct RGB-style controlled noise/counterfactual splits within Sufficient Context's datasets and evaluate the same models with matched correct/abstain/hallucinate definitions. The same retriever, generator backbones, abstention thresholding policy, and shared definitions of 'insufficient context' vs 'noise' would also need to be reported.
notes: RGB's 'negative rejection' testbed is the closest analog to Sufficient Context's insufficient-context stratum, but it uses fully noise contexts rather than partially insufficient natural retrieval, so even that subset is not an apples-to-apples match.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (RAGTruth: naturally generated hallucinations across QA/data-to-text/summarization); naturally occurring conflict and benchmark-constructed stressor (FaithfulRAG: parametric-vs-context conflict on conflict benchmarks)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (RAGTruth corpus + fine-tuned detector); context assembly/compression and generator prompting or training (FaithfulRAG self-fact mining, alignment, self-think)
metric_target: evidence support, citation faithfulness (RAGTruth: span-level hallucination detection P/R/F1); answer correctness (FaithfulRAG: faithful answer accuracy on conflict QA)
action_policy: verify (RAGTruth detectors flag hallucinated spans); answer (FaithfulRAG generates a reconciled response)
rationale: Both papers concern faithfulness failures of RAG outputs, but they occupy fundamentally different roles in the pipeline. RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact: a span-annotated corpus of naturally occurring hallucinations (including evident conflicts) used to benchmark and fine-tune hallucination detectors that operate post-hoc on a generated response. FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that mines self-facts, aligns them with context chunks, and runs a self-think module to reconcile parametric/context conflicts before producing the answer. The metric targets (span detection F1 vs answer correctness on conflict benchmarks) and action policies (verify/flag vs answer with reasoning) are distinct, so leaderboard-style ranking would be misleading; they are best framed as complementary (one could evaluate FaithfulRAG outputs using RAGTruth's annotation protocol).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) evaluate FaithfulRAG-generated outputs on RAGTruth's span-level hallucination annotations using the same detectors/judges, comparing whether FaithfulRAG reduces hallucination incidence vs baseline RAG; or (b) compare a RAGTruth-fine-tuned detector + abstain/verify policy against FaithfulRAG on the same conflict QA benchmarks with matched retriever, generator, prompt, action policy (answer vs abstain vs flag), and a shared metric family (faithfulness + answer correctness). Without these, the two papers address different operating regions and stages of the RAG stack.
notes: Benchmark-vs-method asymmetry is the dominant break; failure-type overlap (consistency/conflict, unsupported claims) is genuine but insufficient for a direct ranking.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B counterfactual noise only)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (Paper A); benchmark-constructed stressor incl. counterfactual passages (Paper B)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator training (Paper A); generator training only (Paper B)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, EM/F1-style)
action_policy: filter + answer (Paper A NLI gate discards non-entailing passages); answer only (Paper B)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA with LLaMA-2-class generators and use a training-based mitigation, and they overlap on NQ. However, Paper A scopes noise to irrelevant (benign) retrieval and combines two distinct interventions — an NLI filter that exercises a 'filter' action policy plus fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts — whereas Paper B expands the failure surface to include counterfactual passages (a consistency/conflict regime), constructs adversarial training stressors, and exposes only an 'answer' action policy with no filtering or abstention. Because the noise typology, evidence assumption, and especially the action policy differ, a leaderboard ranking would compare systems operating under different threat models and pipelines. The work is genuinely complementary — a filter-then-answer pipeline vs. an adversarially robust generator — so 'partial' is the appropriate verdict rather than 'valid' or 'invalid'.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared protocol: same retriever (e.g., DPR top-k), same base generator (LLaMA-2 7B), identical noise mixtures spanning irrelevant AND counterfactual passages, and a common metric suite (EM/F1) on the same query splits (NQ at minimum, ideally TriviaQA/WebQ). Critically, report results under a declared action policy: either (i) ablate Paper A's NLI filter so both systems are answer-only generators, or (ii) extend Paper B with a filtering/abstention front-end, and report selective-risk/coverage alongside accuracy. Counterfactual-noise robustness must be evaluated for Paper A's model, and irrelevant-only robustness for Paper B's, to align failure-type coverage.
notes: Partial — methods are best framed as complementary (filter+train vs. adversarial train) rather than substitutable on a single leaderboard.

failure_type: relevance/noise (shared); Paper B additionally covers consistency/conflict (counterfactual) and sufficiency (negative rejection)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real retrievers on ODQA; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios plus injected counterfactual documents
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (robust fine-tuning); Paper B: evaluation artifact (RGB benchmark, no mitigation proposed)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness (EM/accuracy on 5 ODQA benchmarks); Paper B: answer correctness plus selective risk/coverage (rejection rate, counterfactual identification rate)
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (fall back to no-context answer when NLI says non-entailing); Paper B: explicitly evaluates abstain via negative-rejection testbed, otherwise answer
rationale: Both papers concern RALM robustness to noisy/irrelevant retrieved context, so the high-level failure type overlaps. However, Paper A is a method paper proposing two concrete deployment-time controls (an NLI passage filter and robust fine-tuning) evaluated on five ODQA benchmarks with answer-correctness, while Paper B is a diagnostic benchmark (RGB) that decomposes RAG into four abilities including negative rejection and counterfactual robustness that Paper A never tests. The operational action policies are different — Paper A's pipeline filters then answers from parametric memory, whereas RGB explicitly scores abstain behavior — and the intervention coordinate is incommensurate (mitigation vs evaluation artifact). They are best discussed as complementary (Paper A's methods could be scored on RGB's noise-robustness testbed), not as alternatives on the same leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI filter and fine-tuned RALM on RGB's noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds with matched retrievers, prompts, and decoding; jointly report accuracy and rejection/abstain rate so that the filter's fallback action and RGB's abstain action are scored under one selective-prediction metric; extend Paper A or restrict Paper B so the failure-type scope (noise only vs noise+counterfactual+integration) coincides.
notes: Method-vs-benchmark mismatch and explicit-abstain vs filter-fallback action policies are the decisive operational differences from a deployment-controls perspective.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (raat2024); evaluation artifact (rgb2023)
metric_target: answer correctness (F1/EM) for raat2024; answer correctness plus selective risk/coverage (rejection rate) for rgb2023
action_policy: answer (raat2024); answer + abstain (rgb2023, via negative rejection testbed)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RAG and both explicitly treat counterfactual/misleading retrieved evidence as a stressor, sharing the failure-type and evidence-assumption coordinates. However, raat2024 is a training-side intervention (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 on a curated noise benchmark) evaluated only on answer correctness (F1/EM) under a single 'answer' action policy, while rgb2023 is purely an evaluation artifact (a bilingual benchmark) that decomposes RAG into four abilities including negative rejection, which explicitly evaluates an 'abstain' action policy alongside answering. Because one artifact is a method and the other is a benchmark, and because their action-policy and metric coverage differ (raat2024 never measures abstain behavior; rgb2023 proposes no intervention), they cannot occupy a single leaderboard as substitutable methods. They are best framed as complementary: RAAT could be scored on RGB's testbeds, but as published they break on intervention_point, action_policy, and metric_target. Therefore the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate RAAT (and a non-RAAT baseline LLaMA-2 7B) on RGB's four testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) using RGB's metrics including rejection rate, and conversely add an abstain-capable variant of RAAT so that both papers report the same action-policy set and metric family. Alternatively, fix the retriever, generator, noise construction protocol, and reporting of answer/abstain/expose-conflict outcomes across both works so that any reported numbers are directly substitutable.
notes: Asymmetric artifact types (training method vs. benchmark) is the dominant reason this falls short of valid even though the problem framing overlaps substantially.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Paper A additionally addresses uncertainty/OOD (unknown-answer cases)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both); Paper A includes naturally occurring out-of-knowledge cases via RealTimeQA
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting/training (note-taking + fine-tune). Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator training (mixed-context fine-tune)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (rejection rate). Paper B: answer correctness (with vs without retrieval; multi-hop accuracy)
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain ('unknown'). Paper B: filter (NLI drop non-entailing passages) + answer (fallback to no-retrieval LLM when filtered)
rationale: Both papers target the same failure type—generator distraction by irrelevant retrieved passages in ODQA under benign retrieval errors—and each defines an explicit, evaluated action policy, so this is not under-specified. However, the operational levers differ: Chain-of-Note intervenes at the generator with a per-document note-taking step and trains for an explicit 'unknown' abstention, whereas Yoran et al. intervene upstream with an NLI passage filter (falling back to a no-context LLM) plus mixed-context fine-tuning, with multi-hop reasoning as a central testbed. The reported metrics also diverge—Paper A reports both EM and rejection rate as first-class outcomes, while Paper B emphasizes accuracy delta relative to a no-retrieval baseline. A leaderboard-style ranking would conflate an abstention-aware system with a filter-and-answer system on metrics that reward different behaviors, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on the same retriever + generator backbone over a shared benchmark suite spanning single-hop, multi-hop, and known-unknown questions; report a common metric bundle including accuracy, abstention/rejection rate, accuracy-on-answered (selective risk), and accuracy delta vs no-retrieval baseline; explicitly label each system's action policy (answer / abstain / filter+fallback) and evaluate them under matched protocols, including an ablation that pipelines NLI filtering before CoN to disentangle filter-stage vs generator-stage contributions.
notes: Both action policies are explicitly evaluated, so the case is partial (complementary mechanisms) rather than under-specified.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: Sufficient Context: verifier (autorater) + system-control policy (selective generation at inference time); Self-RAG: generator training (reflection tokens) + retriever (on-demand) + verifier (self-critique)
metric_target: Sufficient Context: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (abstention vs hallucination rates); Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: Sufficient Context: answer, abstain (explicit selective generation); Self-RAG: answer, re-retrieve, filter (adaptive retrieval and irrelevance filtering via reflection tokens)
rationale: Both papers tackle RAG reliability by adding a self-evaluation signal to decide how the generator should behave given retrieved context, and both report explicit action policies (a key prerequisite often missing in this area). However, Sufficient Context operates as an inference-time selective-generation policy gated by an autorater's sufficiency judgement combined with self-confidence, and is scored primarily on hallucination/abstention trade-offs (selective risk/coverage). Self-RAG, in contrast, retrains the generator to emit reflection tokens that trigger on-demand retrieval and passage filtering, and is scored on citation faithfulness and evidence support in addition to correctness. Because the intervention points (inference-time controller vs. trained generator+retriever loop), action policies (abstain vs. re-retrieve/filter), and metric families differ substantively, a direct leaderboard ranking would conflate orthogonal capabilities; the two are better discussed as complementary control mechanisms operating in different regions of the RAG pipeline.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both systems on a shared benchmark with (a) the same retriever and corpus, (b) the same generator backbone where feasible (or matched parameter budgets), (c) a unified evaluation that jointly reports answer correctness, abstention rate, citation faithfulness, and selective-risk/coverage curves, and (d) an explicit action-policy taxonomy so that 'abstain' (Sufficient Context) and 'trigger retrieval / filter passage' (Self-RAG) are reported on comparable axes. Ideally also report retrieval cost/latency so adaptive-retrieval costs of Self-RAG are visible against the cheaper post-hoc Sufficient Context controller.
notes: Both papers do specify an action policy explicitly, so this is not under-specified; the obstacle to direct ranking is misaligned intervention point and metric coverage, hence partial.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence driving over-reliance); Self-RAG: relevance/noise + sufficiency (indiscriminate retrieval, unsupported generations)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval errors (no adversary). CalibRAG assumes the retrieved doc set is the source of decision uncertainty; Self-RAG assumes some queries do not require retrieval and that retrieved passages may be irrelevant.
intervention_point: CalibRAG: retriever/reranker (calibration-oriented forecasting function over (t,q,d) used to rerank) + generator confidence signaling. Self-RAG: generator prompting/training (reflection tokens) + adaptive retrieval gating + verifier-style critique.
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness for downstream decisions. Self-RAG: answer correctness, factuality, citation faithfulness.
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence (no explicit abstain/escalate evaluated, though calibration enables downstream gating). Self-RAG: re-retrieve (on-demand), filter (critique/select via ISREL/ISSUP/ISUSE tokens), answer. Different action repertoires; neither is evaluated under the other's policy.
rationale: Both papers aim to make RAG more reliable, but they target distinct failure modes with distinct mechanisms. CalibRAG attacks miscalibration of decision-confidence by training a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) used for reranking and confidence reporting, with ECE/calibration as a primary metric. Self-RAG attacks indiscriminate retrieval and unsupported generation by training a generator that emits reflection tokens to decide when to retrieve, judge relevance, and check support, with factuality and citation faithfulness as primary metrics. Their action policies differ qualitatively (confidence reporting for decision-making vs. on-demand retrieval + critique-based filtering), and their headline metrics are not interchangeable. A leaderboard-style ranking would mislead, but the two are coherent as complementary modules: hence partial, not invalid or under-specified.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a single (retriever, generator, dataset) stack and evaluate both under the same explicit action policy (e.g., answer-or-abstain with a calibration threshold, or selective-risk/coverage curves). Report a shared metric battery including ECE/Brier, accuracy at matched coverage, factuality/citation support, and any abstain or re-retrieve rates. Either retrofit Self-RAG with calibrated confidence outputs (e.g., probability from reflection-token logits) or have CalibRAG perform on-demand retrieval, so both produce comparable action labels and confidence signals on the same decision-making benchmarks.
notes: Both are 'control-flavored' RAG enhancements, but the control surface differs: calibration of confidence vs. discrete reflection-token gating. Without a shared action policy and metric family, ranking one above the other is not meaningful.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflict on benign retrieval; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target questions, both black-box and white-box retriever visibility, black-box generator access, ~5 injected passages per target question, objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious text injection) — no defender intervention proposed
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and evidence support / context faithfulness; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (with internal self-think reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (offensive paper, no defender action policy evaluated)
rationale: Both papers touch the RAG context-vs-knowledge interface, but FaithfulRAG is a defender-side generation-time method targeting benign knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and retrieved context, measured by answer faithfulness/correctness, while PoisonedRAG is an offensive corpus-poisoning attack assuming write access to the knowledge base and an attacker-chosen target answer, measured by attack success rate. Every coordinate diverges: the failure type (consistency vs adversarial integrity), evidence assumption (natural conflict vs attacker-created), intervention point (generator prompting vs corpus injection), metric target (correctness vs ASR), and action policy (answer-with-reconciliation vs none reported). FaithfulRAG is never evaluated under a poisoning threat model, and PoisonedRAG does not propose a defense whose effectiveness could be ranked against FaithfulRAG. Putting them on a shared leaderboard would conflate a benign-conflict mitigation method with an attack methodology, which is misleading rather than merely partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) re-evaluate FaithfulRAG as a defense on the PoisonedRAG benchmark (same target questions, injection budget, retriever/generator, and ASR metric) alongside other defenses, with explicit action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine), or (b) compare FaithfulRAG only against other conflict-resolution baselines on naturally-conflicting corpora with faithfulness metrics — and PoisonedRAG only against other attack methods on ASR. A direct head-to-head ranking is not meaningful without aligning threat model, intervention side (attack vs defense), metric family, and a declared action policy on the RAG side.
notes: Classic attack-paper vs defense-method mismatch; the 'conflict-security' framing of the pair masks that the conflict is benign in one and adversarially manufactured in the other.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict (with secondary mention of integrity/adversarial corruption); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption only
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict + benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB worst-case). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence; threat model: corpus write access = yes, query control = targets attacker-chosen questions, retriever visibility = both black-box and white-box studied, generator access = black-box, insertion budget = 5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free, source-aware consolidation, post-retrieval). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (poisoning, pre-retrieval).
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness (with worst-case robustness). PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR).
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (after reliability comparison of internal vs external candidates). PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper; defense action policy is not the artifact's role).
rationale: Both papers concern the reliability of RAG outputs when retrieved evidence is harmful, and Astute RAG even names 'malicious information' as a motivation. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack artifact that operates at corpus/index with explicit adversarial assumptions (write access, 5-text insertion budget, attacker-chosen target answer) and reports attack success rate, whereas Astute RAG is a generator-stage defense evaluated on benign/benchmark imperfect retrieval (NQ, TriviaQA, BioASQ, RGB worst-case) using answer correctness, without testing against PoisonedRAG-style optimized injections. The metric targets (ASR vs accuracy) and intervention points (corpus vs generator) are not interchangeable, and Astute RAG's action policy is 'answer with reliability comparison' while PoisonedRAG has no defender-side action policy. The artifacts are complementary (one could plug Astute RAG in as a defense against PoisonedRAG) but cannot be ranked on the same leaderboard as alternative methods to the same problem.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Astute RAG as a defender against PoisonedRAG attacks under matched conditions: same corpus (e.g., NQ/HotpotQA Wikipedia), same retriever, same target-question set, identical insertion budgets (1, 5, 10 malicious texts) in both black-box and white-box attacker settings, and report defender-side metrics (ASR reduction, clean accuracy retention, abstention rate) alongside answer correctness. Additionally, both should agree on an explicit action policy for the generator (answer/abstain/expose conflict) so the defense's behavior under poisoning is measurable, not just its accuracy on benign noise.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pairing within the same threat surface; partial rather than invalid because the defense paper explicitly motivates malicious retrieval and could plausibly be benchmarked against this attack, but as published neither evaluates the other.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume corpus write access with bounded insertion budget (PoisonedRAG ~5 malicious texts per target question, black-box/white-box retriever knowledge; RobustRAG adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge and bounded corrupted passages); query control and generator access broadly aligned
intervention_point: corpus/index for PoisonedRAG attack; context assembly/compression plus generator prompting for RobustRAG defense
metric_target: attack success for PoisonedRAG; answer correctness with certified robustness lower bound for RobustRAG
action_policy: unreported for PoisonedRAG; abstain plus isolate-then-aggregate explicitly evaluated for RobustRAG
rationale: Both papers address the same failure type (integrity/adversarial corruption in RAG) and assume largely compatible threat models: an attacker with corpus write access and a bounded insertion budget targeting a standard RAG pipeline. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack contribution whose intervention is at the corpus/index level and whose primary metric is attack success rate, with no explicit defensive action policy. RobustRAG is a defense contribution whose intervention is at context assembly/generation via isolate-then-aggregate, whose primary metric is certified/empirical answer correctness under corruption, and which explicitly evaluates an abstain action. They are complementary pieces of an attack-defense ecosystem rather than alternative methods on a shared leaderboard, so direct ranking would be misleading; the verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A joint evaluation rather than direct ranking: instantiate RobustRAG and at least one undefended baseline on the same corpus, retriever, generator, and target query set, then attack each with PoisonedRAG under matched insertion budgets (k', m'), reporting attack success rate, certified accuracy, empirical accuracy, and abstain rate on identical target questions. Any comparison should frame PoisonedRAG as the threat model evaluated against RobustRAG's defense, not as a competing method on a shared leaderboard.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pairs are structurally complementary; partial rather than invalid because threat model and failure type align cleanly.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict (RAGTruth: naturally generated LLM hallucinations over retrieved contexts); benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactuals)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); verifier (RAGTruth additionally fine-tunes detectors)
metric_target: evidence support, citation faithfulness (RAGTruth word/span hallucination detection); answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (RGB accuracy across 4 abilities including rejection rate)
action_policy: verify (RAGTruth, detector flags spans); answer + abstain (RGB explicitly scores negative rejection); otherwise unreported for generator-side action
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation artifacts probing generator reliability, but they instrument fundamentally different phenomena. RAGTruth measures word-level faithfulness of naturally generated responses against given contexts (a consistency/support metric, with a verifier-style detection action), whereas RGB measures answer correctness across four constructed stressors (noise, all-noise rejection, multi-doc integration, counterfactual conflict) and explicitly scores abstention as 'negative rejection.' The evidence assumption (naturally produced hallucinations vs. controlled, synthetically injected stressors), the metric family (span-level faithfulness vs. answer accuracy / rejection rate), and the evaluated action policy (verify vs. answer+abstain) all diverge. They are complementary diagnostics, not alternatives on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To compare directly, one would need a shared task definition with (a) the same generators and retrievers, (b) a common metric family — either both report span-level faithfulness on the same noise/counterfactual partitions, or both report answer accuracy plus rejection rate on naturally generated and adversarially constructed contexts, and (c) explicit, matched action-policy labels (answer / abstain / flag-and-verify) scored under the same scheme. Without aligning the failure-type partitions and the metric+action axes, any ranking across these benchmarks would conflate distinct robustness dimensions.
notes: Both are benchmarks, but the operational decision they evaluate (post-hoc span verification vs. in-loop answer-or-reject) is different, which is what blocks leaderboard comparability rather than the corpus-construction details alone.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (noise injected at controlled ratios, counterfactual documents constructed); Sufficient Context: benign retrieval error analyzed via autorater on natural RAG outputs
intervention_point: RGB: evaluation artifact only; Sufficient Context: evaluation artifact (autorater) + generator prompting + system-control policy (selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context only adds abstention/hallucination decomposition and selective risk)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB as 'negative rejection' ability; Sufficient Context as guided abstention via selective generation)
rationale: Both papers study how LLMs behave under imperfect retrieved contexts and explicitly treat abstention as a first-class behavior, which is unusual overlap and prevents a strict 'invalid'. However, RGB is a benchmark artifact that fixes four abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) using constructed stressors at controlled noise ratios, whereas Sufficient Context introduces an autorater-based analytic lens plus a selective generation method that intervenes at the generator/system-control layer based on a sufficiency signal combined with self-confidence. The intervention points differ (pure evaluation versus evaluation + selective answering policy), evidence is constructed vs. naturally retrieved-and-rated, and the failure type scope is broader in RGB. They are complementary perspectives — RGB scores LLMs on abilities including rejection; Sufficient Context stratifies/improves abstention via sufficiency — so leaderboard-style ranking would conflate a benchmark with a method.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the Sufficient Context autorater + selective generation pipeline on RGB's four testbeds (with the same retriever/generator stack) and report RGB's per-ability metrics alongside Sufficient Context's correct/abstain/hallucinate decomposition and selective-risk curves; conversely, evaluate RGB-tested LLMs on Sufficient Context's datasets with the same abstention scoring. Only when both papers' artifacts are evaluated on the same (query, context, action label) tuples with shared correctness, abstention, and hallucination metrics could direct comparison be claimed.
notes: Action policy is explicit in both papers (rare in this benchmark area), which is why this is partial rather than under-specified.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and naturally occurring conflict for RAGTruth; naturally occurring conflict (parametric vs retrieved) for FaithfulRAG
intervention_point: evaluation artifact plus generator prompting/training for RAGTruth; context assembly/compression plus generator prompting for FaithfulRAG
metric_target: evidence support, citation faithfulness, answer correctness for RAGTruth; answer correctness for FaithfulRAG
action_policy: unreported for RAGTruth; answer for FaithfulRAG
rationale: Both papers fall under RAG faithfulness, but they operate at fundamentally different layers: RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact (corpus with word-level hallucination annotations, used to benchmark and fine-tune detectors) while FaithfulRAG is a generator-side intervention that mines parametric self-facts, aligns them with context chunks, and reasons through conflicts before generation. The intervention points (evaluation artifact/detector vs generator prompting plus context assembly), metric targets (span-level hallucination detection vs QA answer correctness), and action policies (detect-only/unreported vs always-answer-after-reconciliation) differ materially. RAGTruth's failure-type scope is also broader (evident conflict, subtle conflict, baseless info across QA, data-to-text, summarization) while FaithfulRAG narrowly targets parametric-vs-context conflicts. They are complementary (FaithfulRAG could be evaluated against RAGTruth's annotations) rather than direct leaderboard alternatives, so the comparison is partial, not valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) re-cast both as generation methods and evaluate on the same RAG QA benchmark with identical retriever and generator backbones, reporting answer correctness, faithfulness, and an explicit action policy (answer vs abstain on detected conflict); or (b) re-cast both as faithfulness/hallucination detectors evaluated on RAGTruth's span-level annotations with the same precision/recall protocol. In addition, both should declare conflict definitions (parametric-vs-context vs naturally generated hallucinations) and report a common action policy (answer, abstain, expose conflict).
notes: Artifact-type mismatch (benchmark plus detector vs generation framework) is the primary reason for partial rather than valid.

failure_type: relevance/noise; consistency/conflict (Paper B's counterfactual subtype)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (naturally retrieved irrelevant passages); Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor mixing relevant, irrelevant, and counterfactual noise
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (fine-tune on mixed contexts); Paper B: generator prompting or training (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-awareness classification)
metric_target: answer correctness (Paper A: EM/accuracy on 5 ODQA sets; Paper B: F1/EM on RAG-Bench/3 ODQA sets)
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (NLI-based decision to drop context and fall back to closed-book); Paper B: answer (auxiliary noise-type classification, but no abstain/filter action reported)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs in open-domain QA and share answer-correctness as the primary metric, so they sit in the same broad research area. However, Paper A scopes noise to irrelevant/distracting retrievals and intervenes either by NLI-filtering passages (an explicit filter action) or by fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts, whereas Paper B expands the noise taxonomy to include counterfactual (conflicting) passages and intervenes only via adaptive adversarial training plus a noise-type classifier, with the model still always answering. The intervention mechanism, noise construction protocol, evaluation benchmark (5 datasets vs. RAG-Bench's 3), and action policy therefore diverge in non-trivial ways, so a leaderboard-style head-to-head would conflate a filter-and-fall-back system with an always-answer adversarially trained system over partially disjoint noise distributions. They are best discussed as complementary mitigations rather than ranked, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared benchmark with (a) identical retriever and generator backbones, (b) a unified noise taxonomy that separates irrelevant vs. counterfactual subsets with matched proportions, (c) the same QA datasets and answer-matching metric, and (d) explicit reporting of the action policy per method (e.g., evaluate Paper B with and without an abstain/filter wrapper, and evaluate Paper A on counterfactual noise). Also report calibration/abstention or selective-risk curves so the filter-based and pure-generation approaches can be compared at matched coverage.
notes: Paper B explicitly cites Yoran et al. as prior work, but evaluation protocols and noise definitions still diverge enough to block direct ranking.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); sufficiency and consistency/conflict (Paper B only via negative rejection and counterfactual testbeds)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor (both); Paper B additionally injects naturally occurring and counterfactual evidence
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) and generator prompting or training (robust fine-tuning); Paper B: evaluation artifact only
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness; Paper B: answer correctness plus selective risk/coverage (rejection rate) and evidence support under conflict
action_policy: Paper A: answer (with upstream filter), abstention not evaluated as a labeled action; Paper B: answer and abstain (negative rejection explicitly scored), plus expose-conflict implicit in counterfactual testbed
rationale: Both papers target the noise-robustness aspect of RAG, so the failure type partially overlaps on distraction by irrelevant retrieved context. However, Paper A is a methods contribution that intervenes at the context-assembly stage (NLI filtering) and at training (mixed relevant/irrelevant fine-tuning) and measures answer correctness on five ODQA benchmarks; it does not score an abstain action. Paper B is a diagnostic benchmark that decomposes RAG into four abilities, two of which (negative rejection and counterfactual robustness) require an abstain or conflict-exposure action and lie outside Paper A's evaluation. Because the intervention point (method vs. benchmark), action-policy scope (answer-only vs. answer+abstain), and metric family (accuracy vs. accuracy+rejection rate+counterfactual sensitivity) differ, the two cannot be ranked as alternatives on a single leaderboard; they are complementary, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robust fine-tuned models on RGB's four testbeds with the same retriever, generators, and prompt template, and additionally have Paper A explicitly report a labeled abstain/negative-rejection action and a counterfactual-robustness metric. Equivalently, restrict the comparison to the noise-robustness testbed only, with matched noise-ratio definitions and a shared accuracy metric, and document that abstention/conflict behaviors are out of scope.
notes: Method-vs-benchmark asymmetry is the dominant comparability obstacle; Paper A's methods could be benchmarked on RGB but neither paper does this directly.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage and evidence support (RGB only, via negative rejection and counterfactual detection)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer and abstain (RGB, via negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers address noise robustness in RAG with explicit attention to counterfactual/misleading documents, and both construct curated benchmarks to probe LLM behavior under noisy retrieval. However, they are different kinds of artifacts: RAAT is a training-side intervention (adaptive adversarial training plus noise-aware multi-task classification on LLaMA-2 7B) evaluated by F1/EM on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ, while RGB is a diagnostic benchmark evaluating 6 frozen LLMs across four separable abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) using news-derived passages in English and Chinese. The intervention point, the action policy space (RGB explicitly scores abstention via negative rejection; RAAT scores answering), and the metric family (RGB adds rejection rate and error-detection/correction beyond F1/EM) all differ, so they cannot occupy the same leaderboard slot, though they are clearly complementary in the same problem area.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate the RAAT-trained generator on RGB's four testbeds with the same retriever and noise-ratio settings, and conversely run RGB's baseline LLMs on RAG-Bench with matched noise types; report answer correctness, negative-rejection rate, and counterfactual-detection rate jointly, with an explicit action-policy specification (when to answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict) that is consistent across both benchmarks.
notes: Method paper vs. benchmark paper; overlap is real but the intervention and action axes prevent direct ranking.

failure_type: relevance/noise; CoN additionally addresses uncertainty/OOD (unknown questions)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor for both; CoN additionally constructs noisy-document and real-time (out-of-knowledge) stressors, Paper B emphasizes naturally occurring distractors plus a multi-hop adversarial-decomposition setting
intervention_point: CoN: generator prompting/training (note-taking reasoning step); Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI entailment filter) plus generator training on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts
metric_target: answer correctness (EM) for both; CoN additionally reports selective risk/coverage via rejection rate on real-time/unknown questions; Paper B does not report a comparable abstention metric
action_policy: CoN: answer or abstain ('unknown') — explicitly evaluated; Paper B: filter then answer (fallback to no-retrieval answer when NLI rejects) — abstain is not an evaluated action
rationale: Both papers target the same failure mode — RALM degradation when retrieved passages are irrelevant or distracting — and both evaluate on open-domain QA with overlapping datasets (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA). However, they intervene at different points: Paper B filters at the context-assembly stage via an NLI entailment check and additionally fine-tunes on mixed contexts, while Chain-of-Note restructures generator reasoning with per-document notes. They also operate under different action policies — CoN explicitly evaluates an abstain ('unknown') action and reports rejection rate, whereas Paper B's pipeline answers (with or without retrieved context) and reports no comparable abstention metric. These differences in intervention point, action policy, and metric coverage mean the two should be framed as complementary modules at different operating points rather than ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Same retriever and retrieval depth, identical document pools across the same benchmark splits (including a controlled multi-hop subset and a controlled unknown/out-of-knowledge subset), a shared action-policy specification where both systems are allowed and scored on abstain, and a common metric suite reporting answer correctness, rejection/abstention rate, and selective risk-coverage. Ideally also an ablation combining NLI filtering with Chain-of-Note to separate context-level from generator-level contributions.
notes: From a faithfulness lens, CoN's note generation provides per-document support traces that Paper B's NLI filter does not, but neither paper directly measures citation faithfulness, so that axis is uninformative for ranking.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, system-control policy, verifier
metric_target: answer correctness, evidence support, citation faithfulness, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: abstain (Sufficient Context, explicitly evaluated via selective generation); re-retrieve, filter, verify (Self-RAG, via reflection tokens)
rationale: Both papers target RAG factuality and the question of whether to trust retrieved context, but they operate at fundamentally different points and execute different action policies. Sufficient Context is a post-hoc selective-generation method: an LLM autorater labels (Q,C) sufficiency and is combined with self-confidence to gate abstention, with metrics centered on selective-risk/coverage and correctness-when-answered. Self-RAG retrains a generator end-to-end to emit reflection tokens that trigger on-demand re-retrieval and per-passage critique, with primary metrics on factuality and citation accuracy across diverse tasks. The action policies (abstain vs. adaptive re-retrieve + verify) and the intervention points (inference-time control vs. training-time generator + adaptive retriever) diverge, and the headline metric families only partially overlap, so a direct leaderboard ranking would conflate orthogonal interventions; they should be discussed as complementary modules.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared evaluation suite with the same retriever, base LM family, and corpus; report a common metric set including (a) selective-generation metrics (coverage, accuracy-when-answered, abstention rate on insufficient context) and (b) citation/attribution metrics (supportedness, citation precision/recall). Use an explicit shared action-policy taxonomy that distinguishes answer / abstain / re-retrieve / verify, and align the operating point (e.g., match coverage or match retrieval budget) before comparing correctness or factuality.
notes: Both fit a broad 'control RAG hallucinations' theme, but the protocols, training regimes, and reported action policies are different enough that head-to-head ranking would mislead.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence in decision support); Self-RAG: relevance/noise + sufficiency + consistency/conflict (when/whether passages support claims)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval errors from standard corpora; neither targets adversarial corruption or stale-source threats. CalibRAG additionally assumes a decision-making context where user reliance scales with confidence; Self-RAG assumes passages may be irrelevant or unsupported and trains the LM to detect this.
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker (forecasting function f(t,q,d) used to score/rerank documents) plus generator confidence calibration; Self-RAG: generator prompting/training (reflection tokens added to vocabulary) and retriever (on-demand retrieval triggered by Retrieve token)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer (with calibrated confidence; no explicit abstain/re-retrieve evaluation reported); Self-RAG: answer + re-retrieve + filter + verify (via ISREL/ISSUP/ISUSE reflection tokens) — substantively different action repertoires
rationale: Both papers aim to improve RAG reliability beyond plain retrieve-and-generate, so they sit in the same broad 'robust RAG' family. However, CalibRAG targets miscalibration of decision-support confidence and intervenes at the reranker via a learned forecasting function f(t,q,d), optimizing calibration error alongside accuracy. Self-RAG targets retrieval necessity and passage relevance/support, intervening inside the generator via trained reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval, filtering, and self-critique, and it optimizes factuality and citation accuracy. The intervention point, primary metric family, and action repertoire (calibrated answer vs. retrieve/filter/critique tokens) differ substantively, so a leaderboard-style ranking would compare apples to oranges; they are best framed as complementary modules addressing different failure modes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark reporting both calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, selective risk/coverage) and citation/support metrics (citation precision/recall, attribution faithfulness) under an identical retriever and base LM; explicit action-policy reporting for both systems (when each abstains, re-retrieves, or filters); and cross-application ablations (e.g., apply CalibRAG's forecasting function on top of Self-RAG outputs, and evaluate Self-RAG's reflection-token mechanism under CalibRAG's decision-calibration protocol) so that mechanism contributions can be disentangled rather than ranked head-to-head.
notes: Both are well-specified individually; the issue is incommensurate objectives, not missing information, so 'partial' fits better than 'under-specified'.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs contextual); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and retrieved context; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target questions, black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per question, objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious text injection); defenses evaluated in PoisonedRAG sit at context assembly/filter
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness, evidence support; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (with internal reconciliation), no explicit abstain/expose-conflict evaluation; PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy beyond filter baselines)
rationale: Both papers concern trust in retrieved evidence for RAG, but they occupy fundamentally non-overlapping problem settings. FaithfulRAG is a defense that resolves naturally occurring conflicts between an LLM's parametric knowledge and benign retrieved context via fact-level reconciliation, reported on answer-correctness benchmarks with no adversarial threat model. PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that injects 5 attacker-crafted malicious passages per target question into the corpus to flip generations toward attacker-chosen answers, reported via attack success rate; the only defenses it evaluates are perplexity/duplicate filters at the corpus/context stage. Failure type, evidence assumption, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge, and neither paper instantiates the other's setup (FaithfulRAG never reports ASR under corpus poisoning; PoisonedRAG never measures parametric-vs-context faithfulness). A leaderboard-style ranking would conflate attack effectiveness with conflict-resolution accuracy and would mislead readers.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG as a candidate defense inside the PoisonedRAG threat model on the same datasets (NQ/HotpotQA/MS-MARCO), same retriever (e.g., Contriever), same generator, and same insertion budget, then report a common metric set including ASR, clean accuracy, accuracy under attack, and a defender action policy (answer/abstain/expose-conflict/filter). Conversely, PoisonedRAG would need to report fact-level faithfulness metrics on natural-conflict benchmarks. Both papers must explicitly declare the threat model and the action policy under evaluation.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pair where the defense is not designed for adversarial corpus poisoning; partial would understate the threat-model gap.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict (worst-case all-negative retrieval, not attacker-optimized). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence; threat model — corpus write access YES, query control NO (attacker chooses target question), retriever visibility black-box and white-box, generator access black-box, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (source-aware consolidation, reliability comparison); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious passage injection)
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness (worst-case robustness); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (with internal/external reliability arbitration); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy evaluated)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, evidence_assumption, action_policy, role (attack vs defense)
rationale: Both papers concern robustness of RAG under non-ideal retrieval, but they occupy opposite sides of the attack-defense ecosystem and cannot be ranked on a shared leaderboard. PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that assumes corpus write access and an insertion budget (~5 malicious texts per question) to induce a chosen target answer, reporting Attack Success Rate. Astute RAG is a defensive, training-free generator-side method that elicits LLM-internal knowledge and performs source-aware consolidation, reporting answer correctness under worst-case retrieval without modeling adversarial optimization or insertion budgets. The intervention point (corpus vs generator), metric target (ASR vs correctness), evidence assumption (attacker-created vs imperfect/conflicting), and defender action policy (explicit reliability arbitration vs none) all diverge, so direct comparison would conflate an attack's success with a defense's accuracy and mislead readers.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make these comparable, one would need to evaluate Astute RAG explicitly as a defense against PoisonedRAG-style injections: shared retriever and generator, identical corpus with the same insertion budget (e.g., 5 malicious texts per target question across NQ/HotpotQA/MS-MARCO as in PoisonedRAG), and shared metrics reported on both sides — Attack Success Rate, target-question accuracy, and clean-question accuracy — plus an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/expose-conflict) measured under attack. Only then could one rank Astute RAG against PoisonedRAG (or against other defenses under PoisonedRAG) on a common leaderboard.
