notes: Astute RAG mentions 'malicious information' rhetorically but does not evaluate against an optimized corpus-poisoning attacker; the worst-case RGB setting is constructed noise, not attacker-created evidence with an insertion budget.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume corpus write access and a bounded insertion budget (PoisonedRAG: ~5 malicious texts per target question, black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, attacker-chosen target QA pair with goal of inducing a specific target answer; CertifiedRAG: adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense and ability to inject up to k' malicious passages, defender controls aggregation but not corpus)
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG, attack-side injection) vs. context assembly/compression + generator prompting (CertifiedRAG, isolate-then-aggregate defense)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG: ASR) vs. answer correctness with certifiable lower bound (CertifiedRAG)
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy under evaluation); CertifiedRAG: answer + abstain ('I don't know') + filter (keyword aggregation)
breaking_coordinates: role asymmetry (attack vs. defense), intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat space—adversarial corruption of a RAG knowledge base via injected malicious passages with a bounded insertion budget—so the failure_type and evidence_assumption families overlap. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack method whose metric target is attack success rate and whose intervention point is the corpus, while CertifiedRAG is a defense method whose metric target is certifiable answer correctness and whose intervention point is isolate-then-aggregate at context assembly/generation with an explicit abstain/filter action policy. An attack and a defense cannot be ranked as substitutable methods on a single leaderboard; they are complementary components of an attack–defense pair. The comparison is therefore partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) restrict the comparison to a defense-vs-defense or attack-vs-attack leaderboard, or (b) re-cast as a joint attack/defense evaluation: instantiate CertifiedRAG and any baseline defenses on the exact PoisonedRAG threat model (same corpus, retriever, generator, target queries, k and k' insertion budget, and attacker knowledge level), then report a shared metric pair such as ASR-under-defense and certified accuracy lower bound, plus explicit action labels (answer/abstain/filter). Only then can the two papers be discussed quantitatively against each other rather than as complementary attack and defense contributions.
notes: Classic attack-paper vs. defense-paper asymmetry; partial (not invalid) because the threat model and corruption assumption are compatible enough that CertifiedRAG could in principle be evaluated against PoisonedRAG-style injections.

failure_type: sufficiency, consistency/conflict, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations from LLM generations on standard RAG inputs; RGB: benchmark-constructed stressors (noise ratios, counterfactual documents, all-noise contexts)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally targets verifier/detector training; RGB targets generator prompting behavior
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support, citation faithfulness (hallucination detection F1/span); RGB: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (rejection rate), information integration accuracy
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (detector flags spans); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection explicitly evaluated)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation benchmarks concerned with trustworthiness, and both touch hallucination/conflict phenomena (RAGTruth's span-level hallucinations, RGB's counterfactual robustness). However, RAGTruth is a corpus of naturally generated LLM responses annotated for word-level hallucinations, designed to score and train hallucination detectors (verifier-side, evidence support metric). RGB is a constructed bilingual testbed that probes generator behavior across four axes (noise robustness, negative rejection, integration, counterfactual robustness) using synthesized noisy/counterfactual contexts, with answer-correctness and explicit abstain/rejection as primary metrics. Because the units of evaluation (annotated spans of natural hallucinations vs. constructed stressor instances), metric targets (detection quality vs. generation accuracy + rejection), and action policies (verify vs. answer/abstain) differ, the two cannot be placed on a single leaderboard. They are complementary diagnostic instruments rather than substitutable benchmarks, so the verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A common task definition where the same RAG inputs are used to (a) evaluate generator outputs under specified stressors and (b) evaluate detector/abstain decisions on those outputs, with a shared action policy schema (answer/abstain/verify), shared metric family (e.g., joint correctness + faithfulness + selective risk), and shared evidence-construction protocol (natural vs. synthetic explicitly matched). At minimum, one would need to run RGB-style stressors through RAGTruth's annotation pipeline (or vice versa) and report aligned detection-vs-generation metrics on the same models.
notes: Both classify as evaluation_benchmark, but their evaluation objects (detector quality vs. LLM RAG abilities) are distinct enough that ranking is not meaningful even though they overlap topically.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict (RGB covers all three across its 4 abilities; Sufficient Context centers on sufficiency)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB) vs. benign retrieval error / naturally occurring insufficient context (Sufficient Context)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (RGB benchmark + RGB autorater scoring) vs. evaluation artifact + generator prompting (Sufficient Context autorater plus selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, retrieval-conditioned accuracy (RGB) vs. answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, hallucination rate stratified by sufficiency (Sufficient Context)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB as 'negative rejection'; Sufficient Context as guided selective generation)
rationale: Both papers explicitly evaluate whether LLMs in RAG abstain versus hallucinate when retrieved context is insufficient, and both treat abstention as a first-class action policy (RGB's 'negative rejection' and Sufficient Context's selective generation), so the abstention axis is genuinely comparable. However, RGB is a fixed multi-ability benchmark built from constructed stressors (noise ratios, swapped/counterfactual passages, all-noise documents) that scores models on four pre-specified axes, while Sufficient Context introduces a (Q,C) sufficiency autorater applied to natural QA datasets and additionally proposes a generator-side intervention (selective generation combining sufficiency with self-confidence). The evidence assumption (synthetic stressor vs. naturally occurring sufficient/insufficient context), intervention point (eval-only vs. eval + generator prompting), and metric framing (per-ability accuracy vs. coverage/risk stratified by sufficiency) differ enough that a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate distinct constructs. The pair is therefore best read as complementary lenses on the same abstention problem rather than substitutable methods, supporting a 'partial' verdict.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make this directly comparable, one would need: (i) a shared dataset stratified both by RGB's constructed conditions and by the Sufficient Context autorater's binary sufficiency label; (ii) a unified abstention metric (e.g., risk-coverage or accuracy-when-answered alongside abstention rate) computed identically for both; (iii) the same backbone LLMs and retrieval pipeline; and (iv) reporting Sufficient Context's selective-generation method on RGB's four testbeds, plus running RGB's negative-rejection protocol on the natural QA sets used by Sufficient Context, so the intervention point (eval artifact vs. eval + generation policy) is held constant.
notes: Action policy is explicitly evaluated in both papers (not inferred), so the abstention axis itself does not break; the break is on evidence construction, intervention scope, and metric family.

failure_type: consistency/conflict for both; RAGTruth also covers relevance/noise and sufficiency
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations from LLM RAG outputs with word-level labels (benign retrieval error plus naturally occurring conflict); FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflict on conflict-oriented QA benchmarks
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) plus optional detector fine-tuning; FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support and citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection F1; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness on knowledge-conflict QA
action_policy: unreported in both; RAGTruth detects post-hoc, FaithfulRAG always answers after self-think with no abstain or expose-conflict policy
rationale: Both papers concern faithfulness in RAG and both touch consistency/conflict as a failure mode (RAGTruth annotates 'Evident Conflict' spans; FaithfulRAG explicitly targets parametric-vs-context conflict). However, RAGTruth is an evaluation corpus plus detector benchmark whose intervention is an evaluation artifact and a fine-tuned span-level hallucination detector, while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that produces answers. Their metric targets are therefore in incompatible families: span-level detection F1 over naturally generated hallucinations vs. answer correctness on constructed knowledge-conflict QA, and neither evaluates a comparable action policy. Putting them on a single leaderboard would mistake a dataset/detector for a generation method, so the comparison is invalid rather than merely partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) run FaithfulRAG's generator on the RAGTruth corpus tasks and report span-level hallucination rate using RAGTruth's annotation protocol against a RAGTruth-trained detector baseline, with matched retriever and generator; or (b) evaluate a RAGTruth-trained detector coupled with an explicit action policy (abstain or re-retrieve on flagged spans) against FaithfulRAG on the same knowledge-conflict QA benchmarks with identical retriever, generator backbone, conflict construction, and a shared metric such as answer correctness plus faithfulness-to-context.
notes: Pairing a benchmark/detector paper with a generation-time conflict-resolution method is a classic category mismatch; comparability would require choosing one common axis (detection F1 or answer correctness) and aligning the rest.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B only, via counterfactual noise)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper A: naturally-occurring irrelevant DPR/Google retrievals plus low-ranked distractors); benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper B: explicitly synthesized relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual noise via RAG-Bench)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (Paper A: NLI filter + fine-tuning on mixed contexts); generator prompting or training (Paper B: adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-type classification head)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: filter + answer (Paper A: NLI filter discards non-entailing passages, then answers); answer (Paper B: produces answer; noise-type head is internal, not gated as an action)
rationale: Both papers target training/structural robustness of RALMs to noisy retrieval on open-domain QA and share answer-correctness metrics (EM/F1) and partial dataset overlap (e.g., NQ). However, Paper A scopes 'noise' to irrelevant/distracting passages and intervenes via an NLI filter plus mixed-context fine-tuning, whereas Paper B explicitly broadens the failure type to include counterfactual (conflicting) noise and intervenes via adaptive adversarial training with a noise-aware multi-task head. The action policies also diverge: Paper A evaluates an explicit filter→answer pipeline, while Paper B reports only answer outputs without a gated abstain/filter action tied to its classifier. These mismatches in failure type, intervention scope, and action policy make a direct leaderboard ranking misleading, though the two methods are clearly complementary within the noise-robustness space, so 'partial' rather than 'invalid' is appropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark using the same retriever (e.g., DPR), generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), and an identical noise construction protocol that separates irrelevant vs. counterfactual conditions; report EM/F1 per noise type; fix and report the action policy (pure answer vs. filter-then-answer vs. abstain) consistently; and ablate Paper A's NLI filter as a preprocessing module composable with RAAT training so that intervention-point overlap is controlled.
notes: Paper B's counterfactual condition straddles relevance/noise and consistency/conflict; treating it as the same failure family as Paper A's irrelevant-only setting would conflate distinct robustness phenomena.

failure_type: relevance/noise; consistency/conflict (RGB also includes counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (naturally retrieved irrelevant passages across 5 ODQA sets). Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios) plus naturally occurring conflict / counterfactual injections in separate testbeds.
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (robust fine-tuning). Paper B: evaluation artifact (RGB benchmark) only; no method intervention.
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness on ODQA. Paper B: multi-dimensional — accuracy at varying noise ratios, plus rejection rate (negative rejection), integration accuracy, and counterfactual error rate.
action_policy: Paper A: filter, then answer. Paper B: answer + abstain (negative rejection is explicitly scored).
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG and overlap on the relevance/noise failure type, but they sit on opposite sides of the method/benchmark divide. Paper A contributes two concrete interventions (NLI passage filtering and mixed-context fine-tuning) and reports ODQA answer accuracy under naturally retrieved noise on five existing benchmarks. Paper B contributes the RGB evaluation artifact with four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness), constructed-noise ratios, and scores LLMs with metrics including a rejection rate — i.e., it explicitly evaluates an abstain action that Paper A never measures. Because the intervention point, metric family, action policy, and noise construction all differ, the two cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as alternative methods; they are complementary (a method paper and a diagnostic benchmark). Hence partial, not valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robust-trained generator on the RGB noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds using the same backbone LLM, and report both accuracy at matched noise ratios and the rejection rate; conversely, evaluate RGB-style baselines on Paper A's five ODQA benchmarks under the same retriever, prompt, and answer/abstain protocol. Without aligning retriever, noise construction (natural vs ratio-controlled), action labels (answer vs abstain), and a shared metric family, head-to-head ranking is not meaningful.
notes: Asymmetry is fundamental: Paper B has no proposed mitigation, so 'which method wins' is ill-posed; only cross-evaluation of Paper A's methods on RGB would yield a comparable result.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor, naturally occurring conflict
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage via negative rejection (RGB only)
action_policy: answer (RAAT, unreported abstention); answer + abstain (RGB explicitly evaluates negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers address retrieval noise in RAG and overlap on the failure types of relevance/noise and counterfactual/conflicting evidence. However, RAAT is a generator-training intervention (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-awareness) evaluated with F1/EM on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ using DPR-retrieved Wikipedia passages, while RGB is purely an evaluation benchmark built from bilingual news articles that measures four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) including an explicit abstain action policy. The intervention point differs categorically (training vs. no intervention), the action policy in RGB includes abstain while RAAT only scores answer correctness, and the noise construction and datasets differ. They are complementary—RGB could evaluate RAAT—but they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as alternative methods, hence partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT-fine-tuned and baseline LLMs through the RGB testbeds (or run RGB-style noise ratios on RAG-Bench) using the same base model, retriever, noise construction protocol, and dataset; report both answer correctness (F1/EM/accuracy) and abstention/rejection rate; clarify and evaluate an identical action policy (answer vs. abstain) under matched insertion budgets of noisy/counterfactual passages.
notes: Method paper vs. benchmark paper; comparison is fundamentally asymmetric unless one is re-run inside the other's evaluation harness.

failure_type: relevance/noise; CoN additionally covers uncertainty/OOD (unknown handling)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (irrelevant/noisy passages); CoN also probes OOD/unknown questions via RealTimeQA
intervention_point: CoN: generator prompting/training (per-document note-taking). Yoran et al.: retriever-side filtering (NLI) + generator fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts
metric_target: answer correctness (both); CoN additionally reports rejection rate; Yoran et al. emphasizes preserving performance on relevant cases and multi-hop accuracy
action_policy: CoN: answer + abstain ('unknown'). Yoran et al.: filter + answer (fallback to closed-book LLM when NLI rejects, no model-emitted abstention)
rationale: Both papers target RAG distraction by irrelevant retrieved context in ODQA, sharing the failure-type (relevance/noise) and a benign-error + benchmark-stressor evidence assumption. However, the intervention points diverge: Chain-of-Note inserts a generator-side note-taking reasoning step and trains the model to emit explicit 'unknown', whereas Yoran et al. apply an NLI filter at the retriever side and fine-tune the generator on intentionally mixed contexts. The action policies are also different first-class behaviors—CoN evaluates abstention as a metric (rejection rate on RealTimeQA), while Yoran et al.'s 'filter then fall back to closed-book LLM' is a system-control choice not measured as abstention quality and instead foregrounds multi-hop accuracy. Benchmarks overlap only partially (NQ, TriviaQA) and Yoran et al.'s multi-hop focus is not present in CoN. Direct leaderboard ranking would conflate distinct mechanisms and action regimes, so the comparison is partial (complementary modules), not valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation harness with the same retriever and base generator, the same irrelevant-context construction protocol, a benchmark suite covering both single-hop and multi-hop ODQA plus an unknown/OOD slice, and a common metric panel reporting (i) answer correctness when retrieval is relevant, (ii) answer correctness/no-harm when retrieval is irrelevant, and (iii) abstention/rejection quality with both systems configured to expose an explicit abstain action (e.g., add an 'unknown' option to the Yoran et al. fine-tune, or remove CoN's abstain head for a no-abstain comparison). Without aligning intervention stage, action policy, and the abstention metric, the two methods can only be discussed as complementary.
notes: Both methods could plausibly be stacked (NLI filter + CoN-style notes + abstain); this further argues for partial/complementary rather than direct ranking.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error, benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: Sufficient Context: verifier (autorater) + system-control policy + generator prompting (selective generation at inference); Self-RAG: generator training (reflection tokens) + retriever (adaptive on-demand)
metric_target: Sufficient Context: answer correctness conditional on responding, hallucination/abstention rates; Self-RAG: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support (factuality on long-form)
action_policy: Sufficient Context: answer/abstain (explicitly evaluated selective generation); Self-RAG: answer + re-retrieve + verify (reflection tokens), abstention not the evaluated policy
rationale: Both papers target RAG quality issues stemming from problematic retrieved context (insufficient or irrelevant evidence) and both add some form of self-judgment about retrieval/generation quality, so the failure types overlap. However, Sufficient Context is an inference-time analysis lens plus a selective generation method whose central evaluated action is sufficiency-conditioned abstention, with metrics dominated by correct-among-answered and hallucination reduction. Self-RAG is an end-to-end training framework introducing reflection tokens that primarily evaluates adaptive on-demand retrieval and citation-grounded long-form generation, with metric targets including citation accuracy and factuality, and does not evaluate abstention as the policy of interest. Because the intervention point (inference-time verifier+policy vs. training-time token-augmented LM), the explicit action policy (abstain vs. re-retrieve+critique+answer), and the headline metric family differ, direct leaderboard ranking would be misleading; they are better framed as complementary modules operating in different regions.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation that fixes (i) the same base generator and retriever, (ii) the same datasets covering both short-form QA and long-form citation-grounded generation, (iii) a common action-policy space (e.g., both methods must produce answer/abstain decisions and both must support optional re-retrieval), and (iv) a common metric suite reporting correctness, hallucination, abstention rate, citation faithfulness, and a coverage-risk curve. Concretely, one could apply Sufficient Context's selective generation on top of a Self-RAG model and evaluate both at matched coverage, or constrain Self-RAG to a verifier-only inference pipeline; without such alignment of intervention layer and action labels, the comparison remains partial.
notes: Both are 'control' rather than security; threat-model coordinates not applicable.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise + sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; no adversarial threat model
intervention_point: reranker + verifier (CalibRAG forecasting function); generator prompting/training + system-control policy (Self-RAG reflection tokens)
metric_target: calibration error + answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness + evidence support + citation faithfulness (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer with calibrated confidence (CalibRAG, abstention not explicitly evaluated); re-retrieve + answer with self-critique tokens (Self-RAG)
rationale: Both papers fall under the broad 'control/reliability' umbrella for RAG, but they target distinct failure modes with non-overlapping primary mechanisms. CalibRAG addresses miscalibration in decision-support: it trains a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) used for reranking and confidence calibration, with calibration error as a core metric. Self-RAG addresses indiscriminate retrieval and unfaithful generation: it trains the generator with reflection tokens that adaptively trigger retrieval and critique relevance/support, with citation faithfulness and factuality as headline metrics. The intervention points (reranker/verifier vs. generator training + control tokens), primary metric targets (calibration error vs. citation faithfulness), and action policies (calibrated confidence output vs. on-demand retrieve/critique) all diverge, so a leaderboard-style direct ranking would misrepresent both. They are better positioned as complementary modules operating in different regions.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require: (1) a shared benchmark and task where both calibration quality (e.g., ECE, selective risk/coverage) and factuality/citation metrics are reported for both systems on identical retriever + base LM; (2) explicit action policies measured for both (e.g., abstain thresholds for CalibRAG, retrieval-trigger precision/recall for Self-RAG); (3) ablations isolating the reranker/verifier contribution of CalibRAG vs. the generator-side reflection tokens of Self-RAG; (4) ideally, a stacked condition (Self-RAG + CalibRAG calibration on top) to test complementarity rather than substitution.
notes: Both clearly belong to 'control,' but they control different things; treating them as substitutes on one leaderboard would conflate calibration with adaptive retrieval/self-critique.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs. retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between model parametric knowledge and benign retrieved context; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target questions (query control), black-box and white-box retriever visibility, no generator access required, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts, attack objective is inducing a target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, contextual alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attacker injection) — it is an attack, not a defense
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and context faithfulness; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR)
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after fact-level reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (no defender action policy; the paper proposes the attack and only briefly tests existing defenses)
rationale: Both papers touch the broad theme that retrieved context can mislead an LLM, but they sit on opposite sides of the pipeline and assume incompatible threat models. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense for naturally occurring parametric/retrieved knowledge conflicts and is measured by answer correctness/faithfulness, with no adversary in the loop. PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that assumes an adversary with corpus write access and query control, injecting ~5 malicious passages to induce a target answer, and is measured by ASR. Because the failure type, evidence assumption, intervention point, and metric target all differ — and one paper is an attack while the other is a mitigation for a non-adversarial phenomenon — a direct leaderboard-style comparison would conflate distinct problems and mislead readers.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a meaningful comparison, FaithfulRAG would need to be evaluated as a defense under PoisonedRAG's threat model (same corpus, same insertion budget, same target QA set, both black-box and white-box attacker settings) and reported with ASR alongside clean accuracy; conversely, PoisonedRAG would need to report a downstream answer-correctness metric on naturally conflicting (non-adversarial) corpora. Both papers would also need to declare an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine) on identical benchmarks to compare on the same axis.
notes: Classic attack-vs-method mismatch; FaithfulRAG could be a candidate defender against PoisonedRAG, but neither paper conducts that experiment, so they are not interchangeable methods.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict (with passing mention of integrity/adversarial corruption); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption only
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict + benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB worst-case); PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, no query control (attacker chooses target question), black-box and white-box retriever visibility, no generator access required, insertion budget = 5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free post-retrieval consolidation); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (injection of malicious passages)
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness under imperfect retrieval; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR)
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer via reliability-based selection over internal vs external candidates (no explicit abstain/filter/quarantine evaluation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (it is an attack, not a defense, so no system-side action policy)
rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior when retrieved evidence can be unreliable, but they sit on opposite sides of the system: PoisonedRAG is an attack that writes malicious passages into the corpus and reports attack success rate, while Astute RAG is a generator-side, training-free defense whose target metric is answer correctness under noisy/conflicting retrieval (with adversarial content only mentioned, not the principal threat model). The intervention point, the metric target, the evidence assumption (attacker-crafted poisoning vs. mixed noise/conflict including benchmark-constructed worst case), and the action policy (no defender action in PoisonedRAG; reliability-based answer selection but no abstain/quarantine evaluation in Astute RAG) all diverge. Astute RAG is not evaluated against PoisonedRAG-style poisoning, and PoisonedRAG's reported 'defenses' section does not include Astute RAG. Treating them as alternative methods on a shared leaderboard would be a category error, hence invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require placing both papers inside a common attack-vs-defense evaluation: fix retriever, generator, corpus, and target-question set; run PoisonedRAG (and at least one baseline poisoning attack) at matched insertion budgets and threat-model assumptions (corpus write access, black-/white-box retriever); then evaluate Astute RAG together with other defenses (e.g., majority/consistency filtering, RobustRAG, certified defenses) on the same poisoned corpus, reporting both attack success rate and clean-task answer correctness, plus an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/filter). Only then can one paper's contribution be ranked against the other on a shared axis.
notes: Attack paper vs. defense paper with non-overlapping deliverables; partial would understate the category mismatch.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG assumes corpus write access with ~5 injected passages per target question, no query control, both black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, targeted-answer objective; RobustRAG assumes an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense who can inject a bounded number k' of malicious passages, defender controls context assembly and generator prompting
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack); context assembly/compression, generator prompting, verifier (RobustRAG defense)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG ASR) vs answer correctness under bounded corruption plus certified accuracy and selective risk/coverage (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported for PoisonedRAG (attack paper, no defender action evaluated); answer, abstain ('I don't know'), filter for RobustRAG
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, role (attacker vs defender)
rationale: Both papers operate on the same threat surface—retrieval corruption via attacker-injected passages into the RAG knowledge base—and share the failure type (integrity/adversarial corruption) and evidence assumption (attacker-created evidence with bounded insertion budget). However, PoisonedRAG is an attack contribution whose intervention is corpus injection and whose metric is attack success rate, while RobustRAG is a defense whose intervention is isolate-then-aggregate at context-assembly/generator-prompting time and whose metric is certified/empirical answer correctness plus abstention coverage. They occupy complementary roles (attacker vs defender) and cannot be ranked as alternative methods on a single leaderboard, but they are naturally co-evaluable as an attack-defense pair. Therefore the comparison is partial: meaningful as complementary modules, not as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) compare like-for-like—PoisonedRAG against other retrieval-corruption attacks under a common defended/undefended baseline, retriever, generator, dataset, insertion budget, and attacker knowledge; or RobustRAG against other defenses (e.g., perplexity filtering, voting) under a common attack suite—or (b) reframe as joint evaluation: run RobustRAG against PoisonedRAG with matched threat-model parameters (k' = insertion budget, identical retriever/generator/corpus, same target questions), and report a shared metric family such as certified accuracy, empirical accuracy under attack, ASR reduction, and abstention rate with explicit action-policy labels.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pair; threat-model overlap is genuine but role asymmetry precludes leaderboard-style ranking, hence partial rather than invalid.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict (real LLM-generated hallucinations against provided contexts); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally targets verifier (detector training)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness at span level (detector precision/recall); RGB: answer correctness, rejection accuracy, error rate under counterfactuals
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (detection-only, no system action evaluated); RGB: abstain (negative rejection) and answer explicitly evaluated
rationale: Both papers are evaluation artifacts in the broad robust-RAG space and both touch consistency/conflict between generations and retrieved evidence. However, RAGTruth is a span-annotated corpus of naturally generated hallucinations whose primary metric is hallucination detector performance (a verifier-side metric), while RGB is a constructed bilingual testbed that probes four LLM abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) via end-task answer correctness and abstention rates. The two benchmarks therefore reward different systems: RAGTruth scores a detector's span-level precision/recall, RGB scores a generator's QA accuracy and refusal behavior under stressors. Action policy is explicit in RGB (abstain vs answer) but unreported as a system action in RAGTruth. They are complementary diagnostics rather than substitutable leaderboards, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Define a single shared task (e.g., decide-and-cite under noisy/counterfactual contexts) evaluated on overlapping data (apply RGB-style noise/counterfactual injections to RAGTruth contexts, or run RAGTruth-style span annotation on RGB outputs), use a common metric family (joint answer correctness + span-level evidence support + abstention rate), fix the same retriever and generator backbones, and explicitly report the same action policy (answer/abstain/expose-conflict) for both benchmarks. Without this, the two benchmarks measure different system properties.
notes: Both are 'RAG benchmarks' but at different levels of the stack (detector evaluation vs end-to-end ability diagnosis); shared label does not imply comparability.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents) vs naturally occurring conflict / benign retrieval error (Sufficient Context: autorater applied to existing QA datasets like HotPotQA, Musique, FreshQA)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); generator prompting (Sufficient Context only, via selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, calibration error (Sufficient Context); answer correctness, abstention/rejection rate, error-on-counterfactual (RGB)
action_policy: abstain (both evaluate explicitly); expose conflict (RGB counterfactual testbed); answer (both)
rationale: Both papers study how RAG systems behave when retrieved context is noisy or insufficient and both explicitly evaluate abstention as an action, so the failure-type axis overlaps substantially (sufficiency and noise robustness). However, RGB is a fixed bilingual benchmark with four hand-constructed testbeds where noise ratios and counterfactual documents are injected by design, while Sufficient Context defines sufficiency as a property of (query, context) pairs measured by an LLM autorater on naturally retrieved contexts, and additionally proposes a selective-generation intervention on the generator side. The metric families therefore diverge: RGB reports per-ability accuracy and rejection rates, whereas Sufficient Context reports stratified hallucination/abstention rates and selective-risk/coverage curves tied to a confidence + sufficiency signal. These differences in evidence construction, intervention scope (eval-only vs eval + generator policy), and metric target make them complementary lenses rather than entries on the same leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's autorater and selective-generation method on RGB's four testbeds (especially Noise Robustness and Negative Rejection) using the same LLMs, and conversely apply RGB-style controlled noise/counterfactual injection to Sufficient Context's datasets; report a common metric suite (answer accuracy, abstention rate, hallucination rate, and selective-risk/coverage) under matched retriever, generator, and action-policy definitions, with the sufficiency label operationalized identically across both setups.
notes: Action policy is explicitly evaluated in both (not inferred), so the break is in evidence construction, intervention point, and metric target rather than in unreported action.

failure_type: RAGTruth: consistency/conflict + sufficiency (broad hallucination types including unsupported claims and evident conflict); FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict only (parametric vs. retrieved knowledge)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations from standard RAG with benign retrieval; FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and retrieved context
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) + verifier (fine-tuned hallucination detector); FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think reasoning)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / hallucination detection precision-recall-F1 at span/response level; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness on QA benchmarks with conflict
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (benchmark itself does not prescribe an action; detector flags spans); FaithfulRAG: answer (regenerate after conflict reconciliation)
rationale: Both papers address faithfulness in RAG, but they are fundamentally different artifact types: RAGTruth is an evaluation benchmark/corpus with word-level hallucination annotations spanning QA, data-to-text, and summarization (with detection methods as a secondary contribution), while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention specifically targeting parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflicts via self-fact mining and self-think reasoning. The intervention points differ (evaluation artifact + post-hoc detector vs. pre-generation reasoning module), the metric targets differ (span-level hallucination detection F1 vs. downstream answer correctness on conflict QA), and the action policies differ (flag/detect vs. answer-after-reconcile). They address overlapping but non-coextensive failure modes, so leaderboard-style ranking would mislead; they are better framed as complementary—one provides the measurement substrate, the other a generation method that could be measured on that substrate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: FaithfulRAG would need to be evaluated on the RAGTruth corpus (or its knowledge-conflict subset) using RAGTruth's span/response-level hallucination metrics, with a fixed retriever and generator backbone shared with RAGTruth's baselines. Conversely, RAGTruth's fine-tuned detector would need to be compared against FaithfulRAG on the same conflict-QA datasets (e.g., the benchmarks FaithfulRAG uses) with explicit action policies (detect-and-abstain vs. detect-and-regenerate). A common evaluation harness covering both detection metrics and downstream answer faithfulness, plus an explicit, identical action policy, would be required.
notes: Asymmetry of contribution type (benchmark + detector vs. generation method) is the dominant break; even with shared faithfulness framing, they cannot be cast as alternative entries on one leaderboard without substantial additional experiments.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B only, via counterfactual noise)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (naturally irrelevant passages from real retriever). Paper B: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (synthetically injected counterfactual passages alongside relevant/irrelevant categories).
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (fine-tune on mixed contexts). Paper B: generator prompting or training (adversarial training + multi-task noise classification head).
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) in both; Paper B adds an internal noise-type classification objective but does not report it as a deployed selective-action metric
action_policy: Paper A: filter (NLI) then answer. Paper B: answer (noise-awareness is internal classification, not a separate output action). Neither paper evaluates abstain/escalate.
rationale: Both papers target noise-robust RALMs on open-domain QA with the same metric family (EM/F1) and overlapping datasets (e.g., NQ), and both modify the generator via fine-tuning, so they sit in the same broad problem area. However, Paper A scopes noise to naturally retrieved irrelevant passages and combines an NLI-based context-assembly filter with mixed-context fine-tuning, while Paper B explicitly enlarges the noise taxonomy to include counterfactual (conflict-inducing) passages and uses adaptive adversarial training plus a noise-awareness classification head, with no filtering stage. The failure-type coverage (relevance/noise vs. relevance/noise + consistency/conflict), the evidence construction (organic vs. benchmark-constructed stressor), the intervention surface (filter+train vs. train-only), and the effective action policy (filter-then-answer vs. answer) all differ, so a single leaderboard number would conflate operating regimes rather than rank methods on a shared task. They are best framed as complementary modules over a shared robustness desideratum, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix base generator (e.g., Llama-2 7B), retriever (DPR or equivalent), and evaluation set (a common subset of NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ). Re-construct retrieval contexts under one shared noise protocol that explicitly partitions irrelevant vs. counterfactual buckets, report EM/F1 per bucket, and evaluate each method under identical action policies (either both answer-only with no filtering, or run Paper A's NLI filter as a separately reported pipeline stage). Additionally report any abstention/coverage behavior so the action policy is explicit rather than implied by ordinary QA.
notes: If restricted only to the irrelevant-noise slice and answer-only setting, a narrower head-to-head could approach valid; as published, the scope and pipeline asymmetry warrant partial.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B also covers sufficiency (negative rejection) and consistency/conflict (counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real ODQA retrievers; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios over news-derived passages (plus synthetic counterfactual edits)
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts); Paper B: evaluation artifact only
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness (EM/F1 on ODQA); Paper B: answer correctness plus rejection rate and counterfactual-acceptance metrics
action_policy: Paper A: filter then answer (explicitly evaluated); Paper B: answer and abstain (negative-rejection testbed explicitly scores abstention)
rationale: Both papers share a noise-robustness framing for RAG, but they are fundamentally different artifact types: Paper A proposes interventions (NLI-based passage filtering and fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts) and evaluates them on five real ODQA benchmarks where noise comes from genuine retriever errors, while Paper B contributes the RGB benchmark with four constructed testbeds, synthetic noise ratios drawn from news articles, and explicit abstention scoring. The intervention point (real method vs. evaluation artifact), the evidence construction (organic retrieval error vs. controlled stressor), the metric family (correctness only vs. correctness plus rejection/counterfactual acceptance), and the action policy assessed (filter+answer vs. answer+abstain) all diverge. They cannot be ranked as alternative methods on a single leaderboard, but they are clearly complementary—Paper A's interventions are the kind of system that Paper B's benchmark is designed to score.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate Paper A's NLI-filter and fine-tuned generator on RGB's noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds (same retriever-free passage pool, same noise ratios, same correctness and rejection metrics), and/or reciprocally apply RGB-style controlled noise to Paper A's ODQA setups with matched generators, retrievers, and action labels (answer vs. abstain). Without a shared corpus construction, matched action policy, and a common metric that captures both correctness and abstention, only complementary discussion is supported.
notes: From an IR standpoint, the corpus and retrieval pipelines are not aligned (real Wikipedia/web retrieval vs. curated news passages with injected noise), which alone blocks leaderboard-style ranking even before considering the intervention-vs-benchmark asymmetry.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict (RGB only via counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both, but constructed differently: RAAT uses DPR retrieval over Wikipedia QA datasets filtered into relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual buckets; RGB uses news articles plus search-engine retrieval with controlled noise ratios)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training + evaluation artifact (RAAT); evaluation artifact only (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (RGB only, via negative rejection rate)
action_policy: answer (RAAT, no abstain or conflict-exposure tested); answer + abstain + expose conflict (RGB, explicitly evaluates negative rejection and counterfactual error detection)
rationale: Both papers target retrieval noise in RAG and even share a roughly aligned noise typology (irrelevant / counterfactual contexts), so the failure type overlaps. However, RAAT is a training-side intervention (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B) that reports only F1/EM under an implicit 'always answer' policy, while RGB is a diagnostic benchmark over 6 frozen LLMs that explicitly scores additional action policies—negative rejection (abstain) and counterfactual error identification (expose conflict)—and uses news+search-engine evidence rather than DPR-on-Wikipedia. Because the intervention points (train vs. evaluate only), action policies tested, evidence construction pipelines, and the breadth of metric families differ, the two cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitutable methods. They are best treated as complementary: RAAT as a candidate solution and RGB as one of several noise-robustness diagnostics on which RAAT-style methods could be scored. Hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and a non-adversarial baseline) on RGB's four testbeds in matched language (English) using the same base LLM(s) RGB evaluated, reporting accuracy under graded noise ratios, negative rejection rate, information-integration accuracy, and counterfactual error-identification rate; conversely, evaluate RGB-style stock LLMs on RAAT's RAG-Bench with identical retriever (DPR/Wikipedia) and prompts. Both papers should explicitly disclose and score the action policy (answer / abstain / expose conflict) under a common protocol before any ranking claim.
notes: Asymmetry is intrinsic: RGB is purely a benchmark, RAAT is method+benchmark, so 'comparison' is only meaningful at the benchmark layer or as method-vs-baseline on a shared benchmark.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Paper A also covers uncertainty/OOD (unknown/RealTimeQA)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both); Paper A additionally treats naturally occurring unknown/OOD queries (RealTimeQA) where no relevant evidence exists
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting/training (per-document reading notes before answer). Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI-based passage filtering) + generator training on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts
metric_target: answer correctness (both); Paper A additionally reports selective risk/coverage (rejection rate on real-time/unknown questions); Paper B emphasizes delta vs. no-retrieval baseline including multi-hop
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain ('unknown'); Paper B: answer + filter (drop non-entailing passages, then answer with/without retrieval); abstention is not a first-class behavior in B
rationale: Both papers target distraction by irrelevant retrieved context in open-domain QA and modify the generator side to make RALMs more robust, so the failure type and high-level problem overlap substantially. However, Chain-of-Note inserts a per-document note-taking reasoning step and explicitly supports an 'unknown' abstention action, evaluated via rejection-rate on RealTimeQA, while Yoran et al. intervene earlier via an NLI filter on the context and fine-tune on mixed-quality contexts, with no explicit abstention behavior or selective-prediction metric. The intervention points (generator reasoning vs. context filter + training), the action policy (abstain vs. filter-then-answer), and the metric families (selective risk/coverage vs. accuracy delta including multi-hop) differ, and the retrievers, corpora, and backbones (DPR + GPT-4/LLaMA-2-7B vs. multiple retrievers + LLaMA-2-13B) are not aligned. They should be discussed as complementary mechanisms (filter-before vs. note-while-reading, with/without abstention), not ranked on a single leaderboard, so the verdict is partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, corpus, and generator backbone; run both methods on a shared benchmark suite that includes both multi-hop QA (B's strength) and unknown/OOD questions (A's strength); report a common metric family covering (i) EM/F1 with relevant context, (ii) EM/F1 degradation under irrelevant/noisy context, and (iii) selective-prediction metrics (abstain rate, risk-coverage, accuracy on answered subset) with an explicit, identically-defined action policy {answer, abstain} for both systems; additionally ablate B with an added abstention head and A without the abstention option so that the action policy is held constant when comparing accuracy.
notes: From an IR perspective the corpus/retriever setups (DPR vs. mixed retrievers across 5 ODQA sets) are not aligned, which further weakens direct ranking even if action policy were matched.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: evaluation artifact, generator prompting or training, retriever (adaptive)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, citation faithfulness
action_policy: abstain (Sufficient Context); re-retrieve, verify (Self-RAG)
rationale: Both papers target generation quality when retrieved evidence may be irrelevant or insufficient, and both can be framed as improving factuality under noisy retrieval. However, Sufficient Context introduces an external autorater for context sufficiency and uses it together with self-confidence to drive selective generation (the action policy is explicitly answer-vs-abstain at inference time), whereas Self-RAG retrains an LM with reflection tokens to decide on-demand retrieval and to self-critique, with action policy centered on retrieve/continue/critique rather than abstention. The intervention points (post-hoc selective layer over an unchanged generator vs. end-to-end trained LM with new tokens), the evaluated action policies (abstain vs. adaptive retrieve+critique), and the headline metrics (hallucination/coverage on QA vs. citation accuracy and multi-task factuality) only partially overlap. Therefore they should be discussed as complementary mechanisms operating at different control points, not ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark suite (e.g., PopQA, TriviaQA, HotPotQA, ASQA) with the same retriever, corpus, and base generator backbone; report a common metric set including %correct-when-answered, abstention/coverage curves, citation precision/recall, and selective risk; force both systems to expose a comparable action policy (answer/abstain/re-retrieve) and measure each on the same axis; ideally include an ablation where Sufficient Context's selective layer is wrapped around the Self-RAG generator to isolate the contribution of the autorater vs. the reflection-token training.
notes: Both papers have explicit action policies, so this is not under-specified; the break is structural difference in intervention and policy, not missing information.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence); Self-RAG: relevance/noise + sufficiency (unnecessary or unhelpful retrieval)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval errors from standard corpora (Wikipedia-like); neither targets adversarial or stale evidence
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker via forecasting function f(t,q,d) + context assembly; Self-RAG: generator training with reflection tokens + on-demand retriever invocation
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer/decision correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence score (no abstain reported); Self-RAG: answer with self-critique tokens, conditional re-retrieve based on reflection tokens — unreported abstain semantics
rationale: Both papers aim to make RAG more reliable, but they target fundamentally different failure modes: CalibRAG addresses confidence-correctness alignment for decision support via a forecasting-based reranker, while Self-RAG addresses unnecessary or noisy retrieval and unsupported generations via trained reflection tokens that gate retrieval and critique generations. The primary metric families diverge (calibration ECE vs. citation faithfulness/factuality), and the intervention points sit at different stages of the pipeline (reranking score vs. generator self-control). Neither paper evaluates the other's primary metric (Self-RAG does not report calibration; CalibRAG does not report citation faithfulness or adaptive-retrieval triggering), so a direct leaderboard ranking would systematically favor whichever metric one chose. The verdict is partial because they share the broad goal of trustworthy RAG and could be combined or compared as complementary modules, but they are not substitutable methods on the same task definition.
what_valid_comparison_requires: (1) A shared evaluation suite that includes BOTH calibration metrics (ECE/Brier on decision correctness) and factuality/citation metrics (e.g., FactScore, citation precision/recall); (2) identical retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; (3) decision-making tasks where Self-RAG produces a usable confidence signal (e.g., aggregated from reflection tokens) and CalibRAG produces a usable retrieval/critique policy; (4) explicit action policies (abstain thresholds, re-retrieve triggers) reported for both systems; (5) ablations isolating reranking vs. generator-side reflection contributions.
notes: Both are 'control/reliability' RAG papers but on orthogonal axes — calibration vs. adaptive retrieval/citation — making leaderboard-style ranking misleading without a multi-metric harness.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs. contextual knowledge); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and retrieved benign context; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, target-question query control, both black-box and white-box retriever visibility, black-box generator access, insertion budget of ~5 malicious passages per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive injection, not a defense)
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support (faithfulness); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (with reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy evaluated)
rationale: Both papers concern how RAG systems behave when retrieved context conflicts with the 'true' answer, but the resemblance ends there. FaithfulRAG addresses naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflicts in benign retrieval and proposes a generator-side fact-alignment defense measured by answer correctness/faithfulness. PoisonedRAG is an offensive paper assuming an attacker with corpus write access who injects ~5 crafted passages per target question to maximize attack success rate; it has no defender action policy and does not evaluate faithfulness. The threat models, intervention points (generator reasoning vs. corpus poisoning), and metric families (correctness vs. ASR) are non-overlapping, so direct leaderboard-style ranking would be misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require co-locating both works on a shared evaluation: (1) construct a benchmark with both benign parametric-context conflicts and PoisonedRAG-style injected adversarial passages under a specified insertion budget, retriever, and generator; (2) run FaithfulRAG as a defense against PoisonedRAG attacks and report ASR reduction alongside clean-task faithfulness; (3) report a common metric set (answer correctness, attack success rate, possibly abstention/selective risk) with an explicit defender action policy; (4) hold the threat model (corpus write access, retriever visibility, query control) constant across both methods. Without this, the papers solve different problems and cannot be ranked as alternatives.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense asymmetry; the only bridge would be using FaithfulRAG as a candidate mitigation evaluated under PoisonedRAG's threat model, which neither paper does.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict (with brief mention of malicious info); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption only
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (e.g., RGB worst-case negative docs); PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model — corpus write access = yes, query control = yes (chosen target question), retriever visibility = black-box and white-box settings, generator access = output-only, insertion budget ≈ 5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free post-retrieval consolidation/verification); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (passage injection into knowledge database)
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness (incl. worst-case accuracy); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (with reliability-based candidate selection); PoisonedRAG: unreported / not applicable — it is an attack paper that does not implement a defender action policy
rationale: Both papers fall under the broad umbrella of RAG robustness, and Astute RAG nominally lists 'malicious' content as one source of imperfect retrieval, but the two are categorically different research objects: PoisonedRAG is an attack that crafts malicious passages and reports attack success rate under a corpus-write threat model, while Astute RAG is a generator-side defense reporting answer correctness under largely benign noise and conflict, plus a worst-case-negative benchmark stressor. They differ on every coordinate — failure type, evidence assumption (attacker-created vs benign/benchmark), intervention point (corpus vs generator), metric target (ASR vs correctness), and action policy (none vs answer with reliability selection). A leaderboard-style ranking is therefore meaningless: one cannot place an attack and a defense on the same axis, and Astute RAG never evaluates against PoisonedRAG-style optimized injections, while PoisonedRAG never evaluates Astute RAG as a defender. The comparison is invalid as currently scoped.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To enable meaningful comparison, both papers would need to be re-framed within a shared defense-vs-attack evaluation: (1) fix retriever, generator, corpus, and target-question set; (2) apply PoisonedRAG black-box and white-box attacks with the same insertion budget (e.g., 1/3/5 texts); (3) evaluate Astute RAG alongside other defenses (e.g., RobustRAG, perplexity/duplicate filtering) on shared metrics — attack success rate, clean accuracy, and worst-case accuracy; (4) explicitly report defender action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine) and threat-model assumptions (corpus write access, query control, retriever visibility). Only then could Astute RAG be ranked against attack-aware baselines on the PoisonedRAG benchmark, or PoisonedRAG be reported as one of several stressors in the Astute RAG worst-case suite.
notes: Classic attack-paper vs defense-paper mismatch; even the partial verdict is too generous because the metric families (ASR vs correctness) are orthogonal and Astute RAG's 'malicious' mentions are not operationalized into an evaluated threat model.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG assumes corpus write access with small insertion budget (~5 malicious passages per target query), attacker-chosen target Q/A, both black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, attack objective = induce specific target answer. RobustRAG assumes the same threat surface (bounded number k' of corrupted passages in top-k) but treats the attacker as an adaptive adversary with full knowledge of the defense; it does not constrain insertion semantics or instantiate the attacker.
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG, attacker-side); context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG, defender-side via isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success rate (PoisonedRAG); answer correctness with certified robustness lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported for PoisonedRAG (attack paper, no defender action evaluated); filter + abstain (RobustRAG returns 'I don't know' in isolated branches and aggregates via keywords/decoding)
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat space of adversarial corpus poisoning for RAG and share the failure type (integrity/adversarial corruption) and evidence assumption (attacker-created passages injected into the retrieval corpus). However, PoisonedRAG is an attack contribution that intervenes at the corpus and measures attack success rate against an undefended RAG pipeline, while RobustRAG is a defense that intervenes at context assembly/generator prompting via isolate-then-aggregate and measures certified answer quality under bounded corruption. Their metric families (ASR vs. certified robust accuracy) and roles (offense vs. defense) are not interchangeable on a single leaderboard, and PoisonedRAG does not evaluate a defender action policy while RobustRAG explicitly evaluates filter/abstain behavior. They are best framed as complementary attack–defense components rather than alternative methods, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require either (a) evaluating RobustRAG explicitly against PoisonedRAG attacks under matched retriever, generator, corpus, top-k, and insertion budget while reporting both certified bounds and empirical ASR/accuracy, or (b) re-casting both works under a unified attack-defense benchmark with shared metric targets (empirical robust accuracy and ASR), shared adversary capabilities (corpus write access, query knowledge, retriever/generator visibility, insertion budget m'), and explicit action policy labels (answer vs abstain vs filter) on both sides.
notes: Classic attack vs defense pairing in security; even though they share threat model coordinates, leaderboard-style ranking is conceptually ill-posed without a shared evaluation harness.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error / naturally occurring hallucinations during RAG generation; RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth also touches generator prompting/training via fine-tuned detector
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection F1; RGB: answer correctness, abstention/rejection rate, integration accuracy, counterfactual error-correction rate
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (detection task only, no action policy evaluated); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection is an explicit evaluated ability)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation artifacts concerned with model behavior under imperfect retrieval, so they share a high-level motivation around trustworthy RAG. However, RAGTruth supplies a word-level hallucination corpus from naturally generated LLM responses and measures span-detection performance, while RGB constructs synthetic testbeds with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injections to score four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness). The evidence model (natural vs. constructed stressor), metric family (span detection vs. capability-specific correctness and rejection rates), and action policy (none vs. explicit abstain) all differ materially. These are complementary diagnostic tools rather than interchangeable leaderboard entries, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make them directly comparable, one would need (a) a shared task instance pool labeled both with RAGTruth-style span-level hallucination annotations and RGB-style ability tags, (b) a unified metric (e.g., answer correctness plus span-grounded faithfulness) computed on the same generators and retrievers, and (c) an explicit common action policy (answer vs. abstain) evaluated across both datasets so that detection performance and capability scores can be aligned on the same axis.
notes: Both classified as evaluation_benchmark but they probe different failure surfaces; treating them as substitutes on a single leaderboard would conflate naturally occurring hallucinations with constructed stressor responses.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise (RGB also includes consistency/conflict via counterfactual testbed)
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (synthetic noise ratios, injected counterfactuals from news corpus); SufficientContext: naturally occurring retrieval errors labeled by an LLM autorater over existing QA datasets
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); SufficientContext additionally proposes verifier (autorater) and system-control policy (selective generation with confidence)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (SufficientContext); answer correctness and abstention rate decomposed by ability (RGB)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention — RGB via 'negative rejection' testbed; SufficientContext via selective generation and stratified hallucination/abstain analysis)
rationale: Both papers evaluate RAG behavior under imperfect retrieval and explicitly probe abstention vs. answering, so the failure type and action policy overlap meaningfully. However, RGB is a fixed bilingual benchmark with four discrete ability testbeds built from synthetic noise ratios and injected counterfactuals, while Sufficient Context defines a per-instance (Q,C) property scored by an LLM autorater on standard QA datasets and additionally proposes a selective-generation method combining sufficiency with self-confidence. The intervention point therefore diverges (pure evaluation artifact vs. evaluation lens + verifier + control policy), the evidence assumption diverges (constructed stressors vs. autorater-labeled natural retrieval), and the metric operationalization diverges (ability-wise accuracy/rejection scores vs. selective risk-coverage style metrics). They are complementary — RGB supplies controlled stressors, SufficientContext supplies a stratification lens and a method — so leaderboard-style ranking is not warranted, but cross-use is sensible.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Cast both onto a shared task: e.g., run the Sufficient Context autorater + selective-generation method on each of RGB's four testbeds (especially Noise Robustness and Negative Rejection) with matched LLMs, retrievers, prompts, and abstention/coverage metrics; conversely, apply RGB's noise-ratio and counterfactual construction to Sufficient Context's QA datasets so that the same context-quality strata are compared. Reporting must align action labels (correct/abstain/hallucinate), use a common selective-risk metric, and fix the generator and any retriever so differences are attributable to method rather than benchmark.
notes: Both papers do report abstention behavior explicitly, so action_policy is not the breaking coordinate here; the break is in evidence construction and the scope of intervention (benchmark only vs. benchmark + method).

failure_type: consistency/conflict for FaithfulRAG; broader hallucination including relevance/noise, sufficiency, and consistency/conflict for RAGTruth
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error and naturally occurring conflict in standard RAG pipelines; FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflict, often instantiated via counterfactual conflict QA benchmarks
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) and generator prompting or training (fine-tuned detector); FaithfulRAG: context assembly/compression and generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support and citation faithfulness (span-level hallucination detection); FaithfulRAG: answer correctness on conflict QA
action_policy: unreported for both (RAGTruth detects/flags spans post-hoc; FaithfulRAG answers after self-think but does not evaluate abstain/expose-conflict policies)
rationale: Both papers target faithfulness failures in RAG, but they operate on different slices of the problem. RAGTruth is an evaluation benchmark with word-level hallucination annotations across QA, summarization, and data-to-text, used to score detectors and fine-tune them; its metric target is span-level hallucination detection (evidence support / citation faithfulness). FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention specifically for parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflicts, measured by answer correctness on conflict QA. The intervention points (evaluation artifact + detector training vs. context assembly + self-think prompting), metric families, and the scope of the evidence assumption differ, and neither evaluates an explicit action policy such as abstain or expose-conflict. They are complementary rather than substitutable on a single leaderboard, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG generations on the RAGTruth QA subset and score them with RAGTruth's span-level hallucination annotations, and conversely evaluate RAGTruth-trained detectors plus a baseline RAG generator on FaithfulRAG's conflict QA benchmarks using the same answer-correctness metric. Fix retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; report a common action policy (e.g., answer-only, or answer-with-abstain) so both methods are measured on identical inputs, metrics, and decision behavior.
notes: RAGTruth is primarily a benchmark/detector paper while FaithfulRAG is a conflict-resolution generation method; they could be combined in a pipeline but cannot be ranked head-to-head as-is.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); RAAT additionally addresses consistency/conflict via counterfactual noise
evidence_assumption: Yoran: benign retrieval error / naturally occurring irrelevant passages from real retrievers across 5 ODQA sets. RAAT: benchmark-constructed stressor with three engineered noise types (relevant, irrelevant, counterfactual) on RAG-Bench (NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ).
intervention_point: Yoran: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning). RAAT: generator prompting or training (adaptive adversarial training + noise-aware multi-task head).
metric_target: answer correctness (Yoran: EM/accuracy on ODQA; RAAT: F1 and EM on RAG-Bench)
action_policy: Yoran: filter (NLI rejects non-entailing passages and falls back to no-retrieval answer) + answer. RAAT: answer only (no abstention, no filtering reported, despite the multi-task noise-classification head, the downstream action is still to answer).
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs and share an answer-correctness objective on open-domain QA, and Yoran's fine-tuning component and RAAT's adversarial training are conceptually related generator-side defenses. However, RAAT explicitly broadens the failure type to counterfactual (conflicting) evidence — a different stressor than Yoran's irrelevant-context regime — and constructs noise synthetically on RAG-Bench rather than relying on natural retriever errors over five ODQA benchmarks. The action policies also diverge: Yoran couples training with an NLI filter that abstains from using retrieval, while RAAT keeps an always-answer policy and only adds an internal noise-recognition head. Because the noise taxonomy, intervention surface, and action policy all differ, the two systems should be treated as complementary defenses operating in overlapping but non-identical regimes rather than as ranked entries on the same leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on the same base generator (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B) and the same retriever/corpus, evaluate on a unified noise suite covering irrelevant AND counterfactual passages, report EM/F1 separately per noise type, and either (a) disable Yoran's NLI filter so both systems share an answer-only action policy, or (b) add an abstention/filter variant to RAAT so the action policy is matched. Additionally, report selective-risk / coverage-accuracy curves so the filter-based abstention in Yoran is not unfairly credited as accuracy gain.
notes: From a selective-risk lens, conflating a filter+fallback policy with an always-answer policy under a single EM number is exactly the kind of comparison that misleads readers; this is the main reason I prefer partial over valid.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); plus sufficiency, consistency/conflict in Paper B (negative rejection, counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real retrievers over ODQA corpora; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injection
intervention_point: Paper A: reranker/context-assembly filter (NLI) + generator training (robust fine-tuning); Paper B: evaluation artifact (benchmark only, no mitigation)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness (EM/F1 on ODQA); Paper B: answer correctness decomposed into noise-robustness accuracy, rejection rate, integration accuracy, and counterfactual rejection
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (fallback to no-retrieval generation when NLI rejects); Paper B: answer + abstain (explicit negative rejection evaluated) + implicit expose-conflict for counterfactual
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, evidence_assumption, metric_target, action_policy, failure_type scope
rationale: Both papers target LLM behavior under noisy retrieval, but they operate at fundamentally different levels of the stack: Paper A proposes concrete interventions (NLI-based passage filtering plus mixed-context fine-tuning) and measures answer correctness on five ODQA benchmarks with naturally-occurring retrieval noise, whereas Paper B (RGB) is a diagnostic benchmark that constructs controlled stressors and decomposes capability into four separate abilities, including explicit evaluation of abstention (negative rejection) and counterfactual conflict. The intervention point (method vs. evaluation artifact), evidence construction (benign retrieval error vs. synthetic stressors with counterfactuals), action policy (filter+answer vs. answer+abstain), and metric decomposition all differ. They are complementary rather than alternative leaderboard entries, so the comparison is partial.
