what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI filter and robust fine-tuning on Paper B's four RGB testbeds with matched generators and retrievers, reporting noise-robustness accuracy, rejection rate, integration accuracy, and counterfactual rejection under a common, explicit answer/abstain action policy; or restrict comparison to the single noise-robustness slice of RGB with identical evidence-construction and metric definitions and add an abstention head to Paper A's pipeline so both sides report the same calibration/selective-risk outputs.
notes: Method paper vs. benchmark paper asymmetry is the dominant break; selective-risk view also flags abstention asymmetry.

failure_type: relevance/noise, integrity/adversarial corruption (counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT) vs evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage implied by RGB's negative rejection testbed only
action_policy: answer (RAAT only); answer + abstain (RGB explicitly evaluates negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RAG under benchmark-constructed stressors and both reason about counterfactual/misleading evidence, so the failure-type and evidence-assumption coordinates partially overlap. However, RAAT is a training-time intervention on the generator measured by F1/EM under an answer-only policy on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ, while RGB is an evaluation artifact with four separately scored testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) on bilingual news data and explicitly probes abstention via rejection rate. From a selective-risk/calibration perspective this asymmetry is decisive: RGB rewards correct abstention whereas RAAT never reports a coverage/risk tradeoff. They are therefore complementary (RGB could serve as a testbed for RAAT-like methods) but not directly rankable on the same leaderboard, so partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate RAAT-trained LLaMA-2 (and matched baselines) on RGB's four English-Chinese testbeds using RGB's exact metrics, including the negative rejection rate; symmetrically, report selective-risk/coverage curves on RAG-Bench so that abstention behavior is measured on both sides. Then align retriever, corpus, noise construction, language, and especially the action policy (answer vs abstain) before any ranking is claimed.
notes: Method paper vs benchmark paper is the structural mismatch; the missing abstention/calibration axis in RAAT is the trustworthy-ML-relevant break.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency, uncertainty/OOD (CoN); relevance/noise (Paper B)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error, benchmark-constructed stressor; both assume natural distractor passages from a standard retriever, no adversary
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (CoN, note-taking step + SFT); context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (Paper B, NLI filter + robust fine-tuning)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (CoN only, via rejection rate on RealTimeQA / unknown)
action_policy: answer, abstain (CoN explicitly evaluates 'unknown'); answer, filter (Paper B routes to no-retrieval fallback but does not evaluate abstention)
rationale: Both papers target distraction by irrelevant retrieved context in open-domain QA and propose training/prompting interventions to make RALMs more robust. However, CoN explicitly adds and evaluates an abstain action ('unknown') and reports rejection rate as a selective-risk metric for OOD/unknown questions, whereas Paper B's NLI filter + robust fine-tuning approach only filters context or falls back to a no-retrieval answer—it never abstains and is evaluated almost entirely on accuracy. Their intervention points also differ (per-document note generation inside the generator vs. upstream NLI filtering plus mixed-context SFT). A direct leaderboard ranking would either suppress CoN's selective-prediction contribution or compare on a metric family Paper B does not optimize, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods with the same retriever, generator backbone, and benchmark suite that mixes relevant, noisy, and unanswerable/OOD questions; report a shared metric set including standard QA accuracy AND selective-risk/coverage metrics (rejection rate, risk-coverage curves, calibration) with explicit action-policy labels (answer vs. abstain vs. filter+answer); add ablations isolating the contribution of filtering, fine-tuning, and abstention so the two designs are compared in operating regions where their action policies are commensurate.
notes: From a selective-prediction lens the abstention gap is the decisive break: comparing an abstaining system to a non-abstaining one on accuracy alone is systematically misleading.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting + system-control policy (post-hoc selective generation wrapper); Paper B: generator prompting or training + retriever (reflection tokens, on-demand retrieval)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (hallucination/abstention/correct stratified by sufficiency); Paper B: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: Paper A: answer or abstain (explicit selective generation); Paper B: re-retrieve + answer + implicit self-critique, abstention not explicitly evaluated as a policy
rationale: Both papers tackle RAG unreliability when retrieved context is irrelevant or insufficient, and both try to make the generator more self-aware about when context is useful. However, Sufficient Context is a post-hoc selective-generation method that uses an external sufficiency autorater plus self-confidence to govern an explicit abstain action and is evaluated on selective-risk/coverage tradeoffs, whereas Self-RAG trains the generator with reflection tokens to support adaptive retrieval and citation-grounded self-critique, optimizing factuality and citation accuracy rather than a coverage-vs-risk curve. The intervention point (inference-time policy wrapper vs. trained generator + adaptive retriever), action policy (abstain vs. re-retrieve/answer), and metric target (selective risk vs. citation faithfulness) all diverge. They are therefore complementary mechanisms for RAG trustworthiness, not substitutable entries on the same leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold retriever, generator backbone, corpus, and QA datasets fixed; evaluate both methods on a shared selective-prediction protocol that reports risk-coverage curves, abstention rate, hallucination rate at fixed coverage, AND citation/grounding metrics. Self-RAG's reflection tokens (e.g., ISSUP/ISREL) would need to be operationalized as an explicit abstain action and scored on the same selective-generation benchmark, while Sufficient Context would need to report citation/support metrics. Without a shared action policy (abstain) and a shared metric family covering both selective risk and citation faithfulness, head-to-head ranking is misleading.
notes: From a calibration/abstention perspective, the asymmetry is decisive: only Paper A explicitly measures selective risk; Paper B's reflection tokens could in principle support it but do not in the reported evaluation.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise, sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; neither assumes adversarial corpus or attacker-created evidence
intervention_point: retriever + context assembly via learned forecasting function (CalibRAG); generator prompting/training with reflection tokens (Self-RAG)
metric_target: calibration error + answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer with calibrated confidence score for downstream human decision (CalibRAG); re-retrieve adaptively + answer with self-critique tokens (Self-RAG); neither explicitly evaluates abstain as a first-class action
breaking_coordinates: metric target, intervention point, action policy, failure type
rationale: Both papers can be loosely framed as 'control mechanisms' over RAG outputs, but they target fundamentally different reliability failures. CalibRAG's core contribution is a forecasting function f(t,q,d)→c that produces a calibrated probability of decision correctness, primarily evaluated by calibration error (ECE) plus accuracy, intervening at the retriever/reranking stage. Self-RAG instead trains reflection tokens into the generator so it adaptively retrieves and critiques relevance/support, evaluated by factuality and citation accuracy. The metric targets do not overlap on calibration (Self-RAG reports no ECE) nor on citation/support (CalibRAG does not target attribution), and the intervention points and action policies differ. A direct leaderboard ranking would conflate calibration with generation quality, so the comparison is partial—complementary modules rather than substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-evaluate both systems on a shared benchmark with a common retriever and generator backbone, reporting (i) ECE / Brier / selective-risk curves, (ii) exact-match or factuality answer accuracy, and (iii) citation/support metrics. Action policies must be aligned—either both produce a calibrated confidence usable for abstain/defer at matched coverage, or both must commit to answer-only outputs. Without this, one paper's main metric is invisible to the other.
notes: From a calibration/selective-risk lens, Self-RAG's ISSUP/ISUSE tokens could in principle be repurposed as a confidence signal, but the paper does not evaluate them as calibrated probabilities, so the comparison cannot be promoted to valid on those grounds.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (FaithfulRAG) vs integrity/adversarial corruption (PoisonedRAG)
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict (FaithfulRAG) vs attacker-created evidence (PoisonedRAG); PoisonedRAG threat model: corpus write access = yes, query control = yes (attacker chooses target Q/A), retriever visibility = both black-box and white-box evaluated, generator access = black-box, insertion budget = ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer; FaithfulRAG specifies no threat model
intervention_point: generator prompting/training (FaithfulRAG self-fact mining + self-think) vs corpus/index (PoisonedRAG injects malicious passages)
metric_target: answer correctness / evidence support / citation faithfulness (FaithfulRAG) vs attack success rate (PoisonedRAG)
action_policy: answer with reconciliation (FaithfulRAG) vs unreported / not applicable (PoisonedRAG is an attack paper, not a defense, so no defender action policy)
rationale: Both papers concern what happens when retrieved context disagrees with what the LLM should say, but they occupy opposite roles in the robust-RAG stack. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense that assumes naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflicts and is scored on answer correctness/faithfulness, whereas PoisonedRAG is an offensive paper that assumes an attacker with corpus write access and ~5-passage insertion budget and is scored on attack success rate. Every coordinate breaks: failure type (benign conflict vs adversarial corruption), evidence assumption (natural vs attacker-crafted), intervention point (generator vs adversary-controlled corpus), metric target (correctness vs ASR), and action policy (reconciled answer vs no defender action at all). A leaderboard ranking would be category-error: one is a method, the other is an attack, and neither evaluates the other's regime.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) run FaithfulRAG as an explicit defense against PoisonedRAG-style injections on the same QA datasets, retriever, generator, and insertion budget, reporting matched metrics (ASR, clean accuracy, abstention/selective-risk curves), or (b) report a head-to-head defender benchmark where both papers are positioned as defenses with declared threat models, action policies (answer/abstain/quarantine/re-retrieve), and shared evaluation on both natural-conflict and poisoned-corpus splits. Without that, the two papers should be discussed as orthogonal contributions, not ranked.
notes: From a trustworthy-ML view, FaithfulRAG also lacks any abstention or selective-risk reporting, so even reframed as a defense it would not directly answer PoisonedRAG's threat model.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption (both); Astute RAG also covers relevance/noise and consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor + attacker-created evidence (treated generically as 'imperfect retrieval'). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model — corpus write access: yes (inject 5 texts per target question); query control: yes (attacker chooses target question and target answer); retriever visibility: both black-box and white-box variants; generator access: black-box; insertion budget: ~5 malicious texts in a million-document index; attack objective: induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (post-retrieval consolidation) + verifier-like reliability selection. PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (poisoning).
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness (incl. worst-case accuracy). PoisonedRAG: attack success rate.
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (after source-aware consolidation and reliability comparison among candidate answers). PoisonedRAG: unreported / not applicable — it is an attack, not a system action policy.
breaking_coordinates: role (attack vs defense), metric_target, intervention_point, action_policy, evidence_assumption framing
rationale: Both papers concern the integrity of retrieved evidence and overlap on the failure type 'adversarial corruption,' and Astute RAG explicitly cites PoisonedRAG as motivation. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive method measured by attack success rate at the corpus/index intervention point under an explicit attacker threat model (write access, chosen target Q/A, 5-text budget, black/white-box retriever), while Astute RAG is a defensive generation-stage method measured by answer correctness under generic 'imperfect retrieval' that does not adopt PoisonedRAG's adversarial protocol or evaluate against it as a stressor. Because one paper's metric (ASR) and another's metric (accuracy) move in opposite directions, and because attacks and defenses are not substitutable entries on the same leaderboard, direct ranking would conflate orthogonal contributions and mislead. The intervention point, metric target, and action policy all break simultaneously, so this is invalid rather than partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To support any direct comparison, both works would need to share a common evaluation harness: (1) Astute RAG evaluated explicitly under PoisonedRAG's threat model (same corpus, retriever, insertion budget, target question set, and black/white-box variants), reporting both clean accuracy and post-attack accuracy/ASR; (2) PoisonedRAG paired with at least one defense baseline that occupies Astute RAG's role at the generator stage, so attack and defense are measured as a (attack, defense) tuple rather than ranked head-to-head; and (3) shared action-policy reporting (answer vs abstain vs expose-conflict) so that defended ASR is comparable across systems. Without this, the two papers should be discussed as complementary (attack benchmark vs defense mechanism), not ranked.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pairs in robust RAG are a recurring invalid pattern; partial would only be appropriate if Astute RAG had run on PoisonedRAG-corrupted corpora with the same metric basis.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG assumes corpus write access, attacker-chosen target questions/answers, both black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, ~5 malicious texts per target query, objective = induce specific target answer; RobustRAG assumes adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge, bounded insertion budget m of corrupted passages, defender controls context assembly and generator prompting
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (injection); RobustRAG: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success (ASR); RobustRAG: answer correctness with certified lower bounds (selective risk/coverage proxy via abstention)
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action evaluated); RobustRAG: answer, abstain ('I don't know'), implicit aggregate/filter via isolation
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, role (attacker vs defender)
rationale: Both papers concern the same failure type (integrity/adversarial corruption of RAG via attacker-created evidence injected into the knowledge base), and they share the same threat surface — bounded passage injection into the retriever's corpus. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that proposes and measures an attack via ASR with no defender action policy, while RobustRAG is a defensive contribution that intervenes at context assembly/generation with an explicit abstain-or-answer policy and reports certifiable accuracy lower bounds. Because one paper's success metric is the inverse of the other's and they occupy complementary roles (attack vs. defense), they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable methods, but they are clearly co-applicable: RobustRAG should be evaluated against PoisonedRAG-style attacks. This makes the relationship partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct comparison would require both papers to be cast as methods producing the same measurable output under a shared threat model — for example, both reporting attacker-against-defender end-to-end metrics (clean accuracy, accuracy-under-attack at fixed insertion budget m, abstention rate, and certified accuracy where applicable) on identical datasets, retrievers, and generators, with PoisonedRAG instantiated as the attacker against RobustRAG's defense. Alternatively, they could be discussed as a (attack, defense) pair within a shared evaluation matrix rather than ranked head-to-head.
notes: From a trustworthy-ML/selective-risk lens, RobustRAG's abstention and certified lower bounds belong to a defender's risk-coverage frame, whereas PoisonedRAG's ASR is an attacker's effectiveness frame — these are not interchangeable scoreboards.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (RAGTruth); relevance/noise + sufficiency + consistency/conflict (RGB)
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict / benign retrieval error (RAGTruth); benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB, with controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactuals)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); verifier (RAGTruth, via fine-tuned detectors)
metric_target: evidence support / citation faithfulness via span-level detection F1 (RAGTruth); answer correctness + negative rejection rate (RGB)
action_policy: verify (RAGTruth detectors); answer / abstain (RGB negative rejection testbed) — different action families
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation benchmarks concerned with model trustworthiness, but they probe different failure surfaces with non-interchangeable scoring. RAGTruth annotates word-level hallucinations in naturally generated LLM responses across QA/data-to-text/summarization and scores hallucination-detection methods (span-level precision/recall/F1). RGB constructs controlled testbeds for four abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness), scoring LLM end-task accuracy and rejection rate. The failure types only partially overlap (RAGTruth ⊂ consistency/conflict; RGB spans noise + sufficiency + conflict), the evidence assumptions differ (naturally occurring vs. constructed stressors), and the metric targets and action policies differ (detector F1/verify vs. answer/abstain). They are complementary slices of RAG trustworthiness rather than substitutes on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct comparison would require aligning task and metric: either (a) running RAGTruth-style span-level hallucination detection on RGB's counterfactual/noise testbed with matched generators and detectors, or (b) scoring the same LLMs on a shared faithfulness-and-abstention metric across both corpora, using a common evidence-construction protocol (natural vs. injected) and an explicit, evaluated action policy (verify, abstain, answer). Without that, the two should be reported as complementary diagnostics, not ranked alternatives.
notes: Both are benchmarks, so 'better' is not meaningful; the question is whether scores transfer, and they do not.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios and counterfactual documents) vs benign retrieval error / naturally occurring (Sufficient Context: autorater-labeled sufficiency on existing QA datasets)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); plus verifier and generator prompting (Sufficient Context only, via sufficiency autorater and selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, calibration error (Sufficient Context); answer correctness, abstention/rejection rate, error-detection rate on ability testbeds (RGB)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both evaluate abstention; RGB also probes expose-conflict via counterfactual robustness)
rationale: Both papers study RAG behavior when retrieved context is imperfect and both explicitly measure abstention, so the failure-type and action-policy coordinates overlap substantially. However, RGB is a pure evaluation artifact that decomposes RAG into four discrete abilities measured on synthesized testbeds with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injections, reporting ability-specific accuracy and a negative-rejection rate. Sufficient Context instead introduces an autorater-defined sufficiency property over naturally occurring (Q,C) pairs, uses it as an analysis lens, and adds a verifier + selective-generation method that targets a selective-risk/coverage tradeoff combined with self-confidence calibration. Because the evidence construction (constructed stressor vs naturally distributed sufficiency), the intervention type (benchmark only vs benchmark plus method), and the metric family (per-ability accuracy vs selective risk curves) differ, the two cannot be ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard, but they are clearly complementary lenses on the same abstention problem — hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both works on a shared retriever, generator set, and QA corpus; apply RGB's four testbeds while also stratifying instances using Sufficient Context's autorater; report a common set of metrics including per-ability accuracy, abstention rate when context is insufficient, hallucination rate when context is sufficient, and selective risk–coverage curves with explicit answer/abstain labels; additionally evaluate Sufficient Context's selective generation method on RGB's negative-rejection and counterfactual testbeds so that the two interventions are placed on the same operating axis.
notes: From a trustworthy-ML/selective-risk perspective, the deepest mismatch is that RGB scores abstention as a discrete ability while Sufficient Context analyzes the full risk–coverage tradeoff; this alone blocks direct leaderboard ranking even where the underlying phenomenon is shared.

failure_type: RAGTruth: consistency/conflict + relevance/noise + sufficiency (broad hallucination taxonomy across QA/summarization/data-to-text); FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (specifically parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflict)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring LLM hallucinations on standard RAG outputs (benign retrieval, no attacker); FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved context (no adversarial threat model)
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) + verifier (benchmarks detectors and fine-tunes a Llama detector); FaithfulRAG: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think before generation)
metric_target: RAGTruth: detector precision/recall of hallucination spans (and citation faithfulness as ground truth); FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / faithfulness to retrieved context on QA benchmarks
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported as a downstream action (detection only, no abstain/re-retrieve loop evaluated); FaithfulRAG: answer (post-reasoning generation), no abstain or escalate policy evaluated
rationale: Both papers target faithfulness failures in RAG, but they occupy fundamentally different layers of the stack: RAGTruth is a span-annotated corpus and detector benchmark spanning multiple hallucination subtypes (including conflict, baseless info, and over-claiming) across QA, summarization, and data-to-text, while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention narrowly scoped to parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflict that is evaluated by end-task answer accuracy. The intervention point (evaluation artifact + detector vs. context assembly + generator prompting), the metric target (detector P/R on hallucinated spans vs. answer correctness/faithfulness), and the action policy (post-hoc detection vs. self-think-then-answer) are all distinct, and FaithfulRAG does not report results on the RAGTruth corpus. They are best discussed as complementary components of a faithfulness pipeline rather than ranked head-to-head on one leaderboard, so the verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To enable direct comparison: (1) evaluate FaithfulRAG-generated outputs on the RAGTruth corpus using its span-level hallucination annotations, or run RAGTruth's fine-tuned detector on FaithfulRAG outputs; (2) align the failure-type scope by restricting RAGTruth analysis to the 'Evident Conflict' subset that matches FaithfulRAG's parametric-vs-context conflict definition; (3) fix the generator, retriever, and conflict-construction protocol across both; (4) report a common metric family (e.g., faithfulness/factuality score plus detector F1) and explicitly state the action policy (answer-only vs. answer+detect+abstain) used at evaluation time.
notes: Borderline between partial and invalid; chose partial because a shared evaluation harness is conceivable (FaithfulRAG outputs scored by RAGTruth annotations on the conflict subset), even though the papers as published serve distinct roles (benchmark/detector vs. generation method).

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (only Paper B via counterfactual category)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real DPR/SerpAPI retrieval. Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressors with three noise types including counterfactual passages that semantically contradict the gold answer. Neither paper formalizes an attacker threat model (no corpus write access, no insertion budget, no query control, no retriever/generator visibility framing); B's 'adversarial training' refers to worst-case sampling during training, not an attacker model.
intervention_point: Paper A: corpus/index (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning). Paper B: generator prompting or training only (RAAT adversarial training + multi-task noise classification).
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (NLI gating explicitly evaluated as an action). Paper B: answer only (no filter, no abstain, noise-type classification is auxiliary and not an inference-time action).
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA and report answer correctness (EM/F1), and both include generator-side training on mixed-quality contexts, so there is genuine topical overlap. However, Paper A scopes the problem to irrelevant (off-topic) retrieved passages as benign retrieval error and offers two distinct interventions—an NLI filter (a filter action policy) and robust fine-tuning—whereas Paper B expands the noise taxonomy to include counterfactual passages (a consistency/conflict failure type that Paper A does not treat) and evaluates only a single training-based intervention without an inference-time filter or abstain action. The action policies and evidence assumptions therefore do not line up, and the counterfactual subset of RAG-Bench falls outside Paper A's claimed regime. Neither paper specifies an attacker threat model, so this is not a security comparability question, but the noise constructions are still non-substitutable, making a direct leaderboard ranking misleading rather than invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-run both methods on a shared benchmark with the same retriever (e.g., DPR), the same generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), and a noise mixture broken out by type (purely irrelevant vs counterfactual vs mixed) so that Paper A's scope is respected on the irrelevant slice and Paper B's counterfactual slice is reported separately. Both methods should be evaluated under matched action policies (answer-only, and with an optional NLI/filter gate applied uniformly), and the shared dataset (NQ is common) should use identical splits and EM/F1 scoring. Reporting whether each method also supports an abstain or filter action would close the action-policy gap.
notes: From a security lens: 'adversarial' in RAAT is training-time worst-case selection, not an attacker with corpus write access; treating it as a corpus-poisoning defense would be a category error.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency (negative rejection) and consistency/conflict (counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real search; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactuals)
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (fine-tune on mixed contexts); Paper B: evaluation artifact only (no defense proposed)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness; Paper B: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (rejection rate) + a counterfactual identification metric
action_policy: Paper A: answer (with optional skip of retrieval when NLI flags non-entailment); Paper B: answer and abstain (negative rejection explicitly scored); not aligned
rationale: Both papers concern LLM behavior under noisy retrieved context in QA, so the failure type partially overlaps on relevance/noise. However, Paper A is a method paper proposing NLI filtering and robust fine-tuning evaluated on naturally retrieved ODQA passages with answer-correctness as the sole target, whereas Paper B is a benchmark with constructed noise ratios and injected counterfactuals that scores four distinct abilities, including negative rejection (abstain) and counterfactual robustness that Paper A neither targets nor reports. The intervention points are non-comparable (defense vs. evaluation artifact) and the action policies differ (Paper A always answers; Paper B explicitly scores abstention). They cannot sit on one leaderboard as alternative methods, but they are clearly complementary on the noise-robustness slice, hence partial rather than invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and fine-tuned RALM on the RGB noise-robustness subset (matched noise ratios, same generator base, same EM/accuracy metric) and additionally report negative-rejection and counterfactual-robustness scores so the action policy (answer vs. abstain) and the broader ability axes are aligned; alternatively, restrict any head-to-head claim to the shared relevance/noise subset with identical retriever, corpus, and metric definitions.
notes: Method-vs-benchmark asymmetry is the main driver; comparison would also need the same generator family since RGB uses 6 LLMs and Paper A focuses on Llama-2-13B.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAAT: DPR-retrieved Wikipedia passages with injected relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual noise on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ; RGB: ChatGPT-generated QA from news articles with controlled noise ratios and search-engine-retrieved distractors). No adversarial attacker, no corpus write threat model; both are benign stressor benchmarks.
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT), evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both), selective risk/coverage (RGB negative rejection only)
action_policy: answer (RAAT), answer + abstain (RGB evaluates negative rejection explicitly)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, evidence_assumption (different corpora and noise construction)
rationale: Both papers address noise robustness in RAG and share overlapping noise typologies (irrelevant/counterfactual distractors), so they live in the same problem family. However, RAAT is a method paper that fine-tunes a LLaMA-2 7B generator via adaptive adversarial training and evaluates on its own RAG-Bench (NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ + DPR), whereas RGB is purely an evaluation artifact spanning four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) over bilingual news-derived data. Most critically, RGB explicitly evaluates an abstain/negative-rejection action policy, while RAAT only measures answer correctness (F1/EM) with no abstention channel — so they target different action policies and partially different metric families. They should be discussed as complementary (one a training intervention, the other a diagnostic benchmark) rather than placed on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and the relevant baselines) on the RGB testbeds end-to-end, reporting all four RGB abilities including negative-rejection rate and counterfactual robustness, using the same generator backbone and prompts; conversely, evaluate the RGB-tested LLMs on RAAT's RAG-Bench with the same noise-injection protocol. Also align corpus source, retriever, noise-ratio sweep, language (en vs zh), and explicitly define and score an abstain action policy for both systems.
notes: Not a security pair — no attacker capability, corpus write access, or attack objective is in scope for either paper.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Paper A additionally covers uncertainty/OOD (unknown questions)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (naturally noisy DPR/retriever outputs); no adversarial threat model, no corpus write access, no attacker query control — non-security pair
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting/training (note-taking reasoning step); Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator training (fine-tune on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); Paper A additionally reports rejection/abstain rate on RealTimeQA; Paper B reports only QA accuracy across 5 ODQA incl. multi-hop
action_policy: Paper A: answer or abstain ('unknown' explicitly evaluated); Paper B: filter + answer (no explicit abstention semantics; falls back to no-context LLM when NLI contradicts)
rationale: Both papers target the same failure type — RALM brittleness to irrelevant/noisy retrieved context on open-domain QA — under benign retrieval-error assumptions, so they share the core problem framing. However, the intervention points differ: CoN modifies generator reasoning via per-document note-taking, while Yoran et al. intervene at context assembly (NLI-based filtering) plus generator fine-tuning on mixed contexts. Crucially, the action policies diverge: CoN explicitly evaluates abstention ('unknown') and reports a rejection rate, whereas Yoran et al. treat the system as filter-then-answer with no abstention metric, and additionally cover multi-hop decomposition that CoN does not. Because abstention vs always-answer changes what 'robustness' means operationally, and the metric sets only partially overlap, direct leaderboard ranking would misrepresent each system; the papers are better viewed as complementary mechanisms operating at different intervention points with different action contracts.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a common benchmark suite (overlap NQ/TriviaQA plus a multi-hop set such as StrategyQA/2WikiMultiHop), with the same retriever (e.g., DPR) and same base generator (e.g., LLaMA-2-7B), under a shared protocol that (a) defines whether abstention is permitted, (b) reports both QA accuracy and abstain/rejection rate plus accuracy-on-attempted, (c) constructs irrelevant-context stressors with a common recipe (random/top-k-non-gold), and (d) explicitly declares the action policy (answer-only vs answer-or-abstain) so CoN's 'unknown' outputs and Yoran's filter-fallback can be scored on the same axes.
notes: Not a security pair; threat-model coordinates (write access, insertion budget, attacker objective) are not applicable since both assume benign retrieval noise.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both assume non-adversarial retrieval; no attacker model, no corpus write access, no insertion budget — security threat model is not in scope for either paper)
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting + evaluation artifact (sufficient-context autorater + selective generation); Paper B: generator training + retriever + verifier (reflection tokens for adaptive retrieval and self-critique)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage; Paper B: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: Paper A: answer, abstain (selective generation is explicitly evaluated); Paper B: answer, re-retrieve, verify (reflection tokens explicitly trigger on-demand retrieval and critique)
rationale: Both papers target factuality/quality of RAG generation under benign (non-adversarial) retrieval conditions, and both involve some form of self-assessment to decide what to do with retrieved context. However, Paper A intervenes post-hoc with an autorater + confidence-based abstention (action policy: answer/abstain; metric centered on selective coverage and hallucination reduction), while Self-RAG intervenes via end-to-end training with reflection tokens that drive on-demand re-retrieval and citation-grounded critique (action policy: answer/re-retrieve/verify; metric centered on citation faithfulness and evidence support). The failure-type overlap (insufficient/noisy context) is real but the intervention loci, action policies, and primary metric targets diverge enough that direct leaderboard ranking would conflate distinct mechanisms; they are better treated as complementary modules.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation harness with the same retriever, generator base, and datasets where both methods are scored on a common metric bundle that includes (a) selective accuracy/coverage curves with explicit abstain action, (b) citation faithfulness/evidence support, and (c) cost (e.g., extra retrieval calls). Both methods would need to expose the same action policy set (answer/abstain at minimum, ideally also re-retrieve), and the sufficient-context signal would need to be benchmarked head-to-head against Self-RAG's ISREL/ISSUP tokens as alternative gating signals.
notes: Not a security pair; threat-model coordinates (write access, insertion budget, attacker objective) are not relevant.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise + sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; no adversarial threat model in either, so security coordinates (corpus write access, query control, insertion budget, attack objective) are not applicable
intervention_point: reranker + verifier/calibration head (CalibRAG) vs generator prompting/training with reflection tokens and adaptive retrieval (Self-RAG)
metric_target: calibration error + answer correctness (CalibRAG) vs answer correctness + citation faithfulness/evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer-with-calibrated-confidence (CalibRAG, no explicit abstain evaluated) vs re-retrieve + verify via reflection tokens (Self-RAG); not the same action policy
breaking_coordinates: metric target, intervention point, action policy, failure type
rationale: Both papers fall under the broad 'reliable/controllable RAG' umbrella, but they target distinct failure modes with different mechanisms. CalibRAG trains a forecasting function f(t,q,d) that predicts decision correctness, used to rerank documents and produce calibrated confidence; its headline metric is calibration (alongside accuracy) and its action is answer-with-confidence. Self-RAG trains a generator to emit reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval and self-critique, with factuality and citation faithfulness as the headline metrics and re-retrieve/verify-style actions. Because the intervention point (reranker+calibration head vs generator training), metric target (ECE/calibration vs citation/factuality), and action policy (calibrated answer vs adaptive retrieve+critique) all differ, a direct leaderboard ranking would conflate distinct objectives, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both systems on the same datasets with a shared retriever, generator backbone, and inference budget, reporting a unified metric set (ECE/Brier for calibration, FactScore/citation precision-recall for faithfulness, EM/F1 for correctness), with explicit and identical action policies (e.g., answer vs abstain at matched confidence thresholds, and re-retrieve budget). Without this, one cannot tell whether a difference reflects calibration quality, retrieval adaptivity, or citation grounding.
notes: Not a security pair; threat-model coordinates do not apply. Overlap is real (both improve RAG reliability) but objectives differ enough that ranking them on a single leaderboard would mislead.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs. retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict (benign retrieval, no attacker); PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence. Threat model for PoisonedRAG: corpus write access = yes (injection into knowledge DB), query control = attacker-chosen target questions, retriever visibility = both black-box and white-box evaluated, generator access = black-box, insertion budget = ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = targeted misinformation (force attacker-chosen answer). FaithfulRAG specifies no threat model at all.
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, contextual alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attacker side, not a defense intervention)
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / contextual faithfulness on benign QA; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR), plus retrieval recall of malicious texts
action_policy: Both unreported. FaithfulRAG always answers after reconciliation (no abstain/quarantine evaluated); PoisonedRAG is an attack paper and evaluates no defender action policy.
rationale: FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense for naturally occurring knowledge conflicts between an LLM's parametric knowledge and retrieved context, evaluated on standard QA accuracy/faithfulness with no adversarial threat model. PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that assumes an adversary with corpus write access who injects ~5 malicious passages per target question to induce attacker-chosen answers, measured by attack success rate in black-box and white-box retriever settings. The papers occupy opposite roles (defense vs. attack), opposite evidence assumptions (benign conflict vs. attacker-created corruption), different intervention points (generator vs. corpus injection), and incompatible metric targets (correctness/faithfulness vs. ASR); neither evaluates a shared action policy. Placing them on a single leaderboard would conflate a non-adversarial faithfulness method with an adversarial threat surface it was never tested against, which is misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) evaluate FaithfulRAG (and matched baselines) as a defense against PoisonedRAG using identical retriever, generator, corpus, target-question set, and 5-text injection budget, reporting both ASR under attack and clean-task accuracy, with explicit defender action labels (answer/abstain/filter/quarantine); or (b) reframe the comparison as defense-vs-defense by including a separate adversarial-corruption defense baseline alongside FaithfulRAG on the same PoisonedRAG benchmark. Without such matched threat-model evaluation, the two papers cannot be ranked as substitutes.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense-for-different-problem mismatch; 'conflict' in FaithfulRAG and 'corruption' in PoisonedRAG are not the same construct.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption for PoisonedRAG; consistency/conflict and relevance/noise for AstuteRAG
evidence_assumption: PoisonedRAG assumes attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, ~5 malicious texts per target question, attacker-chosen target Q/A, both black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, and no query manipulation. AstuteRAG assumes benign retrieval error plus benchmark-constructed stressor and naturally occurring conflict, with no adversarial threat model and no insertion budget.
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index via injection. AstuteRAG: generator prompting via source-aware consolidation and reliability comparison.
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success. AstuteRAG: answer correctness under imperfect retrieval.
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack-only, no defender action). AstuteRAG: verify, expose conflict, and answer via reliability comparison over internal vs external candidates.
rationale: Both papers live in the robust-RAG space and both touch malicious retrieved content, but they sit on opposite sides of the attack/defense boundary and cannot be ranked on a shared leaderboard. PoisonedRAG is an attack contribution: it assumes corpus write access with a ~5-text insertion budget, attacker-chosen target questions/answers, and reports attack success rate in black-box and white-box settings. AstuteRAG is a generator-side defense against broadly imperfect retrieval (noise and conflict, with 'malicious' only mentioned qualitatively), evaluated by QA correctness without a formal threat model or insertion budget. The intervention point (corpus injection vs generator consolidation), metric target (ASR vs answer correctness), evidence assumption (attacker-crafted vs benchmark stressor/conflict), and action policy (none vs verify+consolidate+answer) all diverge, so direct comparison would conflate attacker capability with defender capability and is misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-run AstuteRAG explicitly under PoisonedRAG's threat model: same target Q/A set, same knowledge base, same retriever and generator, matched 1/3/5/10 malicious-text insertion budgets, and matched black-box/white-box adversary assumptions, then report post-attack accuracy and ASR reduction (ideally alongside benign accuracy and abstention rates) so both papers are scored on a shared attack-defense axis.
notes: Pair is attack vs defense; comparability would require situating AstuteRAG as a PoisonedRAG defense baseline.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; corpus write access = yes for both; query control = attacker-chosen target queries (PoisonedRAG) vs adaptive attacker assumed (RobustRAG); retriever visibility = black-box and white-box (PoisonedRAG) vs full knowledge of defense (RobustRAG); generator access = query-only; insertion budget = ~5 malicious passages (PoisonedRAG) vs bounded m' (RobustRAG); attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer (PoisonedRAG) vs any response corruption (RobustRAG defense scope)
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack); context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (RobustRAG defense)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG); answer correctness + selective risk/coverage with certified lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: answer (PoisonedRAG, forced target answer); abstain + filter + verify via isolate-then-aggregate (RobustRAG)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, role asymmetry (attack vs defense)
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat surface — retrieval corruption via attacker-injected passages with corpus write access — and share the integrity/adversarial-corruption failure type and attacker-created-evidence assumption. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution whose intervention is at the corpus and whose metric is attack success rate against undefended RAG, while RobustRAG is a defensive contribution whose intervention is at context assembly and generator prompting, with metrics on certified answer correctness and explicit abstain/aggregate action policies. They occupy opposite roles on the same problem and therefore cannot be ranked head-to-head on a leaderboard; they are naturally complementary (the attack is a stressor for the defense). This makes the relationship partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-frame both within a single evaluation harness: fix retriever, generator, knowledge base, target-query distribution, and insertion budget; run PoisonedRAG (both black-box and white-box variants) as the adversary against RobustRAG (and at least one undefended/alternative-defense baseline); report a common metric family — attack success rate, clean-task accuracy, certified accuracy lower bound, and abstain rate — under matched threat models so that attack strength and defense robustness can be jointly read off. Without this co-evaluation, PoisonedRAG and RobustRAG should be discussed as complementary attack/defense modules, not as substitutable methods.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pairs are a recurring category that the rulebook should treat as 'partial' by default unless the defense paper explicitly evaluates the attack paper's threat under matched parameters.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (RAGTruth); relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict (RGB)
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict (RAGTruth: organic LLM hallucinations against real retrieved passages); benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios, fabricated counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth also targets verifier (fine-tuned hallucination detectors)
metric_target: evidence support / citation faithfulness (RAGTruth: span-level hallucination detection F1); answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (RGB: accuracy, rejection rate, integration accuracy, counterfactual identification)
action_policy: verify (RAGTruth: detection over generated spans); answer, abstain (RGB: explicitly evaluates negative rejection alongside answering)
rationale: Both are evaluation benchmarks for trustworthy RAG and share concern about ungrounded outputs, but they instrument different phenomena. RAGTruth collects naturally generated RAG responses across QA, data-to-text, and summarization and provides word-level hallucination annotations for training and scoring detectors (a verifier-style metric). RGB constructs synthetic QA testbeds along four orthogonal axes (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and scores end-to-end LLM behavior including explicit abstention. Because the evidence-construction regime (organic vs. controlled), the unit of measurement (span detection vs. answer-level ability scores), and the evaluated action set (verify vs. answer/abstain) all differ, a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate distinct constructs. They are complementary diagnostic resources rather than substitutable benchmarks, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Define a shared task (e.g., RAG answer faithfulness on QA), align task format (single-turn QA only), use the same generators and retrieval/noise distributions, harmonize ground-truth granularity (response-level faithful/abstain/hallucinated label or span-level annotation on both), agree on a common metric family (e.g., faithfulness F1 plus abstention rate at matched coverage), and explicitly report the action policy LLMs are allowed (answer vs. abstain vs. flag) so that both benchmarks score the same decision under the same evidence regime.
notes: Both are benchmarks rather than systems, so 'leaderboard comparability' here means whether scores transfer; they do not, because the constructs measured are distinct.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise (RGB also covers consistency/conflict and integrity/adversarial via counterfactual robustness, which Sufficient Context does not)
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactuals); Sufficient Context: benign retrieval error / naturally occurring (analyzes standard QA retrieval outputs with an autorater label). Not a security pair, so attacker capability fields are not central; RGB's counterfactual subtask is the only adversarial-flavored slice and has no analogue in Sufficient Context.
intervention_point: RGB: evaluation artifact only. Sufficient Context: evaluation artifact + verifier (sufficiency autorater) + system-control policy (selective generation gated by sufficiency and self-confidence).
metric_target: Overlap on answer correctness; RGB additionally reports a rejection/accuracy split per ability; Sufficient Context reports selective risk/coverage (hallucination vs abstention vs correct, stratified by sufficiency).
action_policy: answer, abstain (explicitly evaluated by both — RGB via 'negative rejection' subtask, Sufficient Context via selective generation and stratified abstention behavior)
rationale: Both papers care about whether retrieved context lets an LLM answer correctly, and both explicitly evaluate the answer-vs-abstain action policy, so the action coordinate is unusually well-aligned for this area. However, RGB is a four-ability diagnostic benchmark built from synthetically constructed stressors (fixed noise ratios, injected counterfactuals, multi-doc integration cases) and reports per-ability accuracy/rejection rates, while Sufficient Context introduces a binary (Q,C) sufficiency label produced by an autorater over standard QA corpora and uses it both as an analytic lens and to drive a selective-generation method. The failure-type coverage only partially overlaps (RGB adds conflict and counterfactual/adversarial slices absent in Sufficient Context), the evidence assumptions differ (constructed stressor vs naturally occurring retrieval), and the intervention points differ (pure eval artifact vs eval + verifier + control policy). They are best framed as complementary lenses on overlapping phenomena rather than as substitutable methods on a single leaderboard, so partial is the right verdict.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's autorater + selective-generation pipeline on RGB's four testbeds (especially Noise Robustness and Negative Rejection) using the same generator, retriever, and prompt; report RGB's accuracy and rejection-rate metrics alongside Sufficient Context's stratified correct/abstain/hallucinate breakdown; and either restrict comparison to the answerability slice (excluding RGB's counterfactual/integration testbeds) or extend Sufficient Context's sufficiency label to handle conflict and counterfactual evidence so the failure-type coverage matches.
notes: Not a security pair; counterfactual robustness in RGB has adversarial flavor but uses benchmark-constructed perturbations rather than a defined threat model, so attacker-capability fields do not meaningfully apply.

failure_type: RAGTruth: relevance/noise + sufficiency + consistency/conflict (broad hallucination taxonomy); FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (specifically parametric vs retrieved knowledge)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error producing naturally generated hallucinations across QA/data-to-text/summarization; FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring (and constructed) parametric-vs-context conflicts. Not a security/adversarial setting on either side, so attacker-model fields N/A.
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) plus a fine-tuned post-hoc hallucination detector; FaithfulRAG: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think before answering)
metric_target: RAGTruth: span/response-level hallucination detection performance (precision/recall/F1 of detector against gold annotations); FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / faithfulness on QA with knowledge conflict
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (benchmark + detector flags spans, no downstream generation action evaluated); FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciliation), no abstain/quarantine/expose-conflict evaluated
rationale: Both papers nominally concern faithfulness in RAG, but they are categorically different artifacts. RAGTruth is an annotated evaluation corpus (plus a fine-tuned post-hoc hallucination detector) spanning QA, data-to-text, and summarization with a broad hallucination taxonomy; its metric target is span/response-level detection performance and it does not evaluate any downstream answering action policy. FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention targeting the narrower parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge-conflict subproblem on QA, intervening at context assembly and generator prompting and reporting answer-correctness style metrics. The intervention points (evaluation artifact + detector vs generator-side reconciliation), failure-type scope, metric targets, and action policies are non-overlapping, so they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitute methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison meaningful one would need to (a) evaluate FaithfulRAG (and the RAGTruth-finetuned detector / detect-then-edit pipeline) on a shared task slice — e.g., RAGTruth's QA subset — using the same retriever, generator backbone, and conflict construction; (b) align on a common metric family (e.g., faithfulness/answer-correctness AND hallucination-span detection on the same outputs); and (c) specify a common action policy (answer vs flag-and-abstain vs edit) so the two systems are doing the same job. Alternatively, reframe RAGTruth purely as the benchmark on which FaithfulRAG and competing faithful-generation methods are ranked, rather than treating RAGTruth itself as a competing 'method'.
notes: Pair mixes a benchmark/detector paper with a generation-time intervention; this is a category mismatch rather than a marginal coordinate break, hence invalid rather than partial.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Paper B also covers consistency/conflict (counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor for both; Paper B additionally constructs counterfactual stressors that Paper A does not target
intervention_point: Paper A: reranker/verifier-style NLI filter + generator prompting/training; Paper B: generator training only (adversarial + multi-task noise classification)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: Paper A: filter then answer (NLI-gated); Paper B: answer (no explicit filter/abstain reported)
breaking_coordinates: failure_type scope, intervention_point, action_policy, evaluation artifact (benchmark composition)
rationale: Both papers address noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA and report answer correctness (EM/F1), so the high-level problem overlaps. However, the noise scope differs materially: Paper A targets irrelevant context (including multi-hop), while RAAT explicitly partitions noise into relevant, irrelevant, and counterfactual, with counterfactual conflict central to its claims. The intervention points are also asymmetric — Paper A combines an NLI filter at the context-assembly stage with generator fine-tuning, whereas RAAT operates solely at the generator via adversarial training plus an auxiliary noise-type classifier. Finally, the action policies differ: Paper A explicitly evaluates a filter-then-answer pipeline (with the option to drop retrieval), while Paper B reports an answer-only policy. These differences make leaderboard-style ranking misleading; the methods are better characterized as complementary modules covering partially overlapping operating regions.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever (e.g., DPR), generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), and benchmark set (intersect NQ/TriviaQA with multi-hop subsets if included); define a shared noise mixture covering at minimum irrelevant and counterfactual subsets, and evaluate both systems on each noise slice separately. Require both methods to report under a common action policy (either both filter-then-answer, or both answer-only) with abstention behavior explicit. Match training-data budget and report EM/F1 alongside any selective-risk or noise-classification metric so each system is evaluated on the same target.
notes: Paper A's NLI filter could in principle be stacked on RAAT, reinforcing that these are complementary rather than substitutable along a single leaderboard axis.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict and sufficiency additionally in Paper B (counterfactual, negative rejection, integration)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); Paper A also uses naturally noisy retriever output from 5 ODQA corpora, Paper B uses news-sourced documents with controlled noise ratios and synthetically inserted counterfactuals
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning); Paper B: evaluation artifact only (no method proposed)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness (EM/F1 on ODQA); Paper B: answer correctness plus selective risk/coverage proxy via negative rejection rate and counterfactual error rate
action_policy: Paper A: filter then answer (the NLI gate drops passages but the system still answers); Paper B: explicitly evaluates answer vs abstain (negative rejection) and expose conflict (counterfactual) as separate target behaviors
rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior under irrelevant/noisy retrieved evidence, so the noise-robustness coordinate genuinely overlaps. However, Paper A is a method paper that proposes and trains interventions (NLI filtering and mixed-context fine-tuning) measured by answer correctness on five ODQA benchmarks, while Paper B is an evaluation artifact (RGB) that defines four orthogonal testbeds—noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness—and reports them as separate diagnostic abilities. The intervention point is incompatible (method vs. benchmark), the action policy is explicitly multi-modal in Paper B (answer/abstain/expose-conflict) but only filter+answer in Paper A, and Paper B's metric scope extends well beyond the relevance/noise axis Paper A targets. They are complementary—Paper A could be evaluated on Paper B's noise-robustness testbed—but they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable approaches.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and mixed-context fine-tuned models on the RGB noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds with identical retriever, generator backbones, noise ratios, and matched metric definitions (accuracy plus an explicit abstention/rejection rate). Additionally, report a shared action-policy label (answer vs abstain) so that filtering-then-answering in Paper A is distinguishable from RGB's expected abstention behavior. Without this, any ranking would conflate method quality with benchmark coverage.
notes: Borderline between partial and invalid; the method-vs-benchmark asymmetry pushes against direct ranking but the shared noise-robustness construct preserves a meaningful partial overlap.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict (counterfactual); RGB additionally tests sufficiency via negative-rejection
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAAT filters DPR top-k and injects three noise types on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ; RGB synthesizes noise from news + search-engine documents with varied noise ratios)
intervention_point: RAAT: generator prompting or training + evaluation artifact (RAG-Bench); RGB: evaluation artifact only
metric_target: answer correctness for both (F1/EM in RAAT, accuracy in RGB); RGB additionally reports rejection rate, error detection rate, and error correction rate that RAAT does not
action_policy: RAAT: answer (no explicit abstain evaluation); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection is an explicit ability scored)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG using benchmark-constructed stressors and a similar three-way taxonomy that includes counterfactual/misleading evidence, so the failure type and evidence-construction posture overlap. However, RAAT is a generator-side training intervention scored on its own RAG-Bench with F1/EM only, while RGB is a diagnostic benchmark spanning four abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) without proposing a method. Critically, RGB explicitly evaluates an abstain action via negative rejection and reports rejection/error-correction metrics, whereas RAAT only trains the model to answer correctly under noise and does not report any abstention behavior. The intervention point, metric family, and action policy therefore diverge, making them complementary rather than direct leaderboard substitutes; the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT-trained models on RGB's four testbeds (English and Chinese) using RGB's full metric suite (accuracy, rejection rate, error detection/correction) and, conversely, evaluate RGB's baseline LLMs on RAG-Bench with matched retriever (DPR vs search-engine), matched noise construction, and an explicitly defined and scored action policy (answer vs abstain). Both should also fix the generator family and report counterfactual-handling separately from irrelevant-noise handling so intervention effects can be attributed.
notes: Classic method-paper vs benchmark-paper asymmetry; surface topic overlap masks divergent intervention point and action-policy reporting.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); uncertainty/OOD (Chain-of-Note only, via 'unknown' on RealTimeQA)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor (both inject or use real retriever noise); not security-relevant, so threat-model dimensions do not apply
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (Chain-of-Note: note-taking reasoning + LLaMA-2 fine-tune); context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (Yoran et al.: NLI filter at context assembly plus fine-tune on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM) shared; Chain-of-Note additionally reports rejection rate for out-of-scope queries
action_policy: abstain (Chain-of-Note: explicit 'unknown' output); filter + answer (Yoran et al.: NLI-driven discard of non-entailing passages, then answer with or without retrieved context)
rationale: Both papers target the same robust-RAG failure mode—distraction by irrelevant retrieved context in open-domain QA—and share answer correctness on overlapping benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA). However, the intervention points differ substantively: Chain-of-Note modifies generator reasoning with a note-taking step trained via GPT-4 distillation, while Yoran et al. intervene before generation via an NLI entailment filter and additionally fine-tune on mixed-quality contexts. The action policies are also distinct: Chain-of-Note explicitly evaluates an abstain ('unknown') behavior and reports rejection rate, whereas Yoran et al. evaluates filter-then-answer (optionally answering without context) but not abstention. These are best framed as complementary mitigation modules operating at different pipeline stages with different decision repertoires, so leaderboard-style ranking on a single EM number would conflate intervention stage and action policy. Hence partial, not valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A controlled study using the same retriever, the same set of irrelevant/relevant context constructions (both randomly injected and retriever-natural distractors), the same base generator(s), and a unified evaluation harness reporting (a) EM on relevant-only, irrelevant-only, and mixed conditions; (b) abstain/rejection rate with a common 'unknown' label; and (c) selective-risk/coverage curves. Both methods should be evaluated in single-hop and multi-hop settings, and ablations should isolate the filter component vs. the generator-reasoning/training component so the contribution of each intervention stage is comparable.
notes: Action policy is explicitly reported in both papers (abstain vs. filter), so this is not an under-specified case; the comparability gap is real divergence in intervention stage and decision repertoire.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: evaluation artifact, generator prompting or training, retriever, verifier
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, citation faithfulness
action_policy: abstain, re-retrieve, verify, answer
rationale: Both papers address RAG quality when retrieved context may be unhelpful or insufficient, but they intervene at very different points and evaluate different action policies. Sufficient Context builds an inference-time autorater plus a selective-generation rule whose action policy is answer-or-abstain, scored on selective risk/coverage and hallucination rate. Self-RAG instead trains the generator to emit reflection tokens that trigger on-demand re-retrieval and self-critique, evaluated heavily on citation faithfulness and long-form factuality. The intervention point (inference-time gating vs. training-time reflection tokens), the action policy (abstain vs. re-retrieve/verify), and the headline metric family (selective accuracy vs. citation/factuality) differ enough that a leaderboard-style ranking would misattribute gains. They are better discussed as complementary modules than as substitutes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared benchmark with the same retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; align action policies (e.g., allow both to abstain and to re-retrieve, with a fixed retrieval budget); report a common metric suite covering answer correctness, abstention/selective-coverage curves, and citation faithfulness; and stratify results by sufficient vs. insufficient context so each method is evaluated in its native operating regime.
notes: Both action policies are explicitly evaluated in their respective papers, so the issue is divergence, not absence, of action policy.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG: miscalibrated confidence in decision-making); relevance/noise + sufficiency (Self-RAG: when retrieval is needed and whether passages support the claim)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; neither assumes adversarial corpus or constructed stressors
intervention_point: reranker + generator prompting (CalibRAG forecasting function f(t,q,d) reranks and supplies calibrated confidence); generator training + system-control policy (Self-RAG reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and critique)
metric_target: calibration error + answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer-with-calibrated-confidence (CalibRAG, no explicit abstain/escalate); re-retrieve + answer + verify via reflection tokens (Self-RAG)
rationale: Both papers sit in the RAG 'control' family and aim to make retrieval-augmented generation more reliable, but they target fundamentally different control objectives. CalibRAG learns a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) to produce calibrated decision-confidence and rerank documents; its headline metric is calibration error alongside accuracy on decision tasks. Self-RAG instead trains a generator to emit reflection tokens that govern on-demand retrieval and self-critique, evaluated primarily on factuality and citation accuracy. The failure types (uncertainty/calibration vs. relevance/sufficiency), intervention points (reranker/forecaster vs. generator-with-reflection-tokens), metric targets, and action policies all diverge, so the two systems are complementary control mechanisms rather than substitutable methods on a single leaderboard — hence partial, not valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation suite that (a) fixes retriever and base LM, (b) reports both calibration metrics (ECE/Brier/selective-risk) and factuality/citation metrics on the same tasks, (c) specifies and evaluates a common action policy (e.g., answer vs. abstain with a confidence threshold), and (d) ablates the reranker-forecaster vs. reflection-token mechanisms under identical retrieval budgets. Without joint calibration + factuality reporting and matched action policies, ranking one above the other is not interpretable.
notes: Both lie under 'control' but optimize different objectives; treating them as leaderboard rivals would conflate calibration with adaptive-retrieval/critique.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and benign retrieved context. PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence (threat model: corpus write access = yes; query control = attacker chooses target questions and answers; retriever visibility = both black-box and white-box evaluated; generator access = query-only/black-box LLM; insertion budget ≈ 5 malicious passages per target question; attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer).
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious passage injection).
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support (faithfulness). PoisonedRAG: attack success rate.
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (with internal reconciliation); no abstain/verify reported. PoisonedRAG: unreported (offense paper, defender action policy not in scope).
rationale: Both papers touch the broad theme of RAG robustness, but they sit on opposite sides of the trust boundary. FaithfulRAG treats conflict as a naturally occurring disagreement between an LLM's parametric memory and a benign retrieved passage and intervenes at the generator with a self-think reconciliation module evaluated by answer correctness/faithfulness. PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that injects attacker-crafted passages into the corpus under an explicit threat model (corpus-write access, chosen target Q/A, ≤5 malicious texts, black/white-box retriever) and measures attack success rate. Failure type, evidence assumption, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge; a leaderboard that pits a faithfulness gain against an ASR would be category-confused and would misrepresent both works. The comparison is therefore invalid as written.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe FaithfulRAG as an adversarial defense and evaluate it on PoisonedRAG-poisoned corpora (matched retriever, generator, insertion budget, target Q/A set) reporting ASR, clean-utility, abstention/verification rates, and detection. Alternatively, restrict comparison to conflict-resolution methods on the same naturally-occurring conflict benchmarks (e.g., ConflictQA) for FaithfulRAG, and to other corpus-poisoning attacks (e.g., GARAG, Phantom) for PoisonedRAG. Without aligned threat model and a shared metric family (ASR + utility, or correctness under matched adversary), direct ranking is meaningless.
notes: Defense-vs-attack mismatch; even if some downstream work bridges them, neither paper's own evaluation supports placing them on a single leaderboard.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption shared at a coarse level; Astute RAG also covers relevance/noise and consistency/conflict, while PoisonedRAG is exclusively integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence (corpus write access yes, attacker chooses target questions, retriever visibility evaluated in both black-box and white-box, generator black-box, insertion budget approximately 5 malicious texts per target question, objective is to induce attacker-chosen target answer). Astute RAG: primarily benign retrieval error and naturally occurring conflict, with malicious information mentioned only as motivation; no formal adversary model or insertion budget specified.
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (poisoning the database). Astute RAG: generator prompting (source-aware iterative consolidation post-retrieval). Opposite sides of the pipeline.
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success. Astute RAG: answer correctness under imperfect/worst-case retrieval.
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action). Astute RAG: answer (selects final answer via reliability comparison across internal/external sources); no abstain or quarantine explicitly evaluated.
rationale: Both papers concern the integrity of RAG outputs when the retrieved context is unreliable, so they share a coarse problem space (conflict plus corruption). However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution intervening at the corpus by injecting a small budget of crafted malicious passages and reporting attack success rate, while Astute RAG is a defensive generation-stage method that consolidates internal and external knowledge and reports answer correctness, mostly under benign or RGB-style stressors rather than an explicit adversary. They occupy complementary roles (attack vs. defense) on different pipeline stages with different metric families and threat models, so they cannot be ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard but are clearly related enough to discuss together as partial overlap.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate Astute RAG explicitly under the PoisonedRAG threat model (same corpus, same target questions, same insertion budget of malicious passages, same retriever and generator, both black-box and white-box variants) and report attack success rate alongside answer correctness; or, conversely, evaluate PoisonedRAG against a defender deploying Astute RAG with a declared action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine). A shared benchmark covering both naturally noisy and adversarially poisoned conditions with matched metrics would make direct comparison meaningful.
notes: Attack vs. defense pair; partial rather than invalid because the shared corruption-integrity axis makes them legitimately complementary, and partial rather than under-specified because each paper individually specifies its own setup clearly.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption (shared)
