evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence (shared). PoisonedRAG: corpus write access yes, query control yes (attacker chooses target question and target answer), retriever visibility both black-box and white-box variants, generator access varies, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer. RobustRAG: adaptive attacker with full knowledge of defense, bounded insertion budget m' as a parameter, attack objective = degrade response quality; corpus write access assumed.
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious passage injection). RobustRAG: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (isolate-then-aggregate with keyword and decoding aggregation).
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success (ASR). RobustRAG: answer correctness with certifiable lower bound on response quality under bounded corruption.
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: unreported (system answers as usual; no defensive action evaluated). RobustRAG: explicit abstain ('I don't know') plus aggregated answer, i.e., answer + abstain are both evaluated policies.
rationale: Both papers operate within the same adversarial-corruption-of-RAG threat surface with attacker-created evidence and corpus write access, so they share failure type and evidence assumption. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack contribution that intervenes at the corpus/index and reports attack success rate with no defender action policy, whereas RobustRAG is a defense that intervenes at context assembly and generator prompting, reports certified answer correctness under bounded corruption, and explicitly evaluates an abstain policy. They are complementary components of a security evaluation pipeline (attack vs. defense), not substitutable methods that can be ranked on a common leaderboard. The comparison is therefore partial: meaningful only as defender-evaluated-under-this-attack, not as a head-to-head ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a meaningful comparison, the two must be combined rather than ranked: evaluate RobustRAG under PoisonedRAG-generated corpora with matched retriever (e.g., Contriever/DPR), generator (matched LLMs), datasets (NQ/HotpotQA/MSMARCO), insertion budget (matched k and m'), and report a unified metric suite—clean answer accuracy, empirical accuracy under attack, certified accuracy lower bound, abstention rate, and ASR—against the same target-question set. Without aligning intervention role (attacker vs. defender), metric semantics (ASR vs. certified correctness), and action policy (unreported vs. abstain+aggregate), any leaderboard-style ranking would be misleading.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pair; they belong in the same threat model but are not interchangeable methods. Verdict 'invalid' was considered but 'partial' better captures that they can be jointly used in a single robust-RAG evaluation.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict (hallucinations in naturally generated RAG responses); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally enables generator prompting/training of detectors
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support, citation faithfulness at span level (hallucination detection precision/recall/F1); RGB: answer correctness under noise, selective risk/coverage (rejection rate), and counterfactual error detection/correction
action_policy: RAGTruth: answer (detector flags hallucinated spans post-hoc); RGB: explicitly evaluates answer, abstain (negative rejection), and expose conflict (counterfactual robustness)
rationale: Both papers introduce evaluation artifacts for trustworthy/robust RAG, so they overlap at the failure-type level (hallucination/conflict). However, RAGTruth provides word/span-level annotations over ~18K naturally generated responses across QA, summarization, and data-to-text, with the primary metric being span-level hallucination detection performance and the implicit action policy being 'answer + post-hoc detect'. RGB instead constructs controlled stressors across four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) measured at response level, and explicitly evaluates abstention and conflict exposure as scored behaviors. The metric families (span-F1 for detectors vs ability-wise response accuracy and rejection rate), evidence construction (naturally occurring vs benchmark-injected), and evaluated action policies do not align, so a single leaderboard ranking would conflate different constructs; the two are complementary diagnostic tools rather than substitutable benchmarks.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, one would need (a) a shared task slice (e.g., QA only) with the same retriever, generator pool, and prompt format; (b) a common metric family — either both reporting span-level hallucination detection on the same span-annotated subset, or both reporting response-level correctness/rejection on the same constructed stressors; (c) explicit alignment of evaluated action policies (answer vs abstain vs expose conflict) with the same scoring rubric; and (d) matching evidence-assumption conditions (either both naturally occurring or both benchmark-injected noise/counterfactual at controlled ratios). Without these, papers can only be reported as covering different operating regions of trustworthy RAG evaluation.
notes: Both are 'evaluation_benchmark' artifacts, which tempts a 'valid' label, but benchmark co-membership is not sufficient — the measured constructs and action policies must align for leaderboard-style ranking.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: synthetic noise ratios + counterfactual injection on news QA) vs. naturally occurring sufficiency variation (Sufficient Context: existing HotpotQA/Musique/FreshQA contexts stratified by autorater label)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); plus verifier + generator prompting (Sufficient Context's selective generation method)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context only); RGB also reports rejection rate and error-detection rate per ability
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via 'negative rejection' testbed; Sufficient Context via %Correct/%Abstain/%Hallucinate stratification and guided abstention)
rationale: Both papers evaluate RAG behavior when retrieval is imperfect and both explicitly consider abstention as a desired action, so the action_policy coordinate aligns better than in many evaluation pairs. However, RGB is a fixed bilingual benchmark that constructs four discrete testbeds with controlled noise ratios and synthetically injected counterfactuals on news QA, whereas Sufficient Context introduces a sufficiency autorater applied to pre-existing QA datasets and additionally proposes a selective generation method combining sufficiency with self-confidence. The evidence assumptions differ (constructed stressors vs. naturally stratified retrievals), the intervention extends beyond evaluation into verifier/generator policy on the Sufficient Context side, and the metric families differ (per-ability scores vs. sufficiency-stratified hallucination/abstention plus selective coverage). They are complementary lenses on similar phenomena but cannot share a leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the Sufficient Context autorater on RGB's noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds (and vice versa: apply RGB-style controlled noise ratios to HotpotQA/Musique) using the same generator set, the same answer/abstain decision threshold, and a unified metric family covering both per-ability accuracy/rejection rates and sufficiency-stratified %Correct/%Abstain/%Hallucinate. Selective generation results would also need to be re-reported on RGB testbeds with identical abstention semantics.
notes: Note that RGB does evaluate abstention via 'negative rejection,' so action_policy is not the breaking coordinate here; the breaks are in stressor construction, intervention scope, and metric family.

failure_type: RAGTruth: relevance/noise + sufficiency + consistency/conflict (broad hallucination taxonomy across QA, summarization, data-to-text); FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict only (parametric vs retrieved)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring LLM hallucinations in standard RAG with benign retrieval; FaithfulRAG: benchmark-constructed parametric-vs-context conflicts
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) + generator training (fine-tuned detector); FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining + self-think module)
metric_target: RAGTruth: span-level hallucination detection F1; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness on conflict QA benchmarks
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (flag/detect hallucinated spans), unreported as a generation-time policy; FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciliation), no abstain reported
rationale: Both papers concern faithfulness in RAG, but they occupy fundamentally different roles in the pipeline: RAGTruth is an evaluation corpus and detector-training resource for post-hoc word-level hallucination detection across multiple task types, while FaithfulRAG is an in-process generation method that resolves a narrower failure mode (parametric-vs-retrieved conflict) via self-fact alignment and self-think reasoning. Their intervention points (evaluation artifact + detector vs generator method), metric targets (detection F1 vs answer accuracy), and action policies (verify/flag vs answer-after-reconciliation) do not align, so a single leaderboard ranking would be misleading. They are best discussed as complementary modules — FaithfulRAG could plausibly be evaluated on RAGTruth-style annotations, but the papers as presented do not share the same comparable axis. The overlap on the 'faithfulness' concern is real but insufficient for direct ranking, so partial rather than invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG generations on RAGTruth's QA/summarization/data-to-text prompts and have them word-level annotated under the same RAGTruth scheme, OR have RAGTruth's fine-tuned detector applied to FaithfulRAG outputs on the same conflict benchmarks used in FaithfulRAG. Either direction requires a shared task, shared retrieval/generation backbone, explicit action policy (answer vs abstain vs flag), and a single agreed metric (e.g., hallucination span rate or end-task accuracy under conflict).
notes: Classic benchmark-vs-method asymmetry; the two artifacts are pipeline-complementary, not leaderboard-competitive.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (RAAT's counterfactual noise category, not addressed by Yoran et al.)
evidence_assumption: Yoran et al.: benign retrieval error from real DPR/Google retrieval over ODQA benchmarks. RAAT: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAG-Bench), explicitly mixing relevant, irrelevant, and counterfactual passages constructed for adversarial training.
intervention_point: Yoran et al.: context assembly/compression (NLI filtering) + generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning). RAAT: generator prompting or training (adaptive adversarial training) + auxiliary verifier-like multi-task noise-type classification head.
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: Yoran et al.: filter then answer (NLI gate is explicitly evaluated). RAAT: answer (no explicit filter/abstain/expose-conflict action evaluated; noise-type classification is auxiliary).
rationale: Both papers target generator-side noise robustness for RAG on open-domain QA and share NQ-style evaluation with EM/F1, so they sit in the same broad problem family. However, RAAT explicitly enlarges the noise taxonomy to include counterfactual/conflicting passages and trains adversarially against that distribution, while Yoran et al. scope failures to irrelevant (naturally retrieved) context and mitigate with NLI filtering plus mixed-context fine-tuning. The intervention points (context-assembly filter + training vs. adversarial training + auxiliary noise-type head) and the action policies (filter-then-answer vs. answer-only) are not aligned, and the evidence assumptions differ (benign retrieval error vs. benchmark-constructed adversarial stressor). These are complementary contributions on overlapping but non-identical problems, so the comparison is partial rather than valid; a leaderboard ranking would conflate different noise distributions and action policies.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a single benchmark with an explicit noise taxonomy (e.g., RAG-Bench's relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual split, plus Yoran's naturally retrieved irrelevant set), use the same retriever and base generator (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), evaluate both Yoran's NLI-filter + robust-FT pipeline and RAAT end-to-end under matched action policies (answer-only, and optionally filter/abstain), and report EM/F1 broken down per noise type, ideally with a no-retrieval and oracle-context control. Without this, ranking the two systems on a single number is misleading.
notes: Counterfactual noise in RAAT crosses into consistency/conflict territory, which arguably makes it a different failure type than pure irrelevance; if restricted to the irrelevant-noise slice, the pair would move closer to valid but still differs on action policy.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B also covers consistency/conflict and sufficiency
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (real retriever outputs on ODQA); Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, fabricated counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filtering) + generator prompting or training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts); Paper B: evaluation artifact (benchmark, no intervention)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness; Paper B: answer correctness + rejection rate (selective risk/coverage proxy) + counterfactual identification
action_policy: Paper A: answer (filter then answer with or without context); Paper B: answer + abstain (negative rejection is explicitly scored)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG QA and share the failure type of irrelevant/noisy retrieved context. However, Paper A is a method paper proposing two concrete interventions (NLI-based filtering and robustness fine-tuning) evaluated on existing ODQA benchmarks under an answer-only action policy with naturally noisy retrieval, while Paper B is an evaluation artifact (RGB benchmark) that constructs noise via controlled ratios and additionally tests negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness with abstention as a first-class action. The intervention point, action policy set, and evidence-construction assumption differ, and Paper B spans abilities Paper A does not address, so they are complementary rather than leaderboard-rankable. Verdict: partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robust-FT methods on the RGB Noise Robustness testbed using the same generator backbones; report both answer accuracy under varying noise ratios and explicit rejection rate on the negative-rejection split; hold retriever/generator/prompt fixed; and either restrict the comparison to the noise-robustness ability or extend Paper A's methods to the counterfactual and integration splits with the same action-policy labels (answer vs abstain).
notes: Method-vs-benchmark mismatch is the clearest comparability barrier; abstention being scored only in Paper B is also decisive.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (RGB negative rejection)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer + abstain (RGB via negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG and share overlapping noise typology including counterfactual/misleading documents and irrelevant passages. However, RAAT is a training-based intervention (adaptive adversarial training plus noise-aware multi-task learning on the generator) reporting F1/EM on its own RAG-Bench, while RGB is an evaluation-only benchmark that decomposes RAG into four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and explicitly measures an abstain action via negative rejection. The intervention points are categorically different (method vs. benchmark), and RAAT does not evaluate the abstain/rejection policy that is central to RGB. They are therefore complementary contributions—RGB could serve as an evaluator of RAAT—rather than substitutable methods on a single leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and a non-RAAT baseline) on the RGB testbeds for noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness using RGB's metrics (accuracy, rejection rate, error detection rate, error correction rate) with the same retriever, generator backbone, and noise construction; or, conversely, have RGB report a uniform training-free vs. trained-method comparison under matched action policies (answer vs. abstain) and matched noise-injection budgets so that the two papers' claims can be aligned on the same operating points.
notes: Method paper vs. benchmark paper is the core asymmetry; even if both touch noise robustness, leaderboard-style ranking between them is not meaningful without RAAT being scored on RGB.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Chain-of-Note additionally covers uncertainty/OOD via 'unknown' handling for RealTimeQA
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error; benchmark-constructed stressor (both inject/sample irrelevant or low-rank DPR passages, no adversarial threat model)
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting/training (note-taking step + supervised fine-tuning). Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI passage filter) + generator prompting/training (fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM) for both; Paper A also reports rejection rate / selective risk-like coverage for unknown questions
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain ('unknown') — explicitly evaluated. Paper B: filter (NLI-driven passage drop with fallback to closed-book LLM) + answer — explicitly evaluated; abstention not modeled
rationale: Both papers target the same failure mode — distraction by irrelevant retrieved context in open-domain QA under benign DPR-style retrieval errors and benchmark-constructed noise — and both share answer correctness on overlapping ODQA datasets (NQ, TriviaQA). However, they intervene at different stages: Chain-of-Note rewires generator reasoning with per-document notes and an explicit 'unknown' abstention action, while Yoran et al. add an NLI passage filter and/or fine-tune on mixed-quality contexts, with the action being passage discard plus fallback to no-retrieval (no abstention). Because the action policies (abstain vs. filter) and intervention points differ, a leaderboard EM number conflates two different system contracts: a coverage-trading abstainer vs. an evidence-pruning answerer. The comparison is therefore partial — they are complementary mechanisms that overlap on the distraction axis but should not be ranked head-to-head without harmonizing the action contract.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever (e.g., DPR top-k from same Wikipedia dump), generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), and the same ODQA benchmarks with an identical noise/irrelevance injection protocol. Report a unified action-policy scoring rubric: both systems evaluated as answer-or-abstain (CoN's 'unknown'; Yoran's NLI-filter+closed-book treated either as an answer or as an abstain), with conditional accuracy, coverage, and rejection rate broken out. Additionally report whether the NLI filter is applied upstream of CoN to disentangle filtering gains from note-taking gains, and include multi-hop settings (Yoran covers them; CoN does not) only as a separate operating region.
notes: Both papers do specify an action policy, so this is not under-specified; the partiality comes from non-matching action contracts and intervention loci, not missing information.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: context assembly/compression, generator prompting or training, verifier, retriever
metric_target: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: abstain (Paper A); re-retrieve, filter, answer (Paper B)
rationale: Both papers aim to improve RAG factuality through some form of self-assessment over retrieved evidence, so they share a broad robustness goal. However, Sufficient Context (Paper A) frames the problem as detecting whether (Q,C) contains enough information and uses a post-hoc selective-generation signal combined with self-confidence to drive a guided-abstention action policy; its headline metric is hallucination reduction conditional on answering plus coverage tradeoffs. Self-RAG (Paper B) instead trains a generator with reflection tokens to adaptively decide when to retrieve, to mark passage relevance/support, and to filter passages in parallel, with citation accuracy and long-form factuality as primary metrics; it does not evaluate abstention as the controlled output. The interventions (lightweight autorater + selective generator vs. end-to-end trained reflective LM with on-demand retrieval), action policies (abstain vs. re-retrieve/filter/answer), and headline metrics differ enough that a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate distinct mechanisms; they are better discussed as complementary modules on the sufficiency/adaptive-retrieval axis.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold retriever, generator backbone, and benchmarks (e.g., PopQA, TriviaQA, ASQA, Bio) constant; evaluate both systems under a shared output protocol that reports answer correctness, abstention rate, hallucination rate on answered subset, and citation faithfulness; force both methods to expose the same action set (answer/abstain/re-retrieve) and report selective-risk/coverage curves so that sufficiency-based abstention and reflection-token-based adaptive retrieval can be compared at matched operating points.
notes: Partial rather than invalid because the underlying robustness target (RAG factuality under imperfect retrieval) genuinely overlaps; the break is in action policy and intervention granularity, not problem framing.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence); Self-RAG: relevance/noise and sufficiency (irrelevant/insufficient passages)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval error from a standard corpus; neither models adversarial or stale evidence
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker (forecasting function f(t,q,d)) + evaluation artifact for calibration; Self-RAG: generator prompting/training with reflection tokens + retriever (on-demand triggering)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + decision/answer correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer (with calibrated confidence); abstain not explicitly evaluated. Self-RAG: re-retrieve on demand, answer, and verify via self-critique tokens
rationale: Both papers improve RAG reliability but address different failure modes: CalibRAG targets miscalibrated decision confidence by training a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) used for reranking and confidence reporting, while Self-RAG targets indiscriminate retrieval and ungrounded generation via reflection tokens that adaptively trigger retrieval and self-critique. The failure types (uncertainty/calibration vs. relevance/sufficiency), primary metric targets (ECE/calibration vs. citation faithfulness and factuality), intervention points (reranker/evaluation artifact vs. generator training plus on-demand retriever), and action policies (calibrated answer vs. re-retrieve/verify) all diverge. They could be complementary modules in a reliability stack but not direct leaderboard substitutes, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared benchmark with the same retriever and base generator, and report a common metric family covering BOTH calibration (ECE/Brier on decision correctness) AND grounding (citation precision/recall, supportedness) AND task accuracy. Explicitly state and evaluate identical action policies (e.g., both always answer with a confidence score, or both allowed to abstain/re-retrieve with the same budget). Frame both papers under a unified problem statement (e.g., reliability-aware RAG) rather than comparing a calibration method to an adaptive-retrieval/self-critique method as if they were alternatives for the same coordinate.
notes: Self-RAG's reflection tokens give a soft critique signal that could be mapped to confidence, but it is not evaluated as calibration; conversely CalibRAG does not evaluate citation faithfulness or adaptive retrieval, so any head-to-head ranking would conflate distinct objectives.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs. retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring or benchmark-constructed knowledge conflict, no adversary assumed; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, both black-box and white-box query/retriever/generator visibility, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, self-think reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive injection, not a defense)
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support (faithfulness); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defense action evaluated)
rationale: Both papers concern problematic content reaching the generator in a RAG pipeline, but they occupy orthogonal roles: FaithfulRAG is a generation-side defense for benign parametric-vs-context knowledge conflicts, while PoisonedRAG is an offensive corpus-poisoning attack assuming an adversary with corpus write access and a small insertion budget. The failure types (consistency vs. adversarial corruption), evidence assumptions (benign conflict vs. attacker-crafted texts), intervention points (generator reasoning vs. corpus injection), metric targets (answer correctness vs. attack success rate), and action policies (reconciled answer vs. none) all diverge. Putting them on the same leaderboard would conflate a defense method with an attack methodology and would misrepresent both. The verdict is invalid because the problem settings are fundamentally incompatible, not merely partially overlapping.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require (a) reframing FaithfulRAG as a candidate defense and evaluating it under PoisonedRAG's threat model (same retriever, generator, datasets, target questions, insertion budget, black-box and white-box attacker assumptions), reporting attack success rate and clean accuracy; and (b) likewise evaluating any PoisonedRAG-style defense baselines on FaithfulRAG's benign knowledge-conflict benchmarks with matched faithfulness metrics. Both papers would also need to declare the same action policy (e.g., answer vs. abstain/quarantine) so that defensive behavior is measured consistently.
notes: Attack-paper vs. defense-paper pairs almost always fail comparability unless one explicitly instantiates the other's threat model.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict with some integrity/adversarial framing; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption. Partial overlap only.
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict + benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB worst case). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access (attacker injects ~5 malicious passages per target question), query control (attacker chooses target question and target answer), retriever visibility in both black-box and white-box settings, no generator weight access, explicit insertion budget, targeted-answer attack objective.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free elicitation + source-aware consolidation). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (adversarial injection into knowledge database). Opposite ends of the RAG pipeline.
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness under imperfect retrieval. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR). Different metric families.
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (consolidate and emit final answer; no abstention or escalation evaluated). PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper with no system-side action policy).
rationale: Both papers sit in the RAG-robustness/security space and both acknowledge that retrieved evidence can be malicious, but they play opposite roles: Astute RAG is a generator-side defense that consolidates internal and external knowledge to answer correctly under noisy/conflicting/malicious passages, while PoisonedRAG is a corpus-side attack that crafts a small budget of malicious passages to induce a target answer. The intervention point (generator vs. corpus), metric target (answer correctness vs. ASR), evidence assumption (benign/benchmark conflict vs. attacker-created with explicit threat model and insertion budget), and action policy (answer vs. unreported) all differ. They are complementary along an attack/defense axis rather than substitutable methods on a single leaderboard, so the verdict is partial rather than invalid or valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation in which Astute RAG is run as a defender against PoisonedRAG-style injections on the same corpus, retriever, and target-question set, reporting both ASR (attacker-side) and answer correctness (defender-side) under matched insertion budgets, attacker knowledge (black-box/white-box), and an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine). Without such a co-evaluated attack-vs-defense setup with aligned threat model and metrics, direct leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful.
notes: Astute RAG mentions malicious information but its main evaluation is on noisy/conflicting retrieval benchmarks, not PoisonedRAG-style targeted injections; this asymmetry reinforces the partial verdict.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume bounded passage injection with corpus write access and attacker query control, but PoisonedRAG specifies a budget of ~5 malicious texts per target question in black-box and white-box retriever-visibility settings with the attack objective of inducing a chosen target answer, while RobustRAG assumes an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense, bounded insertion budget m, generator access via prompting, and seeks certifiable lower bounds on response quality
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG, attacker side) vs context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG, defender side via isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG) vs answer correctness with certified robustness bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported for PoisonedRAG (attack paper, no defender action policy evaluated); answer / abstain for RobustRAG via aggregated 'I don't know' detection and keyword/decoding aggregation
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat space—integrity/adversarial corruption of RAG via attacker-injected passages with bounded corpus write access—so they share failure type and evidence assumption. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that intervenes at the corpus/index and reports attack success rate against undefended or weakly-defended RAG, while RobustRAG is a defensive contribution that intervenes at context assembly and generator prompting and reports certified accuracy under a bounded-injection adversary. They cannot be placed on the same leaderboard because one measures ASR achieved and the other measures certified correctness retained; the action policy is also asymmetric (no defender action in PoisonedRAG vs answer/abstain via aggregation in RobustRAG). The natural relationship is complementary—RobustRAG would be evaluated against PoisonedRAG—not directly rankable, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison meaningful, both works would need to be expressed in a common attacker-defender game: fix the same retriever, generator, dataset, target-question set, and identical insertion budget m; then report a shared metric pair (ASR and certified/empirical robust accuracy) for (i) no defense, (ii) RobustRAG, against (a) PoisonedRAG black-box, (b) PoisonedRAG white-box, and ideally adaptive variants aware of the isolate-then-aggregate defense. Explicit action-policy reporting (answer/abstain rates and conditions for abstention) and matched threat-model parameters (corpus write access, query control, retriever visibility) are required.
notes: Attack vs defense pairs in the same threat model are almost never directly comparable as leaderboard alternatives; partial captures the complementary relationship better than invalid because they share the same failure type and evidence assumption and are routinely paired in evaluation.

failure_type: RAGTruth: consistency/conflict, sufficiency (word-level hallucination including evident conflict and unsupported claims). RGB: relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness). Overlap on consistency/conflict only.
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict / benign retrieval error (responses naturally generated by diverse LLMs on standard RAG inputs, then annotated). RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios injected, counterfactual documents fabricated, deliberate absence of answer for rejection testbed).
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) plus generator prompting/training and verifier (fine-tuned hallucination detector). RGB: evaluation artifact only (diagnostic testbeds, no intervention proposed).
metric_target: RAGTruth: span/response-level hallucination detection (precision/recall over hallucinated spans), evidence support, citation faithfulness. RGB: answer correctness, rejection rate, integration accuracy, counterfactual identification rate.
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc detection of hallucinated spans); answer/abstain not evaluated as such. RGB: answer, abstain (negative rejection explicitly scored), expose conflict (counterfactual identification explicitly scored).
rationale: Both papers are evaluation artifacts for trustworthy RAG and share a concern with model outputs that are not supported by retrieved evidence, but they probe different phenomena with incompatible measurement targets. RAGTruth is a span-level hallucination-detection corpus over naturally generated RAG responses across QA, data-to-text, and summarization, scoring detector precision/recall and supporting fine-tuned verifiers. RGB is a constructed multi-ability stress test that scores LLM answer accuracy under controlled noise ratios, rejection rate when no answer is supported, integration over multi-hop evidence, and counterfactual identification rate. Because the unit of evaluation (response spans vs. final answer behavior), the evidence construction (naturalistic vs. injected), and the action policies scored (verify vs. answer/abstain/expose) differ, putting them on a single leaderboard would conflate detector quality with end-to-end answering behavior, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) run the same systems on both corpora and report aligned metric families (e.g., span-level hallucination F1 from RAGTruth and the four RGB ability scores reported separately, not aggregated), or (b) construct a shared task in which the same retrieval setup, generators, and explicitly labeled action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. flag span) are evaluated, with RAGTruth-style span annotations applied to RGB outputs and RGB-style noise/counterfactual conditions injected into RAGTruth contexts. Without such alignment, treating them as substitutable benchmarks for the same robust-RAG question is misleading.
notes: Both are categorized as evaluation_benchmark, but the failure surfaces measured (post-hoc hallucination spans vs. four ability axes) make them complementary diagnostics rather than competing scoreboards.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise (RGB also covers consistency/conflict via counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactuals); benign retrieval error / naturally occurring insufficiency (Sufficient Context: autorater applied to standard RAG datasets like HotPotQA, Musique, FreshQA)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (RGB benchmark); verifier + system-control policy + evaluation artifact (Sufficient Context: autorater + selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context stratifies %Correct/%Abstain/%Hallucinate; RGB uses accuracy, rejection rate, error detection rate)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both evaluate abstention explicitly: RGB's negative rejection testbed; Sufficient Context's selective generation)
rationale: Both papers analyze RAG behavior when retrieved context is imperfect and explicitly treat abstention as a desired action, so failure type (sufficiency/noise) and action policy overlap. However, RGB is a static four-testbed benchmark with synthetically controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactuals, intervening only at the evaluation-artifact layer, whereas Sufficient Context introduces a sufficiency autorater (verifier) and a selective-generation policy that combines sufficiency with self-confidence (system-control policy), evaluated on naturally retrieved contexts in existing QA datasets. The metric operationalizations therefore differ: RGB reports per-ability accuracy/rejection on constructed splits, while Sufficient Context reports hallucination/abstention stratified by autorater-labeled sufficiency and a selective-coverage curve. They are complementary lenses, not alternative entries on the same leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's autorater + selective generation on the RGB testbeds (especially negative rejection and noise robustness) and report RGB's metrics (accuracy, rejection rate, error detection) alongside Sufficient Context's stratified %C/%A/%H and selective-coverage curves; alternatively, have RGB-style methods report sufficiency-stratified outcomes on the same QA datasets (HotPotQA, Musique, FreshQA) with a shared retriever, generator set, and a common abstention threshold so that the rejection/selective behavior is measured on identical (Q,C) pairs.
notes: RGB is primarily a diagnostic benchmark while Sufficient Context is partly analysis + partly an intervention method; mixing benchmark vs. method is a recurring source of incomparability.

failure_type: consistency/conflict for FaithfulRAG; sufficiency plus consistency/conflict plus relevance/noise for RAGTruth
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations from LLMs over standard retrieved contexts (benign retrieval error and naturally occurring conflict). FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge.
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus plus detectors fine-tuned on it). FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training via self-fact mining and self-think pipeline.
metric_target: RAGTruth: span-level hallucination detection performance (detector precision/recall/F1). FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and contextual faithfulness of generated answers.
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify/flag hallucinated spans post-hoc. FaithfulRAG: answer after reconciling parametric vs contextual facts. No shared action policy is evaluated.
rationale: Both papers address RAG faithfulness, but they are fundamentally different artifact types. RAGTruth is an evaluation benchmark with word-level hallucination annotations across QA, summarization, and data-to-text, scoring post-hoc detector F1 over multiple hallucination categories. FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that mines self-facts and runs a self-think module to resolve parametric-vs-context conflict, scored by answer correctness on conflict QA benchmarks. The intervention point, metric target, action policy, and even the scope of failure types differ, so leaderboard-style ranking would conflate a detector benchmark with a generation method.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) evaluate FaithfulRAG's outputs on RAGTruth and report span-level hallucination rates under matched generators and retrieval setup, or (b) build a detector from RAGTruth and apply it to FaithfulRAG outputs vs baselines on the same knowledge-conflict QA benchmarks with shared metrics (answer correctness plus span-level faithfulness) and explicit action policies (answer vs flag vs abstain).
notes: Artifact-type mismatch (benchmark/detector corpus vs generation-time conflict-resolution method) is the dominant reason direct comparison is misleading.

failure_type: relevance/noise for both; consistency/conflict additionally for B via counterfactual noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for A; benign retrieval error plus benchmark-constructed stressor for B (counterfactual passages crafted)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression plus generator training for A; generator training for B
metric_target: answer correctness (F1/EM on ODQA) for both
action_policy: filter for A (NLI-gated fallback to no-retrieval is explicitly evaluated); answer for B (end-to-end generation; multi-task noise classification is a training auxiliary, not a runtime action)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RALMs on open-domain QA and share answer correctness (F1/EM) as the metric family, so they sit in the same general problem area. However, Paper A scopes noise to benign irrelevant retrieval and offers two distinct interventions (an NLI filter that triggers an explicit fallback-to-no-retrieval action, plus robust fine-tuning), while Paper B broadens the noise typology to include counterfactual/conflicting passages and intervenes only at training time via adaptive adversarial training with an auxiliary noise-type classifier. The action policies differ materially: A operationalizes a filter/abstain-from-retrieval policy at inference, while B always answers and never exposes a runtime gating or abstention decision. These differences in evidence assumption (irrelevant-only vs. irrelevant+counterfactual), intervention point (inference-time filter vs. training-only), and action policy make leaderboard-style ranking misleading; they are better framed as complementary mechanisms operating in overlapping but non-identical regimes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark that explicitly partitions retrieval noise into irrelevant and counterfactual subsets (e.g., RAG-Bench plus A's multi-hop ODQA suite), holding retriever (DPR), top-k, and generator backbone constant. Report F1/EM per noise type, and add an explicit action-policy axis: with vs. without the NLI filter/abstention gate applied to each system, so RAAT can be tested under the same filter and Yoran's robust-trained model can be tested without it. Without aligned noise taxonomy, shared backbone, and a common action-policy protocol, the comparison remains partial.
notes: RAAT's noise-type classifier is training-time auxiliary; if a follow-up paper exposed it as a runtime verifier/escalation signal, the action-policy gap would narrow.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); sufficiency and consistency/conflict additionally in Paper B
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real retrievers over Wikipedia/ODQA; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injections from news corpus
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting/training (robust fine-tuning); Paper B: evaluation artifact (no intervention proposed)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); Paper B additionally tracks selective risk/coverage via negative rejection rate
action_policy: Paper A: filter then answer (explicit); Paper B: answer for noise robustness testbed, abstain explicitly evaluated in the negative rejection testbed
rationale: Both papers concern LLM behavior under noisy/irrelevant retrieved context, so they share the relevance/noise failure type and answer-correctness metric. However, Paper A is a methods contribution (NLI filtering + robustness training) evaluated on five standard ODQA benchmarks under retriever-induced noise, whereas Paper B is a diagnostic benchmark (RGB) with synthetically controlled noise ratios over a news-derived corpus and additionally evaluates counterfactual robustness, information integration, and negative rejection as separate abilities. The intervention point differs fundamentally (system-level mitigation vs. evaluation artifact), the noise constructions and corpora are non-comparable, and the action policies only partially overlap — Paper A explicitly evaluates a filter→answer pipeline while RGB's noise-robustness testbed evaluates plain answer and isolates abstention only in its separate negative-rejection testbed. The papers should be discussed as complementary (one provides methods, the other a diagnostic lens), not ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robust-trained model on RGB's noise-robustness (and ideally negative-rejection and counterfactual) testbeds using the same backbone LLM, same retriever or supplied document sets, matched noise ratios, and a consistent action-policy specification (answer-only vs. filter+answer vs. answer+abstain). Report accuracy, rejection rate, and counterfactual override rate under identical prompting and decoding so that both papers' contributions are measured on the same axes.
notes: Methods-paper vs. benchmark-paper pairing — comparable as complementary, not as leaderboard substitutes.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (RGB negative rejection only)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer + abstain (RGB negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in retrieval-augmented LLMs and both construct benchmark-style noise stressors, with overlap on counterfactual and irrelevant noise. However, RAAT is a training-time intervention (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B with a noise-aware multi-task head) evaluated mainly with F1/EM on RAG-Bench built from NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ via DPR, while RGB is purely an evaluation artifact (no method) that decomposes RAG behavior into four separately scored abilities, including explicit negative rejection (abstain) and information integration, on news-derived corpora. Because RGB makes abstention a first-class measured action while RAAT only measures answering, and because the intervention point, noise construction, and metric families do not line up, they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as alternative methods. They are best discussed as complementary contributions (a method paper vs a diagnostic benchmark) within the same problem area, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the RAAT-trained generator and at least one matched untrained baseline on RGB's four ability testbeds (reporting accuracy, rejection rate, integration, counterfactual scores), and conversely run RGB's evaluated LLMs on RAG-Bench under identical noise-ratio definitions and the same retriever pipeline. Align action policy by either (a) requiring both to evaluate abstention with a shared rejection metric or (b) restricting comparison to the answer-only subset. Standardize noise construction (types, ratios, source domain) and use a common metric family before any ranking.
notes: RAAT does not evaluate abstention or rejection; treating its answer-only setup as comparable to RGB's negative-rejection testbed would be misleading.

failure_type: relevance/noise; sufficiency (CoN also handles unknown/insufficient evidence)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both treat distraction from imperfect retrievers, not adversarial insertion)
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting/training (read-judge-answer notes). Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (rejection rate on RealTimeQA). Paper B: answer correctness (no-harm-when-irrelevant, help-when-relevant); no abstention metric
action_policy: Paper A: answer or abstain ('unknown'). Paper B: filter then answer (fallback to no-context LLM); no abstain branch
rationale: Both papers target the same failure type—distraction by irrelevant retrieved passages under benign retrieval error on ODQA—so the high-level problem overlaps. However, the deployment-time action policies diverge: Chain-of-Note explicitly evaluates an abstain ('unknown') action and reports rejection rate, while Yoran et al. evaluate a filter-then-answer pipeline (NLI gating + fallback to no-context LLM) with no abstention metric. Intervention points also differ (generator-only reasoning vs. context-assembly filter plus optional training), and benchmarks/base models only partially overlap (NQ/TriviaQA shared, but Paper B emphasizes multi-hop). These are complementary operating policies on the same problem, not interchangeable systems on a single leaderboard, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same retriever, base generator, and benchmark suite (including a multi-hop subset and an unknown/unanswerable subset); define a shared action-policy taxonomy that scores both abstain and filter-then-answer (e.g., selective accuracy at matched coverage, plus no-harm delta vs. no-retrieval baseline); report both QA accuracy and abstention/rejection metrics for both methods; and run each method's training/prompting under the same compute and data budget.
notes: From a deployment standpoint, abstain vs filter-and-answer are operationally distinct controls and should not be ranked head-to-head without a unified selective-prediction protocol.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, retriever, verifier, evaluation artifact
metric_target: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: abstain (Sufficient Context), re-retrieve + verify (Self-RAG); action policies differ
rationale: Both papers aim to improve RAG factuality under noisy or insufficient retrieval, so the failure-type axis overlaps (sufficiency / relevance-noise). However, their intervention points diverge sharply: Sufficient Context is an inference-time selective generation policy built on an external sufficiency autorater plus self-confidence, while Self-RAG modifies training to embed reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval and self-critique. Their action policies are not the same operational lever—Sufficient Context's headline contribution is abstain-vs-answer (guided abstention), whereas Self-RAG centers on when-to-retrieve, parallel passage selection, and critique tokens without abstention as an evaluated action. Metric targets only partially overlap (answer correctness), with Sufficient Context emphasizing selective risk / coverage tradeoffs and Self-RAG emphasizing citation faithfulness. From a deployment-controls perspective these are complementary modules, not interchangeable systems on a single leaderboard, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods on the same benchmark with the same base generator and retriever, report risk-coverage curves with explicit abstain/answer/re-retrieve action labels for both, add a matched citation-faithfulness metric, and equalize compute/training assumptions (apply Sufficient-Context-style gating on top of a Self-RAG generator, or strip Self-RAG of its retrieval-on-demand head, so the contribution of each control is isolated).
notes: Self-RAG's reflection tokens could in principle support abstention, but the paper does not evaluate it as an action policy, so I treat the action-policy axis as genuinely divergent rather than under-specified.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibration); Self-RAG: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval error; neither addresses adversarial corruption
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker + verifier (forecasting function over (t,q,d)); Self-RAG: generator prompting/training + context assembly (reflection tokens, on-demand retrieval)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence (no explicit abstain/escalate policy evaluated); Self-RAG: answer + re-retrieve (adaptive) + verify (self-critique) — explicitly reported via reflection tokens
rationale: Both papers aim to improve RAG reliability, but they tackle distinct problems with distinct mechanisms. CalibRAG targets miscalibration of decision confidence via a learned forecasting function f(t,q,d) used for reranking and confidence output, optimizing calibration error and decision accuracy. Self-RAG targets factuality and citation accuracy via reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval and self-critique inside the generator. The failure types (uncertainty/calibration vs relevance/sufficiency), intervention points (reranker+verifier vs generator training+context assembly), metric targets (ECE-style calibration vs citation/evidence-support), and action policies (calibrated answer vs adaptive retrieve/critique) all differ. They are best discussed as complementary modules operating in different reliability dimensions, not as substitutes on a single leaderboard — hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared backbone (same base LM and retriever), evaluation on the same QA suite with a unified metric set covering both calibration (ECE/Brier/selective risk) and factuality/citation (attribution accuracy, evidence support), and a common explicit action policy frame (e.g., both methods report abstention thresholds at matched coverage, or both report adaptive-retrieval decisions). Ideally, Self-RAG's reflection-token confidence would be calibrated and CalibRAG would be evaluated on citation/grounding to enable like-for-like ranking.
notes: Self-RAG's action policy is explicitly evaluated via reflection tokens; CalibRAG's action policy is essentially 'answer with calibrated confidence' and does not evaluate abstain/escalate operating points, which compounds the mismatch.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (FaithfulRAG) vs. integrity/adversarial corruption (PoisonedRAG)
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge (benign). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target question, both black-box and white-box retriever visibility, black-box generator access, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining + self-think reasoning). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attack-side injection).
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support under conflict. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate.
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer after fact-level reconciliation (no abstain/escalate/quarantine evaluated). PoisonedRAG: unreported (offensive paper with no defender action policy).
rationale: Both papers concern what happens when retrieved context disagrees with what an LLM 'should' say, but they sit on opposite sides of the RAG pipeline and assume different threat models. FaithfulRAG is a defense-style generator intervention for naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflict, measured by answer correctness, with no explicit abstain/quarantine policy. PoisonedRAG is an offensive corpus-injection attack with explicit write access and an insertion budget, measured by attack success rate, with no defender action policy at all. The failure type (benign conflict vs. adversarial corruption), evidence assumption, intervention point, metric family, and action policy all diverge, and notably FaithfulRAG's push toward stronger context-faithfulness would, if anything, amplify PoisonedRAG's success. Treating these as alternatives on a single leaderboard would be misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Recast both into a shared attacker-vs-defender protocol: hold retriever, generator, corpus, and target-question set fixed; instantiate PoisonedRAG as the attack with stated write access, query control, retriever/generator visibility, and insertion budget; instantiate FaithfulRAG as one of several defenses; report attack success rate, clean-task accuracy, and an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine/expose conflict) under matched threat conditions. Only then can FaithfulRAG be ranked against other defenses, and PoisonedRAG against other attacks, on commensurate axes.
notes: Attack paper vs. conflict-resolution defense paper; their goals are not just different but partly antagonistic, so leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption (both); Astute RAG also covers relevance/noise and consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict + (worst-case) attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, no retriever access required (black-box) or white-box embedding access, query knowledge of target questions, ~5 malicious passages per target, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (post-retrieval consolidation); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (injection)
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness (worst-case accuracy); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (with internal source-aware consolidation/verify); PoisonedRAG: unreported (no defender action policy — it is an offensive method)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, evidence_assumption, action_policy, role (attack vs defense)
rationale: Both papers concern RAG robustness in the presence of harmful retrieved content, but they sit on opposite sides of the security ecosystem: Astute RAG is a training-free defense that operates at the generator by consolidating internal LLM knowledge with external passages, optimizing answer correctness under imperfect retrieval. PoisonedRAG is an offensive method that injects ~5 crafted passages per target question into the corpus and reports attack success rate, with an explicit threat model (corpus write access, known target questions, black-box or white-box retriever). The intervention point (generator vs corpus), metric target (accuracy vs ASR), and role (defender vs attacker) are inverse rather than substitutable, so they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as alternative methods. A direct ranking would be misleading because lowering Astute RAG's error and raising PoisonedRAG's ASR are not commensurable quantities.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct comparison cannot be made valid because attack vs defense are not substitutable. A meaningful joint evaluation would fix the same retriever, corpus, generator (e.g., Gemini/Claude), target question set, and PoisonedRAG injection budget (e.g., 5 malicious passages), then measure Astute RAG's accuracy and abstention behavior versus baseline RAG under PoisonedRAG attacks — reporting paired metrics (ASR↓ and answer accuracy↑) rather than ranking the two as alternatives. To rank as alternatives, one would instead need to pair Astute RAG with other defenses (e.g., RobustRAG, CAD) or pair PoisonedRAG with other attacks (e.g., GARAG, Phantom) under matched conditions.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pairing; the asymmetry of metric targets alone is sufficient to reject leaderboard-style comparison even before considering action policy.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume corpus write access; PoisonedRAG covers black-box and white-box retriever visibility while RobustRAG assumes adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge; PoisonedRAG uses ~5 malicious texts per target question, RobustRAG certifies against a bounded number m of injected passages; PoisonedRAG objective is to induce an attacker-chosen target answer, RobustRAG defends against arbitrary quality degradation
intervention_point: corpus/index for PoisonedRAG; context assembly/compression and generator prompting for RobustRAG
metric_target: attack success for PoisonedRAG; answer correctness and selective risk/coverage for RobustRAG
action_policy: unreported for PoisonedRAG; abstain and answer via secure aggregation for RobustRAG
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat ecosystem of adversarial corpus corruption against RAG with attacker write access and a bounded insertion budget, so failure type and evidence assumption overlap. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack contribution that intervenes at the corpus/index and reports attack success rate with no defensive action policy, while RobustRAG is a defense that intervenes at context assembly via isolate-then-aggregate, evaluates an explicit abstention action, and reports certified answer-quality bounds. Intervention point, metric target, and action policy therefore differ in the structural way that attack and defense papers always do: they are complementary modules where a defense like RobustRAG should be stress-tested with an attack like PoisonedRAG, not substitutable methods on a single leaderboard. The verdict is partial because the comparison is meaningful as an attack-vs-defense pairing but not as a head-to-head ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct leaderboard comparison is structurally impossible because one paper produces attacks and the other produces defenses. To make a meaningful joint evaluation, reframe as either (a) evaluate RobustRAG against PoisonedRAG and other attacks on a shared benchmark with matched retriever, generator, corpus, insertion budget m, query distribution, and reported action policies including abstention/coverage and certified-vs-empirical robustness, or (b) compare PoisonedRAG against other attacks under a fixed defense such as RobustRAG using attack success rate and degradation of certified accuracy as the shared metrics.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pair; partial rather than invalid because they share threat model and are designed to be evaluated against each other, and partial rather than under-specified because both papers explicitly specify their threat model and action policy within their own role.

failure_type: RAGTruth: sufficiency + consistency/conflict (hallucination against retrieved evidence); RGB: relevance/noise + sufficiency + consistency/conflict (multi-ability test split into noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring (naturally generated LLM outputs over standard RAG inputs, then human-annotated); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, all-noise rejection cases, counterfactual document injection)
intervention_point: Both: evaluation artifact. RAGTruth additionally probes verifier-style hallucination detectors (and fine-tuned detector); RGB probes generator behavior directly under stressor contexts.
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness measured at span level, detector precision/recall/F1; RGB: answer correctness, rejection rate (for negative rejection), integration accuracy, counterfactual identification — different metric families and aggregation units.
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc hallucination detection); action policy of the generator itself is unreported. RGB: explicitly evaluates abstain (negative rejection) and answer, with implicit expose-conflict signal for counterfactual subset.
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation benchmarks broadly motivated by reliability under imperfect evidence, but they measure substantively different things and cannot be placed on a common leaderboard. RAGTruth is a corpus of naturally generated RAG outputs annotated for word-level hallucinations, with metrics centered on span-level detection performance of verifier-style methods; it does not evaluate the generator's action policy (abstain, expose conflict). RGB constructs synthetic stressor testbeds and explicitly evaluates four distinct abilities including an abstain action policy (negative rejection) and counterfactual handling, scored via answer accuracy and rejection rate. Because the evidence-construction regime (natural vs. benchmark-constructed stressor), the metric target (detector F1 vs. answer/rejection accuracy), and the action policies actually evaluated diverge, the two should be discussed as complementary diagnostic tools, not as alternatives on the same ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A unified evaluation that (a) runs the same systems on both natural hallucination spans (RAGTruth) and constructed stressor testbeds (RGB), (b) reports both end-to-end answer correctness AND a hallucination-detection metric on the same outputs, (c) explicitly logs action policy choices (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict) with thresholds, and (d) shares retrievers/generators and evidence-construction protocols so that detector-quality gains and abstention-quality gains are separable rather than confounded across benchmarks.
notes: From a deployment-controls perspective the gap is sharp: RGB tells an operator whether the generator will refuse or get fooled by noisy/counterfactual evidence; RAGTruth tells an operator whether a downstream verifier can flag hallucinated spans. Different operational decisions.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: noise ratios, counterfactuals); benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (Sufficient Context: natural retrieval over QA datasets labeled by autorater)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (RGB); evaluation artifact + generator prompting (Sufficient Context selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (both); RGB also reports per-ability accuracy and rejection rate; Sufficient Context reports hallucination/abstention stratified by sufficiency
action_policy: answer, abstain (both explicitly evaluate abstention; Sufficient Context also operationalizes a guided abstention policy)
rationale: Both papers explicitly evaluate when a RAG system should answer vs abstain, and both probe failure modes tied to noise and insufficiency, so action policy is non-trivially shared (RGB via 'negative rejection', Sufficient Context via guided selective generation). However, RGB is purely a constructed diagnostic benchmark with hand-built noise ratios and counterfactuals across four separated abilities, while Sufficient Context defines a runtime sufficiency signal over natural retrieval and uses it to drive a deployment-time abstention controller. The evidence assumption (constructed stressor vs autorater-labeled natural retrieval), intervention point (benchmark-only vs benchmark+generator-prompting controller), and metric formulation (per-ability scores vs sufficiency-stratified hallucination/abstention rates) differ enough that they cannot be ranked on a shared leaderboard, but they are clearly complementary lenses on the same operational question of when to answer.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the Sufficient Context autorater + selective generation controller on RGB's four testbeds (or run RGB's LLMs through the Sufficient Context pipeline on the same QA datasets), report a common metric pair such as correct-when-answered and abstention rate under matched retrieval, and align the action-policy definitions (RGB's 'negative rejection' vs Sufficient Context's guided abstention threshold) so the operating points are directly comparable.
notes: From a deployment-controls perspective these are sibling-but-not-substitute artifacts: RGB is a pre-deployment audit suite, Sufficient Context is a runtime control signal.

failure_type: consistency/conflict for both; RAGTruth also covers relevance/noise and sufficiency
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error and naturally occurring conflict in real LLM outputs; FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflict
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact plus verifier via fine-tuned detector; FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training via self-fact mining and self-think
metric_target: RAGTruth: span/response-level hallucination detection performance; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and contextual faithfulness
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (benchmark-level, no deployment action evaluated); FaithfulRAG: answer (always-answer after reconciliation); neither evaluates abstain, filter, or escalate
rationale: Both papers target faithfulness in RAG and share consistency/conflict as a failure mode (RAGTruth explicitly annotates Evident Conflict spans, FaithfulRAG targets parametric-vs-context conflict). However, they sit at different layers of the stack: RAGTruth is an evaluation corpus supporting detection benchmarking and detector fine-tuning, while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that reconciles conflicts before answering. Their metric targets differ (hallucination-span detection F1 vs end-task answer accuracy/faithfulness), and only FaithfulRAG specifies an action policy (always-answer with reconciliation); RAGTruth reports no deployment-time action. They are complementary rather than rankable as substitute methods on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate FaithfulRAG on the RAGTruth benchmark (or generate RAGTruth-style word-level annotations on FaithfulRAG outputs) using the same generators, retrieval contexts, and a shared metric family (e.g., span-level hallucination rate plus end-task accuracy), and explicitly report a common action policy (answer vs abstain vs flag). Without shared task setup, metric, and action policy, direct ranking remains partial.
notes: Different artifact types (benchmark vs method) typically force partial unless the method is run on the benchmark with matched action labels.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B adds counterfactual noise)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (Paper A); benchmark-constructed stressor including counterfactual passages (Paper B)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator training (Paper A: NLI filter + fine-tuning on mixed contexts); generator training (Paper B: adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-awareness)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: filter + answer (Paper A explicitly drops non-entailing passages via NLI); answer with internal noise classification (Paper B); neither evaluates abstain or expose-conflict
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA and report answer correctness (EM/F1) on partially overlapping benchmarks (NQ in particular). However, Paper A scopes noise to irrelevant retrieval (benign retrieval error) and intervenes with an NLI-based passage filter plus fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts, whereas Paper B broadens the noise taxonomy to include counterfactual (conflict-inducing) passages constructed as a stressor and intervenes purely at the generator via adaptive adversarial training with a noise-awareness auxiliary task. These differences span four coordinates: the failure type (Paper B adds consistency/conflict), the evidence assumption (constructed counterfactuals vs. naturally irrelevant), the intervention point (context-level filter+train vs. generator-only adversarial train), and the action policy (explicit filter vs. answer with internal classification, with no abstain or conflict-exposure evaluated). They are complementary modules in the noise-robustness space rather than direct leaderboard substitutes, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark that includes the same irrelevant and counterfactual noise mixtures, using the same backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B) and retriever, and report identical metrics (EM/F1) alongside an explicit action-policy ledger (filter rate, abstention, conflict exposure). Cross-apply: run Paper A's NLI filter + robust fine-tuning on RAG-Bench's counterfactual subset, and run RAAT on Paper A's multi-hop ODQA setting, so each system is stressed under the other's noise typology with matched training-data budgets.
notes: Neither paper measures citation faithfulness or evidence support directly; both reduce 'robustness' to downstream answer accuracy, which masks differences in how conflict is handled.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency, consistency/conflict (counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (natural noisy retrieval over ODQA); Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios, plus synthetic counterfactual/conflict documents
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting/training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts); Paper B: evaluation artifact (benchmark, no proposed intervention)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness on ODQA; Paper B: answer correctness plus rejection rate and integration/counterfactual-specific accuracy
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (abstention not evaluated as a measured outcome); Paper B: answer + abstain (negative rejection rate explicitly measured)
rationale: Both papers concern noise robustness in RAG and study how irrelevant retrieved passages degrade LLM QA accuracy, so the failure type overlaps on the noise/relevance axis. However, Paper A is a methods paper proposing NLI-based filtering and robust fine-tuning evaluated on five standard ODQA benchmarks with naturally retrieved noisy passages, while Paper B is purely an evaluation benchmark (RGB) that synthesizes noisy contexts at controlled ratios and additionally evaluates negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness as separate abilities. The intervention point (method vs. evaluation artifact), evidence assumption (benign retrieval error vs. benchmark-constructed stressor and counterfactuals), and action policy (filter+answer with no abstention measurement vs. explicit negative-rejection scoring) all diverge, with metric target only partially overlapping. They are therefore complementary—Paper A's methods could be evaluated on Paper B's testbed—but cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable approaches to one shared task.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's two interventions (NLI filter and fine-tuned robust generator) on Paper B's RGB noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds using the same retriever and base LLM, and conversely report Paper B's noise-ratio sweep and rejection metric on Paper A's ODQA setup. Additionally align action policy by explicitly reporting both answer accuracy and abstention/rejection rate for both systems under matched noise constructions (natural and synthetic) so that the same operating point and outcome family are scored.
notes: Asymmetry in paper type (method vs. benchmark) is the dominant break; even if noise robustness were the only ability considered, the missing abstention/rejection measurement in Paper A still prevents direct ranking.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAAT: DPR-retrieved passages categorized into relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual noise; RGB: news articles plus ChatGPT-generated and search-retrieved distractors with controlled noise ratios)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, F1/EM/accuracy); selective risk/coverage (RGB rejection rate only)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer, abstain (RGB explicitly evaluates negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers target retrieval noise robustness and share a taxonomy that includes irrelevant/noisy and counterfactual documents, so the failure types substantially overlap. However, RAAT is a training-time intervention (adaptive adversarial training of LLaMA-2 7B on RAG-Bench built from NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ with DPR retrieval), while RGB is purely a diagnostic benchmark over news articles with ChatGPT-generated distractors and proposes no method. Their action policies differ in a load-bearing way: RAAT only measures answer correctness (F1/EM), whereas RGB explicitly evaluates negative rejection (abstention when all docs are noise) and information integration as separate abilities. Because of the method-vs-benchmark mismatch, divergent stressor construction, and unequal action policies, they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitutable approaches, but they are usefully complementary on the relevance/noise axis.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT-trained and baseline models on all four RGB testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) using RGB's metrics including rejection rate; conversely, evaluate a representative subset of RGB-tested LLMs on RAAT's RAG-Bench with matched noise-ratio sweeps; align the action policy by reporting both answer accuracy and abstention behavior, and use the same retriever and noise-injection protocol so that improvements can be attributed to the training intervention rather than benchmark differences.
notes: RGB is fundamentally an evaluation artifact while RAAT is a training method—direct ranking conflates 'method effectiveness' with 'benchmark difficulty,' which is the central comparability hazard here.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Paper A additionally targets uncertainty/OOD (real-time questions beyond pretraining scope)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; Paper B includes benchmark-constructed stressors via mixed relevant/irrelevant fine-tuning data; neither adversarial
