intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting + generator training (CoN reasoning step, fine-tuned LLaMa-2 on 10K CoN traces). Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI-based passage filtering) + generator training (fine-tune on mixed contexts).
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/accuracy) for both; Paper A also reports selective risk/coverage (rejection rate on unanswerable real-time questions); Paper B focuses on accuracy degradation/recovery, including multi-hop
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain (explicit 'unknown' output is evaluated). Paper B: answer + filter (NLI gate decides whether to use retrieval; abstention is not evaluated).
rationale: Both papers tackle the same failure type—distraction/noise from irrelevant retrieved passages in open-domain QA under benign retrieval errors—and both include a generator-side training component, so they are clearly in the same problem family. However, their intervention mechanisms differ (per-document reading notes in CoN vs. NLI passage filtering plus mixed-context fine-tuning in IrrelevantContext), and crucially their action policies diverge: CoN explicitly evaluates abstention with a rejection-rate metric, while IrrelevantContext's filter governs whether to consult retrieval and never measures an 'unknown' output. The metric families overlap on EM but only CoN reports selective risk, and IrrelevantContext additionally emphasizes multi-hop settings not assessed by CoN. These coordinate breaks mean leaderboard-style ranking would conflate different actions and operating regimes, so the comparison is partial rather than valid—they are best presented as complementary mechanisms.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods with the same retriever and base generator on a shared benchmark suite covering single-hop and multi-hop ODQA plus an unanswerable/real-time slice; report a common metric grid including EM on benign retrieval, accuracy with injected irrelevant passages, and (for the abstention setting) rejection rate, coverage, and selective accuracy. Make action policy explicit for both systems—either equip the NLI/fine-tuned model with a calibrated abstain head or restrict CoN to forced-answer mode for the accuracy-only comparison—so each metric is computed under the same allowed action set.
notes: If one restricts the comparison to forced-answer EM under irrelevant-context injection, a narrow valid comparison is achievable; the partial verdict reflects the published reporting, not in-principle incompatibility.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, retriever, verifier, system-control policy
metric_target: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: abstain (Sufficient Context); re-retrieve, verify, answer (Self-RAG)
rationale: Both papers target hallucination/factuality failures in RAG when retrieved evidence is imperfect, so the failure type (sufficiency/relevance noise) and overall motivation overlap. However, Sufficient Context intervenes post-hoc via a sufficiency autorater plus self-confidence to drive a selective-generation (abstain) policy at inference, with the primary metric being correctness conditional on answering. Self-RAG instead modifies generator training to emit reflection tokens that trigger on-demand re-retrieval and self-critique, and additionally evaluates citation/support faithfulness for long-form outputs. The intervention points (selective-generation policy vs. trained reflective retrieve+verify), action policies (abstain vs. re-retrieve/verify/answer), and metric families (selective risk vs. citation faithfulness) diverge, so they are complementary mechanisms rather than head-to-head alternatives on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared benchmark with (a) the same retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; (b) a unified action-policy schema (answer / abstain / re-retrieve / verify) instrumented for both systems; (c) a common metric suite including selective accuracy (cover-risk curves), citation/support faithfulness, and hallucination rate stratified by sufficiency labels; and (d) explicit reporting of how each system would be evaluated when its native action (Self-RAG's re-retrieve, Sufficient Context's abstain) is exercised. Without this, ranking one above the other conflates different operating regions.
notes: Self-RAG's citation-faithfulness evaluation is a meaningful axis Sufficient Context does not report; treating them as substitutable would hide this asymmetry.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise + sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; no adversarial threat model in either
intervention_point: reranker + generator prompting/training (CalibRAG via forecasting function reranking and confidence calibration); generator training + retriever (Self-RAG via reflection-token training and on-demand retrieval)
metric_target: calibration error + answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer with calibrated confidence (CalibRAG, no abstention/recovery explicitly evaluated); re-retrieve + verify via ISREL/ISSUP reflection tokens (Self-RAG)
rationale: Both papers sit in the broader RAG-control/reliability space but tackle different failure modes: CalibRAG addresses miscalibration of decision confidence by training a forecasting function f(t,q,d) that predicts decision correctness and reranks accordingly, while Self-RAG addresses adaptive retrieval and factual grounding by training an LM to emit reflection tokens (Retrieve/ISREL/ISSUP) that critique its own generations. Their headline metrics diverge - calibration error (ECE) and decision accuracy for CalibRAG versus citation faithfulness, factuality, and answer correctness for Self-RAG - and their action policies are also distinct: CalibRAG outputs an answer with a calibrated confidence score (no evaluated abstain/recover branch), whereas Self-RAG explicitly conditions generation and (non-)retrieval on critique-token outputs. Because the failure type, metric target, and action policy all differ, leaderboard-style ranking would misrepresent both systems; they are better framed as complementary control mechanisms operating on different reliability axes (confidence calibration vs. evidence-support self-critique).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both systems on (1) a shared benchmark suite that reports the same metric family - at minimum calibration error (ECE/Brier) AND citation/support faithfulness for both - (2) a common retriever, generator backbone, and corpus to isolate the intervention, (3) the same explicit action policy (e.g., both required to abstain when uncertainty exceeds a threshold, or both forced to always answer), and (4) a shared decision-making task where calibrated confidence is actually consumed by a downstream simulated user, so that Self-RAG's reflection tokens and CalibRAG's forecasting score can be mapped onto the same operating curve.
notes: Both are framed as 'control' but the control surface (confidence calibration vs. self-reflection tokens) and the quantity being controlled are different; treating them as direct alternatives would conflate calibration with faithfulness.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict (parametric vs legitimately retrieved context); PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, query control over target questions, both black-box and white-box retriever visibility, ~5 malicious texts insertion budget, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, contextual alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious text injection)
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness, evidence support (faithfulness); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR)
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (offensive paper with no defender action policy evaluated as primary contribution)
rationale: Both papers nominally touch on discrepancies in retrieved evidence within RAG, but they operate in fundamentally incompatible problem spaces. FaithfulRAG is a defense-side reasoning method that resolves benign, naturally occurring conflicts between the LLM's parametric knowledge and legitimately retrieved context, measured by answer correctness and faithfulness. PoisonedRAG is an offensive paper that crafts malicious passages and injects them into the corpus (corpus-write threat model with ~5 insertions per target question) to induce attacker-chosen answers, measured by attack success rate. All five coordinates diverge: failure type (consistency/conflict vs integrity/adversarial), evidence assumption (naturally occurring vs attacker-created), intervention point (generator vs corpus), metric target (correctness vs ASR), and action policy (reconciled answer vs no defender action evaluated). A direct leaderboard-style comparison would dangerously conflate parametric-conflict resolution with adversarial-poisoning defense and is therefore invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make any direct comparison meaningful, one would need to (a) evaluate FaithfulRAG as a defense against PoisonedRAG attacks on the same datasets, reporting ASR and ASR reduction under the same insertion budget, retriever, and generator; (b) report defender-side action policies (answer/abstain/expose conflict/quarantine) under poisoned conditions; and (c) align metric families so both papers report attack success, answer correctness, and faithfulness on a common benchmark with explicit threat-model parameters (corpus write access, query control, retriever visibility).
notes: Attack paper vs defense-for-different-problem paper; misclassifying as 'partial' would understate the threat-model incompatibility.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict (with passing mention of malicious info); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict + benchmark-constructed worst-case (RGB all-negative); no explicit threat model. PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model — corpus write access = yes (injects into DB), query control = attacker selects target question, retriever visibility = both black-box and white-box evaluated, generator access = none (goal is induced target answer), insertion budget = ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = force attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free internal-knowledge elicitation + source-aware consolidation). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious text injection).
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness under imperfect retrieval. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR).
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (after iterative consolidation and reliability-based selection). PoisonedRAG: unreported / not applicable — attacker side, no defender action policy evaluated.
rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior under corrupted or imperfect retrieval, but they occupy fundamentally opposite roles: PoisonedRAG is an attacker-side contribution that injects malicious passages into the knowledge database to maximize attack success rate under an explicit threat model (corpus write access, ~5-text insertion budget, attacker-chosen target Q/A), while Astute RAG is a defender-side, generator-stage method that consolidates internal LLM knowledge with retrieved passages to preserve answer correctness under noisy/conflicting/worst-case retrieval. The intervention point (corpus injection vs. generator prompting), the metric target (ASR vs. answer accuracy), and the action policy (none on attacker side vs. answer-after-consolidation) differ on every axis, and the threat model is only explicitly specified by PoisonedRAG. Placing them on the same leaderboard as 'alternative methods' would conflate attack and defense and seriously mislead.
what_valid_comparison_requires: These two papers cannot be ranked head-to-head. A valid use of the pair would treat PoisonedRAG as a stressor and Astute RAG as one of several defenses, then report a 2-D table: (defender method × attacker variant) with matched retriever, generator, corpus, insertion budget, and target-question set, measuring both clean answer accuracy and ASR / accuracy-under-attack. A 'valid' comparison would only arise if Astute RAG were re-cast as a defender baseline against PoisonedRAG (or vice versa, PoisonedRAG used against Astute RAG's pipeline) under a shared evaluation protocol.
notes: Astute RAG mentions 'malicious' information but does not adopt an explicit adversary model or insertion-budget evaluation comparable to PoisonedRAG's; its worst-case RGB setting is benchmark-constructed, not attacker-optimized.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; corpus write access = yes for both; query control = attacker-chosen target questions in PoisonedRAG, adaptive attacker with target query in RobustRAG; retriever visibility = black-box and white-box for PoisonedRAG, full-knowledge adaptive for RobustRAG defense threat model; generator access = black-box query for attacker, defender owns generator for RobustRAG; insertion budget = ~5 malicious texts (PoisonedRAG), bounded k' passages (RobustRAG); attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer (PoisonedRAG) vs. preserve correctness under such attacks (RobustRAG)
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack injects malicious passages); context assembly/compression and generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG ASR); answer correctness with certifiable robustness lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: answer (target-answer induction in PoisonedRAG); answer with explicit abstain ('I don't know') and aggregation in RobustRAG
rationale: Both papers operate within the same threat surface—integrity/adversarial corruption of RAG via attacker-created passages injected into the corpus—so they share failure type and evidence assumption. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution measuring attack success rate when injecting ~5 malicious texts to induce a target answer, while RobustRAG is a defensive contribution measuring certifiable robust accuracy via an isolate-then-aggregate mechanism at context assembly/generation. The intervention points (corpus injection vs. context-assembly aggregation), metric targets (ASR vs. robust correctness with certificates), and action policies (induce-answer vs. answer/abstain-with-aggregation) are fundamentally different roles, not interchangeable methods. They are complementary modules in a single security stack and should be discussed as attack–defense pairing (e.g., does RobustRAG certify against PoisonedRAG's budget?), not ranked on a shared leaderboard—hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) pair PoisonedRAG with another corpus-injection attack under identical retriever, generator, corpus, target-question set, insertion budget, and ASR metric; or (b) pair RobustRAG with another retrieval-corruption defense evaluated against the same attack suite (including PoisonedRAG), with matched k/k' budget, identical certification or empirical-robust-accuracy definition, and shared abstain semantics. To bridge the current pair, both works would need a common attack–defense evaluation harness reporting ASR, clean accuracy, certified robust accuracy, and abstain rate on the same datasets/LLMs with the same threat-model parameters.
notes: Attack vs. defense pairs almost never qualify as 'valid' alternatives; partial captures the legitimate complementary relationship without conflating roles.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring (real LLM-generated hallucinations annotated post-hoc on standard QA/summ/data-to-text RAG); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents, curated negative-rejection cases)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally targets verifier/detector training
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support, citation faithfulness (span-level hallucination detection F1); RGB: answer correctness, plus rejection/integration/counterfactual identification rates
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc hallucination detection over generated spans); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection) + expose conflict (counterfactual robustness)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation artifacts concerned with trustworthiness when retrieved evidence is imperfect, so the failure-type space overlaps (noise, sufficiency, conflict). However, RAGTruth supplies word-level annotations on naturally produced LLM outputs and primarily scores hallucination *detectors* (evidence support / citation faithfulness, with a verify action), while RGB constructs controlled testbeds with engineered noise ratios and counterfactual injections and scores the *generator LLM* on answer accuracy, abstention, and conflict exposure. Because evidence construction, metric family, and the evaluated action policy differ, a number on RAGTruth and a number on RGB cannot be placed on a common leaderboard; they are complementary diagnostics of RAG trustworthiness, hence partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, both works would need to evaluate the same system against the same action-policy contract (e.g., answer/abstain/expose-conflict) on a shared evidence regime — for example, run RAGTruth-trained detectors as verifiers on top of RGB's noisy/counterfactual testbeds, and report a common metric family (faithfulness/support plus rejection and counterfactual-identification rates) with matched retrievers, generators, and stressor construction protocols.
notes: Both are clearly 'evaluation_benchmark', but RAGTruth is a detector-training corpus while RGB is an LLM-ability diagnostic; treating them as alternatives risks category error.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios, counterfactual injections), naturally occurring conflict / insufficiency (Sufficient Context: stratification of existing QA benchmarks via autorater)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (RGB), evaluation artifact + verifier + generator prompting/system-control policy (Sufficient Context)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context selective generation), evidence support (RGB negative rejection / counterfactual)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via 'negative rejection' testbed; Sufficient Context via selective generation)
rationale: Both papers contribute to RAG evaluation and explicitly study when LLMs answer, abstain, or hallucinate under imperfect retrieval, so they share a faithfulness/abstention concern. However, RGB is essentially an evaluation artifact—four disjoint testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) constructed from controlled news data with stressors designed to isolate each ability—whereas Sufficient Context defines a (query, context) sufficiency property, deploys an LLM autorater on existing QA benchmarks to stratify behavior, and adds a selective generation intervention at the verifier/system-control layer. The intervention points, evidence assumptions (constructed stressors vs. naturally occurring sufficiency variation on standard QA), and metric families (per-ability scores vs. correct/abstain/hallucinate stratified by sufficiency + selective-coverage gains) all diverge, so a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate a diagnostic benchmark with a method paper. The comparison is partial: they are complementary lenses on overlapping phenomena.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's autorater + selective generation pipeline on RGB's four testbeds (and conversely re-stratify Sufficient Context's QA datasets by RGB-style noise ratios and counterfactual injections) using the same retriever, generator, prompts, and a unified metric family (correct/abstain/hallucinate + per-ability accuracy and negative-rejection precision). Only then can one report whether the sufficiency-based selective generation improves RGB's negative-rejection score and counterfactual robustness, making the two artifacts directly comparable.
notes: Action policy is not the breaking coordinate here—both papers explicitly evaluate abstention—but intervention point and evidence construction differ substantially.

failure_type: RAGTruth covers broad hallucination (sufficiency, consistency/conflict, relevance/noise); FaithfulRAG narrowly targets consistency/conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error and naturally occurring conflict in LLM-generated outputs across QA, summarization, data-to-text. FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and retrieved context.
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact plus optional fine-tuned detector. FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training via self-fact mining, alignment, self-think.
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support and citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection F1. FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and contextual faithfulness on QA benchmarks.
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc detection of hallucinated spans). FaithfulRAG: answer (after internal reconciliation). Neither evaluates the other's action policy.
rationale: Both papers sit in the RAG-faithfulness space, but they are categorically different artifacts. RAGTruth is an evaluation benchmark with word-level hallucination annotations (plus a fine-tuned detector baseline) measuring detection F1 over already-generated responses, while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that mines self-facts and runs a self-think module to reconcile parametric/contextual conflicts before answering. They differ on intervention point (evaluation artifact vs. generator method), metric target (detection F1 vs. answer correctness), action policy (verify vs. answer), and even failure-type breadth. Direct leaderboard ranking would be misleading because one produces a labeled corpus and a detector, while the other produces a generator-side conflict resolver.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate FaithfulRAG-generated outputs on RAGTruth's tasks/contexts and score them with RAGTruth's span-level hallucination metric, or alternatively fine-tune/evaluate RAGTruth's detector pipeline as a verifier on FaithfulRAG's QA benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, etc.) using identical retrievers, generators, conflict construction, metric definitions, and explicit answer-vs-verify action labels.
notes: RAGTruth is fundamentally a benchmark/detector while FaithfulRAG is a generation method; they are complementary rather than substitutable.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B counterfactual only)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (Paper A, DPR-style natural irrelevance); benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper B, three engineered noise categories incl. counterfactual)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (Paper A: NLI filter + fine-tune); generator prompting or training (Paper B: adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise classifier)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, EM/F1)
action_policy: filter + answer (Paper A NLI baseline explicitly filters non-entailing passages); answer (Paper B, no filter action; internal noise classification is auxiliary, not an action label)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RALMs, train the generator on noisy contexts, and evaluate answer correctness on overlapping ODQA datasets (e.g., NQ), so they share substantial common ground. However, Paper A scopes failure to irrelevant context drawn from natural retrieval and pairs fine-tuning with an explicit NLI-based filter action, whereas Paper B constructs three engineered noise classes (relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual) and trains adaptively without any filtering action, additionally covering consistency/conflict failures. The evidence assumption (natural distractors vs benchmark-constructed adversarial noise mix), the action policy (filter+answer vs answer-only), and the breadth of failure type therefore diverge, so head-to-head leaderboard ranking would conflate different operating regions. The papers are best discussed as complementary mechanisms on partially overlapping noise distributions rather than as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-evaluate both methods under a unified noise construction protocol that includes both naturally retrieved distractors and the three RAAT noise categories, holding retriever (e.g., DPR), corpus, base generator (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), prompt template, and training-set size constant; report EM/F1 stratified by noise type, plus explicit action-policy labels (answer, filter, abstain) and any filtering precision/recall, so that the NLI-filter pipeline and the RAAT-trained generator are scored on identical inputs and identical action spaces.
notes: Paper B cites Yoran et al. (Paper A) as prior work, confirming shared problem space but not equivalent setup; counterfactual noise in B is the main scope-breaking element.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict and sufficiency additionally in rgb2023 (counterfactual robustness, negative rejection)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); irrelevantContext2023 also touches benign retrieval error from real retrievers, while rgb2023 explicitly synthesizes noise ratios and counterfactual documents
intervention_point: irrelevantContext2023: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training; rgb2023: evaluation artifact (no intervention proposed, benchmark only)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); rgb2023 additionally reports selective risk/coverage-like rejection rate and a counterfactual identification metric
action_policy: irrelevantContext2023: answer (after filter; fall back to closed-book when filtered); rgb2023: answer + abstain (negative rejection ability explicitly evaluated)
rationale: Both papers concern LLM behavior under noisy retrieved context within ODQA-style settings, so the failure-type overlap on relevance/noise is real. However, irrelevantContext2023 is a method paper proposing two interventions (NLI-based passage filtering and fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts) measured by answer accuracy with an implicit answer policy, whereas rgb2023 is an evaluation benchmark spanning four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and explicitly scores abstention. The intervention point (method vs. evaluation artifact), the metric family (pure QA accuracy vs. multi-ability scoring including rejection), and the action policy (no abstain in A vs. mandatory abstain evaluation in B) all differ, so a leaderboard-style head-to-head ranking is not meaningful. The two are complementary—A's methods could be evaluated on RGB—but not directly substitutable, hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run irrelevantContext2023's NLI filter + robust fine-tuning on the RGB noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds with the same base LLMs and retrievers, report not only accuracy but rejection rate and counterfactual identification, and explicitly define an action policy (answer/abstain) that both systems honor; alternatively, restrict scope to RGB's noise-robustness testbed only and align corpora, retrievers, and prompts so the two contributions are evaluated under identical conditions.
notes: Core asymmetry is method paper vs. benchmark paper; this alone usually precludes valid direct comparison even when the topical area matches.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAAT: DPR retrieval over Wikipedia with filtered golden contexts; RGB: news articles with ChatGPT-generated and human-filtered noise/counterfactual passages at varying ratios)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT), evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (RAAT: F1/EM; RGB: accuracy, plus rejection rate and error detection rate for separate testbeds)
action_policy: answer (RAAT), answer + abstain (RGB via negative rejection testbed)
rationale: Both papers concern noise robustness in RAG and overlap on relevance/noise and counterfactual conflict failure types. However, RAAT is a method paper proposing adaptive adversarial training of LLaMA-2 7B with a multi-task noise-awareness objective, whereas RGB is a diagnostic benchmark that proposes no intervention and instead decomposes RAG into four separate testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) across 6 LLMs in English and Chinese. The intervention points (generator training vs. evaluation artifact) are categorically different, the corpora and noise-construction protocols differ (DPR/Wikipedia with ≥2 golden contexts vs. news + ChatGPT-generated stressors at controlled noise ratios), and only RGB explicitly evaluates an abstain action policy (negative rejection) while RAAT reports only answer-generation F1/EM. They are complementary—RAAT could be scored on RGB—but cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable methods, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate RAAT (and an equivalent baseline LLM) on RGB's four testbeds using RGB's accuracy, rejection rate, and error detection rate metrics in both languages, or rebuild RAG-Bench with explicit abstain labels and matched noise-ratio conditions, holding retriever, generator, noise typology mapping, and action-policy reporting (answer vs. abstain) constant. Without that, comparisons collapse to qualitative claims about overlapping failure types.
notes: Classic method-vs-benchmark mismatch; verdict driven primarily by intervention_point and action_policy breaks rather than topical disagreement.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Chain-of-Note additionally targets uncertainty/OOD (unknown questions)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor; Chain-of-Note also includes naturally occurring out-of-knowledge cases via RealTimeQA
intervention_point: Chain-of-Note: generator prompting/training only (note-taking pre-answer); Irrelevant Context: reranker/filter (NLI filter) plus generator prompting/training (mixed relevant/irrelevant fine-tuning)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/accuracy) shared; Chain-of-Note adds selective risk/coverage via rejection rate on unknown questions; Irrelevant Context does not evaluate abstention but stresses multi-hop accuracy
action_policy: Chain-of-Note: answer + abstain ('unknown'); Irrelevant Context: filter then answer (no explicit abstain policy evaluated)
rationale: Both papers target the same core failure mode—RALMs being distracted by irrelevant retrieved passages on open-domain QA, evaluated on overlapping benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA)—and both involve generator fine-tuning as part of the fix. However, the intervention points differ materially: Irrelevant Context combines an NLI-based pre-generation filter with robust fine-tuning, while Chain-of-Note operates purely at the generator with explicit note-then-answer reasoning. The action policies also diverge: Chain-of-Note explicitly evaluates an 'unknown' abstention behavior with a rejection-rate metric, whereas Irrelevant Context only evaluates answer accuracy with no abstain channel reported. These differences mean a leaderboard-style ranking on a single accuracy number would conflate distinct mechanisms (filter+train vs. reasoning+abstain) and miss the selective-prediction axis on which Chain-of-Note is partly judged, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods with the same retriever (e.g., DPR) and base generator (e.g., LLaMa-2) on a common evaluation suite that includes (a) standard single-hop ODQA (NQ/TriviaQA), (b) the multi-hop setting used by Irrelevant Context, and (c) a held-out unanswerable/out-of-knowledge slice (RealTimeQA-style). Report a shared metric family covering EM/accuracy with and without injected irrelevant passages, plus selective-prediction metrics (rejection rate, coverage-risk) under an explicitly defined action policy (answer vs. abstain). Additionally, ablate Chain-of-Note + NLI filter and Irrelevant Context's fine-tune + note-taking so the intervention-point contributions are separated.
notes: If one restricts comparison to plain EM on single-hop ODQA with relevant+noisy contexts, the overlap is tighter, but the abstention/coverage axis in Chain-of-Note still has no counterpart in Irrelevant Context.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: verifier, system-control policy, generator prompting or training, retriever
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: abstain, answer, re-retrieve, verify
rationale: Both papers target RAG factuality and incorporate a self-assessment signal about whether retrieved context supports the answer, so they share the sufficiency/relevance failure family under benign retrieval. However, Sufficient Context intervenes post-hoc with an external autorater plus a selective-generation policy whose action space is answer-vs-abstain, evaluated via correct/abstain/hallucinate rates and selective risk. Self-RAG instead bakes the mechanism into generator training via reflection tokens that govern on-demand re-retrieval and self-critique, and reports answer correctness plus citation/support metrics on long-form generation. The intervention points (verifier+policy wrapper vs. trained generator+adaptive retriever), action policies (abstain vs. re-retrieve/critique), and the metric mix (selective coverage vs. citation faithfulness) all diverge enough that leaderboard-style ranking would conflate different design choices, even though the high-level motivation overlaps; this makes the pair partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared QA benchmark with the same retriever, base generator family, and context budget; report a common metric suite that includes selective accuracy at matched coverage, hallucination/abstention rates, and citation/support faithfulness; expose both systems' action policies under identical labels (answer/abstain/re-retrieve) so that Self-RAG's reflection-driven re-retrieval and Sufficient Context's confidence-gated abstention are evaluated on the same operating curve.
notes: Methods are plausibly complementary: Self-RAG's reflection tokens could feed a Sufficient-Context-style selective layer, suggesting partial rather than invalid.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG primary), relevance/noise (Self-RAG primary), sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both); no adversarial threat model
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker + system-control policy (forecasting function over (t,q,d)); Self-RAG: generator prompting/training (reflection tokens) + retriever (on-demand retrieval)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness for decision-making; Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer (with calibrated confidence; abstain not explicitly evaluated); Self-RAG: re-retrieve + filter (via reflection tokens)
rationale: Both papers aim to improve RAG reliability beyond vanilla retrieve-then-generate, but they target fundamentally different failure modes and use different control surfaces. CalibRAG trains a forecasting function f(t,q,d) to predict decision correctness, intervening at reranking to produce calibrated confidence supporting human decision-making (primary metric: calibration error / decision accuracy). Self-RAG trains the generator to emit reflection tokens that govern on-demand retrieval and self-critique, optimizing factuality and citation accuracy. The action policies differ (calibrated answer vs. adaptive retrieve/filter via reflection tokens), the intervention points differ (reranker/scoring vs. generator training), and the primary metric families differ (calibration vs. citation faithfulness). Therefore they should be discussed as complementary mechanisms in a reliability stack rather than ranked on one leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same base LM, retriever, and benchmark; require both systems to report a common metric suite covering (i) calibration (ECE/Brier) on a shared decision task, (ii) factuality/citation faithfulness on long-form QA, and (iii) answer correctness; specify and evaluate identical action policies (e.g., both abstain-enabled or both answer-only); ablate adaptive retrieval and calibrated reranking under matched compute. Without these, only an operating-region or complementary-module comparison is defensible.
notes: Both are non-adversarial robust-RAG work; overlap is conceptual (reliability) but coordinates clearly diverge — partial rather than valid.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict / benchmark-constructed parametric-vs-context discrepancy; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target question, both black-box and white-box retriever visibility, no generator weight access required, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts per target, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think before generation); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious passage injection) — offensive, not defensive
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support / citation faithfulness; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported defender action policy — paper is an attack, not a defense
rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior when retrieved evidence is problematic, but they sit on opposite sides of the system: FaithfulRAG is a defense/reconciliation method for naturally occurring parametric-vs-context knowledge conflicts, operating at the generator with fact-level alignment and self-thinking, and is scored by answer correctness. PoisonedRAG is an offensive paper that assumes corpus write access and attacker-chosen target questions/answers, injects ~5 malicious passages, and is scored by attack success rate. The failure type, evidence assumption (organic conflict vs adversarial corpus poisoning), intervention point (generator-side reasoning vs corpus-side injection), metric family (accuracy vs ASR), and action policy (answer with reconciliation vs no defender policy at all) all diverge. They cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitute methods because one produces the attack and the other mitigates a different threat surface.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Reframe both under a shared defender-side benchmark: instantiate FaithfulRAG (and any baselines) as a defense evaluated against PoisonedRAG-style adversarial corpus injection alongside natural knowledge-conflict perturbations, using the same retriever, generator, corpus, insertion budget, and threat model. Report a common metric set (clean accuracy, accuracy-under-attack, attack success rate, and an explicit answer/abstain/expose-conflict action policy) so the two interventions can be compared on the same axes; without that shared defender protocol, direct ranking remains category-error.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense category mismatch; even if FaithfulRAG were stress-tested with PoisonedRAG injections, that would be a complementary evaluation, not a same-leaderboard substitution.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption (PoisonedRAG); relevance/noise + consistency/conflict + some integrity/adversarial corruption (Astute RAG)
evidence_assumption: PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model (corpus write access via insertion of 5 malicious texts per target question; black-box and white-box retriever visibility; no generator access; query control limited to attacker-chosen target questions; attack objective = induce target answer). Astute RAG: mixture of benign retrieval error, benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB worst-case), naturally occurring conflict; does not formalize an attacker.
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive). Astute RAG: generator prompting (defensive, training-free consolidation).
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success rate. Astute RAG: answer correctness (incl. worst-case accuracy).
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: unreported / not applicable (attack paper, no defender action). Astute RAG: answer (after source-aware reliability comparison); no explicit abstain/quarantine evaluated.
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, evidence_assumption (role asymmetry: attack vs defense)
rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior under corrupted or imperfect retrieved evidence, but they occupy fundamentally different roles: PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that injects malicious passages into the knowledge database and reports attack success rate under specified attacker capabilities, while Astute RAG is a defensive, generator-side consolidation method whose primary metric is answer correctness (including worst-case accuracy on RGB). The intervention point (corpus vs. generator), the metric family (ASR vs. accuracy), and the very objective (induce wrong answer vs. preserve right answer) do not align, so they cannot occupy the same leaderboard as substitutable methods. They are complementary—PoisonedRAG can serve as a stressor for Astute RAG—rather than alternative robust-RAG methods, hence the comparison is invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) compare Astute RAG against another defense (e.g., RobustRAG, conflict-aware decoding) under a shared attack such as PoisonedRAG, using matched retriever, generator, insertion budget, and a common metric (post-attack accuracy and/or ASR), or (b) compare PoisonedRAG against another attack (e.g., GARAG, Phantom) under the same defender, threat model, and ASR definition. Direct A-vs-B ranking would also require a single shared metric family and explicit reporting of the defender's action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine).
notes: Asymmetry of attack vs defense is the core break; even if one treats both as 'robust RAG' work, they cannot be ranked on a common leaderboard without choosing a side and matching the missing role.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; corpus write access assumed by both; PoisonedRAG: attacker chooses target Q and target A, ~5 injected passages, black-box and white-box retriever knowledge; RobustRAG: adaptive attacker with full knowledge of defense, bounded number m' of corrupted passages, arbitrary user queries
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attack-side injection); RobustRAG: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (isolate-then-aggregate decoding/keyword)
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success rate; RobustRAG: answer correctness with certified robustness lower bound (also implicitly cost/latency of multi-group decoding)
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: answer (induce attacker-chosen target answer, no abstain reported); RobustRAG: answer + abstain ('I don't know' aggregation rule)
rationale: Both papers operate on the same threat surface—knowledge-database corruption of RAG by an attacker who can inject a bounded number of malicious passages—so failure type (integrity/adversarial corruption) and evidence assumption (attacker-created evidence, corpus write access) overlap. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack contribution whose intervention point is the corpus and whose metric target is attack success rate against attacker-chosen target QA pairs, while RobustRAG is a defense whose intervention point is context assembly plus generator prompting via isolate-then-aggregate, with a metric target of certified accuracy and an explicit answer-vs-abstain action policy. These are complementary attack/defense artifacts rather than substitutable methods on the same leaderboard, so a direct ranking would be category-confused. The relation is partial: they belong in a joint evaluation matrix, not in a head-to-head comparison.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To upgrade to valid, the pairing must be reframed as 'attack vs. defense evaluation' rather than 'alternative methods.' Concretely: (1) run RobustRAG against PoisonedRAG attacks under matched retriever, generator, corpus size, and insertion budget m'; (2) report both attack-side (ASR on attacker-chosen targets) and defense-side (certified accuracy, clean accuracy, abstention rate) metrics on the same datasets; (3) align action policies so both papers explicitly state when the system answers vs. abstains vs. flags corruption; (4) for true substitutability one would instead compare RobustRAG against another defense (e.g., perplexity-based filtering, majority voting) under the same PoisonedRAG threat model.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense asymmetry; leaderboard-style ranking is the wrong frame even though the two papers cite the same threat model.

failure_type: RAGTruth: consistency/conflict (word-level hallucination/unsupported claims); RGB: relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict (counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring (LLM-generated responses over standard RAG contexts, then human-annotated); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, synthesized counterfactual documents, all-noise negatives)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally supports verifier (fine-tuned hallucination detector)
metric_target: RAGTruth: detector precision/recall/F1 at span and response level (evidence support / citation faithfulness as detector task); RGB: answer correctness plus negative-rejection / counterfactual-rejection rates (selective risk/coverage)
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (flag hallucinated spans); RGB: answer and abstain (negative rejection is explicitly scored)
breaking_coordinates: metric_target, action_policy, evidence_assumption, intervention_point (unit of evaluation: detector vs generator)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation benchmarks aimed at trustworthiness, and both touch hallucination/conflict between generated text and retrieved evidence. However, RAGTruth is a meta-evaluation corpus whose scored object is a hallucination detector (span/response-level precision/recall over naturally generated outputs), while RGB scores the LLM generator's RAG abilities under synthetic stressors via answer accuracy and explicit rejection rates. The evidence-construction regime (natural generations vs controlled stressor mixtures), the metric target (detector F1 vs answer correctness/rejection rate), and the evaluated action policy (verify/flag vs answer/abstain) all differ. They are complementary diagnostics of RAG reliability rather than substitutable methods on a shared leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Pick a single evaluated object (either detector or generator) and a shared task formulation. For example, run the same LLMs and the same hallucination detectors on both corpora, report a common metric family (e.g., span-level support F1 plus answer correctness and abstention rate), align the evidence regime (natural vs constructed noise/counterfactual), and explicitly score the same action policy (answer/abstain/flag) on both benchmarks before any direct ranking.
notes: Shared 'evaluation_benchmark' category masks that one benchmarks detectors and the other benchmarks generator abilities; leaderboard-style ranking across them would conflate units of evaluation.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: RGB uses benchmark-constructed stressors (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactuals); Sufficient Context uses naturally occurring QA datasets (HotPotQA, Musique, FreshQA) stratified post hoc by an LLM autorater for sufficiency
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); plus verifier and generator prompting (Sufficient Context only, via selective-generation method)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (both report abstention/rejection); Sufficient Context additionally reports hallucination vs abstention rates stratified by sufficiency
action_policy: answer, abstain (both explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via 'negative rejection' testbed, Sufficient Context via selective generation and abstention-rate analysis)
rationale: Both papers explicitly probe RAG behavior under insufficient or noisy context and both score answer-vs-abstain as a first-class action policy (RGB's 'negative rejection', Sufficient Context's selective generation), so the action-policy and failure-type axes overlap substantially. However, RGB is a pure diagnostic benchmark constructed via controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual passages over a curated bilingual news corpus, whereas Sufficient Context is a hybrid analysis-plus-method paper that stratifies existing open-domain QA datasets using an LLM autorater for sufficiency and proposes a verifier-driven selective-generation intervention. The evidence-construction methodology, the unit of evaluation (4 ability-specific testbeds vs. sufficiency-stratified slices), and the intervention scope (benchmark only vs. benchmark + method) differ enough that putting their numbers side-by-side on a single leaderboard would mislead. They are best treated as complementary lenses on the same underlying phenomenon (RAG abstention under insufficient evidence), not as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's autorater + selective-generation pipeline on RGB's noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds (and conversely, apply RGB's noise-ratio and counterfactual stressors to HotPotQA/Musique slices), using the same LLMs, the same correct/abstain/hallucinate scoring rubric, and the same definition of an abstention success. Report both RGB's per-ability accuracies and Sufficient Context's sufficiency-stratified C/A/H rates so the two evaluation lenses can be cross-walked on identical (model, dataset, retriever) triples.
notes: The papers genuinely agree on action policy (abstention is evaluated in both), which prevents an 'under-specified' verdict; the gap is in evidence construction and evaluation granularity, hence partial rather than invalid.

failure_type: consistency/conflict for both; RAGTruth additionally covers sufficiency and relevance/noise at the annotation level
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth assumes naturally occurring hallucinations from LLMs over standard RAG benchmarks (QA, data-to-text, summarization); FaithfulRAG assumes benchmark-constructed and naturally occurring parametric-vs-context knowledge conflicts
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (annotated corpus plus fine-tuned detector); FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, alignment, and self-think before generation)
metric_target: RAGTruth: span/case-level hallucination detection performance; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and context faithfulness on conflict QA
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (detector flags spans, no end-to-end action); FaithfulRAG: answer (final response after reconciling conflicts)
rationale: Both papers sit in the faithfulness area and touch the consistency/conflict failure type, since RAGTruth annotates 'evident conflict' spans and FaithfulRAG explicitly models parametric-vs-context conflict. However, RAGTruth is fundamentally an evaluation artifact, an 18K-response annotated corpus used to benchmark and fine-tune hallucination detectors, whereas FaithfulRAG is a generator-side intervention that reconciles conflicting facts before producing an answer. Their intervention points (evaluation corpus vs. generator prompting), metric targets (detection F1 over annotated spans vs. answer correctness on conflict QA), and action policies (flag vs. answer) are categorically different kinds of contributions, and the evidence assumptions only partially overlap. Placing them on the same leaderboard would conflate a measurement instrument with a generation method and mislead readers, so the pair is invalid for direct comparison even though RAGTruth could legitimately serve as one evaluation harness for FaithfulRAG-style methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG and a RAGTruth-derived pipeline (e.g., detector plus regenerate/abstain) on a shared task suite covering both RAGTruth's QA/summarization splits and a knowledge-conflict QA benchmark, fix retriever, generator, and decoding, and report a common metric family (answer correctness, faithfulness/support, and hallucination span detection) together with an explicit, identical action policy such as answer-or-abstain after conflict resolution.
notes: Comparability is about kind-of-contribution: benchmark/detector vs. generation-time conflict resolver; they are complementary rather than substitutable.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B's counterfactual noise only)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real DPR/retriever output across 5 ODQA benchmarks; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with three engineered noise types (relevant, irrelevant, counterfactual) built on top of DPR retrievals from NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ. No adversarial corpus-write threat model in either.
intervention_point: Paper A: reranker/filter (NLI entailment filter) + generator prompting/training (mixed-context fine-tuning); Paper B: generator prompting/training (adaptive adversarial training with noise-aware multi-task auxiliary head)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: Paper A: filter (NLI-based discard then fall back to closed-book) is explicitly evaluated as an action; Paper B: answer (no abstain/filter/verify action reported)
rationale: Both papers tackle noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA with EM/F1 as the metric, and both touch generator-side training as one mitigation, so there is genuine overlap. However, Paper B explicitly adds a counterfactual (conflict) noise class that Paper A does not model, and constructs noise through a curated benchmark rather than reporting natural retriever errors. Paper A additionally evaluates an NLI filter with a filter+fallback action policy, while Paper B only evaluates an answer policy with adversarial training. A leaderboard ranking would conflate two different problem scopes and two different action regimes, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Use a shared retriever and generator backbone; evaluate both methods on a common noise taxonomy (matching irrelevant-only and counterfactual splits separately); report results under the same action policy (either both answer-only, or both with an explicit filter/abstain option and matched coverage); use the same evaluation datasets and noise construction protocol; and report EM/F1 plus a calibration or coverage metric so the filter action in Paper A is comparable to RAAT's answer-always policy.
notes: Paper B explicitly cites and contrasts with Paper A (Yoran et al., 2023), so the authors themselves treat the comparison as partial/complementary rather than as substitutable methods.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); rgb2023 additionally covers sufficiency and consistency/conflict via negative rejection and counterfactual subtests
evidence_assumption: irrelevantContext2023: benign retrieval error from real retrievers over ODQA corpora; rgb2023: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injections built from news + search-engine documents
intervention_point: irrelevantContext2023: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) plus generator prompting/training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts); rgb2023: evaluation artifact (a benchmark; no proposed mitigation)
metric_target: irrelevantContext2023: answer correctness on ODQA; rgb2023: answer correctness plus rejection/error-detection rates across four ability dimensions
action_policy: irrelevantContext2023: answer (with implicit filter→fallback-to-no-retrieval when NLI rejects); rgb2023: explicitly evaluates abstain (negative rejection) and expose conflict as targeted behaviors
rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior under noisy retrieved context, so they share the noise/relevance failure type and overlap conceptually. However, irrelevantContext2023 is a method paper proposing NLI-based filtering and robust fine-tuning evaluated on naturally retrieved ODQA passages with answer-accuracy as the target, while rgb2023 is a benchmark paper that constructs controlled noise ratios and counterfactual documents to score LLMs across four abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) using rejection/accuracy/error-detection metrics. The intervention points differ (context-assembly + generator training vs evaluation artifact), the evidence is constructed differently (real retrieval vs benchmark-engineered noise), and only rgb2023 explicitly evaluates abstention as an action policy. They are therefore complementary rather than directly rankable on the same leaderboard, making the comparison partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the irrelevantContext2023 methods (NLI filter and the fine-tuned robust generator) on rgb2023's four testbeds with identical retriever, generator backbone, and prompt template; report rgb2023's full metric suite (accuracy, rejection rate, error-detection rate) alongside ODQA accuracy; and explicitly evaluate an abstention/fallback action so both systems are scored under the same action-policy regime and the same noise-construction protocol.
notes: Core asymmetry is method-paper vs benchmark-paper; even where their noise framings overlap, the metric and action-policy scopes only partially align.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAAT: DPR-retrieved Wikipedia passages over NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ filtered for >=2 golden contexts, with relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual noise injected; RGB: news-article corpus with search-engine retrieval and controlled noise ratios, plus separately constructed counterfactual and rejection testbeds)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, via F1/EM or accuracy); selective risk/coverage (RGB only, via negative-rejection rate)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer and abstain (RGB negative-rejection testbed)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG and overlap on the relevance/noise and consistency/conflict failure types, including a counterfactual-noise category that appears in both designs. However, the contributions sit at different coordinates: RAAT is a generator-side training intervention (adaptive adversarial training + noise-aware multi-task learning on LLaMA-2 7B), whereas RGB is an evaluation-artifact contribution with no method intervention. The action policies also diverge: RAAT only evaluates 'answer' under noisy contexts, while RGB explicitly evaluates abstention via its negative-rejection testbed, so they are not measuring the same operating behavior. Evidence assumptions further differ (Wikipedia/DPR with golden-passage filtering vs. news + web-search with engineered noise ratios), so they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitutable methods; they are complementary (one is a method, one is a benchmark), justifying partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and a matched non-adversarially-trained baseline of the same backbone) on RGB's four testbeds at the same noise ratios and in both English and Chinese, reporting answer correctness AND the rejection rate / accuracy under the negative-rejection condition; symmetrically, evaluate the RGB-tested LLMs on RAAT's RAG-Bench under the three RAAT noise types with the same F1/EM protocol. Comparability also requires aligning retriever (DPR vs. web search), corpus (Wikipedia vs. news), and an explicit action-policy column (answer vs. abstain) so that the methods are scored on identical inputs and decision options.
notes: Asymmetry is the main blocker: a method paper vs. a benchmark paper can be cited together but cannot be ranked head-to-head without a shared evaluation harness and a declared action policy.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both rely on standard dense retrievers like DPR over Wikipedia returning some irrelevant passages; no adversarial corpus writes assumed)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (CoN); reranker/filter + generator prompting or training (Yoran et al., NLI filter + fine-tuning)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (CoN reports rejection rate on RealTimeQA), retrieval recall (implicit in Yoran's filter analysis)
action_policy: answer + abstain ('unknown') for CoN; filter + answer (fallback to no-context LLM) for Yoran — no explicit abstain
rationale: Both papers target the same failure mode — RALM brittleness to irrelevant/noisy retrieved passages in open-domain QA over standard dense-retriever pipelines — and both propose training-time mitigations using small amounts of synthetic data, so the problem framing and evidence assumption overlap strongly. However, the intervention points differ: CoN modifies the generator's reasoning to produce per-document notes and an 'unknown' abstain option, while Yoran et al. add a pre-generation NLI filter (a reranker-style component) and train the LLM to ignore mixed irrelevant context, without an abstain action. The metric targets also differ — CoN explicitly reports a rejection rate (selective-risk dimension) on RealTimeQA, whereas Yoran et al. focus on EM with and without filtering, treating filtered-context fallback as a recall/precision trade. These differences in action policy (abstain vs. filter-and-answer) and in where the intervention is placed mean the two should be discussed as complementary modules within the same problem family, not ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared retriever (e.g., DPR top-k from the same Wikipedia dump), same generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), same QA benchmark set (intersection of NQ/TriviaQA + a multi-hop set like StrategyQA), and report a common metric grid: EM on relevant-context subset, EM on irrelevant-context stressor subset, abstention/rejection rate on an unanswerable subset, and effective coverage. Each method must be evaluated under both an answer-only policy and an abstain-allowed policy so the action-policy axis is controlled, and Yoran's filter must be ablated against CoN's note-judge step on the same passages.
notes: From an IR perspective the retriever/corpus assumptions align well, but the placement of the robustness mechanism (generator reasoning vs. NLI rerank/filter) and the abstain-vs-filter action policy are the decisive non-comparabilities.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both assume non-adversarial corpus; Sufficient Context analyzes existing RAG retrieval behavior; Self-RAG operates with standard Wikipedia/web retrieval)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (Sufficient Context: post-hoc autorater + selective generation); retriever + generator prompting or training (Self-RAG: trained reflection tokens for on-demand retrieval and critique)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context); answer correctness, citation faithfulness (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer, abstain (Sufficient Context, explicitly evaluated via selective generation); re-retrieve, filter, answer (Self-RAG, via reflection tokens)
rationale: Both papers address the failure mode of RAG systems using retrieved context indiscriminately—each tries to make the system smarter about when/whether to use retrieved passages and when to refrain. However, the intervention points differ substantially: Sufficient Context applies a post-hoc autorater on (query, context) pairs and combines a sufficiency signal with self-confidence for selective generation, while Self-RAG trains a single LM with reflection tokens to adaptively trigger retrieval, judge relevance, and critique support inline. Their action policies also diverge—answer/abstain for Sufficient Context versus re-retrieve/filter/answer for Self-RAG—and the primary metric families emphasize hallucination-rate-at-coverage versus factuality and citation accuracy. They are complementary modules in a RAG quality stack rather than substitutable systems on a shared leaderboard, so partial is the appropriate verdict.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold retriever, corpus, generator family, and task suite fixed; evaluate both methods on a common set of QA/long-form factuality benchmarks with matched abstention/coverage curves and matched citation-support metrics; force both systems to expose the same action set (at minimum answer vs. abstain, ideally also re-retrieve) so the operating policies are aligned; and ablate the trained reflection-token mechanism against a post-hoc sufficiency+confidence gate on the same base LM to isolate intervention effects.
notes: Both clearly evaluate an action policy (abstention vs. on-demand retrieval), so this is not under-specified, but the action policies themselves are non-overlapping enough that leaderboard ranking would conflate distinct mechanisms.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD; Self-RAG: relevance/noise + sufficiency
evidence_assumption: both benign retrieval error (no adversarial corpus, naturally retrieved passages from standard corpora)
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker (forecasting function over (t,q,d)); Self-RAG: generator prompting or training (reflection-token fine-tuning) + system-control policy (adaptive retrieve-on-demand)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: unreported (produces calibrated confidence but no explicit abstain/selective-risk evaluation in the available evidence); Self-RAG: re-retrieve (on-demand retrieval gate) + verify (critique tokens) + answer
rationale: Both papers sit in the 'control of RAG behaviour' family and share a benign-retrieval evidence assumption, but they target genuinely different failures: CalibRAG addresses miscalibration / over-reliance by training a (t,q,d) forecasting function that reranks documents and reports a calibrated decision-correctness probability, whereas Self-RAG addresses indiscriminate retrieval and ungrounded generation by training a generator to emit retrieve/critique reflection tokens. Intervention points differ (reranker/calibration head vs. generator training + adaptive retrieval gate), metric targets only partially overlap (ECE/calibration vs. citation faithfulness and evidence support), and action policies diverge sharply—Self-RAG explicitly evaluates retrieve-or-not and critique decisions, while CalibRAG's downstream action (abstain, defer, escalate) is not explicitly evaluated. The two methods are complementary control modules rather than substitutable systems on one leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both on the same QA benchmarks using a shared retriever and generator base model, and report (a) calibration metrics (ECE, AURC, selective risk-coverage) AND (b) citation/grounding metrics (citation precision/recall, factuality) together, plus (c) an explicit, shared action policy such as selective answering with an abstain threshold so both systems are scored on identical decision behaviour. Without aligning at least the metric family and the action policy, any ranking conflates calibration quality with adaptive-retrieval/self-critique quality.
notes: Both are 'control'-area methods but operate on different axes of RAG reliability; combining them is plausible, ranking them is not.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs. contextual); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict / benchmark-constructed conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge, no attacker model. PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence; corpus write access = yes; query control = no (attacker chooses target Q but does not rewrite user queries); retriever visibility = both black-box and white-box variants; generator access = black-box; insertion budget = 5 malicious passages per target question; attack objective = targeted answer induction.
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact extraction, alignment, self-think). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive injection); evaluation artifact (defines an attack benchmark, not a defense).
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness, evidence support / faithfulness. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate.
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciliation); abstain/expose-conflict not explicitly evaluated. PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper; no defender action policy is the contribution).
rationale: Both papers superficially concern situations where retrieved context disagrees with the truthful or parametric answer, but they live in incompatible problem settings. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense for benign / naturally-occurring parametric-vs-context conflict, mining self-facts and running a self-think reconciliation, measured by answer correctness. PoisonedRAG is an offensive corpus-poisoning attack with explicit attacker capabilities (write access to the knowledge database, 5-passage insertion budget, target-answer objective, black/white-box retriever access) measured by attack success rate, with no defender action policy defined or evaluated. All five coordinates diverge, and the role of the artifact is opposite (defense vs attack), so placing them on the same leaderboard would be category-confused and misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) re-cast FaithfulRAG as a candidate defense and evaluate it on the PoisonedRAG benchmark with matched retriever, generator, corpus, target question set, and insertion budget, reporting attack success rate alongside clean accuracy and an explicit defender action policy (answer / abstain / quarantine / verify); or (b) include FaithfulRAG as one of the defenses tested in PoisonedRAG's defense evaluation. Without a shared threat model, shared metric family (ASR vs correctness reconciled), and explicit action policies on both sides, leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful.
notes: Categories are explicitly different in the audit evidence (knowledge_conflict vs adversarial_corruption); attack-vs-defense asymmetry is the decisive break.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption; Astute RAG also covers relevance/noise and consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error and naturally occurring conflict, with attacker-created evidence mentioned but not the primary stressor. PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model - corpus write access yes, query control yes (attacker-chosen target questions), retriever visibility both black-box and white-box, generator access via API only, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per target question into million-text corpus, attack objective is inducing attacker-chosen target answers
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free source-aware consolidation at inference); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (poisoning attack)
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness under imperfect retrieval; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (after internal-vs-external consolidation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (no defender action policy - system is the victim being measured)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, evidence_assumption/threat-model role (defender vs attacker)
rationale: Both papers sit in the robust/secure-RAG space and touch on adversarial or imperfect evidence in the corpus, but they occupy opposite roles in the attack-defense game. PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that constructs an optimization-based corpus poisoning method and reports attack success rate as the primary metric, with the RAG system as victim. Astute RAG is a defense paper that intervenes at the generator via source-aware consolidation and reports answer correctness under noisy/conflicting retrieval, with adversarial corruption only loosely covered. The intervention point, metric target, defender action policy, and even the role of each system in the threat model differ, so they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation in which PoisonedRAG (or an equivalent poisoning attack at matched insertion budget, retriever visibility, and query control) is run against Astute RAG and against baseline RAG, reporting both attack success rate and answer correctness on the same datasets, retriever, generator, and corpus, with an explicit defender action policy (e.g., answer vs abstain vs expose-conflict) so that Astute RAG's robustness can be benchmarked against the attack rather than only against benign noise.
notes: Pair mixes an attack paper with a defense paper; comparability requires re-casting one as the counterpart's evaluation target rather than as a peer method.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume corpus write access; PoisonedRAG attacker chooses target query and injects 5 malicious texts per query under black-box or white-box retriever knowledge with objective of inducing attacker-chosen target answer; RobustRAG defends against an adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge who can inject a bounded number m' of malicious passages
intervention_point: corpus/index for PoisonedRAG; context assembly/compression plus generator prompting for RobustRAG
metric_target: attack success rate for PoisonedRAG; answer correctness plus certified robustness lower bounds for RobustRAG
action_policy: answer for PoisonedRAG (attack induces target answer); answer or abstain via isolate-then-aggregate (keyword/decoding) for RobustRAG
rationale: Both papers address the same failure type (adversarial corruption of retrieved evidence) and share the attacker-created-evidence threat model with corpus write access and bounded injection budgets, making them topically linked as attack vs defense in the same threat surface. However, PoisonedRAG intervenes at the corpus/index to maximize attack success rate, while RobustRAG intervenes at context assembly and generator prompting to provide certified correctness lower bounds with an explicit abstain action; the metric families and action policies therefore do not align for a leaderboard-style ranking. They are naturally complementary (attack benchmark vs certified defense) rather than substitutable methods on a shared axis, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate RobustRAG directly under PoisonedRAG's attack construction (same retriever, generator, datasets, 5-text injection budget, target-question/target-answer protocol) and report a common metric set such as attack success rate and clean answer accuracy alongside certified bounds and abstention rate; conversely, run PoisonedRAG against RobustRAG's isolate-then-aggregate pipeline with matched m' and adaptive-attacker assumptions so both papers report on the same attack-success and answer-correctness axes with explicit action labels.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pairing; comparable as complementary contributions on a shared threat model but not as ranked alternatives.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict (LLM-generated outputs with manual span annotation across QA/summarization/data-to-text); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents, all-noise contexts for rejection)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally informs verifier training via fine-tuned detectors
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support, citation faithfulness (span-level hallucination detection F1); RGB: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (rejection rate, accuracy under noise/counterfactual)
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (hallucination span detection is the evaluated action); RGB: answer and abstain (negative rejection is explicitly scored)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation benchmarks concerned with faithfulness/reliability, and both touch consistency between generation and retrieved evidence. However, RAGTruth is a span-annotated corpus designed to train and score hallucination *detectors* (verify action, span-level support metrics, natural LLM outputs), whereas RGB is a capability-diagnostic testbed for end-to-end LLM RAG behavior across four distinct abilities (answer/abstain actions, accuracy and rejection-rate metrics, synthetically perturbed contexts). A system cannot be ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard because the units of evaluation (spans vs. end answers), the action policies (detect vs. answer-or-reject), and the evidence construction differ. They function as complementary benchmarks covering different slices of RAG reliability, hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) a unified protocol that runs the same RAG pipeline through both benchmarks and reports a shared metric family (e.g., end-to-end answer correctness plus span-level support under matched noise/counterfactual conditions with explicit abstention scoring), or (b) restricting comparison to the narrow overlap (e.g., counterfactual/conflict QA with both span-level faithfulness and rejection-rate reported) with an aligned action policy and matched generators/retrievers.
notes: Both are legitimately cited as 'RAG evaluation benchmarks' but target different problems; treating them as substitutes would conflate detector quality with LLM capability profiling.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict
