evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injection; Sufficient Context: benign retrieval error analyzed on naturally retrieved contexts (HotpotQA, Musique, FreshQA) stratified by an autorater
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); verifier + system-control policy (Sufficient Context only, via selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage; RGB additionally reports rejection rate and counterfactual robustness; Sufficient Context additionally reports hallucination vs abstention rates stratified by sufficiency
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention)
rationale: Both papers evaluate RAG behavior when retrieved evidence is imperfect and both explicitly assess an answer-vs-abstain action policy, so they share the failure-type space of noise/sufficiency and overlap on negative rejection. However, RGB is purely an evaluation artifact with hand-constructed testbeds at fixed noise ratios and counterfactual perturbations, while Sufficient Context introduces a sufficiency autorater that re-stratifies existing QA datasets and additionally proposes a selective-generation intervention combining sufficiency with self-confidence. The metric families therefore differ (ability-level accuracy/rejection/counterfactual scores vs. sufficiency-stratified hallucination/abstention and selective risk-coverage), and the intervention scopes differ (diagnosis-only vs. diagnosis + method). They are best discussed as complementary lenses on imperfect-context RAG rather than placed on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methodologies on a shared dataset+retriever+generator stack: apply the sufficient-context autorater to RGB's noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds to check whether RGB's 'noise' aligns with 'insufficient context'; report a common metric suite (accuracy on sufficient subset, hallucination/abstention on insufficient subset, and RGB's rejection/counterfactual rates); and evaluate Sufficient Context's selective generation on RGB testbeds with the same abstention scoring rule so the two are directly rank-comparable.
notes: Both papers do report an explicit abstain action, which is a strong reason this is not 'under-specified'; the break is in intervention scope and metric construction rather than missing action policy.

failure_type: RAGTruth covers consistency/conflict plus sufficiency and relevance/noise as a broad hallucination taxonomy; FaithfulRAG targets only consistency/conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error with naturally generated LLM hallucinations over standard RAG passages; FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflict
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) plus verifier (fine-tuned detector); FaithfulRAG: context assembly/compression and generator prompting (self-fact mining, self-think)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support and citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection P/R/F1; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness on conflict QA benchmarks
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (corpus and detector, no deployed action); FaithfulRAG: answer after internal reconciliation, no abstain or verify reported
rationale: Both papers sit under the broad umbrella of RAG faithfulness, but they are categorically different contributions. RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact—a span-annotated corpus plus a fine-tuned detector—covering several hallucination subtypes across QA, data-to-text, and summarization, whereas FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention narrowly targeting parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflict and is evaluated on conflict QA benchmarks via answer accuracy. The intervention points (detector/benchmark vs. generation pipeline), metric families (span-level detection F1 vs. QA correctness), failure scopes, and action policies do not align. Direct leaderboard-style comparison would be misleading because one produces a hallucination label and the other produces a reconciled answer.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark with identical retriever, generator, and conflict construction; report both span-level hallucination detection metrics and downstream answer correctness; specify a common action policy (e.g., answer vs. abstain when conflict detected); and ideally apply RAGTruth's detector as a verifier on FaithfulRAG outputs (and vice versa, train a FaithfulRAG-style reconciler evaluated on RAGTruth spans) so both are measured on the same target.
notes: The pair conflates a benchmark/detector contribution with a generation-time conflict resolution method; this is a category mismatch rather than a parameter difference.

failure_type: relevance/noise; consistency/conflict for RAAT counterfactual noise only
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; benchmark-constructed stressor for RAAT adversarial noise mixtures and Yoran irrelevant-context training data
intervention_point: generator prompting or training for both; context assembly/compression for Yoran NLI filter baseline
metric_target: answer correctness via EM and F1 on ODQA
action_policy: answer for both; filter for Yoran NLI baseline; neither evaluates abstention or selective risk
rationale: Both papers target training-based noise robustness for RALMs on open-domain QA and share datasets such as NQ and TriviaQA, so they sit in the same broad research area and RAAT explicitly positions itself against Yoran et al. as a baseline. However, failure-type coverage diverges: Yoran focuses on irrelevant or distracting context (relevance/noise) and adds multi-hop, while RAAT additionally constructs counterfactual noise that introduces a consistency/conflict failure mode not addressed by Yoran. The intervention surface also differs: Yoran offers two distinct mechanisms (NLI-based pre-generation filtering plus mixed-context fine-tuning), whereas RAAT couples adaptive adversarial training with an auxiliary noise-type classification head, so method A vs method B is not a clean controlled comparison. Action policy is implicit answer on both sides (with Yoran's filter being the only explicit policy), and neither evaluates abstention or calibrated selective risk, so leaderboard-style ranking would conflate methods that optimize for partially different noise distributions and intervention points. The relationship is best described as complementary mechanisms on overlapping but non-identical problem instances, which is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-evaluate both methods under a single controlled protocol: identical base generator (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), identical retriever and corpus, identical noise-construction procedure spanning irrelevant, relevant-but-distracting, and counterfactual noise so Yoran is stress-tested on counterfactual conditions and RAAT on multi-hop, identical EM/F1 metric definitions, matched training-data budgets, and an explicit declared action policy (answer-only vs answer+filter vs answer+abstain) reported per condition. Reporting selective risk/coverage and noise-type-stratified accuracy would further justify direct ranking.
notes: RAAT cites Yoran as a baseline, but a single-paper comparison table is not equivalent to a fair head-to-head; counterfactual-noise coverage and intervention differences remain the principal blockers.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); sufficiency and consistency/conflict (Paper B only via negative rejection and counterfactual testbeds)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper A: natural noisy retrieval + constructed mixed contexts for training); benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper B: controlled noise ratios, fabricated counterfactual documents, all-noise contexts)
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (robust fine-tune). Paper B: evaluation artifact only (benchmark, no proposed intervention)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness. Paper B: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (rejection rate) + integration accuracy
action_policy: Paper A: answer (filter is upstream but final policy is answer; abstention not evaluated). Paper B: answer and abstain are both explicitly scored (negative rejection ability)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, action_policy, metric_target, failure_type (partial overlap only)
rationale: Both works are framed around noise in retrieved evidence for RAG, but they are categorically different artifacts: Paper A proposes interventions (NLI-based passage filtering and robust fine-tuning) and measures answer correctness on five ODQA benchmarks, whereas Paper B contributes the RGB benchmark with four separate testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and proposes no method. From a trustworthy-ML standpoint, the action policy differs critically: Paper B explicitly evaluates abstention (negative rejection) as a first-class outcome, while Paper A only reports correctness conditional on answering and does not measure selective risk or coverage. Paper B also covers conflict/integrity failure modes (counterfactual) that lie outside Paper A's scope. Therefore the two are complementary rather than substitutable on a single leaderboard; the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI filter and robust fine-tuned generator on RGB's noise robustness and negative rejection testbeds with the same backbone LLM, and separately report (i) answer accuracy at matched noise ratio, (ii) rejection/abstention rate on all-noise contexts, and (iii) behavior under counterfactual documents. Conversely, RGB would need to fix a generator and report it as a baseline rather than as a benchmark. Without shared intervention scope, an explicit action-policy specification (answer vs abstain), and a common metric family that includes selective-risk/coverage, leaderboard-style ranking is not justified.
notes: Methods paper vs benchmark paper is a recurring partial-comparability pattern; the abstention/selective-risk gap is the decisive coordinate here.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (RGB negative rejection only)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer + abstain (RGB negative rejection testbed)
rationale: Both papers concern noise robustness in RAG and both partition retrieval noise into relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual-style buckets, so the failure-type coordinate clearly overlaps. However, RAAT is a generator-side training method (adaptive adversarial training on LLaMA-2 7B) evaluated with F1/EM on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ assuming the system must always answer, whereas RGB is a diagnostic benchmark with four separate testbeds, including a negative-rejection testbed that explicitly evaluates abstention as a first-class action. From a selective-prediction/calibration standpoint these are categorically different artifacts: a training intervention measured on answer correctness vs. a benchmark that also scores abstention behavior and rejection rate. They are complementary (RAAT could in principle be scored on RGB) but cannot be ranked side-by-side on a single leaderboard without misrepresenting either system, so the verdict is partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and matched baselines) on RGB's noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds using the same retriever, corpus, noise-ratio sweeps, and bilingual splits; report both accuracy AND rejection rate / selective-risk curves under explicit answer-vs-abstain action labels; conversely, RGB-style evaluations should be extended to the NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ-with-DPR noise constructions RAAT uses, with the same counterfactual injection budget. Only then can the two be placed on comparable axes.
notes: Method-vs-benchmark asymmetry and missing abstention evaluation in RAAT are the primary reasons direct comparison would mislead, even though the topical framing is nearly identical.

failure_type: relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error; naturally occurring irrelevant passages from standard ODQA retrieval (no adversary)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (CoN: per-document reading notes); retriever/context assembly filter + generator training (Yoran: NLI entailment filter and mixed-context fine-tuning)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); rejection rate / selective behavior on out-of-knowledge questions (CoN only)
action_policy: CoN: answer or abstain ('unknown'); Yoran: filter then answer (fallback to no-retrieval LLM); abstention not evaluated in Yoran
rationale: Both papers tackle distraction from irrelevant retrieved context in ODQA under benign retrieval errors, so the failure type and evidence assumption align. However, Chain-of-Note intervenes at the generator with sequential note-taking and—critically for selective-prediction users—introduces an explicit 'unknown' abstain action, reporting rejection rate on RealTimeQA. Yoran et al. instead intervene with an NLI-based passage filter plus mixed-context fine-tuning (with a multi-hop focus) and report only answer correctness, with no abstention or calibration/coverage metric. Because the action policies are qualitatively different (answer-or-abstain vs filter-then-answer) and only the correctness sub-metric overlaps, the works are complementary mechanisms covering different slices of robustness rather than substitutable methods on one leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods on a shared benchmark suite (overlap of NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ plus multi-hop sets and an out-of-knowledge slice like RealTimeQA) with a unified retriever and generator backbone; report answer correctness AND selective-risk/coverage curves AND rejection rate under a common abstain protocol (e.g., force both systems to expose 'unknown'/abstain decisions); ablate Yoran's NLI filter against CoN's note-based relevance assessment under matched compute; document action-policy labels explicitly for each system.
notes: From a selective-risk perspective the abstain dimension is the decisive break: CoN's headline gain is partly calibration/coverage, which Yoran's evaluation simply does not measure, so a single ranking on EM would systematically undervalue CoN's intended contribution.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: context assembly/compression, system-control policy (Paper A); generator prompting or training, retriever (Paper B)
metric_target: selective risk/coverage, calibration error (Paper A); answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support (Paper B)
action_policy: answer, abstain (Paper A); re-retrieve, verify, answer (Paper B)
rationale: Both papers target RAG factuality and exploit signals about retrieved-evidence quality to guide generation, but they intervene at different points with incompatible action policies and metric families. Sufficient Context is an inference-time selective-generation method that uses a sufficiency autorater plus self-confidence to drive abstention, and is evaluated primarily through selective-accuracy/coverage tradeoffs (a calibration/selective-risk framing). Self-RAG retrains the generator end-to-end with reflection tokens to perform adaptive retrieval and self-critique, and is evaluated through full-coverage answer correctness and citation faithfulness, with no abstention-coverage curves. Because one method explicitly trades coverage for correctness while the other does not, direct leaderboard ranking would conflate different operating regimes and intervention philosophies; the relationship is complementary rather than substitutive.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold the base LLM, retriever, corpus, and evaluation datasets constant; evaluate both systems on (a) selective-accuracy vs coverage / risk-coverage curves with identical abstention semantics, (b) citation/evidence-support metrics under matched grounding protocols, and (c) explicitly report each method's action policy (answer/abstain/re-retrieve/verify). Ideally, layer Sufficient Context's selective gate on top of a Self-RAG generator to disentangle the training-time reflection contribution from the inference-time sufficiency gate.
notes: From a selective-risk lens, Paper A reports an abstention-aware operating point that Self-RAG never quantifies, so any single-number factuality comparison would be misleading.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD; Self-RAG: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval error in standard open-domain QA; no adversarial threat model in either.
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker (forecasting function over (t,q,d)) plus generator confidence head; Self-RAG: generator prompting/training (reflection tokens) and retriever (on-demand)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer (with calibrated confidence, no abstention reported); Self-RAG: re-retrieve, filter, verify (self-critique tokens)
rationale: Both papers aim to make RAG more reliable, but they target fundamentally different failure modes and optimize for different quantities. CalibRAG explicitly tackles uncertainty/calibration by training a forecasting function that predicts decision correctness so that downstream human decisions are well-calibrated; its headline metric is calibration error alongside accuracy. Self-RAG instead tackles when-to-retrieve and self-critique via reflection tokens, with citation faithfulness and adaptive retrieval as primary goals, and does not evaluate calibration. The intervention points partially overlap (both touch generator behavior) but the failure type, metric family, and action policy diverge: CalibRAG answers with a calibrated probability, Self-RAG re-retrieves and verifies. Direct leaderboard-style ranking would conflate calibration improvements with factuality/citation improvements, so they are best framed as complementary modules.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A common benchmark with both (i) calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, AURC, selective risk-coverage) and (ii) factuality/citation metrics evaluated on identical retriever+generator+corpus; explicit and matched action policies (e.g., both required to produce a confidence and both allowed to abstain or re-retrieve under defined budgets); and an apples-to-apples ablation isolating reranking-by-forecasted-correctness vs reflection-token training, ideally with each method augmented with the other's missing capability.
notes: Neither paper evaluates selective abstention as a first-class action, which limits any comparison framed around selective risk.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge (both sources assumed non-malicious). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, target-question query control, black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, ~5-passage insertion budget, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attacker-side injection); no defensive intervention proposed.
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support under conflict. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR).
action_policy: Both unreported / answer-only; neither evaluates abstain, verify, quarantine, or escalate as a measured action.
rationale: Both papers touch the broader 'robust RAG' umbrella and involve a tension between retrieved content and the model's prior, but they are not alternative methods on the same task. FaithfulRAG is a defender-side generator method that reconciles benign, naturally occurring parametric–context conflicts and is scored by answer correctness; PoisonedRAG is an attacker-side method that writes malicious passages into the corpus under a specific threat model (corpus write access, 5-text insertion budget, target-question control) and is scored by attack success rate. The actors, failure type, evidence assumption, intervention locus, and metric direction are all different (one minimizes error on benign conflict, the other maximizes ASR), and neither paper evaluates the other's setup. A leaderboard-style ranking would be category-confused and misleading, so the comparison is invalid rather than merely partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) re-cast FaithfulRAG as a defense and evaluate it under the PoisonedRAG threat model (same retriever, generator, corpus, insertion budget, target-question pool) reporting ASR reduction, clean-task accuracy retention, and an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine); or (b) report PoisonedRAG ASR with and without FaithfulRAG-style fact-level reconciliation as a defense baseline. Without a shared threat model, shared metric (ASR or robust accuracy under poisoning), and shared action policy, direct comparison is not meaningful.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense category error; the only conceptual overlap is 'parametric-vs-context disagreement,' but the source of the disagreement (benign vs adversarial) is exactly what robust-RAG evaluation must hold fixed.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor + naturally occurring conflict (RGB worst-case). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence; threat model = corpus write access yes (inject ~5 malicious texts), no query control, retriever visibility varies (black-box and white-box), no generator access, insertion budget = 5 texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting + context assembly/compression. PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive injection).
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness (worst-case accuracy). PoisonedRAG: attack success rate.
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (with internal/external reliability-based selection); abstention not explicitly evaluated. PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defense action policy).
rationale: Both papers concern the robustness/security of RAG to imperfect or adversarial retrieval, but they occupy fundamentally opposite roles in the threat-defense pipeline: PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that injects optimized malicious passages into the corpus and measures attack success rate, whereas Astute RAG is a defensive generation-stage method that consolidates internal and external knowledge and is primarily evaluated on noisy/conflicting retrieval (e.g., RGB worst case) using answer correctness. Their intervention points (corpus/index attack vs. generator prompting), metric targets (ASR vs. accuracy), and action policies are not on the same axis, and Astute RAG is never reported under PoisonedRAG-style attacker assumptions with matched insertion budget and retriever visibility. A leaderboard-style ranking is therefore misleading: PoisonedRAG is not an alternative robustness method to Astute RAG but a threat that Astute RAG could be tested against.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) evaluate Astute RAG end-to-end under PoisonedRAG's exact attack protocol—same datasets (NQ/HotpotQA/MS-MARCO), same retriever and generator, same 5-text insertion budget, both black-box and white-box attacker, reporting ASR and clean accuracy and any abstention behavior—or (b) compare both papers within the same axis (defense vs. defense, or attack vs. attack) rather than across roles. A genuinely valid comparison also needs a shared action policy specification (answer/abstain/quarantine) so Astute RAG's selective behavior under poisoning is measurable against other defenses.
notes: Astute RAG mentions 'malicious' retrieval in motivation, creating surface-level overlap, but its evaluation centers on noise and natural conflict rather than optimized poisoning attacks.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG assumes corpus write access with small insertion budget (e.g., 5 malicious passages per target question), full query control, both black-box and white-box retriever visibility, no generator access, and a targeted attack objective; RobustRAG assumes an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense, bounded k' injected passages, and arbitrary attack objective, defending at the generator/aggregation layer
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack) vs. context assembly/compression and generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG ASR) vs. answer correctness with certified lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported for PoisonedRAG (attack only, no defender action evaluated); abstain plus aggregated answer for RobustRAG (keyword/decoding aggregation with explicit 'I don't know')
rationale: Both papers concern the same failure surface—adversarial corruption of retrieved evidence in RAG with attacker-created passages injected into the corpus—so failure type and evidence assumption align. However, the two papers occupy structurally opposite roles: PoisonedRAG proposes an attack whose primary metric is attack success rate under a small injection budget, intervening at the corpus, with no defender action policy evaluated; RobustRAG proposes a defense whose primary metric is certified robust answer quality under bounded k' corruption, intervening via isolate-then-aggregate at context assembly and generator prompting, with an explicit abstain-or-aggregate action policy. Because the intervention point, metric target, and action policy are inverted rather than merely different, the two cannot share a leaderboard—one constructs the threat, the other resists a bounded version of it, and ranking ASR against certified accuracy is a category error. They are best framed as components of an attack–defense ecosystem rather than competing methods on the same axis.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To enable any direct comparison, one would need a shared evaluation harness in which RobustRAG is stress-tested specifically against PoisonedRAG's black-box and white-box variants within RobustRAG's bounded-corruption threat model, or PoisonedRAG is reported as a baseline attack on a common robust-RAG benchmark with matched retriever, generator, corpus, k, k', insertion budget, and target-question distribution, plus joint metrics (ASR, clean accuracy, certified accuracy, abstention rate) under a single explicit action policy. Even then, the two should be reported as attack-vs-defense pairings rather than ranked head-to-head.
notes: Attack paper vs. defense paper with inverted objectives; calibration/selective-risk perspective makes the lack of a shared action policy and metric especially salient.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error with naturally occurring LLM hallucinations on real retrieved passages; RGB: benchmark-constructed stressors (injected noise documents, withheld evidence, counterfactual edits)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally targets a verifier (fine-tuned hallucination detector)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection (P/R/F1); RGB: answer correctness, plus rejection rate and counterfactual identification rate
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc detection of unsupported spans); RGB: answer vs. abstain (negative rejection is explicitly scored)
rationale: Both works are RAG evaluation benchmarks aimed at trustworthy generation, and both touch hallucination/unsupported content in retrieved-context settings. However, RAGTruth instruments naturally generated LLM outputs with word-level annotations to train and score post-hoc hallucination *detectors*, while RGB synthesizes four controlled testbeds to diagnose end-to-end LLM behavior, including an explicit abstention (negative rejection) signal. The evidence assumption (natural vs. constructed stressor), the metric target (span-level detection F1 vs. answer accuracy and rejection/counterfactual rates), and the action policy (verify vs. answer-or-abstain) all diverge. They are complementary instruments at different points of the RAG trustworthiness stack, not interchangeable leaderboards.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared protocol in which the same RAG system produces (i) an answer, (ii) an abstention/confidence signal, and (iii) a span-level support attribution, all evaluated on a unified corpus that includes both natural hallucinations (RAGTruth-style) and constructed stressors with negative-rejection and counterfactual partitions (RGB-style). Metrics would need to jointly report answer correctness, selective-risk/coverage (abstention calibration), and span-level faithfulness P/R/F1 on the same generators and retrievers; without this, neither benchmark alone places the methods on a common axis.
notes: From a selective-risk lens, RGB scores abstention behavior directly while RAGTruth does not evaluate when a model should withhold an answer—this asymmetry is the strongest single reason the comparison cannot be a direct leaderboard.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict (RGB counterfactual testbed only)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB); benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (Sufficient Context, using existing QA datasets with natural and curated retrieval)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); plus verifier and system-control policy (Sufficient Context's selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context); per-ability accuracy and rejection/error-detection rates (RGB)
action_policy: answer, abstain (explicitly evaluated by both)
rationale: Both papers address LLM behavior under noisy or insufficient retrieved context and both explicitly evaluate abstention (RGB's 'negative rejection' ability and Sufficient Context's hallucination/abstention/correctness stratification), so the action_policy coordinate is not the issue. However, RGB is a pure evaluation artifact that constructs four categorically distinct testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and reports per-ability accuracy and rejection metrics, whereas Sufficient Context introduces a unifying binary (Q,C)-sufficiency lens with an autorater plus a selective-generation method that combines sufficiency and self-confidence to trade off coverage against hallucination. The intervention point (benchmark-only vs. evaluation lens + verifier + control policy), metric family (per-ability accuracy/rejection vs. selective risk/coverage on standard QA), and failure-type scope (four separate stressors vs. a single sufficiency axis) differ enough that head-to-head leaderboard ranking would be misleading; they are best read as complementary contributions.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Apply Sufficient Context's autorater and selective-generation policy to the RGB testbeds (especially negative rejection and counterfactual robustness) using the same LLM backbones, and report a common metric set (per-ability accuracy, abstention rate, and selective risk-coverage curves) so that RGB-style diagnostic measurements and Sufficient Context-style selective generation can be evaluated on identical (query, context) instances with explicit, shared action labels.
notes: RGB is a benchmark artifact while Sufficient Context is analysis + method; this asymmetry (artifact vs. system) is itself part of why direct ranking is not meaningful.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (both, but scoped differently); RAGTruth also covers broader hallucination/sufficiency failures
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict and benign retrieval error (RAGTruth, broad RAG outputs); naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge (FaithfulRAG, scoped)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact + verifier (RAGTruth: corpus and detection benchmark); generator prompting/training (FaithfulRAG: self-fact mining + self-think before generation)
metric_target: evidence support / citation faithfulness (RAGTruth: span-level hallucination detection F1); answer correctness (FaithfulRAG: QA accuracy under conflict)
action_policy: verify (RAGTruth detectors flag spans); answer (FaithfulRAG generates a reconciled response); neither evaluates abstain/re-retrieve
rationale: Both papers fall under the umbrella of RAG faithfulness, but they occupy fundamentally different roles in the pipeline. RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact: a word-level hallucination corpus over QA, data-to-text, and summarization, used to benchmark and fine-tune post-hoc detectors whose action is to verify/flag spans. FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that mines parametric self-facts, aligns them with retrieved chunks, and runs a self-think module to reconcile conflicts before producing an answer; it targets answer correctness under knowledge conflict, not span-level detection F1. The intervention point, metric family, and action policy all differ, and FaithfulRAG's scoped knowledge-conflict failure is narrower than RAGTruth's broad hallucination taxonomy, so they cannot be ranked on a single leaderboard. They are complementary—RAGTruth could in principle serve as one evaluation venue for FaithfulRAG—but as published they address different sub-problems with non-overlapping metrics.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG (and the RAGTruth-fine-tuned detector / baseline generators) on a shared task with (a) the same RAG pipeline (retriever, generator, context construction), (b) a common failure-type slice—either knowledge-conflict QA with parametric vs context contradictions, or RAGTruth-style span hallucinations—(c) a common metric family (e.g., span-level evidence-support F1 AND end-to-end answer correctness reported jointly), and (d) explicit, identical action policies (answer vs verify vs abstain) with the same thresholding. Without aligning intervention stage and metric, any head-to-head ranking would mix detection performance with generation faithfulness.
notes: Benchmark-paper vs method-paper pairings are inherently asymmetric; partial is preferred over invalid because the failure-type overlap (faithfulness/conflict) is genuine and one could in principle evaluate FaithfulRAG on RAGTruth-style data.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (raat2024 counterfactual subtype)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (irrelevantContext2023); benchmark-constructed stressor with three injected noise types including counterfactual (raat2024). No adversarial corpus-write threat model in either.
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (irrelevantContext2023, NLI filter + fine-tune); generator prompting or training (raat2024, RAAT + multi-task noise-aware head)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) in both
action_policy: filter + answer (irrelevantContext2023, NLI decides to drop context and fall back to no-retrieval LLM); answer (raat2024, internal noise classification but no explicit abstain/filter action reported)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness for ODQA RALMs, fine-tune LLaMA-family generators, and report answer correctness on overlapping benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA), so they share the high-level problem framing. However, irrelevantContext2023 scopes 'noise' to retriever-induced irrelevance (benign retrieval error) and couples training with an NLI-based filtering+fallback action policy, while raat2024 adds a counterfactual (factually misleading) noise category that crosses into consistency/conflict failure and intervenes purely through adaptive adversarial training plus a noise-type classifier, with no filter or abstain action evaluated. Because the failure typology, evidence assumption, intervention surface, and action policy differ, leaderboard-style ranking would conflate methods that solve overlapping but non-identical problems. The relationship is best described as complementary modules within noise-robust RAG rather than substitutes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold the generator backbone, retriever, and benchmark fixed (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B on NQ/TriviaQA with DPR top-10); evaluate both methods on a shared noise mix that explicitly separates irrelevant vs counterfactual subsets; report EM/F1 per noise subtype; and either (a) add an NLI-filter+fallback variant for RAAT or (b) report irrelevantContext2023 with its filter disabled, so the action policies are aligned. Also report whether either method abstains or just answers, so the action coordinate is explicit.
notes: Counterfactual noise in raat2024 is the main coordinate break; without it the two would be close to valid on the irrelevant-noise slice.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency (negative rejection) and consistency/conflict (counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); Paper A also uses benign retrieval error from real retrievers over 5 ODQA corpora
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (robust fine-tuning); Paper B: evaluation artifact (no intervention proposed)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness; Paper B: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (negative-rejection rate) + a counterfactual-resistance score
action_policy: Paper A: answer (with NLI gate deciding whether to use retrieved context); Paper B: answer + abstain (negative rejection is an explicitly evaluated action)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, evidence_assumption (different stressor construction and corpora)
rationale: Both papers fall under noise robustness for RAG, sharing the failure-type of irrelevant/noisy retrieved evidence. However, Paper A is a methods contribution that intervenes at the context-assembly layer (NLI-based passage filtering) and at the generator (robust fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts), evaluated on 5 ODQA benchmarks with answer-correctness as the sole metric and 'answer' as the action policy. Paper B is a benchmark artifact (RGB) that defines four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and proposes no method; it explicitly measures an abstention action policy and uses controlled noise ratios plus counterfactual injection over a freshly built bilingual corpus. The intervention point, metric family, action policy, and stressor construction therefore differ enough that leaderboard-style ranking would mislead, but the shared focus on noise tolerance makes them complementary rather than incompatible.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robust-FT models on the RGB noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds (and ideally counterfactual robustness) with matched generator backbones, report both answer accuracy and rejection rate (with an explicit abstain policy), and conversely evaluate vanilla and prompted baselines from RGB on the 5 ODQA settings of Paper A using the same retriever and noise definition. Without this matched intervention+benchmark grid and shared action-policy reporting, the two papers cannot be directly ranked.
notes: Classic methods-paper vs. benchmark-paper asymmetry; comparison is meaningful as complementary evidence but not as substitutable methods.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor; RAAT injects relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual passages drawn from DPR retrieval over Wikipedia QA; RGB constructs noise ratios and counterfactual documents from news articles via ChatGPT plus human filtering. Neither is a security/adversarial-attacker setting (no corpus write access, no attacker query control, no insertion-budget threat model).
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, EM/F1 or accuracy); RGB additionally measures rejection rate and error detection rate
action_policy: answer (RAAT, no abstention evaluated); answer + abstain (RGB explicitly scores negative rejection)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, action_policy, evidence_assumption (noise construction protocol), metric_target (RGB adds rejection-specific metrics)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG and both ship a benchmark with multiple noise types, so the failure-type coordinate overlaps substantially. However, RAAT is a training-side intervention (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-awareness) evaluated only on answer correctness with an always-answer policy, while RGB is a pure evaluation artifact with no proposed method that explicitly scores the abstain action policy (negative rejection) and information integration as separate abilities. The noise typologies, datasets (NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ vs. bilingual news), retrievers (DPR vs. search-engine results), and metric families differ. They function as complementary contributions—a training method vs. a diagnostic benchmark—rather than alternative methods on a single leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate RAAT-trained LLaMA-2 (and the same base model without RAAT) on RGB's four testbeds using RGB's noise-ratio protocol and rejection-rate metric, or conversely evaluate RGB's tested LLMs on RAG-Bench with the same noise categories; unify the retriever, the noise-construction procedure, the set of action policies scored (answer vs. abstain), and report a common metric family (EM/F1 plus rejection accuracy) so that any ranking reflects method differences rather than benchmark differences.
notes: Not a security pair; threat-model coordinates (corpus write access, attacker query control, insertion budget) are not applicable—both are benign benchmark-constructed noise settings.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency (CoN only)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (DPR-retrieved noisy/irrelevant passages); no attacker model in either paper (no corpus write access, no query control, no insertion budget, no attack objective). This is a distraction pair, not a security pair.
intervention_point: generator prompting/training (CoN: note-taking step) vs. context assembly/compression + generator training (IrrelevantContext: NLI filter + mixed-data fine-tune)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage and rejection rate (CoN only)
action_policy: CoN: answer or abstain ('unknown'), explicitly evaluated via rejection rate. IrrelevantContext: filter then answer (with fallback to non-retrieval generation); abstain not evaluated.
rationale: Both papers tackle RALM robustness to irrelevant/noisy retrieved context on overlapping ODQA benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA) under a shared benign-retrieval-error assumption, so the failure type aligns. However, Chain-of-Note intervenes at the generator via a per-document note-taking step and explicitly evaluates an abstain action ('unknown') with a rejection-rate metric, whereas IrrelevantContext intervenes earlier with an NLI passage filter (falling back to non-retrieval generation, not abstention) plus mixed relevant/irrelevant fine-tuning, and focuses on multi-hop QA without abstain metrics. The intervention point, action policy, and metric target therefore diverge in non-trivial ways: one is a generator-side selective-prediction mechanism, the other is a context-assembly filter combined with robust training. They are complementary modules in the same operating region, not interchangeable entries on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same retriever (e.g., DPR) and generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B) on a common benchmark suite covering both single-hop (NQ/TriviaQA) and multi-hop QA; evaluate both methods under a common action policy (answer-or-abstain with matched abstain thresholds) and report a shared metric family including EM/F1, rejection rate, and risk-coverage curves on identically constructed noisy/irrelevant-context stressors; ideally also report an ablation isolating filter-only vs. generator-reasoning effects so the two interventions are not confounded with their training recipes.
notes: Non-security pair; threat-model coordinates (write access, insertion budget, attack objective) are not applicable. Verdict is partial because the shared problem framing is genuine but the action-policy and intervention divergence prevent honest leaderboard ranking.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, system-control policy, retriever
metric_target: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: abstain, re-retrieve, filter
rationale: Both papers target benign RAG failure modes where retrieved context is irrelevant or insufficient and both aim to make the generator behave more responsibly, so they share the underlying failure type (sufficiency / noisy retrieval). However, Sufficient Context intervenes at inference time with a post-hoc autorater plus self-confidence signal to drive selective abstention, measuring accuracy-conditional-on-answering and hallucination reduction. Self-RAG instead bakes adaptive retrieval and critique behavior into the model via trained reflection tokens, with primary metrics around factuality and citation accuracy and action options spanning on-demand re-retrieval and segment-level filtering rather than abstention. The intervention point, action policy, and metric target therefore differ substantively, so a leaderboard ranking would compare apples (a selective-generation abstention head) to oranges (a trained adaptive-retrieval/critique LM). They are best treated as complementary control mechanisms operating at different points of the RAG pipeline, which is why the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold the base generator, retriever, and corpus constant; evaluate both methods on the same QA benchmarks using a shared action-policy taxonomy (answer / abstain / re-retrieve) with matched abstention budgets; report a common metric family (accuracy at coverage, hallucination rate, and citation faithfulness) so selective abstention and adaptive retrieval/critique can be placed on the same risk-coverage or factuality-coverage curve. Ideally, also ablate whether stacking the two (sufficient-context gating on top of Self-RAG) yields additive gains.
notes: Not a security pair; threat-model coordinates (corpus write access, attacker capability) are not applicable here.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise, sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; no adversarial threat model
intervention_point: reranker + generator calibration (CalibRAG); generator prompting or training, retriever (adaptive on-demand) (Self-RAG)
metric_target: calibration error, answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer with exposed calibrated confidence (CalibRAG); re-retrieve, answer, verify via reflection tokens (Self-RAG)
rationale: Both papers enhance RAG to improve reliability of downstream answers, but they target fundamentally different failure modes: CalibRAG addresses miscalibrated decision confidence by training a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) for reranking and confidence exposure, while Self-RAG addresses indiscriminate retrieval and ungrounded generation via reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval and self-critique. The intervention points differ (reranker + calibration layer vs. generator training with new vocabulary + adaptive retrieve policy), and the primary metric targets differ (calibration error and decision correctness vs. factuality, citation accuracy, and task accuracy); Self-RAG never measures calibration, and CalibRAG never measures citation faithfulness or adaptive-retrieval cost. Their action policies also diverge—CalibRAG exposes calibrated confidence to a human decision-maker, while Self-RAG dynamically chooses retrieve/critique/continue. Therefore they are complementary RAG-control mechanisms rather than direct alternatives on a single leaderboard, warranting a 'partial' verdict.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both systems on a shared task suite with (a) identical retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; (b) calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, selective-risk/coverage) reported for both; (c) factuality and citation-faithfulness metrics reported for both; (d) explicit logging of retrieval frequency/cost for both so adaptive-retrieval claims are commensurable; and (e) explicit action policies (abstain thresholds, confidence exposure, re-retrieve triggers) declared and held constant across systems.
notes: Control-area pair; security threat-model coordinates do not apply. The break is methodological scope, not threat model.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs. retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and retrieved context (no adversary). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker chooses target questions and target answers, black-box and white-box retriever/generator settings, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts per target question, targeted attack objective (induce attacker-chosen answer).
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining + self-think reconciliation). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (injection of malicious passages).
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support under natural conflict. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR).
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy evaluated)
rationale: Both papers concern how non-parametric evidence interacts with an LLM in RAG, but they sit on opposite sides of the threat model: FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense for naturally-occurring parametric vs. retrieved knowledge conflicts measured by answer correctness, while PoisonedRAG is a corpus-side attack that assumes write access to the knowledge database, a targeted attacker-chosen answer, and an insertion budget of ~5 malicious passages, measured by ASR. The evidence assumption (benign conflict vs. attacker-created evidence), the intervention point (generator vs. corpus), the metric family (correctness vs. ASR), and the action policy (reconcile-and-answer vs. no defender action at all) all diverge. Placing them on a single leaderboard would conflate an attack with a defense and a natural-conflict benchmark with an adversarial one, which is misleading rather than informative. Therefore the comparison is invalid, not merely partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a meaningful comparison one would need: (1) a shared adversarial benchmark such as PoisonedRAG-style injections evaluated against FaithfulRAG as a defense, reporting ASR and clean-task correctness on the same retriever/generator stack; (2) a matched threat model specifying corpus write access, insertion budget, query control, and retriever/generator visibility; (3) shared metric definitions (ASR plus answer correctness plus an explicit abstain/quarantine action policy); and (4) evaluation of FaithfulRAG's self-fact reconciliation specifically under attacker-created evidence rather than only natural parametric-context conflicts. Without such an experiment, the two papers solve orthogonal problems.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pairs of this kind are a recurring source of false-equivalence claims; the surface keyword 'conflict' should not bridge natural disagreement and adversarial injection.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption for both; AstuteRAG also covers relevance/noise and consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model (corpus write access yes, query control via target-question selection, retriever visibility black-box and white-box variants, generator access output-only, insertion budget 5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective force attacker-chosen target answer). AstuteRAG: mixes benign retrieval error, benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB worst-case), and informally misleading or malicious passages with no formalized attacker model.
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index injection. AstuteRAG: generator prompting (source-aware iterative consolidation at inference).
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success (ASR). AstuteRAG: answer correctness under imperfect/worst-case retrieval.
action_policy: AstuteRAG: answer after reliability comparison among internal/external candidates. PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy is the object of study).
rationale: Both papers sit in the adversarial-corruption area of RAG, but they play opposite roles: PoisonedRAG is an offensive method that crafts malicious passages and injects them into the corpus to maximize attack success rate, while AstuteRAG is a defensive inference-time method that consolidates LLM-internal knowledge with retrieved passages to maximize answer correctness under imperfect retrieval. Their intervention points (corpus injection vs generator prompting), metric targets (ASR vs accuracy), and action policies are inverse, and AstuteRAG never formalizes a threat model matching PoisonedRAG's (write access, 5-text budget, target-question selection, black/white-box retriever knowledge). Putting them on the same leaderboard would be misleading because they are not competing alternatives; at best they form an attacker/defender pair. Therefore the comparison is invalid as a direct ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate AstuteRAG alongside other defenses (e.g., RobustRAG, CRAG, conflict-aware decoding) against PoisonedRAG under a fixed threat model: same corpus, retriever, generator, insertion budget (e.g., 5 malicious texts per target question), target-question set, with both clean accuracy and post-attack accuracy/ASR reported. The defender action policy (answer/abstain/filter/quarantine) must be explicitly defined and scored, and metrics aligned (defender-side accuracy and attack-conditioned ASR) rather than raw ASR of an attack paper compared to accuracy of a defense paper.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pairing; can be linked as adversary/defender in the same threat model but cannot be ranked head-to-head.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume corpus write access with bounded insertion budget, but PoisonedRAG operates as attacker (chosen target question, ~5 injected texts, black-box and white-box generator access) while RobustRAG operates as defender against an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense and a bounded number of malicious passages
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack) vs context assembly/compression and generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate defense)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG) vs answer correctness with certifiable lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported for PoisonedRAG; answer or abstain ('I don't know') via secure aggregation for RobustRAG
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, role (attack vs defense artifact)
rationale: Both papers address the integrity/adversarial corruption failure type in RAG and share the assumption of attacker-controlled passages injected into the knowledge base. However, PoisonedRAG contributes an attack method optimized to maximize attack success rate at the corpus level, while RobustRAG contributes a defense at the context-assembly/generator level that certifies a robustness lower bound and uses an explicit abstain action via keyword/decoding aggregation. They occupy opposite sides of the threat model (attacker artifact vs defender artifact) with different intervention points, different metric targets, and different action policies, so they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as alternative methods. A direct ranking would be category-incoherent rather than merely partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Valid comparison is not achievable by adding experiments because the artifacts play different roles; a meaningful comparison would instead require a shared evaluation harness in which RobustRAG is evaluated against PoisonedRAG (and other attacks) under matched retriever, generator, corpus, insertion budget, attacker knowledge, and a common metric set (ASR, certified accuracy, clean accuracy, abstention rate), reporting both attack-side and defense-side numbers rather than ranking the two papers against each other.
notes: Attack vs defense pairing; treating them as substitutable methods on one leaderboard would be misleading even though they target the same threat surface.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict (LLM-generated hallucinations against reference passages, manually annotated). RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, synthesized counterfactual documents, negative-rejection testbeds). No adversarial corpus-write threat model in either; this is not a security pair.
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally touches generator (fine-tunes a small detector LLM)
metric_target: RAGTruth: span/response-level hallucination detection F1, hallucination frequency. RGB: answer correctness (accuracy), rejection rate, error/integration rate per ability.
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (no abstain/answer/verify decision evaluated; only post-hoc detection). RGB: answer vs abstain (negative rejection ability explicitly scored).
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation artifacts targeting trustworthiness, and both contain a consistency/conflict component (RAGTruth's evident-conflict spans; RGB's counterfactual robustness). However, RAGTruth measures span-level hallucination detection performance on naturally generated LLM outputs, while RGB measures end-task answer accuracy and rejection on deliberately constructed noisy/counterfactual document sets across four distinct abilities. The evidence assumption (natural vs benchmark-constructed), metric family (detector F1 vs accuracy/rejection), and action policy (none vs explicit abstain) differ substantially, so they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as alternative robust-RAG methods, but they are complementary diagnostics of overlapping failure modes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, one would need (a) a shared task definition (e.g., either both score hallucination detection at span level on a common corpus, or both score answer accuracy + abstain under a common noise/counterfactual construction), (b) aligned evidence construction (natural vs constructed held constant), (c) the same generator(s) and retrieval setting, and (d) a shared action-policy protocol (answer/abstain/flag) with matched metrics. Absent that, the two benchmarks should be reported as complementary instruments, not ranked.
notes: Not a security pair; attacker-capability axes (corpus write, query control, insertion budget) are not invoked by either work. RGB's counterfactual documents are stressors, not an adversarial corpus-write attack.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise (RGB also includes consistency/conflict via counterfactual testbed)
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual docs); SC: naturally occurring retrieval results classified by an LLM autorater (mix of benign retrieval error and benchmark stressor). Neither is security/adversarial in the threat-model sense (no attacker corpus write, no insertion budget, no attack objective).
intervention_point: RGB: evaluation artifact only; SC: evaluation artifact (sufficient-context autorater) + system-control policy (selective generation combining sufficiency and self-confidence)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (SC explicit; RGB implicit via rejection rate)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via Negative Rejection testbed; SC via Correct/Abstain/Hallucinate stratification and guided abstention)
rationale: Both papers examine LLM behavior in RAG when retrieved evidence is imperfect, and notably both treat abstention as a first-class action policy (RGB's Negative Rejection ability ≈ SC's abstention-when-insufficient analysis). However, RGB is a purely diagnostic benchmark with four hand-constructed testbeds (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents, multi-doc integration) on bilingual news data, while SC defines a (Q,C) sufficiency property via an LLM autorater on standard QA datasets and additionally proposes a selective generation method. The intervention points (evaluation artifact only vs. autorater + selective-generation policy), evidence assumptions (constructed stressor vs. naturally retrieved context labelled by classifier), and metric stratifications (per-ability accuracy/rejection vs. sufficiency-stratified correct/abstain/hallucinate plus coverage-risk) differ enough that a leaderboard ranking would conflate different operational definitions. They are complementary lenses on RAG evaluation rather than substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run SC's sufficient-context autorater on RGB's four testbeds and report SC-style correct/abstain/hallucinate stratified metrics alongside RGB's accuracy and rejection rates on the same instances; or alternatively, apply SC's selective generation method on RGB's testbeds (especially Negative Rejection and Counterfactual Robustness) with matched accuracy, rejection, and counterfactual-acceptance metrics. Both should fix the same retriever, generator set, datasets, and an explicit shared abstention threshold/policy.
notes: Not a security pair in the adversarial sense; threat-model coordinates (write access, budget, attack objective) do not apply. RGB's counterfactual testbed is misinformation-style but not modelled as an attacker with a budget.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (FaithfulRAG); broader hallucination including relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict (RAGTruth)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and naturally occurring conflict (RAGTruth corpus is naturally generated LLM outputs over standard retrieval); naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge (FaithfulRAG). Neither pair is security/adversarial; no attacker model, no corpus write access, no insertion budget.
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (RAGTruth corpus); generator prompting (FaithfulRAG self-think) plus context assembly (fact-level alignment and chunking)
metric_target: RAGTruth: hallucination detection (span/case-level F1) and indirectly answer faithfulness; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and evidence support on conflict QA benchmarks
action_policy: unreported (RAGTruth, which is a detection/annotation benchmark); answer (FaithfulRAG, after internal reconciliation, but not framed or evaluated as an explicit abstain/expose-conflict policy)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, failure_type (partial overlap only), action_policy
rationale: Both papers concern faithfulness of RAG outputs, but they operate at fundamentally different points in the pipeline: RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact (a word-level hallucination corpus) used to benchmark and fine-tune hallucination detectors, while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that mines self-facts and runs a self-think module to reconcile parametric vs retrieved knowledge conflicts. The failure type overlaps only partially: RAGTruth covers QA, summarization, and data-to-text hallucinations broadly, whereas FaithfulRAG narrowly targets parametric–contextual knowledge conflict. The metric targets differ (detection-quality F1 over annotated spans vs end-task answer correctness on conflict benchmarks), and action policy is unreported in RAGTruth and only implicit (answer-after-reconcile) in FaithfulRAG. Therefore they are complementary contributions to faithful RAG and cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable methods, justifying a partial verdict rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate FaithfulRAG on the RAGTruth corpus using its span/case-level hallucination metrics across the same QA/summarization/data-to-text tasks, against (a) RAGTruth-fine-tuned detection+regeneration baselines and (b) other faithful-RAG methods, holding retriever, generator backbone, and prompt template constant. Both works would additionally need to declare a common action policy (e.g., answer vs abstain vs expose-conflict) and report end-task correctness plus faithfulness on the same benchmark slice so that detection-oriented and generation-oriented interventions can be ranked under one objective.
notes: Not a security/adversarial pair; attacker-capability fields are not applicable. The asymmetry is mostly benchmark-vs-method, which intrinsically blocks direct ranking even though the topical area aligns.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B's counterfactual category only)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (Paper A, naturally occurring irrelevant passages from real retriever); benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper B, especially counterfactual noise injected for training/evaluation)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (Paper A: NLI filter + fine-tune); generator prompting or training (Paper B: adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-type classification)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1 in both)
action_policy: filter + answer (Paper A explicitly gates on NLI entailment, falling back to no-retrieval answer); answer (Paper B trains to answer through noise with no explicit alternative action reported)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA and report EM/F1 on overlapping datasets (e.g., NQ), so the metric family and broad problem framing align. However, Paper A scopes noise narrowly as irrelevant context naturally produced by the retriever and mitigates it via an explicit NLI-based filter plus light fine-tuning, whereas Paper B redefines noise into three types — relevant, irrelevant, and counterfactual — and intervenes purely via adaptive adversarial training and noise-type multi-task learning, with no filtering/abstention action. Because the counterfactual category is a consistency/conflict failure that Paper A's NLI filter is not designed to handle, and because Paper A's action policy includes filter+answer while Paper B reports only answer, head-to-head leaderboard ranking on a single 'noise robustness' score would conflate different failure modes and different action repertoires. The papers are best discussed as complementary (filter-time vs training-time interventions; irrelevant-only vs broader noise taxonomy), justifying a partial verdict.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Restrict comparison to a common protocol: (1) the same retriever, generator backbone (LLaMA-2 size), and overlapping datasets (e.g., NQ); (2) decompose evaluation by noise type so Paper A is only scored on irrelevant-noise slices unless extended to counterfactuals; (3) report a shared action policy — either both report filter+answer (run RAAT with a comparable NLI gate) or both report answer-only (ablate Paper A's NLI filter); (4) report EM/F1 plus, ideally, a selective-risk/abstention metric so the filter action is credited; (5) align the noise construction procedure (same counterfactual perturbation recipe and same irrelevant-passage sampling).
notes: Counterfactual-noise inclusion in Paper B is the strongest non-comparability driver; without it, the pair would be closer to valid on the irrelevant-noise slice.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); RGB additionally covers sufficiency, consistency/conflict (counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (natural distractors from real retrievers on ODQA); Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents
intervention_point: Paper A: retriever (NLI filter) + generator prompting/training (robust fine-tuning); Paper B: evaluation artifact (diagnostic benchmark, no proposed method)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness; Paper B: answer correctness plus rejection rate and counterfactual identification rate across separate testbeds
action_policy: Paper A: filter-then-answer (route to no-retrieval generation if NLI fails); abstention not evaluated. Paper B: explicitly evaluates abstain (negative rejection) as a first-class ability
rationale: Both papers address noise/irrelevant-context robustness in RAG, but they occupy structurally different roles: Paper A proposes two concrete interventions (NLI-based passage filtering and mixed-context fine-tuning) and evaluates them on five natural ODQA benchmarks, while RGB is a diagnostic benchmark that scores off-the-shelf LLMs across four distinct abilities under constructed noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents, without proposing a method. The intervention-point coordinate diverges (method-on-retriever/generator vs. evaluation artifact), and the evidence-assumption differs (natural retrieval noise vs. controlled stressor). Action policies are also misaligned: Paper A's pipeline filters then answers and never scores abstention, whereas RGB explicitly measures negative rejection as a separate metric. The papers therefore illuminate the same phenomenon family but cannot be placed head-to-head on a single leaderboard, making the comparison partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI filter and robust fine-tuned generator on RGB's noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds (and ideally counterfactual robustness) at matched noise ratios using the same base LLMs, reporting accuracy, rejection rate, and counterfactual identification rate jointly; explicitly declare and evaluate a shared action policy (answer vs. abstain) so both systems are scored on the same decision space.
notes: Method-vs-benchmark asymmetry is the central obstacle; even after fixing datasets, the action-policy gap (abstention not evaluated in Paper A) prevents a leaderboard-style ranking.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor; both inject or sample noisy/counterfactual passages, but RAAT draws from DPR retrieval over Wikipedia for NQ/TQA/WebQ while RGB constructs perturbations from news articles in English and Chinese
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT, adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B with multi-task noise-awareness); evaluation artifact (RGB, pure benchmark with 4 ability testbeds across 6 LLMs)
metric_target: answer correctness (F1/EM for RAAT; accuracy for RGB) plus selective risk/coverage (RGB explicitly scores negative rejection, RAAT does not)
action_policy: answer (RAAT, only generated answers scored); answer + abstain (RGB, negative rejection is an explicit measured ability)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RAG and both treat counterfactual passages as a distinct failure mode, so the failure-type coordinate genuinely overlaps. However, RAAT is a training-time intervention on the generator with its own RAG-Bench (NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ, DPR retrieval, F1/EM only), while RGB is purely an evaluation artifact that scores six off-the-shelf LLMs on four separable abilities including negative rejection and information integration over a bilingual news corpus. Crucially, RGB explicitly evaluates an abstain action (negative rejection) and counterfactual rejection accuracy, whereas RAAT reports only answer-correctness on generated outputs and does not measure rejection or selective risk. Because the artifact types differ (method vs. benchmark), the metric families differ, and the action policies differ, a direct leaderboard ranking would be misleading; they are better discussed as complementary contributions to the same problem.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT-trained LLaMA-2 7B on RGB's four testbeds (and run RGB's evaluated LLMs on RAG-Bench) using the same retriever, the same noise-construction protocol, and the same scoring rubric that covers both answer correctness and negative-rejection/abstain accuracy. Report identical metric targets (EM/F1 plus rejection rate and counterfactual-correction rate) and an explicit action policy (answer vs. abstain) so that the method and the baseline LLMs sit on a shared leaderboard.
notes: Classic method-vs-benchmark pair: ability axes partially align on noise robustness and counterfactuals, but RGB's negative-rejection and integration testbeds have no counterpart in RAAT's evaluation.

failure_type: relevance/noise; Paper A additionally addresses uncertainty/OOD via the 'unknown' rejection scenario
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error in both; Paper B also constructs mixed relevant/irrelevant training stressors (benchmark-constructed stressor)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (both); Paper B additionally uses context assembly/compression via NLI filtering
metric_target: answer correctness (both); Paper A additionally reports selective risk/coverage (rejection rate on RealTimeQA); Paper B additionally evaluates multi-hop accuracy
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain (explicitly trains and evaluates 'unknown'); Paper B: answer + filter (NLI discards passages but final action is answer only, no abstention evaluated)
rationale: Both papers target relevance/noise robustness in RALMs against irrelevant retrieved context and both intervene primarily at the generator via training/prompting, sharing failure type and high-level framing. However, Chain-of-Note explicitly evaluates an abstention action policy through a rejection-rate metric on RealTimeQA, while Yoran et al. evaluate only an answer action and add NLI filtering plus multi-hop QA which CoN does not cover. The benchmark suites only partially overlap (NQ in common; CoN uses TriviaQA/WebQ/RealTimeQA, Yoran uses multi-hop sets like 2WikiMQA/StrategyQA). Because action_policy diverges (abstain vs answer-only) and metric targets / benchmark composition only partly align, raw leaderboard ranking on a single EM number would conflate methods that are optimizing for different operating regions; hence partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods on a matched benchmark suite covering both single-hop ODQA (NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ) and multi-hop (2WikiMQA/StrategyQA) with the same retriever and the same base generator (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B/13B). Report a common metric family that includes EM/F1, abstention/rejection rate, and accuracy-on-answered (selective risk), with explicit action-policy labels per method. Add a noise-robustness slice (irrelevant-context injection) and an unknown-question slice so both abstain-capable and answer-only systems are scored under identical action contracts.
notes: Asymmetric action policy is the decisive break: CoN's 'unknown' option means standard QA accuracy is not directly commensurable with Yoran's answer-only setup.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, verifier, evaluation artifact
metric_target: answer correctness, evidence support, citation faithfulness, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: abstain, re-retrieve, filter, verify
rationale: Both papers target RAG reliability under imperfect retrieval and use a self-assessment signal to govern generation behavior, so the failure-type (sufficiency / relevance) and benign-retrieval evidence assumption overlap. However, Sufficient Context contributes an external LLM autorater plus a post-hoc selective-generation rule whose primary action policy is abstain vs. answer, with metrics framed as %Correct/%Hallucinate/%Abstain and a coverage-risk tradeoff. Self-RAG instead trains an LM end-to-end with reflection tokens that drive on-demand re-retrieval, passage filtering, and self-critique, and is evaluated on factuality and citation accuracy for long-form generation. The intervention points (evaluation artifact + prompting-time gate vs. trained generator/verifier), action policies (selective abstention vs. adaptive retrieve/filter/verify), and primary metric targets (selective risk vs. citation faithfulness) diverge enough that placing them on a single leaderboard would conflate different operating regions, so a partial / complementary framing is the right call.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation protocol: identical QA + long-form benchmarks, the same retriever and base generator, a common action-policy taxonomy that scores both abstention and adaptive-retrieval/critique outputs, and the same metric family (e.g., selective-risk curves AND citation/support metrics computed for both systems). Also need either (a) plugging Self-RAG's reflection tokens into a sufficient-context-style abstention rule, or (b) running Sufficient Context's autorater on Self-RAG's retrieved passages, so the two interventions are evaluated on the same axis rather than each on its native one.
notes: Both could be valid baselines for one another in a unified selective-RAG benchmark, but as published their headline tables are not directly rankable.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (confidence miscalibration for decision support); Self-RAG: relevance/noise and sufficiency (indiscriminate retrieval, irrelevant passages, ungrounded generation)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval (no adversary). CalibRAG assumes standard retrieved documents from open-domain corpora and focuses on whether the LLM's expressed confidence tracks decision correctness. Self-RAG assumes standard retrieval but additionally that some queries do not require retrieval at all.
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker / verifier (forecasting function f(t,q,d) used to rerank and produce calibrated confidence). Self-RAG: generator prompting and training (reflection tokens) plus retriever (on-demand retrieval gating).
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness for decision tasks. Self-RAG: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support / factuality on long-form generation.
