action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with a calibrated confidence score (abstain/escalate not explicitly evaluated as an action). Self-RAG: re-retrieve on demand and emit critique/support tokens that gate continuation. The action surfaces differ and are not evaluated under a shared policy.
rationale: Both papers fall under 'control of RAG generation quality' and share the broad goal of making RAG outputs more trustworthy, and both report some accuracy numbers. However, CalibRAG targets confidence calibration for downstream decisions via a trained forecasting function used at rerank/verify time, whereas Self-RAG targets factuality and citation accuracy through adaptive retrieval and self-critique tokens at the generator. The primary metric targets (ECE/decision calibration vs. citation faithfulness/factuality), intervention points (reranker/verifier vs. generator+retriever), and operational action policies (calibrated-confidence output vs. on-demand retrieve + critique tokens) differ, so a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate distinct problems. They are best discussed as complementary control mechanisms rather than substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both systems on a shared benchmark with (a) identical retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; (b) a common metric suite that includes both calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, selective-risk/coverage) and factuality/citation metrics on the same tasks; (c) an explicit, shared action policy (e.g., answer vs. abstain vs. re-retrieve) so each method's reflection/forecast signal is mapped to the same decision interface; and (d) the same decision-task framing (decision correctness) so CalibRAG's forecasting target and Self-RAG's critique tokens can be compared head-to-head.
notes: Both are 'control' papers but operate on different failure modes (calibration vs. retrieve-when-needed/grounding); without harmonized action policy and metrics, head-to-head ranking would mislead.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and benign retrieved context; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, ~5 malicious passages per target question, black-box and white-box retriever visibility, attacker-chosen target Q/A as attack objective, no query control over real users
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (injection); no shared intervention surface
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support (faithfulness); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciliation, no abstain/quarantine reported); PoisonedRAG: unreported (it is an attack paper, not a defense)
rationale: Both papers concern how retrieved context can mislead an LLM in RAG, but that is essentially the only overlap. FaithfulRAG targets benign, naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflicts and intervenes at the generator via self-fact alignment, measuring answer correctness/faithfulness. PoisonedRAG is an offensive paper that assumes an attacker with corpus write access injecting ~5 malicious passages per target question to induce a chosen answer, measured by attack success rate, with no defensive action policy reported. The two artifacts therefore differ on failure type, evidence/threat model, intervention point, metric target, and action policy simultaneously — a defense method against benign conflict cannot be leaderboard-ranked against a corpus-poisoning attack.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A common evaluation in which (i) FaithfulRAG is run as a defense against PoisonedRAG-injected corpora and PoisonedRAG is run against vanilla-RAG and FaithfulRAG-protected RAG on the same retriever/generator/datasets; (ii) shared metrics include both ASR under attack and answer correctness on clean queries; (iii) the action policy (answer / abstain / quarantine) is explicitly evaluated for both systems; and (iv) the threat model (insertion budget, retriever/generator visibility) is held constant. Without re-instrumenting both as defense candidates under one threat model, they are not on the same leaderboard.
notes: Classic attack-paper vs conflict-defense-paper mismatch; some readers may downgrade to 'partial' because both involve context trust, but the threat models are categorically different.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict (with peripheral mention of malicious content); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict + benchmark-constructed stressor (no formal threat model). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model — corpus write access = yes, query control = attacker knows target questions, retriever visibility = both black-box and white-box variants, generator access = black-box, insertion budget = 5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting + context assembly/compression (post-retrieval defense). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attack injection).
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness under imperfect retrieval. PoisonedRAG: attack success rate. These are not comparable scales — one is maximized by the defender, the other by the attacker.
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (after source-aware consolidation), implicit verify/expose conflict. PoisonedRAG: unreported / not applicable — this is an offensive method, no defender action policy is evaluated.
rationale: Both papers touch the integrity/adversarial-corruption axis of RAG, but they occupy opposite roles: PoisonedRAG is an offensive method that crafts and injects malicious passages into the corpus and reports attack success rate, while Astute RAG is a defensive generation-stage method that mitigates noisy/conflicting retrieved evidence and reports answer correctness. The intervention point (corpus vs generator), metric target (ASR vs correctness), evidence assumption (attacker-created vs primarily benign-error/conflict), and action policy (attack vs answer-after-consolidation) are all incompatible. Placing them on the same leaderboard would be category-confused — there is no shared score where 'better' means the same thing. They are attack/defense counterparts, not alternative methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To produce a meaningful joint result, PoisonedRAG should be used as the stressor and Astute RAG (alongside other defenses such as instructional prompting, RobustRAG, paraphrase filters) should be evaluated as candidate defenses under a fixed threat model (same retriever, same generator, same target-question set, same insertion budget, identical malicious-text generation procedure), reporting defense-side metrics (clean accuracy, accuracy under attack, ASR reduction, abstention rate). Only the defenses can then be ranked against one another; PoisonedRAG itself belongs on a separate axis as the evaluation artifact, not as a competing system.
notes: Astute RAG mentions 'malicious' information in motivation but its main empirical stressors are RGB-style noise and natural conflict, not PoisonedRAG-style optimized injection; this further widens the gap.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; corpus write access = yes for both; query control = attacker selects target Q in PoisonedRAG, RobustRAG assumes adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge; retriever visibility = black-box and white-box variants in PoisonedRAG, RobustRAG threat model assumes full knowledge; generator access = none for attacker beyond corpus injection; insertion budget = ~5 passages (PoisonedRAG) vs bounded m (RobustRAG certificate parameter); attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer (PoisonedRAG) vs preserve correctness/abstain (RobustRAG)
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attacker-side); context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG defender-side isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG ASR); answer correctness + certified robustness lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: answer (PoisonedRAG evaluates standard answering under attack); abstain + aggregate/filter (RobustRAG explicitly uses 'I don't know' and keyword/decoding aggregation)
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat space of corpus-injection corruption against RAG and share the failure type and broad evidence assumption (attacker-created passages with bounded insertion budget). However, PoisonedRAG is an offense paper whose intervention is at the corpus and whose metric is attack success rate against a standard answer-only policy, while RobustRAG is a defense whose intervention is isolate-then-aggregate at context assembly/generation, measures certified answer correctness, and explicitly permits abstention. These are complementary artifacts (attack vs defense), not substitutable methods on a single leaderboard; one would naturally be used to evaluate the other rather than ranked against it. Hence partial, not valid—and not invalid because the threat-model coordinates align well enough that a joint attack-vs-defense evaluation is meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared adversarial benchmark fixing corpus, retriever, generator, target-question set, and insertion budget m, where attacks (including PoisonedRAG) are scored by ASR / certified-bound violation rate and defenses (including RobustRAG) are scored by clean accuracy, accuracy-under-attack, abstention rate, and certified robust accuracy at matched m. Each paper would need to report results under both roles—e.g., RobustRAG evaluated specifically against PoisonedRAG's black-box and white-box variants at identical budgets, and PoisonedRAG evaluated against RobustRAG's keyword/decoding aggregation—with a common action-policy specification (answer vs abstain) so the two artifacts populate complementary rows of the same evaluation matrix rather than a single ranked list.
notes: Classic attack/defense asymmetry: same coordinate system, opposite roles. 'Partial' captures their complementary leaderboard role without conflating them as substitutable methods.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict (hallucinations arising from real LLM generations over retrieved passages); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents, deliberately insufficient sets)
intervention_point: RAGTruth: verifier (hallucination detector) + evaluation artifact; RGB: evaluation artifact targeting generator prompting behavior
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection P/R/F1; RGB: answer correctness, rejection rate, error detection/correction rate
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc detection of hallucinated spans); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection is an explicitly scored action)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation artifacts concerned with trustworthiness, and both touch consistency/conflict failures (RAGTruth annotates 'evident conflict' spans; RGB tests counterfactual robustness). However, the artifacts target fundamentally different objects: RAGTruth scores a downstream hallucination *detector* over naturally generated outputs at the span level, while RGB scores the *generator's* answer-or-abstain behavior under controlled noise, counterfactual, and insufficient-evidence conditions. The action policies (verify vs. answer/abstain), metric families (span-level detection F1 vs. task accuracy and rejection rate), and evidence construction (natural vs. synthetically stressed) all diverge, so a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate detector quality with generator robustness. The two benchmarks are best treated as complementary slices of robust RAG rather than substitutable testbeds.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require either (a) running the same system under both benchmarks with a shared metric family (e.g., evaluating RGB-style answer correctness on RAGTruth's QA subset and conversely running a hallucination detector against RGB-generated outputs with span-level ground truth), or (b) reporting a common operating point: same retriever, same generator(s), aligned evidence assumptions (natural vs. constructed), and an explicit, shared action-policy label (answer/abstain/flag) with matched metrics. Without that bridge, only complementary discussion is defensible.
notes: Both are benchmarks rather than methods, so 'leaderboard comparability' here means whether systems' scores transfer between them; they do not.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (varying noise ratios, injected counterfactuals over news articles); Sufficient Context: naturally occurring retrieval on standard QA (HotPotQA, Musique, etc.) labeled by an LLM autorater for sufficiency
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); generator prompting (Sufficient Context only, via selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (SC), negative-rejection / abstention rate (RGB rejection rate; SC %Abstain vs %Hallucinate)
action_policy: answer, abstain (explicitly evaluated in both: RGB's 'negative rejection' testbed; SC's selective generation and abstain/hallucinate stratification)
rationale: Both papers explicitly treat answer-vs-abstain as a first-class action and care about model behavior when retrieved context is insufficient or noisy, so the failure-type axis and action policy align well. However, RGB is a constructed bilingual benchmark with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injection over news passages, evaluated with task-specific accuracy/rejection/error-detection metrics, while Sufficient Context defines sufficiency over naturally retrieved contexts on standard QA datasets and operationalizes it through an LLM autorater and a selective-generation intervention scored with a selective-risk/coverage frame. Because the evidence construction, datasets, metric families, and scope (pure benchmark vs benchmark + intervention) differ, raw numbers from one cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as the other. They are best read as complementary lenses on the same underlying phenomena (sufficiency, abstention, noise), justifying partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's autorater and selective-generation method on RGB's four testbeds (or run RGB-style noise/counterfactual constructions on HotPotQA/Musique), report a shared metric set covering accuracy, abstention rate, hallucination rate, and selective risk/coverage at matched coverage, hold the retriever and generator fixed across both setups, and align the action-policy definitions (what counts as a valid 'I don't know') so the negative-rejection rate and SC abstention are measured identically.
notes: Sufficient Context is partly methodological (selective generation) while RGB is purely diagnostic; this asymmetry alone prevents leaderboard-style ranking even though both explicitly evaluate the abstain action.

failure_type: consistency/conflict for both; RAGTruth additionally covers sufficiency and relevance/noise hallucinations beyond conflict
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval with naturally generated LLM responses across QA, summarization, and data-to-text; FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring and elicited parametric-vs-context conflict on knowledge-intensive QA
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus plus fine-tuned detector baseline); FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training via self-fact mining, alignment, and self-think before answering
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support and citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection performance; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness under knowledge conflict
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (post-hoc detection, no generation policy evaluated); FaithfulRAG: answer (reconciled output after self-think)
rationale: Both papers concern faithfulness and hallucination in RAG, and RAGTruth's evident/subtle conflict category overlaps thematically with FaithfulRAG's parametric-versus-contextual conflict. However, RAGTruth is fundamentally an evaluation artifact (an 18K-response annotated corpus plus benchmarked detectors) whose metric target is span-level hallucination detection, while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention whose metric target is end-task answer correctness under conflict. Their action policies also differ: RAGTruth does not define or evaluate any runtime action (detection is post-hoc), whereas FaithfulRAG commits to an answer after reconciling conflicting facts. They are best treated as complementary (a benchmark vs. a generator-side mitigation) rather than as alternatives on a shared leaderboard, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG on the RAGTruth QA split with the same retriever/generator base models and report (a) span-level hallucination rates using RAGTruth's annotation schema and (b) downstream answer correctness under matched conflict conditions; conversely, instantiate a RAGTruth-trained detector as a runtime verifier with an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/re-retrieve) and compare end-to-end faithfulness and accuracy against FaithfulRAG under identical contexts, metrics, and decoding settings.
notes: Benchmark-vs-method asymmetry is the dominant reason for partial; if RAGTruth were used purely as a shared eval substrate with matched metrics and an explicit action policy, the pair could approach valid.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (raat2024 counterfactual noise only)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); benign retrieval error (irrelevantContext2023 analyzes real DPR/retriever errors across 5 ODQA sets)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (irrelevantContext2023: NLI filter and fine-tuning); generator prompting or training (raat2024: adaptive adversarial training + noise-aware multi-task head)
metric_target: answer correctness (F1/EM) for both
action_policy: filter + answer (irrelevantContext2023, NLI baseline explicitly abstains from context use); answer with internal noise-type classification (raat2024, no explicit filter/abstain action evaluated)
rationale: Both papers tackle noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA and report answer correctness, so they sit in the same general problem space. However, raat2024 expands the failure scope to include counterfactual (conflicting) passages, which irrelevantContext2023 does not target, and uses a single generator-side adversarial training intervention, whereas irrelevantContext2023 evaluates an additional pre-generator NLI filtering action alongside fine-tuning. The action policies therefore differ (filter+answer vs. answer-only with internal noise classification), and benchmark composition / noise mixture proportions are not aligned. Direct leaderboard ranking would conflate these scope and mechanism differences, so the pair is best treated as partial / complementary.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same retriever (e.g., DPR) and generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), evaluate on a shared noise mixture covering irrelevant and counterfactual passages with reported per-noise-type proportions, run both methods (NLI-filter + Yoran-style fine-tune vs. RAAT) under identical EM/F1 protocols on the same QA sets (e.g., NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ), and explicitly report action policy (answer vs. filter/abstain) per condition; ideally also report a counterfactual-only slice so the conflict-handling gap is visible.
notes: raat2024 cites Yoran et al. as prior work, confirming related but expanded scope rather than substitutable methods.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency and consistency/conflict (counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error plus benchmark-constructed irrelevant passages from natural ODQA retrieval. Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents from curated news.
intervention_point: Paper A: retriever (NLI filter) and generator prompting/training (robust fine-tuning). Paper B: evaluation artifact only (no proposed intervention).
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness (EM/F1 on 5 ODQA datasets). Paper B: answer correctness under varying noise ratio, rejection rate, integration accuracy, and counterfactual error identification rate.
action_policy: Paper A: filter (NLI baseline) and answer (after robust training); abstention not explicitly evaluated. Paper B: answer and abstain (negative rejection is an explicitly scored ability).
rationale: Both papers center on noise robustness in retrieval-augmented generation, but they are categorically different contributions: Paper A proposes interventions (NLI filtering plus mixed-context fine-tuning) and measures answer accuracy on ODQA, while Paper B is a diagnostic benchmark (RGB) that decomposes RAG into four abilities including noise robustness, negative rejection (abstention), information integration, and counterfactual robustness. The intervention point differs (method vs. evaluation artifact), the metric target is strictly broader in Paper B, and the action policies evaluated diverge — Paper A does not explicitly score abstention while Paper B treats negative rejection as a first-class metric. They cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable methods, but they are clearly complementary: Paper A's mitigations could be scored on Paper B's testbeds. Hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robust-tuned generator on RGB's four testbeds (matching noise ratios, the rejection prompt protocol, and the counterfactual identification metric), holding retriever and base generator constant. Conversely, RGB would need to report an answer-accuracy track comparable to ODQA EM/F1 used in Paper A. Both papers must also state and score the same action-policy set (at minimum answer vs. abstain, and ideally filter), with identical thresholds and metric definitions, before a leaderboard-style ranking would be meaningful.
notes: Method paper vs. benchmark paper is the dominant axis; partial is preferred over under-specified because both papers are fully specified, just non-substitutable.

failure_type: relevance/noise; consistency/conflict (RGB also covers sufficiency via negative rejection)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor; RAAT additionally relies on benign retrieval errors from DPR over Wikipedia, RGB synthesizes/curates from news with human adjustment
intervention_point: RAAT: generator prompting or training (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA2-7B with multi-task noise classification); RGB: evaluation artifact only (no proposed intervention)
metric_target: answer correctness (F1/EM for RAAT; accuracy for RGB noise testbed); RGB additionally measures rejection rate and error detection rate
action_policy: RAAT: answer (no abstain mechanism evaluated); RGB: answer plus abstain (negative rejection testbed explicitly probes refusal)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, action_policy, failure_type scope, metric_target scope
rationale: Both papers target robustness of RAG pipelines to noisy retrieved evidence and overlap on the relevance/noise and counterfactual-conflict failure types in open-domain QA. However, RAAT is primarily a training-side intervention (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning with auxiliary noise classification) plus its own RAG-Bench, while RGB contributes only a diagnostic benchmark with no method and explicitly evaluates additional abilities—negative rejection (abstain) and information integration—that RAAT does not address or measure. The intervention point thus mismatches (training method vs. evaluation artifact), and the action-policy spaces differ (answer-only vs. answer+abstain), so a leaderboard-style ranking of 'RAAT vs RGB' is not meaningful. They are best treated as complementary: RGB is a measurement instrument whose noise-robustness testbed could be applied to evaluate RAAT, rather than a competing method.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, one would need to (1) treat RGB as the evaluation surface and run RAAT (and a vanilla LLaMA2-7B baseline) on the RGB noise robustness, negative rejection, counterfactual, and integration testbeds using RGB's metrics including rejection and error-detection rates; (2) align the retriever, document construction, and noise ratio definitions across the two benchmarks; and (3) explicitly evaluate RAAT's action policy under insufficient evidence (abstain) since RAAT currently only reports answer-correctness. Without these, the two works occupy different roles (method+own benchmark vs diagnostic benchmark) and cannot be ranked head-to-head.
notes: Pair mixes a method paper with a pure benchmark paper; partial is more informative than under-specified because the coordinate mismatches are clearly identifiable from the available materials.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); sufficiency and uncertainty/OOD additionally for Chain-of-Note (unknown handling)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor for both; Chain-of-Note also stresses real-time/out-of-pretraining questions; Irrelevant Context emphasizes multi-hop distractor passages
intervention_point: generator prompting/training (Chain-of-Note: note-taking before answering, fine-tuned on 10K CoN traces); context assembly/compression + generator training (Irrelevant Context: NLI-based passage filtering plus fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts)
metric_target: answer correctness for both; Chain-of-Note additionally reports rejection/abstention rate (selective risk/coverage); Irrelevant Context reports retrieval-helps-vs-hurts deltas without abstention metric
action_policy: Chain-of-Note: answer + abstain ('unknown') explicitly evaluated; Irrelevant Context: answer (with filter step preceding generation, no abstain policy reported)
rationale: Both papers target distraction by irrelevant retrieved passages in open-domain QA and share the failure-type framing that RALMs are brittle to noisy context. However, the intervention points differ substantively: Chain-of-Note modifies generator reasoning via per-document reading notes, while Yoran et al. operate primarily at context assembly via an NLI filter plus a fine-tuning recipe on mixed-quality contexts. Their action policies are also asymmetric: Chain-of-Note explicitly evaluates an abstain action ('unknown') and reports rejection rate on RealTimeQA, whereas the Irrelevant Context paper does not evaluate an abstention action and confines itself to answer correctness (including multi-hop). Benchmarks, retrievers, and noise constructions only partially overlap (both touch NQ; the rest diverge, and Yoran et al. emphasize multi-hop). These are therefore complementary mechanisms operating in different parts of the pipeline rather than directly rankable alternatives on a single leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-run both methods with a shared retriever and generator backbone on a common benchmark suite (e.g., NQ + a multi-hop set like StrategyQA/2WikiMultihopQA) using identical noise/irrelevance construction; report a common metric bundle including answer EM/F1, retrieval-helps-vs-hurts delta, and a calibration/abstention metric (rejection rate, selective risk-coverage) with an explicitly declared action policy (answer vs abstain vs filter-then-answer) for both systems; also disclose whether NLI-filtering is applied before Chain-of-Note's note generation as an ablation to isolate filtering vs reasoning contributions.
notes: Both papers are clearly in the distraction/noise family, but the abstention dimension in Chain-of-Note and the filtering dimension in Yoran et al. push them into complementary roles rather than head-to-head leaderboard competitors.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: Paper A: evaluation artifact (sufficiency autorater) + generator prompting (selective generation) + verifier; Paper B: generator training (reflection tokens) + retriever (on-demand) + verifier (critique tokens)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage; Paper B: answer correctness, evidence support, citation faithfulness
action_policy: Paper A: abstain (selective generation); Paper B: re-retrieve, filter, answer (with critique)
rationale: Both papers address RAG quality when retrieved context may be irrelevant or insufficient, and both incorporate forms of self-assessment, so the failure-type and evidence-assumption coordinates substantially overlap. However, Sufficient Context contributes an external autorater plus an inference-time selective-generation rule that enacts an explicit abstention policy and is measured by hallucination reduction among answered queries (selective risk/coverage), whereas Self-RAG trains a single LM end-to-end with reflection tokens that govern on-demand re-retrieval, relevance filtering, and citation-aware self-critique, evaluated primarily on factuality and citation accuracy. The intervention point (inference-time verifier+abstain vs. training-time integrated retrieve/critique LM), action policy (abstain vs. re-retrieve/filter/answer-with-critique), and primary metric target (selective answer correctness vs. evidence support and citation faithfulness) all differ enough that a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate qualitatively different mechanisms. They are better framed as complementary modules or different operating regions of the broader 'use context only when it helps' problem.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold retriever and generator backbones constant, evaluate both systems on the same QA benchmarks under a unified action-policy regime (e.g., enable abstention for both, or enable adaptive re-retrieval for both), and report a common metric suite covering answer correctness, hallucination/abstention rates, evidence support, and citation accuracy. Ideally also probe both methods at matched coverage levels (risk-coverage curves) and on the same sufficiency-stratified slices so that selective generation and reflection-token gating are compared on equivalent decision tasks.
notes: Both action policies are explicitly evaluated in their respective papers, so under-specified is not warranted; the issue is structural mismatch in what each method does and measures.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence in decision-making); Self-RAG: relevance/noise and sufficiency (indiscriminate retrieval, off-topic passages)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval errors; no adversarial threat model in either paper. CalibRAG assumes a decision-making query with candidate documents; Self-RAG assumes general knowledge-intensive QA/long-form tasks where retrieval may or may not help.
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker (forecasting function over (t,q,d)) plus generator confidence calibration; Self-RAG: generator prompting/training with reflection tokens plus retriever (on-demand triggering)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error and decision/answer correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer (with calibrated confidence; abstention not explicitly evaluated); Self-RAG: answer plus on-demand re-retrieve and filter via reflection tokens (Retrieve/ISREL/ISSUP)
rationale: Both papers sit in the broad 'control/reliability of RAG' space and share a benign-retrieval evidence assumption, but they target different failure modes: CalibRAG addresses miscalibration of model confidence to improve human decision-making, while Self-RAG addresses indiscriminate retrieval and unsupported generation via on-demand retrieval and self-critique tokens. Their primary metric families differ (ECE/calibration + decision correctness vs. factuality, citation faithfulness, and answer correctness), and their action policies are categorically different (calibrated-confidence answering vs. token-driven retrieve/filter/critique). The intervention points only partially overlap (forecasting-based reranking vs. reflection-token-trained generator with adaptive retriever). They could be reported as complementary modules in a reliability stack, but a direct leaderboard ranking would conflate calibration quality with factuality/adaptive-retrieval quality and therefore mislead.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark that (1) fixes the retriever and base generator, (2) reports both calibration metrics (ECE/Brier/selective risk under abstention) AND citation/support metrics on the same outputs, (3) specifies and evaluates a common action policy set including answer/abstain/re-retrieve, and (4) covers both decision-making-style tasks (CalibRAG's regime) and open-domain/long-form factuality tasks (Self-RAG's regime), so each method is exercised on the failure mode the other targets.
notes: Pair is 'control' area but the two systems control different things (confidence vs. retrieval/critique), which is the core reason partial rather than valid is appropriate.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict / benchmark-constructed stressor between parametric and retrieved knowledge. PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, known target questions, black- and white-box retriever visibility, black-box generator access, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting or training (self-fact mining, contextual alignment, self-think). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive injection, not a defensive intervention).
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness, evidence support (faithfulness). PoisonedRAG: attack success (ASR).
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after fact-level reconciliation). PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defensive action policy evaluated).
rationale: Both papers concern reliability of retrieved evidence in RAG, but they occupy fundamentally different problem settings and roles. FaithfulRAG is a defense/method paper that resolves naturally occurring conflicts between parametric knowledge and retrieved context by reasoning at the fact level inside the generator, measured by answer correctness/faithfulness with an 'answer' action. PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that exploits corpus write access to inject ~5 malicious passages per target question and is measured by attack success rate against target answers; it does not implement or evaluate a defensive action policy. All five coordinates diverge, and crucially the two have opposite normative stances toward the retrieved context (trust it vs. distrust it because it is poisoned). Placing them on the same leaderboard would conflate an attacker with a context-faithfulness defender and is therefore invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Comparability would require recasting both as defenses evaluated on a shared benchmark that includes (a) naturally occurring parametric–context conflicts and (b) adversarially poisoned passages crafted under the PoisonedRAG threat model (same insertion budget, retriever/generator stack, query control). Both methods would need to report the same metric family (end-to-end answer accuracy plus ASR-under-poisoning, and ideally selective risk/coverage) and an explicit, measured action policy (answer vs. abstain/quarantine). Without re-purposing PoisonedRAG as a defense (or pairing FaithfulRAG against a defense baseline tested under PoisonedRAG attacks), no direct head-to-head ranking is meaningful.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pairing with incompatible threat models; cleanly invalid rather than partial because the prescribed action toward retrieved context is opposite in the two settings.

failure_type: Astute: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Astute: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor + naturally occurring conflict; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence. Threat model for PoisonedRAG: corpus write access = yes (inject 5 malicious texts per target question), query control = attacker chooses target Q/A, retriever visibility = black-box and white-box variants, generator access = black-box and white-box, insertion budget = 5 texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer.
intervention_point: Astute: generator prompting (post-retrieval source-aware consolidation, internal-knowledge elicitation); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious-text injection). Opposing pipeline stages.
metric_target: Astute: answer correctness (worst-case accuracy under imperfect retrieval); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate. Metrics are inverted — high ASR is success for PoisonedRAG and failure for ASTUTE.
action_policy: Astute: answer (with source-aware reasoning over consolidated candidates) — abstain not evaluated; PoisonedRAG: unreported (it is an attack-construction pipeline, not a deployed answering system).
rationale: Both papers nominally inhabit the robust-RAG space, but they occupy opposite roles: ASTUTE RAG is a generator-side defense that elicits LLM-internal knowledge and performs source-aware consolidation to resolve conflicts under imperfect (mostly benign or benchmark-noisy) retrieval, while PoisonedRAG is a corpus-poisoning attack that optimizes malicious passages to coerce attacker-chosen target answers. All five coordinates diverge: failure type (noise/conflict vs adversarial corruption), evidence assumption (benign/benchmark vs attacker-created), intervention point (generator prompting vs corpus injection), metric target (answer correctness vs attack success), and action policy (answer with consolidation vs no system action). Although ASTUTE mentions 'malicious' information in motivation, it is not evaluated against PoisonedRAG-style optimized injections, and PoisonedRAG does not propose or evaluate a defense, so the two cannot sit on the same leaderboard as alternative methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, one would need a shared evaluation harness where (a) PoisonedRAG is run as the adversary that injects k malicious passages into the same corpus/retriever/generator stack, (b) ASTUTE RAG is evaluated as one of several defenses on the resulting poisoned retrieval, (c) both papers report the same metric pair (clean-task accuracy and attack success rate / target-answer rate) on the same datasets (e.g., NQ, HotpotQA, MS-MARCO), (d) threat-model parameters (insertion budget, retriever visibility, generator access, query control) are held constant, and (e) explicit action policy (answer vs abstain vs flag) is reported for the defended system. Only then is leaderboard-style ranking meaningful — and even then, ASTUTE would be a defense entry and PoisonedRAG an attack/benchmark entry, not interchangeable methods.
notes: Attack paper vs defense paper — comparability is at the benchmark level, not the method level.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; corpus write access (yes for both threat models), query control (attacker selects target questions in PoisonedRAG; arbitrary queries in RobustRAG eval), retriever visibility (PoisonedRAG: black-box and white-box; RobustRAG assumes adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge), generator access (varies), insertion budget (small bounded; ~5 in PoisonedRAG; bounded m' in RobustRAG certification), attack objective (induce attacker-chosen target answer)
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack) vs. context assembly/compression + verifier (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG ASR) vs. answer correctness with certified robustness lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported (PoisonedRAG is an attack, no defender action) vs. answer + abstain ('I don't know' in keyword aggregation) for RobustRAG
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat space (adversarial corruption of RAG via injection of a small bounded number of malicious passages into the knowledge database), and their threat models are largely compatible. However, PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that intervenes at the corpus and measures attack success rate against undefended RAG, while RobustRAG is a defense paper that intervenes at context assembly/verifier via isolate-then-aggregate and measures certified accuracy under bounded corruption with an explicit abstain option. Because one paper proposes an attack and the other proposes a defense, the intervention points, metric targets, and action policies are categorically different and they cannot be ranked as substitutable methods on a single leaderboard. They are, however, clearly complementary: RobustRAG is naturally evaluable against PoisonedRAG-style attacks, which justifies a 'partial' rather than 'invalid' verdict.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct comparison is not appropriate at all (attack vs. defense are not substitutes). To produce a meaningful joint evaluation, both works should be placed inside a shared attack-defense benchmark with a fixed retriever/generator, fixed insertion budget m, identical target-question sets, and paired metrics (ASR before defense, ASR after RobustRAG, certified robust accuracy, abstain rate, clean-task utility). Only under such a co-evaluation can the two papers be discussed together, and even then they should be reported as complementary axes (attacker capability vs. certified defender robustness), not as competing entries on the same leaderboard.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pair; same threat type but different roles. 'partial' captures the complementary-but-not-substitutable relationship better than 'invalid'.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations from standard RAG pipelines (benign retrieval, generator-side faithfulness failures). RGB: benchmark-constructed stressors with controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents.
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally evaluates verifier/detector methods, RGB evaluates generator prompting behavior
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness (span-level hallucination detection F1). RGB: answer correctness plus rejection rate and counterfactual resistance.
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (post-hoc detect/annotate, no action labels). RGB: answer vs abstain (negative rejection explicitly evaluated).
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation benchmarks broadly concerned with unfaithful or incorrect generation under retrieved context, and both publish reusable corpora for diagnosing LLM behavior. However, RAGTruth measures word-level hallucination in naturally produced RAG outputs and benchmarks detector methods (faithfulness / evidence-support metric, no explicit answer-vs-abstain policy), while RGB constructs controlled testbeds for four separable abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) with answer correctness and explicit abstention as targets. The evidence-construction assumption (organic generator errors vs. constructed stressors and counterfactual injections), the metric family, and the action policy all differ, so a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate distinct phenomena. They should be reported as complementary diagnostics, not as substitutes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make these directly comparable, one would need: (i) a common evaluation slice where the same retrieved contexts are used and both span-level faithfulness and answer correctness (plus abstention rate) are scored; (ii) alignment of evidence construction (either both natural or both constructed stressors with matched noise/counterfactual ratios); (iii) an explicit, identical action policy (e.g., answer-or-abstain with the same threshold protocol); and (iv) shared generators and prompting so that detector-vs-generator interventions can be separated from corpus differences.
notes: Both are categorized as evaluation benchmarks, but RGB's counterfactual-robustness and negative-rejection axes have no analogue in RAGTruth, and RAGTruth's span-level faithfulness has no analogue in RGB.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise (RGB also: consistency/conflict via counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactuals); Sufficient Context: naturally occurring retrieval over standard QA datasets plus autorater-derived sufficiency labels
intervention_point: RGB: evaluation artifact only; Sufficient Context: evaluation artifact + verifier (sufficiency autorater) + system-control policy (selective generation)
metric_target: RGB: answer correctness, rejection rate per ability testbed; Sufficient Context: answer correctness, hallucination/abstention rates stratified by sufficiency, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate these; RGB via negative-rejection testbed, Sufficient Context via selective generation)
rationale: Both papers examine LLM behavior under imperfect retrieval, with clear overlap on the sufficiency/abstention axis: RGB's negative-rejection testbed measures whether models abstain when documents lack the answer, while Sufficient Context defines a sufficient-context property and stratifies hallucination/abstention by it. However, RGB is purely a four-ability diagnostic benchmark built from controlled stressors (noise ratios, injected counterfactuals), whereas Sufficient Context combines a sufficiency autorater lens on naturally-occurring retrieval with a proposed selective-generation intervention; one contributes only an evaluation artifact while the other adds a verifier and a control policy. Their metric families differ accordingly (per-ability accuracy/rejection vs. sufficiency-stratified correctness and selective risk). They cannot sit on the same leaderboard as substitutable methods, but they are complementary on the shared sufficiency dimension, so partial—not invalid—is appropriate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's autorater and selective-generation method on RGB's negative-rejection and noise-robustness testbeds, and conversely evaluate RGB-style models on Sufficient Context's stratified datasets, reporting a shared metric family (e.g., abstention precision/recall, selective accuracy at fixed coverage) under a common retriever, generator, and explicit answer/abstain action policy. Alternatively, restrict the comparison to the negative-rejection vs. insufficient-context slice with matched stressor construction so both papers report the same answer-vs-abstain decisions on identical (query, context) pairs.
notes: RGB is fundamentally a benchmark; Sufficient Context is a lens+method that happens to evaluate on QA datasets. The asymmetry of contribution type is the main barrier to direct ranking.

failure_type: RAGTruth covers broad hallucination (relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict in generation); FaithfulRAG narrowly targets consistency/conflict (parametric vs. retrieved)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict and benign retrieval producing organic LLM hallucinations across QA/data-to-text/summarization; FaithfulRAG: benchmark-constructed knowledge-conflict scenarios where retrieved context contradicts parametric knowledge
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (and optionally fine-tuning data for a detector); FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining + self-think reasoning module)
metric_target: RAGTruth: detector-side hallucination identification (span/case-level detection F1); FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and evidence support on knowledge-conflict QA
action_policy: unreported for both (RAGTruth defines no action policy; FaithfulRAG implicitly always answers after reconciliation but does not formally evaluate abstain/expose-conflict)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, evidence_assumption, failure_type scope, action_policy
rationale: Both papers concern faithfulness in RAG, but they are fundamentally different artifacts: RAGTruth is an evaluation corpus with word-level hallucination annotations across QA, data-to-text, and summarization, intended to benchmark and train hallucination *detectors*, while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time *method* that mines self-facts and runs a self-think module to specifically reconcile parametric vs. retrieved knowledge conflicts. They differ on intervention point (eval artifact vs. generator), on failure-type scope (broad hallucination including noise/sufficiency vs. narrow knowledge-conflict), on metric target (span-level detection vs. answer correctness/faithfulness), and on evidence assumption (naturally generated hallucinations vs. constructed conflicts). They are complementary tools rather than competing methods on the same leaderboard, so the verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make this directly comparable, FaithfulRAG would need to be evaluated on RAGTruth's QA subset with the same retriever, generator backbones, and span-level hallucination scoring, OR RAGTruth-derived detector baselines would need to be applied to FaithfulRAG's knowledge-conflict benchmarks using a shared task definition, identical input/output protocol, matched action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. expose-conflict), and the same metric family (e.g., answer accuracy plus faithfulness/grounding rate).
notes: Classic benchmark-vs-method mismatch within the same broad area; they can cite each other but cannot be ranked side-by-side.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B's counterfactual noise category only)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (both); Paper B additionally constructs counterfactual passages as a benchmark stressor
intervention_point: Paper A: retriever (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning). Paper B: generator prompting or training only (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-type classification)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: Paper A: filter (NLI gating) + answer (fall back to no-context LLM on contradiction). Paper B: answer (with internal noise-type recognition but no operational policy reported beyond generation) — effectively unreported as a deployable action policy
breaking_coordinates: failure_type, intervention_point, action_policy, evaluation_artifact (different benchmark slices and noise construction)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA and share answer correctness as the primary metric, with partial dataset overlap (NQ). However, Paper A scopes the failure to irrelevant context and uses a hybrid intervention (NLI filtering at retriever stage + light fine-tuning with mixed contexts), while Paper B broadens the failure typology to include counterfactual/conflicting passages and intervenes purely at the generator via adaptive adversarial training plus multi-task noise classification. Action policies also diverge: Paper A explicitly routes contradicted contexts to a no-retrieval fallback (filter+answer), whereas Paper B has no comparable gating action — its noise-type head is internal and not converted to an operational policy. Because the noise distributions, intervention surfaces, and action policies differ, leaderboard-style ranking would conflate a filtering-plus-training system against a pure adversarial-training system on incomparable noise mixes, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared benchmark with a fixed retriever (e.g., DPR top-k on Wikipedia), the same base LLM (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), an identical noise injection protocol covering irrelevant AND counterfactual passages at matched rates, identical EM/F1 evaluation, and a declared action policy (answer-only vs. filter+fallback vs. abstain) reported separately so each system is judged under the same operational regime. Also report performance with and without the NLI filter for Paper A and with/without the multi-task head for Paper B to isolate the training-only contribution.
notes: Paper B cites Paper A as prior work but does not re-evaluate Paper A's filter+train pipeline on RAG-Bench, so head-to-head numbers in Paper B are not directly comparable; the partial verdict reflects scope and action-policy mismatch rather than methodological incompatibility.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency and consistency/conflict via negative rejection and counterfactual testbeds
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); Paper A also uses benign retrieval error from real retrievers on 5 ODQA datasets
intervention_point: Paper A: filter (NLI) + generator prompting/training; Paper B: evaluation artifact only (no intervention proposed)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness; Paper B: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (negative rejection rate) + counterfactual robustness
action_policy: Paper A: filter then answer (fall back to no-retrieval when NLI rejects); Paper B: evaluates both answer and abstain (negative rejection explicitly measured); action policies differ
rationale: Both papers target noise/irrelevant context in RAG and share the failure-type axis. However, Paper A is a method paper proposing a concrete NLI-filter and robust fine-tuning intervention with answer-correctness as the headline metric, while Paper B is a diagnostic benchmark that does not propose any intervention and explicitly scores LLMs along four distinct abilities including selective abstention (negative rejection) and counterfactual handling. The intervention point (method vs. evaluation artifact), the metric family (single accuracy vs. multi-ability with abstention), and the evaluated action policies (filter+answer vs. answer/abstain) all diverge. They are best framed as complementary—Paper B could serve as a probe for Paper A's mitigations—rather than as alternatives on the same leaderboard, so the verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robust-FT models as systems-under-test on the RGB benchmark using the same backbone LLMs, and report all four RGB scores (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) plus accuracy on Paper A's 5 ODQA datasets. Standardize the action policy (e.g., explicitly allow and score abstention in both setups), report selective-risk/coverage curves, and align retrieval pipelines and noise-construction recipes so the same operating point is being compared.
notes: Method-vs-benchmark asymmetry is the dominant reason for 'partial' rather than 'invalid'; the underlying noise-robustness construct is genuinely shared.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (RAAT F1/EM); answer correctness plus selective risk/coverage (RGB accuracy + rejection rate + error detection)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer + abstain (RGB explicitly evaluates negative rejection)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG and both construct controlled noise stressors (RAAT splits noise into relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual; RGB defines noise robustness, counterfactual robustness, integration, and negative rejection). However, the artifacts are categorically different: RAAT is a generator-side training method (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B) measured by F1/EM on its own RAG-Bench, while RGB is a diagnostic benchmark with no method contribution, and crucially evaluates an abstain/negative-rejection action that RAAT never reports. Because intervention point, metric family, and action policy differ, the two cannot be ranked head-to-head on the same leaderboard, but they are clearly complementary (RAAT could be scored on RGB). The relationship is therefore partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and an untrained baseline) on the RGB testbeds using the same retriever, noise construction, and language, and report all four RGB metrics including negative-rejection/error-detection rates; conversely, RGB would need to host a method track with an explicit action-policy protocol (answer vs abstain) so that training-time interventions like RAAT can be compared on matched accuracy and selective-risk axes. Without aligned action labels and shared metric targets, only partial/complementary statements are warranted.
notes: Asymmetry of artifact type (method vs benchmark) is the dominant break; even at the failure-type layer both papers agree, the missing abstain evaluation in RAAT alone precludes valid.

failure_type: relevance/noise; CoN additionally covers uncertainty/OOD ('unknown' questions)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor (both papers inject or analyze irrelevant retrieved passages on ODQA benchmarks); no adversarial threat model
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting/training (note-taking reasoning step). Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator training (mixed relevant/irrelevant fine-tuning).
metric_target: answer correctness for both; Paper A also reports selective risk/coverage (rejection rate on RealTimeQA)
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain ('unknown'). Paper B: filter (drop non-entailing passages, optionally fall back to no-retrieval) + answer. Abstain is not an evaluated action in B.
rationale: Both papers target distraction by irrelevant retrieved context in open-domain QA and aim to make the RALM behave as if retrieval is helpful when relevant and harmless when not. However, they intervene at different points: Chain-of-Note inserts a per-document note-taking reasoning step inside the generator and explicitly trains/evaluates an 'unknown' abstain action, while Yoran et al. filter passages with an NLI model and fine-tune the generator on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts without an abstain output. The action policies (abstain vs. filter-then-answer) and the operating regions (single-hop noise + unknowns vs. single- and multi-hop with non-entailing passages) differ, and only CoN reports a rejection/selective-risk metric. They should be discussed as complementary mechanisms operating at different stages of the pipeline rather than ranked head-to-head, so partial is the appropriate verdict.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on the same retriever, same base generator, same set of ODQA benchmarks (including the multi-hop subset used by Yoran and the RealTimeQA-style unknown subset used by CoN), with a unified action-policy protocol: either both systems expose an 'abstain/unknown' option scored with the same selective-risk/coverage metric, or both restrict to forced-answer and report identical EM/F1. Also report a shared definition of 'irrelevant context' (BM25/DPR noise vs. NLI-non-entailing) and ablate the filter and the note-taking step under matched compute/latency.
notes: Action policies are explicitly reported in both papers (abstain in A, filter in B), so this is not an under-specified case; the break is genuine divergence in intervention and action.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error, naturally occurring insufficiency (benchmark QA contexts; no adversary)
intervention_point: Sufficient Context: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (selective generation post-hoc) + evaluation artifact (autorater); Self-RAG: generator training (reflection tokens) + retriever decision policy
metric_target: Sufficient Context: answer correctness conditional on responding, abstention/hallucination rates stratified by sufficiency; Self-RAG: answer correctness, evidence support, citation faithfulness
action_policy: Sufficient Context: answer / abstain (explicit selective generation); Self-RAG: re-retrieve (on-demand retrieval) + filter/verify (critique tokens select among continuations); explicit abstain is not a first-class action in Self-RAG
rationale: Both papers address how RAG systems should behave when retrieved context is imperfect or unnecessary, but they operationalize different deployment-time controls. Sufficient Context bolts a post-hoc selective-generation policy on top of an existing LLM, using an autorater plus self-confidence to drive an explicit answer-vs-abstain decision, and reports conditional correctness/hallucination/abstention stratified by sufficiency. Self-RAG instead retrains the generator with reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval and self-critique-based filtering, optimizing aggregate task accuracy, factuality, and citation accuracy without an abstain action. The intervention point (post-hoc selector vs trained reflection model), the action policy (abstain vs adaptive-retrieve+filter), and the metric family (selective conditional correctness vs aggregate accuracy/citation) all diverge, so direct leaderboard ranking would conflate distinct operational mechanisms even though the underlying failure type (insufficient/noisy context) overlaps.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on the same QA datasets with the same retriever and the same generator backbone (or hold one fixed and ablate the other); define a common action set including answer/abstain/re-retrieve with reported rates; report a shared selective-prediction metric family such as risk-coverage curves, hallucination rate at fixed coverage, and citation accuracy where applicable; use a common threshold/decoding tuning protocol; and either give Self-RAG an abstain head (e.g., via Isrel/Issup thresholds) or apply Sufficient Context's selector on top of Self-RAG outputs so the action policies are comparable.
notes: From a deployment-controls lens these read as complementary modules (a runtime selector vs a trained adaptive policy) rather than interchangeable leaderboard entries.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise + sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; no adversarial threat model
intervention_point: reranker + verifier (CalibRAG forecasting function); generator prompting/training + system-control policy (Self-RAG reflection tokens)
metric_target: calibration error + answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer with calibrated confidence (CalibRAG, no explicit abstain evaluated); re-retrieve + verify + answer via reflection tokens (Self-RAG)
rationale: Both papers aim to make RAG more reliable, but they target different failure modes and operate at different points in the pipeline. CalibRAG trains a forecasting function over (t,q,d) to produce calibrated decision-correctness probabilities, with calibration error (ECE-style) as a first-class metric and a reranker/verifier intervention. Self-RAG trains the generator itself to emit retrieval and critique tokens (ISREL/ISSUP), targeting factuality and citation accuracy via adaptive retrieval and self-selection. The action policies differ operationally—calibrated confidence to support a human decision vs. token-driven on-demand retrieval and self-critique—and the headline metrics (calibration vs. citation faithfulness) are not interchangeable. They are best framed as complementary control modules rather than substitutes on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same retriever, generator, corpus, and task suite; report a common metric family that includes both calibration (ECE/Brier/selective risk-coverage) and factuality/citation metrics for both systems; explicitly evaluate a shared action policy (e.g., answer vs. abstain at matched coverage) so both methods produce confidence-or-critique signals that gate the same downstream decision; and ablate Self-RAG's critique tokens as a confidence signal against CalibRAG's forecasting score on identical decision-making benchmarks.
notes: From an operational-policy view, CalibRAG produces a confidence to feed human escalate/abstain decisions; Self-RAG produces a critique-token trace to self-gate generation—neither paper evaluates the other's action surface, which is what breaks direct ranking.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict (benign retrieval that disagrees with parametric knowledge); PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target questions (query control), variable retriever visibility (black-box/white-box), small insertion budget (~5 malicious texts), attack objective = induce specific target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attacker side) with no defender intervention proposed
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / faithfulness to context; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR)
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (with reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy evaluated)
rationale: Both papers concern situations where retrieved context drives the LLM toward an answer that diverges from what would otherwise be produced, so they share the umbrella of 'context vs. model' tension. However, every operational coordinate diverges: FaithfulRAG assumes naturally occurring parametric/contextual conflict and proposes a generator-side reconciliation method evaluated by answer correctness, while PoisonedRAG assumes an adversary with corpus write access who injects ~5 crafted passages to maximize attack success rate. They occupy opposite roles (defense against benign conflict vs. attack exploiting corpus integrity) and are not measured by overlapping metrics or evaluated under a shared threat model. A leaderboard-style ranking would be meaningless and would mislead readers about whether FaithfulRAG defends against poisoning or whether PoisonedRAG addresses faithfulness.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a meaningful comparison, one would need to (1) evaluate FaithfulRAG as a defense against PoisonedRAG-style corpus poisoning using the same retriever, generator, corpus, target question set, and insertion budget; (2) report shared metrics (e.g., ASR under attack plus answer correctness on clean queries) rather than separate faithfulness and ASR scores; (3) explicitly state the defender action policy (answer, abstain, filter, quarantine, etc.); and (4) align threat-model assumptions (corpus write access, attacker query control, retriever visibility). Without such a shared evaluation harness, the two works should be discussed as orthogonal contributions to different failure types.
notes: Conflict-vs-security pair: one defense for naturally conflicting evidence and one attack on corpus integrity; categorically distinct settings.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor + naturally occurring conflict; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence. Threat model for PoisonedRAG: corpus write access yes, query control yes (attacker chooses target Q/A), retriever visibility black-box and white-box variants, generator access no, insertion budget ~5 malicious passages per target, attack objective induce attacker-chosen target answer. Astute RAG does not specify or evaluate an attacker model.
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free post-retrieval consolidation) + system-control policy; PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (poisoning injection)
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness (worst-case accuracy under imperfect retrieval); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (always answer after source-aware consolidation and reliability-based selection); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no system-side action policy)
rationale: Both papers concern RAG robustness and Astute RAG explicitly mentions malicious retrieval, but they sit on opposite sides of the security pipeline: PoisonedRAG is an attack that writes adversarial passages into the corpus and reports ASR, while Astute RAG is a generator-side defense evaluated on RGB-style noise and conflict using answer correctness, with no declared threat model, no insertion budget, and no ASR measurement. The intervention points (corpus vs. generator), metric targets (ASR vs. accuracy), evidence assumptions (attacker-created vs. benign/benchmark noise), and action policies (none vs. answer-after-consolidation) all diverge. Treating them as alternatives on a single leaderboard would misrepresent both: PoisonedRAG would appear without a defense to score, and Astute RAG would appear without an attack it was designed against. Therefore the comparison is invalid rather than partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Astute RAG (and matched baselines) against PoisonedRAG-style injections on shared datasets, retriever, generator, and insertion budgets, and report ASR alongside answer correctness under both black-box and white-box attacker assumptions; symmetrically, evaluate PoisonedRAG against the Astute RAG defense as one of multiple defenses with a declared action policy (answer/abstain/filter). Only then can they be ranked as attack-vs-defense pairs on the same axis.
notes: Astute RAG's worst-case RGB setup is benchmark-constructed noise, not an attacker-budgeted poisoning; passing mention of 'malicious' retrieval does not constitute a threat model.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume corpus write access and attacker query control; PoisonedRAG covers black-box and white-box retriever visibility with insertion budget ~5 malicious passages per target question and targeted-answer objective; RobustRAG assumes an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense and a bounded number of injected passages
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attack artifact, no defense intervention); RobustRAG: context assembly/compression and generator prompting (isolate-then-aggregate defense)
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success rate; RobustRAG: answer correctness with certified robustness lower bounds
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action); RobustRAG: answer, abstain ('I don't know'), filter via keyword/decoding aggregation
rationale: Both papers address adversarial retrieval corruption with attacker-created evidence and shared assumptions of corpus write access plus a bounded insertion budget, so the failure type and threat surface overlap. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that intervenes at the corpus/index level and measures attack success rate without any defender action policy, while RobustRAG is a defensive contribution that intervenes at context assembly and generator prompting, reports certified accuracy under bounded corruption, and explicitly evaluates answer/abstain/filter actions. Because one paper produces an attack artifact and the other a certified defense, they cannot be ranked as substitutable methods on the same leaderboard; they are best discussed as attack vs. defense in the same threat model. A valid comparison would require either evaluating RobustRAG against PoisonedRAG-style injections under matched retriever, generator, and budget, or comparing RobustRAG against other defenses on a common benchmark that includes PoisonedRAG as the attacker.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RobustRAG (and competing defenses) against PoisonedRAG injections at matched insertion budgets, retrievers, generators, and datasets; report both attack success rate and certified/empirical answer correctness plus abstention rate under a shared action-policy taxonomy. Alternatively, restrict the comparison to defenses vs. defenses or attacks vs. attacks rather than cross-role ranking.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pair; comparability is about role mismatch, not method quality.

failure_type: RAGTruth: consistency/conflict + sufficiency (word-level hallucinations including evident conflicts and unsupported claims); RGB: relevance/noise + sufficiency + consistency/conflict (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict / benign retrieval error (responses naturally generated by LLMs in standard RAG, then annotated); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios and synthetically injected counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: Both: evaluation artifact. RAGTruth additionally evaluates verifier/detector models fine-tuned on its corpus; RGB evaluates generator prompting behavior across 4 testbeds
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection F1; RGB: answer correctness, rejection rate, integration accuracy, counterfactual error rate
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc detection of hallucinated spans); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection is explicitly scored) — different policies that are not jointly evaluated
rationale: Both papers are evaluation benchmarks for trustworthy RAG and overlap on the high-level concern of LLMs producing unsupported or conflicting content given retrieved context. However, RAGTruth is a corpus of naturally generated responses with word-level hallucination annotations whose primary use is training/benchmarking span-level detectors (a verifier action), while RGB is a constructed-stressor benchmark that scores generator behavior along four distinct response-level abilities including an explicit abstain (negative rejection) policy and a counterfactual-robustness regime that RAGTruth does not isolate. Because the units of evaluation (span vs. response), metric families (detection F1 vs. correctness/rejection/integration/counterfactual rates), evidence assumptions (natural vs. constructed), and action policies (verify vs. answer/abstain) all differ, leaderboard-style ranking would conflate genuinely different capabilities. The papers are best treated as complementary benchmarks covering different slices of robust RAG, hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To enable direct comparison, both benchmarks would need to (a) align on the same evaluation unit (e.g., span-level support OR response-level correctness), (b) share a common failure-type taxonomy with matched evidence construction (natural vs. injected, with identical noise ratios and counterfactual rates), (c) report the same metric family on the same task slices (e.g., hallucination span F1 measured on RGB instances, or rejection/correctness measured on RAGTruth contexts), and (d) explicitly evaluate the same action policies — at minimum answer vs. abstain vs. verify — under a shared retriever/generator configuration so that a single system can be scored on both.
notes: Both are 'evaluation_benchmark' artifacts, but the protocol's metric_target and action_policy axes diverge enough that ranking systems across them would be misleading; this is the prototypical partial case rather than under-specified, since both papers are quite explicit about what they measure.

failure_type: RGB covers relevance/noise, sufficiency, and consistency/conflict (counterfactual) across separate testbeds; Sufficient Context primarily targets sufficiency with secondary relevance/noise concerns
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, manually injected counterfactual documents). Sufficient Context: benign retrieval error plus benchmark-constructed stressor over existing QA datasets stratified by an autorater-defined sufficiency label
intervention_point: RGB: evaluation artifact only. Sufficient Context: evaluation artifact (sufficiency autorater) PLUS verifier and system-control policy (selective generation combining sufficiency with self-confidence)
metric_target: Both touch answer correctness and selective risk/coverage. RGB reports per-ability accuracy/rejection/integration scores; Sufficient Context reports hallucination vs abstention vs correct rates stratified by sufficiency, plus calibration-style selective generation gains
action_policy: Both papers explicitly evaluate answer and abstain. RGB measures 'negative rejection' as a first-class ability; Sufficient Context's selective generation directly governs answer/abstain decisions
rationale: Both papers study LLM behavior when retrieved evidence is imperfect and both explicitly evaluate the answer-vs-abstain action policy, which is a meaningful overlap. However, RGB is a pure evaluation artifact spanning four disjoint failure types (noise, negative rejection, integration, counterfactual), while Sufficient Context is principally an analytical lens plus an intervention (selective generation using a sufficiency autorater and self-confidence). Their metric structures are not commensurable: RGB reports per-ability scores on its own bilingual constructed testbeds, whereas Sufficient Context reports hallucination/abstention/correctness stratified by autorater-labeled sufficiency on existing QA sets. They are best treated as complementary—one diagnoses where RAG breaks, the other proposes a deployment-time abstention controller—rather than as direct alternatives on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To be directly comparable, the Sufficient Context selective-generation policy would need to be evaluated on RGB's four testbeds (especially negative rejection and counterfactual robustness) using RGB's metric definitions, with the same generator(s) and retriever fixed; conversely RGB would need to report sufficiency-stratified hallucination/abstention rates. A shared answer/abstain operating-point curve (e.g., selective risk-coverage) on identical (query, context) pairs with a common ground-truth answerability label would let the two contributions be ranked or composed.
notes: Action policy is explicit on both sides, so the gap is not under-specification but a scope mismatch: benchmark vs analytical framework + deployment-time controller.

failure_type: RAGTruth covers consistency/conflict plus sufficiency (general hallucination including evident/subtle conflicts and baseless additions); FaithfulRAG focuses narrowly on consistency/conflict (parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflict)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations from standard RAG over benign benchmarks; FaithfulRAG: benchmark-constructed knowledge-conflict stressors with retrieved context. Neither is an adversarial/security setting.
