intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus) plus verifier (fine-tuned or prompted hallucination detectors); FaithfulRAG: context assembly/compression plus generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness measured as span-level hallucination detection F1; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness on conflict QA benchmarks
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc detection), generation action itself unreported; FaithfulRAG: answer with internal reconciliation. No shared action policy is evaluated.
rationale: Both papers target faithfulness in RAG, but they occupy different roles: RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact and detector-training corpus measuring span-level hallucination detection across QA, data-to-text, and summarization, whereas FaithfulRAG is a generation-time intervention that mines self-facts and runs a self-think module to resolve parametric-vs-context conflicts, measured by end-task answer correctness. The failure-type overlap is only partial (RAGTruth includes baseless info and subtle hallucinations beyond knowledge conflict), and the intervention points, metrics, and action policies do not align. They could complement each other (e.g., RAGTruth as a testbed for FaithfulRAG), but they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable methods. Therefore the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate FaithfulRAG's generated outputs on the RAGTruth corpus using span-level hallucination annotations (or evaluate RAGTruth-fine-tuned detectors and FaithfulRAG on the same conflict QA benchmarks with identical retriever, generator, and metric definitions). Both systems would need to report the same action policy (e.g., answer-with-verify) and the same metric family (answer correctness plus span-level faithfulness) under matched evidence conditions.
notes: Asymmetric artifact-vs-method pair; complementary rather than competitive.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B only, via counterfactual noise type)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (Paper A, natural DPR/Google retrieval noise); benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper B, especially synthesized counterfactual passages)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (Paper A: NLI filter + fine-tuning); generator prompting or training (Paper B: adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise classification)
metric_target: answer correctness (Paper A accuracy; Paper B F1/EM) — broadly aligned metric family
action_policy: filter + answer (Paper A, NLI gate is explicit); answer (Paper B, with internal noise-type classification head, but no abstain/filter action evaluated)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RALMs and both report answer-correctness style metrics on open-domain QA, and both include a generator-side training intervention, so the topical overlap is real. However, Paper A scopes the failure strictly to irrelevant context and uses an explicit NLI filtering action plus mixed-context fine-tuning, while Paper B broadens the failure space to three noise types — relevant, irrelevant, and counterfactual — where counterfactual passages introduce a consistency/conflict dimension that Paper A never evaluates, and Paper B's intervention is adaptive adversarial training with a noise-type classification head rather than a passage filter. The evidence assumptions also diverge (Paper A's noise is largely naturally retrieved, Paper B's includes benchmark-constructed counterfactual stressors), and the action policies are not the same primitive (filter+answer vs. answer with internal awareness). These differences make the two methods complementary modules in the noise-robustness space rather than direct substitutes that can be ranked on a single leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared retriever, corpus, and benchmark (e.g., NQ/TriviaQA with identical DPR top-k); restrict Paper B's evaluation to the irrelevant-only noise slice (and separately report counterfactual) so the failure-type scope matches Paper A; standardize the action policy by either (a) reporting both with pure answer-only outputs, or (b) adding an explicit filter/abstain option to Paper B; align metrics (EM/F1/accuracy) and noise construction protocol; and ideally include each paper's method as a baseline in the other's setup, including Paper A's NLI filter on Paper B's RAG-Bench and Paper B's adversarial training on Paper A's multi-hop benchmarks.
notes: Counterfactual noise in Paper B is the most consequential coordinate shift — it implicitly reframes part of the task as conflict handling, which Paper A does not address.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); rgb2023 also covers consistency/conflict (counterfactual) and sufficiency (negative rejection)
evidence_assumption: irrelevantContext2023: benign retrieval error from real retrieval pipeline; rgb2023: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injections
intervention_point: irrelevantContext2023: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting/training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts); rgb2023: evaluation artifact only
metric_target: answer correctness (both); rgb2023 additionally tracks rejection rate and counterfactual identification
action_policy: irrelevantContext2023: filter then answer (implicit, not labeled as policy); rgb2023: answer and abstain (negative rejection explicitly evaluated)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG, but they sit at different layers of the stack: irrelevantContext2023 is a method paper proposing NLI-based passage filtering and robust fine-tuning, evaluated on standard ODQA accuracy with naturally retrieved passages, while rgb2023 is an evaluation benchmark that constructs controlled noise ratios and adds three additional abilities (negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) absent from Paper A. The intervention points diverge (concrete filter+train vs. evaluation artifact), the evidence-construction assumptions differ (organic retrieval noise vs. engineered stressors), and only rgb2023 explicitly evaluates an abstain action policy. They are complementary—Paper A's methods could be scored on RGB—but a direct leaderboard ranking would misrepresent both: Paper A never reports negative-rejection or counterfactual numbers, and Paper B never proposes a mitigation method to rank. Verdict is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Apply irrelevantContext2023's NLI filter and fine-tuned model to the RGB testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) using the same base LLM, the same retriever, and matched noise-ratio settings; report accuracy, rejection rate, and counterfactual identification under a single explicit action policy (answer vs. abstain). Conversely, RGB would need a baseline-method track with declared interventions to be a comparator rather than only a probe.
notes: Asymmetry of paper type (method vs. benchmark) is the dominant comparability gap; partial is appropriate over under-specified because both papers are individually well-specified.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (raat2024); evaluation artifact (rgb2023)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (rgb2023 only, via negative rejection)
action_policy: answer (raat2024); answer, abstain (rgb2023)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RAG with benchmark-constructed noisy contexts, and both include a counterfactual/misleading noise condition. However, RAAT proposes a training-time intervention (adaptive adversarial training of LLaMA-2 7B with multi-task noise-awareness) evaluated on DPR-retrieved Wikipedia passages for NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ with answer-only F1/EM, while RGB is purely a diagnostic benchmark over news-derived bilingual QA that scores four distinct abilities including negative rejection (an abstain action) and information integration. Because RGB does not propose a method and explicitly evaluates an abstain policy while RAAT only evaluates answer correctness without abstention, they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as alternative methods; they are complementary (a method vs. a multi-ability diagnostic). Hence the verdict is partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT-trained and baseline LLMs on RGB's four testbeds (including negative rejection and information integration) using RGB's metrics, and conversely evaluate RGB-tested LLMs on RAG-Bench's three noise types with identical retriever, corpus, prompt, and answer/abstain action labels. Report both answer correctness and an explicit abstain/coverage metric on a shared noise construction so the two interventions (training vs. no training) can be ranked on the same axis.
notes: RAAT is method+benchmark; RGB is benchmark-only with broader ability coverage — overlapping noise focus is real but scope and action policy diverge.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); uncertainty/OOD (CoN only via 'unknown' handling)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor (both papers use ODQA benchmarks with naturally noisy DPR/retrieved passages, plus constructed irrelevant-context conditions)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (CoN: note-taking before answer; IrrelevantContext: fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant); context assembly/compression and verifier (IrrelevantContext: NLI-based filtering of non-entailing passages)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, via EM/accuracy); selective risk/coverage (CoN reports rejection rate for real-time/unknown questions; IrrelevantContext does not)
action_policy: answer + abstain (CoN explicitly evaluates 'unknown' responses); answer + filter (IrrelevantContext explicitly drops non-entailed passages, then answers)
rationale: Both papers target the same core failure mode — RALM brittleness to irrelevant/noisy retrieved context in ODQA — and both motivate the work with cascading-error examples from DPR-style retrieval. However, the intervention points diverge: CoN modifies generator reasoning via per-document note-taking and adds an 'unknown' abstain pathway, while IrrelevantContext intervenes earlier with an NLI verifier that filters non-entailing passages plus mixed-context fine-tuning, and never instantiates an abstain action. Consequently the evaluated action policies differ (abstain vs. filter-then-answer) and metric coverage diverges (CoN reports rejection rate on real-time/unknown questions; IrrelevantContext emphasizes single- and multi-hop EM/accuracy with no selective-risk reporting). Because the systems occupy overlapping but distinct operating regions and their action policies are not commensurable, they should be discussed as complementary modules rather than ranked head-to-head — hence partial, not valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct comparison would require (1) a shared retriever, generator backbone, and corpus across the same ODQA benchmark suite (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, plus a multi-hop set like StrategyQA or 2WikiMultiHop and a real-time/unknown set); (2) a unified action-policy harness that evaluates both abstain and filter behaviors with explicit labels (answered/abstained/filtered); (3) reporting both answer correctness and selective-risk/coverage (e.g., risk-coverage curve, rejection rate on unanswerable/OOD subsets) for both systems; (4) matched noise/irrelevance construction protocols so the 'distraction' stressor is identical; and (5) an ablation where CoN's note-taker is swapped with the NLI filter (and vice versa) to isolate the intervention-point effect.
notes: Not a security pair, so threat-model coordinates (corpus write access, attacker budget, etc.) are not applicable; both assume benign-but-imperfect retrieval.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, retriever, evaluation artifact
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: abstain, re-retrieve, answer, verify
rationale: Both papers target reliability of RAG when retrieved context is imperfect, and both broadly aim to reduce hallucinations, so the failure-type axis (sufficiency / relevance) overlaps. However, Sufficient Context is an inference-time selective-generation method: it constructs an autorater for (Q,C) sufficiency and combines it with self-confidence to decide answer vs. abstain, reporting selective accuracy and hallucination/abstention rates. Self-RAG trains a generator end-to-end with reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval and self-critique, and its headline metrics are factuality and citation/attribution accuracy on long-form generation. The intervention point (post-hoc autorater vs. trained reflection-token policy with adaptive retrieval), the explicit action policy (abstain vs. re-retrieve+critique+answer-with-citations), and the metric family (selective risk/coverage vs. citation faithfulness) all diverge, so a leaderboard ranking would conflate different problems; they are better framed as complementary modules.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on the same benchmarks with the same retriever and base generator, and report a shared metric family: either selective accuracy/coverage curves (forcing Self-RAG to expose an abstain action via its ISSUP/ISREL tokens) or citation precision/recall on attribution-evaluable tasks (forcing Sufficient Context to emit citations). Explicit, matched action-policy labels (answer / abstain / re-retrieve) and identical sufficiency-stratified evaluation slices would be needed before any direct ranking is meaningful.
notes: Both papers are 'control' methods but operate at different layers of the RAG stack; partial rather than invalid because the underlying failure type (sufficiency/relevance of retrieved evidence) is genuinely shared.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence in decision support); Self-RAG: relevance/noise and consistency/conflict (indiscriminate retrieval and ungrounded generation)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval; neither posits adversarial corpus, attacker-created evidence, or naturally occurring conflict. CalibRAG additionally assumes a forecasting model trained on synthetic decision-correctness data.
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker/context assembly via a learned forecasting function f(t,q,d). Self-RAG: generator prompting/training with reflection tokens plus retriever on-demand triggering.
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness for decision-making. Self-RAG: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support (factuality).
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence (abstention/escalation not explicitly evaluated → effectively unreported as an action policy). Self-RAG: re-retrieve (on-demand) + answer with self-critique tokens.
rationale: Both papers aim to improve RAG reliability and share an interest in factuality, but they tackle distinct failure modes: CalibRAG targets miscalibrated confidence so that human decisions are well-calibrated, whereas Self-RAG targets indiscriminate retrieval and ungrounded generation via reflection-token training. The intervention points differ (a learned forecasting/reranking function vs. an LM trained with retrieval and critique tokens), and the headline metrics belong to different families (ECE/decision calibration vs. citation faithfulness and factuality). Neither paper evaluates the other's primary metric on the same operating point, and their action policies (calibrated answering vs. on-demand re-retrieve + self-critique) are not directly substitutable. They are complementary mechanisms rather than substitutable methods on the same leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both systems on a shared benchmark with (i) the same retriever, generator backbone, and corpus; (ii) a common metric suite covering both calibration (ECE, Brier, selective risk/coverage) and citation/grounding (citation precision/recall, attribution F1); (iii) an explicitly defined and evaluated action policy (e.g., answer vs. abstain vs. re-retrieve thresholds) for both systems; and (iv) a matched decision-making task so that CalibRAG's forecasting signal and Self-RAG's reflection tokens can be compared as alternative confidence/grounding signals at equivalent operating points.
notes: Self-RAG's reflection tokens do produce a controllability signal that could in principle be mapped to a calibration score, but the original paper does not report ECE-style calibration, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG=consistency/conflict (parametric vs retrieved); PoisonedRAG=integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG=naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and retrieved context; PoisonedRAG=attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker query control over target questions, both black-box and white-box retriever visibility, no generator access required, insertion budget of ~5 malicious passages per target, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG=generator prompting (self-fact mining + self-think before generation); PoisonedRAG=corpus/index (malicious-text injection); they sit on opposite sides of the pipeline and opposite sides of the attack/defense boundary
metric_target: FaithfulRAG=answer correctness and contextual faithfulness; PoisonedRAG=attack success rate (target-answer induction)
action_policy: FaithfulRAG=answer (reconcile facts then generate; no abstain/expose-conflict evaluated); PoisonedRAG=unreported (attack paper has no defender action policy)
rationale: Both papers concern situations where retrieved context disagrees with the 'true' answer, so they share surface vocabulary about RAG reliability. However, FaithfulRAG targets naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflicts and intervenes at the generator with a fact-level self-think module measured by answer correctness, while PoisonedRAG is an offensive paper that injects attacker-crafted passages into the corpus and measures attack success rate under an explicit threat model (corpus write access, target-question control, ~5 malicious texts). The failure type (benign conflict vs adversarial corruption), evidence assumption, intervention point (defense at generator vs attack at corpus), metric target, and action policy all diverge. A leaderboard-style ranking would be misleading because one paper is an attack and the other is a defense for a different failure mode; they are not substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make any direct comparison meaningful, FaithfulRAG would need to be re-evaluated as a defense against PoisonedRAG-style injected passages on the same corpora (NQ, HotpotQA, MS-MARCO), using the same retriever and generator, the same insertion budget and threat model, and reporting attack success rate alongside answer correctness and an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/expose-conflict). Conversely, PoisonedRAG would need to report downstream faithfulness/correctness under a defender like FaithfulRAG. Without a shared (attack model, defense, metric family, action policy) tuple, only an attack-vs-defense robustness study—not a leaderboard ranking—would be defensible.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pairing across different failure types; not rescuable to 'partial' because even the underlying problem (natural conflict vs adversarial corpus poisoning) differs.

failure_type: ASTUTE RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict (with passing mention of integrity); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: ASTUTE RAG: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB worst-case negatives), with naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge. PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence; threat model = corpus write access (yes), query control (chosen target questions/answers), retriever visibility (black-box and white-box variants), generator access (not required), insertion budget (~5 malicious passages per target question), attack objective (induce attacker-chosen target answer).
intervention_point: ASTUTE RAG: generator prompting (training-free post-retrieval consolidation). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (injection into the knowledge database).
metric_target: ASTUTE RAG: answer correctness (especially worst-case accuracy under noisy/conflicting retrieval). PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR) toward attacker-chosen target answers.
action_policy: ASTUTE RAG: answer (with source-aware reliability-based selection among candidate answers). PoisonedRAG: unreported (no defender action policy is evaluated; it is an attack paper).
rationale: Both papers touch the broader robust-RAG security space and ASTUTE RAG even cites PoisonedRAG when motivating malicious-context risk, but they occupy opposite roles: ASTUTE RAG is a generator-side defense evaluated on answer correctness under noisy/conflicting (mostly benign-stressor) retrieval, while PoisonedRAG is a corpus-poisoning attack evaluated by ASR with an explicit insertion budget and target-question/target-answer threat model. The intervention point (generator prompting vs corpus/index injection), metric target (accuracy vs ASR), evidence assumption (benchmark noise/conflict vs attacker-created passages), and action policy (source-aware answer selection vs no defender action) all diverge. Putting them on the same leaderboard would be a category error - they are not alternative methods for one problem but complementary attack and defense artifacts that target inverse objectives. The comparison is therefore invalid, not merely partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would first require both works to occupy the same role - e.g., evaluate ASTUTE RAG (and another defense) against PoisonedRAG-style attacks under a shared threat model: same retriever, same generator, same target questions, identical insertion budget, fixed black-box/white-box attacker assumptions, and a common metric suite reporting both ASR and clean answer correctness, plus an explicit defender action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine). Only then can attack-resilience be benchmarked directly. As-is, the only meaningful joint use is to treat PoisonedRAG as a stressor and ASTUTE RAG as one candidate mitigation, reported in an attack×defense matrix.
notes: Attack paper vs defense paper with inverse objectives - classic invalid pairing for leaderboard-style comparison; ASTUTE RAG does not run PoisonedRAG-style targeted poisoning in its own evaluation.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG threat model: attacker has corpus write access, knows target question, evaluated in black-box and white-box generator-access settings, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per target question, objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer; RobustRAG threat model: adaptive attacker with full knowledge of defense, corpus write access, bounded number of corrupted passages, retriever visibility assumed, objective = degrade response quality
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious text injection); RobustRAG: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (isolate-then-aggregate with keyword/decoding aggregation)
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success (ASR); RobustRAG: answer correctness with certifiable lower bounds on response quality
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: answer (induce attacker-chosen target); RobustRAG: answer after secure aggregation, with explicit abstain ('I don't know') option
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat space—integrity/adversarial corruption of RAG via attacker-created evidence injected into the knowledge database—so failure type and evidence assumption overlap. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that crafts malicious passages at the corpus level and reports attack success rate, whereas RobustRAG is a defensive contribution that intervenes at context assembly and generation via isolate-then-aggregate and reports certifiable robust accuracy with an explicit abstain action. The intervention point, metric target, and action policy therefore diverge in role (attacker vs defender), not just in implementation. They function as complementary modules in the same security stack and could be co-evaluated (defense tested against this attack), but they cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitutable methods, which makes the comparison partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct leaderboard comparison would require both papers to occupy the same role on the same metric. Concretely: either (a) compare PoisonedRAG against other corruption attacks (e.g., GCG-style or prompt-injection attacks) under a shared retriever/generator/budget on ASR, or (b) compare RobustRAG against other defenses (e.g., voting, filtering, anomaly detection) under the same attacker model on certified/empirical robust accuracy. A co-evaluation (running RobustRAG against PoisonedRAG with matched retriever, generator, target-question set, insertion budget k, and reporting both ASR and certified accuracy curves) would yield a meaningful interaction study but still not a substitutable ranking.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pairing in the same threat model; complementary rather than substitutable. Co-evaluation is natural and informative but does not constitute leaderboard comparability.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error with natural LLM-generated outputs in standard RAG; RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, counterfactual documents, all-noise testbeds)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally trains a verifier (fine-tuned detector)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection F1 and hallucination frequencies; RGB: answer correctness, rejection rate (selective risk/coverage), integration accuracy, counterfactual identification rate
action_policy: RAGTruth: answer + verify (detector); abstention unreported. RGB: answer and explicit abstain (negative rejection testbed)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation resources probing LLM reliability when grounded on retrieved evidence, and both touch consistency/conflict (RAGTruth's 'evident conflict' annotations; RGB's counterfactual robustness). However, RAGTruth produces ~18K naturally generated responses across QA, data-to-text, and summarization with word/span-level hallucination labels intended to train and benchmark detectors, while RGB constructs four separate stressor testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) measured by answer-level accuracy and rejection rate. The evidence-construction protocols (natural vs. controlled stressor), units of measurement (span-level detection F1 vs. answer-level accuracy/rejection), and action policies (verifier output vs. explicit abstention) are incommensurate, so a leaderboard-style ranking would be meaningless. They are best framed as complementary diagnostics of overlapping reliability dimensions, hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Align on a single failure dimension (e.g., evident conflict or counterfactual evidence) at a shared granularity (span or answer); use the same retriever, generator set, and prompt; report a common metric family (e.g., both detection F1 and abstention rate at matched thresholds) on overlapping QA instances; and explicitly evaluate the same action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict) for both systems. Cross-mapping a subset of RAGTruth QA conflicts into RGB-style counterfactual evaluation, or scoring RGB outputs with RAGTruth-style span annotations, would produce a comparable axis.
notes: RAGTruth's tasks extend beyond QA (data-to-text, summarization), further limiting one-to-one comparison with RGB's QA-only testbeds.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: synthetic noise mixes, counterfactual injections, all-noise sets); naturally occurring conflict/insufficiency labeled by an LLM autorater (SufficientContext)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); generator prompting + verifier/system-control policy (SufficientContext's selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, evidence support (RGB's information integration & counterfactual robustness); selective risk/coverage and abstention/hallucination rates (SufficientContext)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via 'negative rejection' ability; SufficientContext via abstention vs. hallucination stratification and selective generation)
rationale: Both papers evaluate RAG behavior when retrieved evidence is imperfect and both explicitly score abstention as a first-class outcome, so they share a non-trivial overlap on the noise/sufficiency failure axis and on answer/abstain policy. However, RGB is a static, benchmark-constructed diagnostic with four distinct testbeds (noise ratio sweeps, all-noise negative rejection, multi-doc integration, counterfactual injection) using accuracy-style metrics per ability, while SufficientContext introduces a (Q,C)-level sufficiency autorater applied to existing QA datasets and adds a selective-generation intervention scored by hallucination/coverage trade-offs. The two operationalize 'insufficient context' differently (engineered all-noise / counterfactual stressors vs. autorater-labeled natural insufficiency), and SufficientContext additionally evaluates an intervention while RGB does not, so they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard. They are best framed as complementary lenses on RAG abstention rather than alternative methods, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both works' models on a common dataset using both labeling schemes simultaneously: (i) apply the SufficientContext autorater to RGB's noise/negative-rejection/counterfactual instances to get sufficiency labels, (ii) report RGB's accuracy and rejection rates alongside SufficientContext's hallucination/abstention/coverage curves, (iii) hold retriever, generator, and prompt fixed, and (iv) evaluate the selective-generation method on RGB's testbeds (and, conversely, RGB's counterfactual stressor under SufficientContext's selective policy) so that both the diagnostic axis and the intervention are scored under one protocol.
notes: Both papers do report explicit abstention policies, so action_policy is not the breaking axis here; the break is in stressor construction and what is being measured/intervened on.

failure_type: consistency/conflict for both; RAGTruth additionally covers sufficiency and relevance/noise hallucination types
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring LLM-generated responses on standard RAG inputs, annotated for unsupported/contradictory spans. FaithfulRAG: benchmark-constructed stressor plus naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflict scenarios.
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus/benchmark). FaithfulRAG: generator prompting or training (self-fact mining and self-think reasoning module).
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support and citation faithfulness via hallucination detection performance. FaithfulRAG: answer correctness on conflict QA benchmarks.
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (benchmark does not prescribe an action policy; detectors only flag spans). FaithfulRAG: answer after internal reconciliation of conflicting facts.
rationale: Both papers sit under the faithfulness umbrella for RAG, but they are fundamentally different artifact types. RAGTruth is a word-level hallucination annotation corpus used to benchmark and fine-tune detection methods across QA, data-to-text, and summarization; FaithfulRAG is a generation-time method that mines self-facts, aligns them with retrieved chunks, and runs a self-think module to reconcile parametric-vs-context conflicts before answering. The intervention points (evaluation artifact vs. generator-side reasoning) sit at different pipeline layers, the metric targets (hallucination span detection vs. end-task answer correctness on conflict sets) differ, and only FaithfulRAG specifies an action policy. Leaderboard-style ranking of these two contributions would conflate a measurement instrument with a method, so direct comparison is invalid as posed.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Treat RAGTruth as the evaluation ground and run FaithfulRAG on RAGTruth's QA/summarization splits, reporting span-level hallucination rates with RAGTruth's protocol alongside end-task correctness; or compare FaithfulRAG against other faithfulness/conflict-resolution methods on identical conflict benchmarks with shared retriever, generator, and explicit action labels (answer vs. abstain vs. expose-conflict). Without this shared substrate, the two works are complementary (benchmark vs. method), not rankable.
notes: Classic benchmark-vs-method mismatch; partial would understate the categorical difference in artifact type.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B only via counterfactual noise)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from actual DPR-style retrieval over 5 ODQA benchmarks. Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAG-Bench) that synthetically mixes relevant, irrelevant, and counterfactual passages; counterfactual injection is closer to a constructed conflict than to naturally occurring noise.
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning). Paper B: generator prompting or training (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-awareness head).
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (NLI-decided drop of non-entailing passages, then answer with or without context). Paper B: answer (no filtering; generator trained to be internally robust). Neither paper evaluates abstain.
breaking_coordinates: evidence_assumption, intervention_point, action_policy, failure_type (partial overlap), evaluation artifact (different benchmarks)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs in open-domain QA and share the relevance/noise failure type with answer-correctness as the metric, so there is genuine thematic overlap. However, Paper A scopes noise to irrelevant retrieved context (benign retrieval error) and intervenes at two points—an NLI filter (explicit filter action) and light mixed-context fine-tuning—evaluated on 5 ODQA benchmarks. Paper B expands the noise typology to include counterfactual passages, which adds a consistency/conflict failure type and a benchmark-constructed stressor (RAG-Bench over NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ), and intervenes only at the generator via adaptive adversarial training plus an auxiliary noise-type classification head with no filtering. The action policies, noise construction, and evaluation suites do not align, so a leaderboard-style head-to-head would conflate interventions operating at different points under different stress models; the methods are better discussed as complementary (filter+train vs. adversarially trained generator) rather than ranked.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever and generator backbones; harmonize the noise mixture so both methods are evaluated under matched proportions of irrelevant and counterfactual passages on the same dataset split (e.g., both on RAG-Bench and on Paper A's 5-ODQA suite); report identical EM/F1 plus an explicit action-policy breakdown (filtered vs. answered, and ideally abstention rate); cross-apply interventions (NLI filter in front of a RAAT-trained generator, and RAAT-trained generator without the filter) so the contribution of each intervention point is isolated.
notes: Paper B explicitly cites Paper A as motivation, but uses a broader noise taxonomy and a different evaluation artifact, which prevents direct substitution.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency and consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (real Google retrievals) plus some constructed distractors; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios from news corpus
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filtering) + generator prompting or training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts); Paper B: evaluation artifact (no method proposed, only a diagnostic benchmark)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness on ODQA; Paper B: answer correctness under noise PLUS selective risk/coverage (negative rejection rate) and counterfactual-handling accuracy
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (abstention not explicitly evaluated); Paper B: answer and abstain (negative rejection is a first-class ability)
rationale: Both papers center on noise robustness in RAG, so they share the relevance/noise failure type and the general concern that irrelevant retrieved context degrades LLM performance. However, Paper A is a methods paper proposing NLI-based filtering and robust fine-tuning, evaluated on ODQA accuracy with naturally retrieved noisy passages, whereas Paper B is a diagnostic benchmark (RGB) constructing controlled noise ratios and additionally measuring negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness as separable abilities. The intervention points differ fundamentally (mitigation method vs. evaluation artifact), and Paper B explicitly evaluates an abstention action policy that Paper A does not. They are complementary—Paper A's methods could be scored on Paper B's benchmark—but they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as alternative robust-RAG methods, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a valid head-to-head comparison, both works would need to be cast as methods evaluated on a shared benchmark with: (1) identical retriever and generator backbones, (2) a single noise-construction protocol (either naturally noisy retrieval or RGB-style controlled noise ratios, not mixed), (3) a shared metric family including both answer correctness on noisy contexts AND an abstention/negative-rejection metric, and (4) explicit, matched action policies (answer vs. abstain vs. filter) reported per system. In practice this would mean running Paper A's NLI-filter and fine-tuned model on the RGB testbeds (noise robustness and negative rejection) and reporting RGB's accuracy and rejection-rate metrics alongside any new baselines.
notes: The method-vs-benchmark mismatch is the dominant obstacle; even where failure types overlap, the contribution categories are not substitutable on a leaderboard.

failure_type: relevance/noise; RGB additionally covers sufficiency (negative rejection) and consistency/conflict (counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both papers construct curated noisy contexts: RAAT via DPR retrieval over NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ filtered for golden contexts plus injected noise types; RGB via ChatGPT-generated questions over recent news with controlled noise ratios)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT: adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-awareness on LLaMA-2 7B); evaluation artifact (RGB: pure benchmark, no method)
metric_target: answer correctness (RAAT: F1/EM); answer correctness plus selective risk/coverage (RGB: accuracy, rejection rate, error detection rate, error correction rate across four testbeds)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer + abstain (RGB explicitly evaluates negative rejection as a required ability)
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, evidence_assumption (noise taxonomy mismatch)
rationale: Both papers address noise robustness in RAG and both construct benchmarks with controlled noise stressors, but their contributions are categorically different: RAAT is a training-time method (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning on LLaMA-2 7B) evaluated with F1/EM on its own RAG-Bench, whereas RGB is a benchmark-only contribution that decomposes RAG capability into four separate abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and measures rejection/integration in addition to correctness. The intervention points differ (generator training vs evaluation artifact), the action policies differ (RAAT only answers; RGB explicitly scores abstention behavior), and the noise taxonomies do not align (RAAT's relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual ≠ RGB's four-ability split). They are complementary—RAAT could be scored on RGB's testbeds—but cannot be placed on a single leaderboard as substitute methods, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To upgrade to valid: (1) evaluate RAAT-trained LLaMA-2 7B on all four RGB testbeds using RGB's metric suite (accuracy, rejection rate, error detection/correction); (2) report RAAT's behavior under an abstention-enabled action policy with the same prompt/threshold protocol as RGB; (3) align noise definitions (map RAAT's relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual to RGB's noise ratio and counterfactual settings); (4) hold retriever, generator base model, and prompt template constant; or alternatively reframe the comparison as method-vs-benchmark rather than method-vs-method.
notes: RGB is fundamentally an evaluation artifact, so any leaderboard-style ranking against a method like RAAT is a category error unless reframed.

failure_type: relevance/noise; uncertainty/OOD (Paper A only, via unknown/real-time questions)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (DPR/standard retriever noise on ODQA); Paper A additionally stresses real-time/out-of-pretraining-scope questions
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (Paper A: note-taking before answer; Paper B: robust fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts); context assembly/compression (Paper B: NLI-based passage filtering)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, EM on ODQA); selective risk/coverage (Paper A: rejection rate on RealTimeQA)
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain (explicit 'unknown'); Paper B: filter + answer (fallback to no-retrieval LLM when NLI rejects)
rationale: Both papers target RALM brittleness to irrelevant/noisy retrieved passages on open-domain QA and share overlapping benchmarks (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA), so the failure-type axis aligns. However, the interventions are placed differently: Chain-of-Note rewrites the generator's reasoning trace via per-document notes, while Yoran et al. intervene at context assembly (NLI filter) and via robust fine-tuning. The action policies also diverge in a substantive way: CoN's headline contribution is explicit abstention ('unknown') with a rejection-rate metric, whereas Yoran et al. evaluate answer accuracy after filtering and never report an abstention/coverage curve. Because the systems optimize partly different objectives (accuracy + selective risk vs. accuracy after filtering) with different intervention points, they are better framed as complementary mitigations than as directly rankable alternatives on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the retriever (e.g., DPR top-k) and base generator (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), evaluate both methods on the same ODQA suite with the same noise/irrelevance construction, and report a common metric bundle: EM/F1 on relevant+irrelevant mixes, selective-risk/coverage curves with an explicit abstention option for both systems, and a controlled real-time/unknown subset. Also disambiguate the action policy (filter-then-answer vs. note-then-abstain) and ablate the filter+CoN combination so any ranking reflects mechanism rather than evaluation protocol.
notes: Action policy is explicitly reported in both (abstain vs. filter), so this is not under-specified; the breaks are real but non-fatal, hence partial rather than invalid.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, evaluation artifact, retriever, context assembly/compression
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, citation faithfulness
action_policy: abstain, re-retrieve, filter
rationale: Both papers target factuality failures in RAG that stem from imperfect retrieved context, so the failure-type space overlaps on sufficiency/noise. However, Sufficient Context is a post-hoc, evaluation+selective-generation framework: it introduces an autorater label and uses sufficiency plus self-rated confidence to drive an answer-vs-abstain policy, measured primarily through selective-risk/coverage and hallucination-vs-abstention rates. Self-RAG instead trains a generator end-to-end to emit reflection tokens that govern on-demand retrieval, passage filtering, and self-critique, and is evaluated on answer correctness and citation faithfulness over long-form generation. The intervention point (post-hoc selective wrapper vs. trained generator with adaptive retrieval), action policy (abstain vs. retrieve/critique/select), and headline metric family thus diverge, so a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate orthogonal mechanisms. They are best treated as complementary modules over the same underlying problem.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation harness on the same QA datasets with (i) identical retriever and base LM backbone, (ii) explicit abstain option scored with the same selective-risk/coverage curve and the same hallucination/citation metrics, (iii) matched action-policy labels (answer/abstain/re-retrieve) reported for both systems, and (iv) ablations isolating the sufficient-context autorater signal vs. Self-RAG reflection tokens as alternative confidence/abstention signals at equal compute.
notes: Both papers are well-specified individually; the issue is mismatched intervention surface and action policy, not missing information.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise, sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error for both; neither addresses adversarial corruption
intervention_point: reranker + system-control policy (CalibRAG forecasting function f(t,q,d) for reranking and confidence); generator prompting/training + retriever (Self-RAG reflection tokens for on-demand retrieval and self-critique)
metric_target: calibration error + answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer with calibrated confidence (CalibRAG, no explicit abstention reported); re-retrieve + filter + answer (Self-RAG via reflection tokens)
rationale: Both papers improve RAG reliability beyond naive retrieve-and-generate, but they target fundamentally different robustness coordinates. CalibRAG attacks the uncertainty/OOD axis by training a forecasting function over (temperature, query, document) to calibrate decision confidence, intervening at the reranker and reporting calibration error against decision correctness. Self-RAG attacks relevance/noise and sufficiency by training reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval, self-critique, and citation, intervening at the generator and reporting factuality and citation faithfulness. The failure types, intervention points, primary metrics, and action policies (calibrated-confidence answer vs. adaptive retrieve/filter/answer) all diverge, so leaderboard-style ranking would conflate calibration quality with retrieval-adaptivity and citation quality.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-evaluate both methods on a shared task with (1) identical retriever and base generator, (2) a unified metric suite that simultaneously reports calibration (ECE/Brier or decision-calibration), answer correctness, AND citation/support faithfulness, (3) an explicit action-policy harness specifying whether the system may answer/abstain/re-retrieve and scoring it accordingly, and (4) controlled noise conditions so each method's contribution at its native coordinate can be isolated. Without aligning at least intervention point or metric family, only complementary-module discussion is defensible.
notes: Calibration vs. self-reflective adaptive retrieval are plausibly stackable rather than competing; treating them as alternatives on one leaderboard would mislead.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge (benign); PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, target-question query control, black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, insertion budget of ~5 malicious passages, attack objective of inducing an attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining + self-think before generation); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive injection, no defense intervention proposed)
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support / faithfulness; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciling conflicting facts); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy is evaluated)
rationale: Both papers touch on situations where retrieved content disagrees with what an LLM would otherwise produce, but they occupy opposite sides of the RAG pipeline. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense that assumes naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflicts and is scored on answer correctness/faithfulness with an explicit answer-after-reconciliation policy. PoisonedRAG is an offensive corpus-injection attack with an attacker threat model (write access, ~5 malicious passages, target-answer objective, black/white-box variants) measured by attack success rate, and it proposes no defender action policy. Every one of the five coordinates diverges, and the roles (defense vs attack) are categorically different, so leaderboard-style ranking would be misleading rather than merely incomplete.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require recasting both works into a shared defense evaluation: FaithfulRAG and a PoisonedRAG-style defense (or FaithfulRAG itself) would need to be tested against the same PoisonedRAG attack corpus under matched retriever/generator, identical insertion budget and target-question set, and report a shared metric family (e.g., ASR plus clean-task accuracy and abstention/verification action labels). Without such a defender-vs-attacker reformulation and explicit action-policy reporting on both sides, the two papers cannot be ranked as substitutes.
notes: Attack paper vs benign-conflict defense paper; threat models are categorically incompatible, so even partial is too generous.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict (with passing mention of malicious info); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (e.g., RGB worst-case); PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target Q (query control), both black-box and white-box retriever visibility, black-box generator access, insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts per target, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (post-retrieval source-aware consolidation); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious passage injection)
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness / worst-case robustness; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR)
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer (with reliability-based candidate selection); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy)
rationale: The two papers sit on opposite sides of the RAG security problem and are not alternative methods for the same task. Astute RAG is a defender-side, training-free generation strategy that consolidates internal and retrieved knowledge to mitigate noise and conflicts, measured by answer correctness. PoisonedRAG is an attacker-side optimization that injects ~5 malicious passages into the corpus to maximize attack success rate against a target question, and explicitly shows existing defenses are insufficient (without specifically evaluating Astute RAG). Their intervention points (generator vs corpus), metric targets (accuracy vs ASR), threat-model roles (defender vs attacker), and action policies are incompatible, so any leaderboard-style ranking would be misleading rather than informative.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A unified attack-defense evaluation: instantiate PoisonedRAG as the stressor (same target questions, same insertion budget, same retriever/generator) and report Astute RAG's accuracy and ASR against it alongside baseline RAG and prior defenses. Both papers would need to share corpus, retriever, LLM, target-question set, and report a common metric pair (correctness on clean + corrupted, ASR on targeted attacks), plus an explicit defender action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine). Only then can the two contributions be discussed in a comparable frame, and even then as attacker vs defender modules rather than direct substitutes.
notes: Even though Astute RAG mentions 'malicious information' in its motivation, its main evaluations use RGB-style noise and benign imperfect retrieval, not PoisonedRAG-style adversarial corpus injection, so the apparent thematic overlap does not translate into shared experimental ground.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; corpus write access = yes for both; query control = attacker chooses target question (PoisonedRAG) vs arbitrary queries (RobustRAG); retriever visibility = black-box and white-box (PoisonedRAG) vs adaptive attacker with full knowledge of defense (RobustRAG); generator access = fixed LLM in both; insertion budget = ~5 malicious texts (PoisonedRAG) vs bounded m corrupted passages (RobustRAG, certified); attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer (both threat models compatible)
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack) vs context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate defense)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG ASR) vs answer correctness with certifiable robustness lower bounds (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported / answer-only (PoisonedRAG) vs answer + abstain ('I don't know') + filter via keyword/decoding aggregation (RobustRAG)
rationale: Both papers target the same threat surface—adversarial corruption of a RAG corpus by an attacker who injects a bounded number of malicious passages to manipulate generation—so failure type and evidence assumption align closely. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution that measures attack success rate against undefended RAG, while RobustRAG is a defensive contribution measuring certifiable lower bounds on response quality via an isolate-then-aggregate strategy with explicit abstention. The intervention point (corpus-side attack vs context-assembly + generator-side defense), metric target (ASR vs robust correctness with certificates), and action policy (none reported vs explicit 'I don't know' abstention plus filtering) all differ. They are natural complements—PoisonedRAG is a candidate attack one would evaluate RobustRAG against—but they cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head requires placing them on a common attack-defense matrix: e.g., run PoisonedRAG (and other attacks) against RobustRAG (and other defenses) on shared datasets, retrievers, generators, and insertion budgets, then report aligned metrics (ASR under defense, robust accuracy, abstention rate, certified bound coverage). Either (a) compare PoisonedRAG to other attacks against the same defended system, or (b) compare RobustRAG to other defenses under the same PoisonedRAG attack at matched budgets m and threat assumptions, with a uniform action-policy specification (answer/abstain).
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pairing within the same threat model; comparable as components of one evaluation, not as alternatives on a single ranking.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations from LLMs in standard RAG; RGB: benchmark-constructed stressors (controlled noise ratios, all-negative passage sets, counterfactual injections)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally fine-tunes a generator-side detector
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection F1; RGB: answer correctness, plus rejection rate and counterfactual error-detection rate
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc span-level detection), generator action is unreported; RGB: answer and abstain explicitly evaluated (negative rejection testbed)
rationale: Both are RAG evaluation benchmarks concerned with the gap between generated text and retrieved evidence, so the high-level problem area overlaps. However, RAGTruth captures naturally generated LLM responses with word-level hallucination annotations across QA/summarization/data-to-text and scores systems on span-level detection F1, implicitly assuming a verify/flag action. RGB instead constructs synthetic stressor testbeds (noise ratio sweeps, all-noise abstention sets, multi-doc integration, counterfactual document injection) and scores answer accuracy and explicit abstain behavior. Because the evidence construction, the metric family, and the action policies differ, results on one benchmark cannot be mapped to a rank on the other; the two should be discussed as complementary diagnostics rather than placed on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the same set of RAG systems on both benchmarks under a shared retriever/generator stack, report a common metric family (e.g., both span-level faithfulness and answer-level accuracy plus abstain rate), and explicitly define and evaluate the same action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. flag) on matched evidence conditions (both natural and constructed). Without these shared axes, RAGTruth's detection F1 and RGB's accuracy/rejection numbers are not commensurable.
notes: Both are benchmarks rather than methods; comparability question is whether a system's score on one transfers as evidence of robustness measured by the other—it does not.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios + injected counterfactuals); naturally occurring conflict / benign retrieval error (Sufficient Context: organic retrieval over existing QA datasets analyzed via sufficiency autorater)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); generator prompting (Sufficient Context's selective generation method)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: answer, abstain
rationale: Both papers address how RAG behaves when retrieved context is imperfect, and both treat abstention as a first-class outcome rather than only accuracy. However, RGB is purely a diagnostic benchmark with four synthetic testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) using controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents, while Sufficient Context introduces a sufficiency autorater applied to organically retrieved contexts in existing QA datasets and additionally proposes a selective generation intervention. The intervention point (evaluation-only vs. evaluation + generator-side selective generation), the evidence assumption (constructed stressors vs. natural sufficiency stratification), and the metric framing (per-ability accuracy/rejection rate vs. sufficiency-stratified hallucination/abstention/correctness and selective-risk improvement) differ enough that ranking them on a single leaderboard would conflate distinct objects. They are best discussed as complementary lenses on RAG abstention rather than substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) run Sufficient Context's autorater and selective generation method on RGB's four testbeds and report the same per-ability accuracy and negative-rejection rate that RGB uses, or (b) reconstruct RGB-style synthetic noise/counterfactual perturbations within Sufficient Context's sufficiency-stratified evaluation pipeline, using a common retriever, generator, dataset, abstention definition, and a shared selective-risk/coverage metric so that the two approaches address the same operating point.
notes: Both are 'evaluation' papers but one is a benchmark-only artifact and the other is autorater + method; comparing them as alternatives is category-conflated.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (FaithfulRAG); mixed sufficiency + consistency/conflict + relevance/noise (RAGTruth covers multiple hallucination categories)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations in benign RAG outputs across QA/summarization/data-to-text; FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring or benchmark-constructed parametric-vs-context conflict
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (and verifier when fine-tuning detectors on the corpus); FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining + self-think pre-generation)
metric_target: RAGTruth: detection performance over span/response annotations (closest to evidence support / citation faithfulness as a detection F1); FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and faithfulness on conflict QA
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (detect/flag hallucinated spans); FaithfulRAG: answer (after internal reconciliation). Different action families, both only partially reported.
rationale: RAGTruth is fundamentally an evaluation corpus contribution: it provides word-level hallucination annotations on ~18K naturally generated RAG outputs and benchmarks detection methods (including fine-tuned detectors) over QA, summarization, and data-to-text. FaithfulRAG is a generation-time method that explicitly models parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflicts and runs a self-think module before answering. Although both sit under the 'faithfulness in RAG' umbrella, they occupy different layers of the stack: an evaluation artifact / verifier-training resource versus a generator-side intervention. The metric targets (detection F1 over spans vs. answer correctness on conflict QA), the action policies (verify/flag vs. answer), and the failure-type scope (broad hallucination taxonomy vs. narrow parametric-context conflict) all diverge, so a leaderboard-style ranking between them would be category-confused and misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison meaningful, FaithfulRAG would need to be evaluated as a hallucination-mitigation method on RAGTruth's exact test split with the same response-level/span-level faithfulness metrics, against an apples-to-apples baseline family (other generation-side faithful-RAG methods). Conversely, the RAGTruth contribution would need to be reframed as a method (e.g., its fine-tuned detector deployed as a verifier in a pipeline that also chooses an action: answer/abstain/re-retrieve) and compared with FaithfulRAG on a shared end-task metric (faithfulness + answer correctness) under a fixed retriever, generator, and explicit action policy. Without that shared task/metric/action protocol, any head-to-head ranking is invalid.
notes: Could be argued as 'partial' since both target faithfulness, but the benchmark-vs-method asymmetry plus mismatched action policy makes a direct leaderboard comparison categorically inappropriate.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B counterfactual only)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (Paper A: naturally irrelevant top-k passages); benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper B: deliberately categorized and injected noise types including counterfactual)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (Paper A: NLI filter + fine-tuning); generator prompting or training (Paper B: adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise classification)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: filter + answer (Paper A NLI drops non-entailing passages and falls back to no-retrieval LLM); answer (Paper B has no explicit filtering/abstain mechanism, just trained to be robust)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness for retrieval-augmented LLMs on open-domain QA (with NQ overlap) and report EM/F1 on answer correctness, so the problem area and headline metric align. However, Paper A scopes failure to naturally-occurring irrelevant passages and combines NLI-based context filtering with fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts, while Paper B constructs a three-way noise typology (relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual) on its own RAG-Bench and intervenes purely through adaptive adversarial training plus a noise-awareness multi-task head. The counterfactual/conflict axis and the filter-vs-answer action mechanism are not shared, and the retriever, base generator, training data scale, and noise construction protocols differ. The comparison is therefore complementary rather than a direct leaderboard substitution: partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A common evaluation harness with: (1) the same retriever (e.g., DPR) and generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B) for both methods; (2) a shared noise construction protocol covering at minimum irrelevant and counterfactual cases on the same NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ splits; (3) reapplication of Paper A's NLI filter on Paper B's counterfactual noise and Paper B's RAAT training on Paper A's natural-retrieval setting; (4) explicit reporting of the action policy (answer vs. filter vs. abstain) and per-noise-type EM/F1 plus a calibration/abstention slice so the trade-offs between filtering and adversarial training can be read off the same axes.
notes: Both methods could in principle be stacked (filter then RAAT-trained generator); treating them as ranked alternatives understates this complementarity.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); rgb2023 also covers sufficiency, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: irrelevantContext2023: benign retrieval error from real retrievers over Wikipedia/ODQA; rgb2023: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios over news-derived corpus (bilingual)
intervention_point: irrelevantContext2023: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting/training (fine-tune on mixed contexts); rgb2023: evaluation artifact only
metric_target: irrelevantContext2023: answer correctness on 5 ODQA; rgb2023: accuracy, rejection rate, error detection rate, error correction rate across 4 ability testbeds
action_policy: irrelevantContext2023: filter then answer (implicit fallback to non-RAG when NLI flags); rgb2023: answer and abstain (negative rejection explicitly scored as separate ability)
rationale: Both papers target noise/irrelevant retrieved context in RAG and share the failure-type family of relevance/noise, but they are different artifact types: irrelevantContext2023 proposes interventions (NLI-based passage filtering and fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts) and reports answer accuracy on five ODQA benchmarks with naturally-retrieved noise, while rgb2023 is an evaluation benchmark that synthesizes controlled noise ratios over news-derived passages and scores four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) on off-the-shelf LLMs without proposing an intervention. The action policies also diverge: irrelevantContext2023 implicitly fuses filter+answer with non-RAG fallback, whereas rgb2023 explicitly scores abstention/negative rejection as a separate ability. Because the intervention point, corpus/noise construction, metric family, and action policy all differ, a leaderboard-style ranking would be misleading; they are better positioned as complementary (a method and a diagnostic benchmark).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run irrelevantContext2023's NLI-filter and fine-tuned generator (and a no-mitigation baseline) directly on RGB's noise-robustness testbed using RGB's noise ratios, corpus, and metrics, and additionally report RGB's negative-rejection score so the filter+abstain behavior is measured on the same axis; symmetrically, evaluate RGB's LLMs on irrelevantContext2023's five ODQA benchmarks with the same retriever, top-k, and answer/abstain action labels. Fix retriever, generator family, prompt, and answer/abstain decision rule across both setups.
notes: Methods paper vs benchmark paper is the dominant break; the topical overlap on noise robustness is real but does not make them substitutable on a shared leaderboard.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT); evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (F1/EM for RAAT); answer correctness plus rejection/counterfactual-specific metrics (RGB)
action_policy: answer (RAAT); answer + abstain via negative rejection (RGB)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG and both consider counterfactual/irrelevant content as stressors, so the failure type largely overlaps. However, RAAT is a training intervention (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B) with its own RAG-Bench built on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ via DPR over Wikipedia and scored only with F1/EM under an answer-always policy, while RGB is purely a diagnostic benchmark over bilingual news passages retrieved from search engines that explicitly evaluates four distinct abilities including negative rejection (an abstain action) and counterfactual robustness across six untrained LLMs. The intervention point, action-policy coverage, corpus/noise construction, and metric decomposition all diverge, and RGB does not propose a method that could share a leaderboard slot with RAAT. They are best treated as complementary contributions (a training method vs a multi-ability evaluation suite) rather than alternatives to be ranked head-to-head.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and a non-RAAT LLaMA-2 baseline) directly on the RGB testbeds for all four abilities with RGB's prescribed metrics (including negative-rejection rate and counterfactual identification), keeping the same retriever, corpus, noise ratios, and prompt format; alternatively, evaluate the RGB-benchmarked LLMs on RAG-Bench under matched noise definitions, and report an explicit answer/abstain action policy for both systems.
notes: RGB is an evaluation artifact rather than a competing method, which is the main reason direct leaderboard comparison is not meaningful.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); sufficiency + uncertainty/OOD (CoN only, via 'unknown' handling on RealTimeQA)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error from ODQA pipelines (both); CoN also uses benchmark-constructed noise stressors for noise-robustness evaluation
intervention_point: generator prompting/training (CoN: per-document reading notes + SFT on 10K synthetic CoN traces); context assembly/filter + generator training (Paper B: NLI-based passage filtering and SFT on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts)
metric_target: answer correctness / EM (both); CoN additionally reports rejection rate for unanswerable real-time questions
action_policy: CoN: answer + abstain ('unknown') explicitly evaluated; Paper B: answer (and implicit filter when NLI rejects), no abstain evaluation reported
breaking_coordinates: action_policy, intervention_point (partial), metric_target (partial), evaluation artifact (different retrievers/benchmarks/base models)
rationale: Both papers tackle the same failure type—irrelevant/noisy retrieved context in ODQA under benign retrieval-error assumptions—and both intervene on the generator side via supervised fine-tuning with the goal of improving answer correctness, so there is substantial topical overlap. However, CoN explicitly defines and evaluates an abstain action policy (responding 'unknown', measured via rejection rate on RealTimeQA), while Paper B reports only answer-attempting EM/F1 and never operationalizes an abstain action; CoN's intervention is a per-document note-taking reasoning step, whereas Paper B couples robust-context SFT with an upstream NLI filter at context assembly. They also differ on retriever (DPR vs Google/SerpAPI), benchmark mix (NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ/RealTimeQA vs 5 ODQA including multi-hop StrategyQA/2WikiMultiHopQA), and base model, so a single leaderboard number would conflate method, retriever, corpus, and action policy. The methods are best discussed as complementary noisy-retrieval mechanisms (filter+train vs note+abstain) rather than ranked head-to-head, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold retriever, corpus, and base generator fixed; evaluate both methods on the same benchmark suite (including the multi-hop sets and a real-time/unanswerable split); explicitly define a shared action policy—either (a) restrict to answer-only EM/F1 with no abstain, or (b) add an abstain mechanism to Paper B and report rejection rate / selective risk alongside EM for both methods on identical noise-stress conditions; ablate the NLI filter from Paper B and the note-taking step from CoN to separate intervention-point effects.
notes: Strong topical overlap on distraction/noise robustness, but action policy and the additional filter/abstain components make direct ranking misleading.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both assume standard open-domain retrieval where some passages are irrelevant or insufficient; neither addresses adversarial or stale evidence)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact + generator prompting (Sufficient Context: external autorater + selective-generation prompt); retriever + generator training (Self-RAG: trained reflection tokens governing on-demand retrieval and passage filtering)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context); answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer, abstain (Sufficient Context, explicitly evaluated via hallucination vs abstention rates); re-retrieve, filter (Self-RAG, via Retrieve and IsRel/IsSup tokens). No common action policy is jointly evaluated.
rationale: Both papers target the broad robust-RAG concern that retrieval may be irrelevant or insufficient, and both equip the system with some form of context-quality signal. However, the intervention point differs sharply: Sufficient Context adds an external sufficiency autorater used at evaluation and as a feature for inference-time selective generation, while Self-RAG bakes the signal into the LM's vocabulary via trained reflection tokens that govern on-demand retrieval and parallel passage filtering. The action policies are also non-overlapping in what is explicitly evaluated: Sufficient Context measures abstain-vs-answer behavior and selective accuracy, whereas Self-RAG measures factuality, citation faithfulness, and task accuracy under retrieve/filter actions, with no abstention metric reported. Because the two systems intervene at different pipeline stages, optimize different action policies, and report partially disjoint metric families, putting them on the same leaderboard would conflate complementary mechanisms rather than rank substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both systems on a shared QA benchmark (e.g., PopQA, TriviaQA, ASQA) using the same retriever and corpus; report a common metric bundle that includes (a) end-to-end answer accuracy, (b) abstention/selective-risk curves with matched coverage points, and (c) citation faithfulness / evidence-support when generations are emitted. Additionally, fix and document the action policy: either force both to operate in answer-or-abstain mode (giving Self-RAG an abstention rule derived from its reflection tokens) or in answer-always mode. Without these matched action and metric choices, the comparison remains partial.
notes: Self-RAG's reflection tokens could in principle be repurposed as an abstention signal, but the paper does not evaluate that policy, so action-policy alignment cannot be assumed.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD (CalibRAG); relevance/noise + sufficiency (Self-RAG)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both); neither assumes adversarial corpora or stressors
intervention_point: reranker via learned forecasting function (CalibRAG); generator prompting/training with reflection tokens (Self-RAG)
metric_target: calibration error + answer correctness (CalibRAG); answer correctness + evidence support + citation faithfulness (Self-RAG)
action_policy: answer with calibrated confidence (CalibRAG, unreported abstention/escalation policy); re-retrieve + verify + answer via reflection tokens (Self-RAG)
rationale: Both papers are 'control'-style interventions over RAG, but they target distinct failure modes: CalibRAG addresses calibration of decision confidence (uncertainty/OOD) by learning a forecasting function f(t,q,d) used as a reranker, while Self-RAG addresses indiscriminate retrieval and unsupported generations via adaptive retrieval and self-critique tokens trained into the generator. The intervention points (reranker vs generator training), primary metric families (calibration error vs citation faithfulness/factuality), and action repertoires (single calibrated answer vs on-demand retrieve/critique/answer) diverge substantially. They could be discussed as complementary modules in a calibrated-and-adaptive RAG stack, but a leaderboard-style head-to-head would conflate calibration quality with adaptive-retrieval quality. Verdict is partial: overlapping motivation (reliable RAG outputs) but non-substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix a shared retriever, generator backbone, corpus, and benchmark suite; then evaluate BOTH systems on the SAME metric panel including ECE/Brier for calibration AND citation/factuality scores (e.g., FActScore, ALCE) AND retrieval recall, with explicitly reported action policies (when each system answers, abstains, or re-retrieves). Without aligning the metric targets and making action policies explicit and equivalent (e.g., both systems given an abstention option and scored on selective risk/coverage), direct ranking would conflate different objectives.
notes: Self-RAG's ISUSE/ISSUP tokens give it implicit selective behavior; CalibRAG's calibrated confidence supports downstream abstention but the paper does not evaluate an abstention policy directly. This asymmetry in action evaluation is itself a comparability gap.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs contextual knowledge); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
