evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring or benchmark-constructed knowledge conflict from benign retrieval; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access (5 malicious texts/question), attacker-chosen target question and answer, retriever visibility in both black-box and white-box settings, black-box generator access, attack objective = induce specific target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining, contextual knowledge alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (poisoning injection) — note this is the attack surface, not a defense intervention
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support (faithfulness to context); PoisonedRAG: attack success rate (ASR)
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after self-think reasoning); PoisonedRAG: unreported (no defender action policy — it is an attack paper)
rationale: Both papers touch the broad theme of a tension between retrieved context and the LLM's parametric knowledge, but they occupy incompatible roles in the RAG robustness landscape. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense for benign/naturally occurring knowledge conflicts that optimizes answer correctness and context faithfulness via fact-level reasoning, while PoisonedRAG is a corpus-side attack that injects 5 attacker-chosen malicious texts per target question into the knowledge database and reports ASR under explicit threat-model assumptions (corpus write access, query control, white/black-box retriever and generator visibility). The failure type (consistency vs integrity/adversarial), evidence assumption (benign conflict vs attacker-created), intervention point (generator vs corpus), metric target (correctness vs ASR), and action policy (answer vs unreported) all diverge. Placing them on a single leaderboard would conflate attacker and defender roles and is misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Recast FaithfulRAG as a candidate defense against PoisonedRAG-style poisoning: hold retriever, generator, knowledge base, and target-question set constant; instantiate PoisonedRAG's attack with a fixed insertion budget and threat model (black-box and/or white-box); then report both ASR (attack success on target questions) and clean-accuracy/faithfulness for FaithfulRAG alongside other defenses (e.g., perplexity filtering, paraphrasing, majority voting). A symmetric comparison also requires an explicit defender action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine) and the same conflict-vs-poisoning evaluation split so the two operating regions are clearly separated.
notes: Attacker–defender mismatch is the dominant break; even shared 'parametric-vs-retrieved' vocabulary does not make them substitutable methods.

failure_type: Paper A: consistency/conflict + relevance/noise (with passing mention of integrity/adversarial corruption); Paper B: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB worst-case) + naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge; Paper B: attacker-created evidence with explicit threat model — corpus write access (yes, inject ~5 malicious passages), query control (attacker chooses target questions, not user queries), retriever visibility (both black-box and white-box variants), generator access (black-box LLM API), insertion budget (5 texts per target question into a million-scale corpus), attack objective (induce attacker-chosen target answer)
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting + context assembly/compression + verifier (source-aware iterative consolidation in post-retrieval); Paper B: corpus/index (adversarial passage injection into the knowledge database)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness (and worst-case accuracy under imperfect retrieval); Paper B: attack success rate (ASR)
action_policy: Paper A: answer (consolidated from internal + external, with implicit reliability comparison) — abstain/escalate not evaluated; Paper B: unreported (no defender action policy is the subject; it is an attack paper)
rationale: Both papers concern robustness of RAG to harmful retrieved content, and Astute RAG explicitly cites and motivates against PoisonedRAG-style malicious information, so the failure-type space overlaps at integrity/adversarial corruption. However, the two papers sit on opposite sides of the attacker–defender loop: PoisonedRAG intervenes at the corpus/index by injecting optimization-crafted passages under an explicit threat model (write access, ~5 texts per target, black/white-box retriever) and reports attack success rate, while Astute RAG intervenes at the generator via source-aware internal/external consolidation and reports answer correctness on RGB/NQ-style benchmark-constructed noise, not on PoisonedRAG-injected corpora. The metric targets are essentially inverted (ASR vs. accuracy) and Astute RAG never instantiates PoisonedRAG’s threat model, so leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful. They are complementary (one defines the threat, the other proposes a candidate post-retrieval mitigation), which is why the verdict is partial rather than invalid or valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate Astute RAG as a defender inside PoisonedRAG’s exact setup: identical corpus (NQ/HotpotQA/MS-MARCO at the stated scale), identical retriever (e.g., Contriever) and generator, identical target-question set, identical insertion budget (e.g., 5 malicious texts/question) under both black-box and white-box attacker knowledge, and report ASR alongside clean accuracy and abstention behavior. Alternatively, frame the comparison explicitly as attack-vs-defense (not leaderboard) and report a defender action policy (answer / abstain / expose conflict) so both papers expose a comparable operating point.
notes: Attack paper vs. post-retrieval defense paper; even with overlapping vocabulary about 'malicious' information, the evaluation artifacts and metric semantics are not interchangeable.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; both assume corpus write access and adversarial passage injection. PoisonedRAG uses a small insertion budget (e.g., 5 malicious texts per target question) with a targeted attack objective, evaluated in black-box and white-box retriever-visibility settings. RobustRAG threat model is an adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge and a bounded number of injected passages, with an arbitrary corruption objective.
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (crafts and injects malicious passages). RobustRAG: context assembly/compression plus generator prompting (isolate-then-aggregate over passage groups).
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success. RobustRAG: answer correctness plus a certified-robustness lower bound under bounded corruption.
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper; no defender action evaluated). RobustRAG: answer via secure keyword/decoding aggregation, with an explicit abstain branch in isolated responses.
rationale: Both papers operate on the same failure type (integrity/adversarial corruption of RAG via injected passages) and share the core evidence assumption of attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, so they sit in the same problem area. However, PoisonedRAG is an offense paper whose intervention is at the corpus and whose metric is targeted attack success rate, with no defender action policy reported, while RobustRAG is a defense paper whose intervention is at context assembly and generator prompting and whose metric is certified answer correctness with explicit aggregate or abstain action policies. The two are complementary roles in the same attack-defense ecosystem rather than substitutable methods on a single leaderboard, and their headline numbers (ASR vs certified accuracy) are inversely oriented and not commensurable. This makes the comparison partial: legitimate to discuss jointly as attack and defense, but not as ranked alternatives.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both within a single attack-defense protocol: fix retriever, generator, corpus, query set, insertion budget, and attacker knowledge; run PoisonedRAG as the attack against RobustRAG (and a no-defense baseline) and report a shared metric family such as targeted ASR and clean accuracy under matched corruption budgets, plus explicit defender action policy (answer vs abstain). Without this shared harness, only complementary discussion is justified.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pair; comparability is structurally partial regardless of empirical results.

failure_type: sufficiency, consistency/conflict, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring (model-generated hallucinations on standard RAG inputs); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, counterfactual documents, all-negative contexts)
intervention_point: RAGTruth: verifier (evaluates hallucination detection methods); RGB: generator prompting (evaluates LLM RAG abilities); both produce evaluation artifacts
metric_target: RAGTruth: span/response-level hallucination detection (precision/recall of unsupported spans); RGB: answer correctness, rejection rate, integration accuracy
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported for the generation system (post-hoc detection only); RGB: answer / abstain (negative rejection is explicitly evaluated) / expose conflict (counterfactual)
rationale: Both papers are evaluation artifacts for trustworthy RAG and share a concern with ungrounded or unreliable LLM outputs given retrieved evidence. However, RAGTruth is a span-level hallucination-annotation corpus whose target unit is a detector that judges whether generated text is supported by the provided context, while RGB is a generator-side capability benchmark that scores end-task answer accuracy, negative-rejection rate, multi-document integration, and counterfactual resistance under constructed noise. The intervention points (verifier vs generator), metric families (detection F1 vs task accuracy/rejection), and action policies (RAGTruth does not evaluate any system-level action; RGB explicitly probes abstention and conflict handling) all differ. A method's score on one cannot be ranked against a method's score on the other, so the comparison is complementary rather than leaderboard-equivalent.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, both works would need to (a) evaluate the same kind of system (e.g., either both score a hallucination detector or both score an end-to-end RAG generator with the same abstention policy), (b) use a shared metric family (e.g., joint detection-F1 plus task-accuracy on aligned inputs), (c) align evidence construction (naturally generated vs deliberately injected noise/counterfactual), and (d) report identical action labels (answer/abstain/expose-conflict) on the same instances. Absent that, they should be presented as complementary diagnostics for different RAG failure modes.
notes: Both are categorized as evaluation benchmarks, but they probe distinct points in the RAG pipeline and reward different behaviors; treating them as substitutable would mislead a reader.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict (RGB only via counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents from news + search); Sufficient Context: naturally occurring conflict / benign retrieval error on standard QA datasets, labeled post-hoc by an LLM autorater
intervention_point: RGB: evaluation artifact only; Sufficient Context: evaluation artifact + verifier (sufficiency autorater) + generator prompting (selective generation combining sufficiency with self-confidence)
metric_target: RGB: answer correctness per ability + rejection rate; Sufficient Context: stratified correct/abstain/hallucinate rates and selective risk/coverage
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via the negative-rejection testbed; Sufficient Context via guided selective generation)
rationale: Both papers study RAG behavior when retrieved context is imperfect and both explicitly evaluate an abstain action in addition to answering, so the failure-type and action-policy axes overlap. However, RGB constructs a fixed benchmark with deliberately controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactual documents and reports per-ability accuracy/rejection scores, while Sufficient Context defines an answerability property over naturally occurring (Q,C) pairs, trains an autorater to label sufficiency, and uses that signal both to stratify error analyses and to drive a selective-generation intervention. As a result the evidence assumption (constructed stressors vs. autorater-labeled natural data), intervention point (evaluation only vs. evaluation + verifier + selective generation), and metric target (per-ability accuracy vs. stratified hallucinate/abstain/correct and selective-risk curves) differ substantively. The two are best discussed as complementary lenses on noisy/insufficient retrieval rather than as substitutable methods on a shared leaderboard, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's selective-generation method on RGB's noise-robustness, negative-rejection, and counterfactual testbeds (and conversely apply the sufficient-context autorater to RGB instances), report a shared metric family (e.g., accuracy among answered vs. abstain rate, or selective risk-coverage) for the same LLMs and retriever, and align the noise constructions so that 'insufficient context' in B and 'all-noise / negative rejection' in A map onto the same instance partitions.
notes: Action policy is supported in both papers (negative rejection in RGB; explicit selective generation in Sufficient Context), so action_policy is not the breaking axis here; the break is in evidence construction, intervention scope, and metric formulation.

failure_type: RAGTruth covers consistency/conflict plus sufficiency at word level; FaithfulRAG targets consistency/conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge only. Partial overlap on conflict.
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations and benign retrieval errors across QA, data-to-text, and summarization. FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring parametric-vs-retrieved conflict. Neither uses an adversarial threat model.
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus plus detector fine-tuning baseline). FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think reconciliation).
metric_target: RAGTruth: detection precision/recall/F1 on span-level hallucination labels (an evidence-support/faithfulness detector metric). FaithfulRAG: answer correctness and context faithfulness on QA.
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (detection only, no downstream generator action). FaithfulRAG: answer after an internal verify/expose-conflict reconciliation step.
rationale: Both papers sit in the broad RAG faithfulness/hallucination space, but they are categorically different artifacts and cannot occupy the same leaderboard. RAGTruth is an evaluation benchmark whose contribution is a word-level annotated corpus and the benchmarking of hallucination detectors, with a fine-tuned Llama detector as the main empirical result. FaithfulRAG is a generation-time method that mines self-facts, aligns them with retrieved chunks, and runs a self-think module to reconcile parametric vs. retrieved knowledge conflicts before producing an answer. The intervention points (evaluation artifact vs. generator pipeline), metric targets (detector P/R/F1 over span annotations vs. answer correctness/faithfulness on QA), and action policies (flag/no action vs. answer-after-reconciliation) are not commensurable, so direct ranking would mislead.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) evaluate FaithfulRAG on the RAGTruth corpus by reporting span-level hallucination rates of its generated answers under matched LLM backbones, prompts, and retriever, and compare against RAGTruth's reported per-model hallucination frequencies; or (b) treat RAGTruth purely as a training/eval substrate and benchmark FaithfulRAG plus the RAGTruth fine-tuned detector (used as a post-hoc filter/abstain policy) on the same QA task with shared retriever, generator, action policy, and a common metric family (answer correctness plus faithfulness/span-hallucination rate).
notes: Benchmark-vs-method pairings of this kind are structurally non-comparable without an explicit harmonization experiment.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B only, via counterfactual noise)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real retrievers across 5 ODQA benchmarks. Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAG-Bench) with three noise categories including counterfactual passages that are closer to attacker-created/conflicting evidence than to organic retrieval noise.
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning). Paper B: generator prompting or training only (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise classification head).
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) for both
action_policy: Paper A: answer + filter (NLI gating that falls back to closed-book when context fails entailment). Paper B: unreported (multi-task noise-type classification is internal; the system still always answers, no explicit abstain/filter/verify action evaluated).
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on ODQA and overlap on answer-correctness metrics and on a training-based generator intervention (Yoran's mixed-context fine-tuning vs. Fang's RAAT). However, Paper B expands the failure space to include counterfactual (conflicting) passages, which is a different failure type and evidence assumption than Paper A's purely irrelevant/benign-noise framing. Paper A additionally couples training with an explicit NLI filter that operationalizes a filter/abstain-from-retrieval action policy, whereas Paper B reports no comparable action policy and is evaluated under a different benchmark construction (RAG-Bench). The methods are therefore complementary and partially overlap on the irrelevant-noise slice, but a leaderboard-style direct ranking would conflate distinct noise typologies, intervention stacks, and action policies.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared benchmark with a unified noise typology (irrelevant, relevant-but-distracting, counterfactual) using the same retriever, base generator, and evaluation splits; report results separately per noise type; explicitly evaluate Paper A's NLI-filter+abstain pipeline alongside RAAT on the counterfactual slice and evaluate RAAT on Paper A's multi-hop benchmarks; and report a common action-policy protocol (answer-only vs. filter/abstain) so that filtering effects are not conflated with training effects.
notes: Paper B cites Paper A directly, but cross-citation does not establish comparability; the counterfactual category materially shifts the threat/evidence model.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency and consistency/conflict via negative rejection and counterfactual testbeds
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real ODQA retrievers; Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and synthetic counterfactual documents
intervention_point: Paper A: reranker/context assembly (NLI filter) and generator prompting/training; Paper B: evaluation artifact (benchmark only, no proposed intervention)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness on ODQA; Paper B: answer correctness plus rejection rate (selective risk/coverage) and counterfactual identification
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (no explicit abstain channel evaluated); Paper B: explicitly evaluates abstain via negative rejection ability
rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior under noisy/irrelevant retrieved context, but they occupy different layers of the research stack. Paper A proposes concrete mitigations (NLI-based passage filtering and fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts) and measures answer accuracy on five ODQA benchmarks using naturally noisy retrieval. Paper B contributes RGB, a bilingual evaluation artifact that measures four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) via deliberately constructed noise ratios and counterfactual documents, and crucially evaluates abstention as a first-class outcome, which Paper A does not. Because Paper B is a benchmark rather than a competing method, and because the two diverge on intervention point, action policy (abstain vs. filter-then-answer), evidence-construction assumptions, and metric family, they cannot be ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard; they are complementary (a method that could be measured on RGB) rather than substitutable. The verdict is therefore partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and fine-tuned RALM on Paper B's RGB noise-robustness testbed under matched noise ratios, with both accuracy and rejection rate reported, plus explicit action-policy labels (when the system abstains vs. answers vs. re-retrieves). To extend comparability across all of RGB, Paper A would also need to be evaluated on counterfactual and negative-rejection testbeds and report calibration of its abstention/filter decisions. Conversely, Paper B would need to include a methods track (not just diagnostic benchmark) for any leaderboard framing.
notes: Asymmetry of contribution type (method vs. benchmark) is the dominant reason this is partial rather than valid; it is not invalid because the noise-robustness construct genuinely overlaps.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict, integrity/adversarial corruption (counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both inject synthetic noise; RAAT also uses adversarially constructed counterfactuals during training; RGB constructs noise from search-engine returns over news)
intervention_point: RAAT: generator prompting or training (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B); RGB: evaluation artifact (no intervention proposed)
metric_target: RAAT: answer correctness (F1/EM); RGB: answer correctness + selective risk/coverage (rejection rate) + a form of error detection
action_policy: RAAT: answer (no abstention evaluated); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection is an explicit testbed)
rationale: Both papers target retrieval-noise robustness and share overlapping noise typologies (irrelevant and counterfactual passages), but they play structurally different roles: RAAT is a training-time method on LLaMA-2 7B evaluated with F1/EM on NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ with DPR, whereas RGB is a bilingual diagnostic benchmark that explicitly evaluates four distinct abilities including negative rejection (abstention) and information integration. Crucially, RAAT never evaluates an abstention or selective-risk action policy, while RGB treats abstention as a first-class measured behavior with its own rejection rate metric — so even the operating definition of 'robust' differs. The intervention point also differs (generator training vs. evaluation artifact), so the two cannot be ranked as alternative methods on a common leaderboard. They are best framed as complementary: a training method that could be slotted into the benchmark, not a head-to-head comparison.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT (and a non-RAAT baseline) directly on RGB's four testbeds in matched languages, reporting accuracy, rejection rate, and error-detection metrics under aligned noise ratios; or, conversely, port RGB-style noise construction and abstention evaluation onto RAG-Bench so that both papers share retriever, generator, noise construction, action-policy labels (answer vs. abstain vs. integrate), and the same metric family covering both correctness and selective risk.
notes: From a selective-risk lens this is a clear partial rather than valid: any leaderboard that omits abstention/rejection metrics would systematically reward RAAT-style answer-always policies and misrepresent the trustworthiness dimension RGB is specifically designed to surface.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); uncertainty/OOD also in Chain-of-Note via 'unknown' handling
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor; CoN additionally treats unanswerable/RealTimeQA as an OOD stressor
intervention_point: Chain-of-Note: generator prompting or training (note-taking before answer). IrrelevantContext: context assembly/compression (NLI-based passage filtering) + generator prompting or training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts)
metric_target: Both: answer correctness (EM). Chain-of-Note additionally: selective risk/coverage (rejection rate on real-time/unknown questions). IrrelevantContext does not report a selective-risk metric.
action_policy: Chain-of-Note: answer + abstain ('unknown'). IrrelevantContext: answer + filter (fall back to no-retrieval LLM when NLI rejects). Both are explicit but materially different.
rationale: Both papers target distraction/relevance noise in RALMs and propose training-based mitigations on overlapping ODQA benchmarks (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA). However, the intervention points differ: CoN modifies generator reasoning via sequential reading notes, while IrrelevantContext inserts an NLI filter at context assembly and fine-tunes the generator on mixed-quality contexts. Crucially, the action policies are different first-class objects—CoN explicitly evaluates abstention via 'unknown' responses and rejection-rate gains on RealTimeQA (a selective-risk metric), whereas IrrelevantContext's action is to skip retrieval but always answer and reports only accuracy. From a calibration/selective-risk standpoint these are complementary operating modes, not interchangeable systems, so direct leaderboard ranking would conflate accuracy-only and abstention-aware regimes. Verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared benchmark suite (overlap of NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ plus a multi-hop set like StrategyQA or HotpotQA) with matched retriever and generator backbones; report both EM/F1 and an abstention/coverage curve (e.g., risk-coverage AUC, rejection rate on unanswerable subset, calibration error); evaluate CoN with and without the 'unknown' option, and evaluate IrrelevantContext with an added abstention head; use matched noise construction (real DPR retrievals vs. injected irrelevant passages) so the same distraction stressor drives both systems.
notes: From a trustworthy-ML lens, abstention vs. filter are different selective-prediction policies; treating them as drop-in replacements on accuracy alone would hide CoN's coverage trade-off.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error, naturally occurring conflict (no adversarial component in either paper)
intervention_point: Paper A: evaluation artifact (sufficient-context autorater) + system-control policy (post-hoc selective generation). Paper B: generator training (reflection tokens) + retriever (on-demand adaptive retrieval).
metric_target: Paper A: selective risk/coverage, answer correctness conditional on answering, hallucination rate. Paper B: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, factuality (no selective-risk curve).
action_policy: Paper A: abstain (explicitly evaluated via selective generation thresholds). Paper B: re-retrieve and answer-with-citation (no abstention evaluation).
rationale: Both papers target RAG reliability and use self-assessment signals to improve answer quality, but they operate on different axes. Sufficient Context is a post-hoc selective-generation method that explicitly measures a coverage/risk tradeoff using an external sufficiency autorater plus self-confidence to drive abstention. Self-RAG instead trains an end-to-end LM with reflection tokens to decide when to retrieve and to critique passages, and reports factuality and citation accuracy without an abstain operating point. The intervention point (train-time reflection vs. inference-time selective gating), the metric family (factuality/citation vs. selective risk under abstention), and the action policy (re-retrieve/answer vs. abstain) all diverge, so they cannot be ranked head-to-head on a single leaderboard but can be discussed as complementary modules.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both systems on a shared QA benchmark with the same retriever and generator backbone, expose an explicit abstention action for Self-RAG (e.g., abstain when ISREL=irrelevant or ISSUP=no-support), and report a common metric family: selective-risk/coverage curves, hallucination vs. abstention rates, and citation faithfulness. Without an abstain operating point and matched selective-risk reporting for Self-RAG, the two systems are measuring different objectives.
notes: From a trustworthy-ML/selective-risk perspective, Self-RAG's reflection tokens could in principle support abstention, but the paper as written evaluates factuality/citation rather than calibration or coverage tradeoffs, so action policy is not equivalently reported.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD (miscalibrated confidence under decision-making); Self-RAG: relevance/noise and sufficiency (indiscriminate retrieval, unsupported generations)
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval error; no adversarial corpus, no threat model in either paper
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker plus a learned forecasting function over (temperature, query, document); Self-RAG: generator prompting/training (reflection tokens) and retriever (on-demand triggering)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error and decision/answer correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness, evidence support, and citation faithfulness
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence reported to the human (no explicit abstention/escalation evaluated); Self-RAG: re-retrieve on demand and filter via critique tokens, then answer — different action surfaces, neither explicitly evaluates abstention as a calibrated risk
rationale: Both papers attempt to make RAG more reliable, but they target distinct failure modes: CalibRAG addresses confidence miscalibration so that humans using RAG outputs for decisions do not over-rely on overconfident answers, while Self-RAG addresses unnecessary or unsupported retrieval by learning when to retrieve and to self-critique via reflection tokens. The intervention points (a learned forecasting reranker vs. a retrained generator with retrieval/critique tokens), the headline metrics (ECE/decision correctness vs. citation faithfulness and factuality), and the action policies (report calibrated confidence vs. on-demand re-retrieval and filtering) do not line up. They could be reported side-by-side as complementary modules or in different operating regions of a reliability stack, but a direct leaderboard ranking would conflate calibration quality with factuality/adaptive-retrieval quality and would mislead readers.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix the same retriever, generator backbone, corpus, and task suite (e.g., PopQA, TriviaQA, ASQA, plus a decision-style benchmark); evaluate both systems on a shared metric battery covering ECE/Brier, accuracy, citation faithfulness, and selective risk/coverage curves under an explicit, identical action policy (e.g., abstain at threshold τ, or report confidence on a fixed scale); additionally measure Self-RAG calibration (treat critique-token probabilities as confidence) and measure CalibRAG retrieval adaptivity/citation support. Without these alignments, the comparison is partial.
notes: Self-RAG's reflection tokens could in principle yield a calibration signal, but the paper does not evaluate calibration error, so it is unsafe to treat the two systems as substitutable on a calibration leaderboard.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (FaithfulRAG) vs integrity/adversarial corruption (PoisonedRAG)
evidence_assumption: naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and retrieved context (FaithfulRAG) vs attacker-created evidence (PoisonedRAG). PoisonedRAG threat model: corpus write access = yes (inject malicious passages), query control = target-question chosen by attacker, retriever visibility = both black-box and white-box studied, generator access = query-only, insertion budget = ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer. FaithfulRAG assumes no adversary.
intervention_point: generator prompting/training via self-fact mining and self-think reasoning (FaithfulRAG) vs corpus/index poisoning (PoisonedRAG)
metric_target: answer correctness and faithfulness to context (FaithfulRAG) vs attack success rate (PoisonedRAG)
action_policy: answer with parametric/contextual reconciliation (FaithfulRAG); unreported / not applicable (PoisonedRAG is an attack paper that does not propose a defender action policy)
rationale: Both papers touch retrieved-context reliability, but they sit on opposite sides of the RAG pipeline: FaithfulRAG is a generation-time defense that resolves naturally occurring parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflicts via fact-level alignment and self-think, measured by answer correctness and faithfulness. PoisonedRAG is an offensive method that writes adversarial passages into the corpus to coerce attacker-chosen target answers, measured by attack success rate under a specified threat model (corpus write access, ~5 malicious texts per target question, black/white-box retriever knowledge). The failure type, evidence assumption, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge, so any direct leaderboard-style ranking would be category-confused (attack vs benign-conflict defense) and misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) restrict comparisons within the same role — FaithfulRAG vs other faithfulness/conflict-resolution defenses on natural-conflict benchmarks, or PoisonedRAG vs other corpus-poisoning attacks under matched threat models; or (b) reframe as an attack+defense study where FaithfulRAG is explicitly evaluated against PoisonedRAG injections on shared retriever, generator, dataset, and budget, reporting both ASR and clean answer accuracy, with an explicit defender action policy (e.g., answer, abstain, or quarantine on conflict).
notes: Pair is an attack-vs-defense-for-different-failure-mode mismatch; could become a meaningful joint study but is not a direct alternative-method comparison.

failure_type: Astute: relevance/noise + consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Astute: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict + benchmark-constructed stressor; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access yes, query control chooses target questions, retriever visibility both black-box and white-box, generator access black-box, insertion budget 5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: Astute: generator prompting + context assembly/compression; PoisonedRAG: corpus/index
metric_target: Astute: answer correctness under imperfect retrieval; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate plus retrieval recall of malicious texts
action_policy: Astute: answer (selects among candidates via reliability comparison; no explicit abstain/escalate); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action evaluated)
rationale: Astute RAG is a training-free defense that consolidates internal LLM knowledge with retrieved passages using source-aware reliability comparison to improve answer correctness under noisy, conflicting, or malicious retrieval, while PoisonedRAG is an offensive method that crafts and injects 5 malicious passages per target question into the corpus to maximize attack success against an unmodified RAG. They occupy opposite roles in the attack-defense ecosystem: intervention points differ (generator/context-assembly defense vs corpus poisoning attack), metric targets are opposed (correctness vs ASR), and Astute supplies no formal attacker model while PoisonedRAG specifies write access, BB/WB retriever visibility, and a concrete insertion budget. Placing them on the same leaderboard would be a category error since neither is an alternative method for the other's problem, and Astute does not evaluate against PoisonedRAG-style optimized attacks. The pair is therefore invalid for direct comparison.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Astute RAG (and baseline defenses) against PoisonedRAG attacks at matched insertion budgets (e.g., 1/5/10 malicious passages per query), under identical retriever, generator, corpus, and target-question set; report both ASR (attacker metric) and answer correctness/abstention rate (defender metric) with explicit action policy (answer vs abstain vs flag). Alternatively, compare PoisonedRAG only to other attacks and Astute only to other defenses on shared benchmarks; cross-comparison requires a joint attack-vs-defense evaluation protocol.
notes: Astute mentions malicious information in motivation but evaluates primarily on noise/conflict benchmarks (RGB worst-case), not on optimized poisoning attacks; role asymmetry (defense vs attack) is the dominant break.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG: corpus write access = yes, insertion budget = 5 malicious texts per target question, retriever visibility = black-box and white-box variants, generator access = query-only, attack objective = induce specific attacker-chosen target answer; RobustRAG: assumes adaptive attacker with full defense knowledge and bounded number of injected passages, defender controls generator prompting and aggregation
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG attack) vs context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate defense)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG, to be maximized) vs answer correctness with certified robustness lower bounds plus coverage (RobustRAG, to be maximized under attack)
action_policy: answer (PoisonedRAG forces target answer generation) vs answer + abstain (RobustRAG explicitly evaluates an 'I don't know' abstention path within its keyword/decoding aggregation)
rationale: Both papers operate in the integrity/adversarial-corruption setting for RAG and share the assumption of attacker-injected passages, but they sit on opposite sides of the attack-defense ledger: PoisonedRAG is an offensive method that injects malicious texts at the corpus/index level and reports attack success rate, while RobustRAG is a defensive method that intervenes at context assembly and generator prompting via isolate-then-aggregate and certifies a lower bound on response quality, with an explicit abstain action. The intervention point, the metric direction (maximize ASR vs maximize certified accuracy/coverage), and the action policy (forced answer vs answer-or-abstain) are all incompatible for a single leaderboard. Treating them as substitute methods would be misleading because 'better' literally means opposite outcomes; the natural relationship is that RobustRAG should be evaluated against PoisonedRAG-style attacks, not ranked alongside it.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A comparison only becomes meaningful as an attack-vs-defense evaluation: fix a shared threat model (corpus write access, insertion budget k, retriever and generator access, attack objective), run PoisonedRAG as the attacker against RobustRAG as the defender on the same datasets, retriever, and LLM, and report a paired metric set (ASR and certified/empirical accuracy plus abstention rate) at matched insertion budgets. Direct leaderboard ranking of the two methods on a single scalar is not appropriate.
notes: Pair is a classic attack-vs-defense mismatch; comparability is structural, not a matter of missing detail.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict (naturally-generated LLM hallucinations under standard RAG); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (curated noise ratios and counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness (span-level hallucination detection F1, hallucination frequency); RGB: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (rejection rate, integration accuracy, counterfactual accuracy)
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (detection is post-hoc, no system action evaluated); RGB: answer, abstain (negative-rejection ability explicitly tests abstention)
rationale: Both papers are RAG-reliability evaluation artifacts, sharing concern for hallucination and conflicting/noisy evidence, but they measure fundamentally different quantities. RAGTruth provides a corpus of naturally generated responses with word-level hallucination spans and benchmarks span-level detectors (and detector fine-tuning), with no system-level action policy evaluated. RGB constructs scenario testbeds for four pre-defined abilities and measures task accuracy and explicit rejection behavior under controlled noise and counterfactual-document stressors. Because the evidence assumption (natural vs. constructed), the metric family (span detection vs. ability accuracy + rejection), and the action policy (none vs. answer/abstain) all diverge, results from one cannot be ranked against the other on a shared leaderboard. The papers are best discussed as complementary diagnostic suites rather than alternatives.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) run identical hallucination detectors on both corpora and report a common detection metric (e.g., span-level or response-level F1) with matched generators and retrieved contexts, or (b) define a shared task split with a unified metric family — answer correctness, abstention/coverage, and citation faithfulness — and an explicit action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict) that both benchmarks evaluate identically, ideally including matched stressor categories (natural hallucination vs. injected counterfactual/noise).
notes: Both are 'evaluation_benchmark' but operate at different levels (corpus of detection labels vs. ability testbeds); leaderboard substitution is not meaningful.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios and injected counterfactuals); benign retrieval error / naturally occurring conflict (Sufficient Context: real QA datasets stratified by an LLM autorater for sufficiency)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); generator prompting (Sufficient Context's selective generation only)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context: %correct/%abstain/%hallucinate, selective-generation lift); answer correctness, plus a 'rejection rate' style metric (RGB: negative-rejection accuracy, noise-robustness accuracy, integration, counterfactual identification)
action_policy: abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate an abstain behavior, but operationalized differently: RGB's 'negative rejection' on all-noise testbeds vs. Sufficient Context's selective generation gated by sufficiency + self-confidence)
rationale: Both papers diagnose RAG failures when retrieval quality is imperfect and both treat abstention as a first-class behavior, so they share the failure-type space (noise/sufficiency) and an interest in selective-risk-style outcomes. However, RGB is a fixed benchmark whose stressors are synthetically constructed (specific noise ratios, all-noise testbeds, injected counterfactuals) and only scores models, while Sufficient Context introduces an autorater that re-labels existing QA data by answerability and then proposes a generator-side selective-generation method. The abstention construct itself differs: RGB's 'negative rejection' is rate of refusal on all-noise inputs, whereas Sufficient Context measures hallucination/abstain rates stratified by autorater-judged sufficiency and reports correct-when-answered lift. Because the stressor construction, intervention point (evaluation-only vs. evaluation+method), and the abstain metric definitions are not aligned, the two cannot sit on the same leaderboard, though they are clearly complementary lenses on RAG selective risk—hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: (1) Run Sufficient Context's autorater over RGB's four testbeds (especially negative-rejection and noise-robustness sets) to confirm whether RGB's 'all-noise' inputs are indeed 'insufficient context' and whether RGB's noisy-mixed inputs span both sufficient and insufficient regimes; (2) report a shared selective-risk metric (e.g., coverage–accuracy or risk–coverage curves, or AUARC) on both setups using the same generator(s), retriever output, and abstention threshold; (3) align the abstain action policy operationally (same refusal string / scoring rubric); (4) ideally evaluate Sufficient Context's selective-generation method on RGB and evaluate RGB-style counterfactual robustness within Sufficient Context's framework so the two can be compared as methods+benchmark on the same axes.
notes: Both papers do report an explicit action policy, so this is not an action-policy under-specification case; the break is in operationalization and stressor construction, not absence.

failure_type: RAGTruth: consistency/conflict + sufficiency + relevance/noise (multi-task hallucination); FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs retrieved). Partial overlap on conflict subtype only.
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error / naturally occurring (LLM-generated hallucinations in standard RAG over real corpora). FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge (no adversarial threat model).
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (benchmark) + post-hoc verifier (detector fine-tuning baselines). FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact mining + self-think before generation).
metric_target: RAGTruth: detection-side metrics (span/case-level hallucination detection precision/recall/F1). FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support / faithfulness on downstream QA.
action_policy: unreported (both default to answer; RAGTruth's detectors flag spans but no abstain/re-retrieve/quarantine policy is evaluated; FaithfulRAG answers after reconciliation without abstention).
rationale: Both papers target unfaithful generation in RAG, but they are fundamentally different artifact types: RAGTruth is a word-level hallucination benchmark whose primary metric is detector performance (span/response-level F1) against naturally occurring LLM hallucinations across QA, data-to-text, and summarization, while FaithfulRAG is a pre-generation intervention (self-fact extraction, alignment, self-think) whose metric is downstream answer correctness/faithfulness on knowledge-conflict QA. The intervention points (evaluation artifact + post-hoc detector vs. generator prompting) and the metric families (detection F1 vs. answer accuracy) do not align, and neither paper evaluates a common action policy such as abstain or re-retrieve. They are complementary—FaithfulRAG could in principle be evaluated on RAGTruth—but cannot be directly ranked on a single leaderboard as alternative methods to the same problem; hence partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG generations through RAGTruth's annotation/detection protocol (or run RAGTruth's detector baselines as a downstream filter/verifier paired with a vanilla generator) on a shared task slice (e.g., QA), with a common retriever, LLM backbone, and conflict construction, and report a shared metric family—either (a) span-level hallucination rate of generated answers, or (b) end-task accuracy/faithfulness with explicit action labels (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict). Without this shared evaluation harness and aligned metric/action policy, leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful.
notes: Asymmetry: RAGTruth is largely a dataset/benchmark contribution; FaithfulRAG is a method. Treating them as comparable systems mis-categorizes the contribution type.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict additionally in Paper B via counterfactual noise
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (imperfect retriever produces distracting passages); Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with three noise types (relevant, irrelevant, counterfactual). Neither models a real attacker: no corpus write access, no query control by adversary, no insertion budget, no explicit attack objective. Paper B's counterfactual noise is adversarial-flavored but benchmark-synthesized, not from a threat model.
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filtering) + generator prompting or training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts). Paper B: generator prompting or training only (adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-aware classification head).
metric_target: answer correctness (both, EM/F1 on ODQA)
action_policy: answer (both); filter appears in Paper A as a pre-generator intervention but neither paper evaluates abstain, expose conflict, or re-retrieve as an action policy
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on overlapping ODQA benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA appear in both) and both train the generator to better tolerate noisy retrieved contexts. However, Paper A confines noise to benign irrelevant/distracting passages and pairs training with an NLI-based filtering module, while Paper B defines a broader three-type taxonomy (relevant, irrelevant, counterfactual) and proposes a pure training-side solution combining adaptive adversarial training with a noise-aware multi-task objective. The counterfactual noise in Paper B drifts into a consistency/conflict failure mode that Paper A does not address, and Paper A's filtering intervention has no counterpart in Paper B. Neither paper explicitly reports an action policy beyond answering, so abstain/escalate behaviors cannot be ranked. Direct leaderboard comparison would therefore conflate different noise mixtures and different intervention surfaces; the works are complementary rather than head-to-head substitutes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods with a shared retriever (e.g., DPR), shared generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), and a single noise protocol: either restrict Paper B's evaluation to irrelevant-only noise matching Paper A, or extend Paper A's evaluation to relevant + irrelevant + counterfactual noise per RAG-Bench. Ablate filtering and training contributions separately, report identical EM/F1 plus an explicit action-policy column (answer vs abstain vs filter-then-answer), and disclose how counterfactual contexts are constructed so the failure type is unambiguous.
notes: Not a security pair in the adversarial-attacker sense; counterfactual noise is synthesized rather than attacker-injected, so threat-model coordinates (write access, insertion budget) are not actually instantiated by either paper.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency, consistency/conflict, and integrity-adjacent counterfactual content
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error from real retriever over ODQA corpora. Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor with controlled noise ratios and synthetic counterfactual documents. Neither pair is attacker-driven, so corpus write access, query control, retriever visibility, generator access, insertion budget, and attack objective are not applicable; the closest analog is Paper B's counterfactual testbed which simulates corrupted evidence without an explicit threat model.
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting/training. Paper B: evaluation artifact only (no proposed intervention).
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness. Paper B: answer correctness plus rejection rate and an error-detection/correction rate for counterfactual content.
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (NLI-gated). Paper B: answer + abstain (negative rejection is explicitly scored). Action policies are reported on different axes.
rationale: Both papers target robustness of RAG systems to noisy or irrelevant retrieved context, so the failure-type axis overlaps. However, Paper A is a methods paper proposing NLI-based filtering and mixed-context fine-tuning evaluated against natural retriever noise on five ODQA datasets, while Paper B is a benchmark (RGB) that constructs four separate testbeds at controlled noise ratios and explicitly scores abstention (negative rejection) and counterfactual handling alongside correctness. The intervention point (method vs. evaluation artifact), evidence assumption (organic retrieval error vs. synthesized controlled noise/counterfactuals), action policy (filter+answer vs. answer+abstain), and metric set differ enough that placing them on the same leaderboard would conflate a proposed mitigation against an evaluation suite. The relationship is complementary rather than substitutive, which warrants partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and robust-fine-tuned models on RGB's noise-robustness and negative-rejection testbeds (and ideally counterfactual robustness), using the same retriever, generator backbone, prompt template, and noise-ratio sweep; report both answer correctness and abstention/rejection rate with an explicit action-policy label (when filtered, does the system answer without context, abstain, or escalate?). Conversely, evaluate RGB-style baselines on Paper A's five ODQA benchmarks under the same retrieval pipeline. Only then can the two be ranked as alternative approaches to a shared noise-robustness problem.
notes: Not a security pair in the adversarial sense; Paper B's counterfactual testbed is the only integrity-adjacent component but lacks an attacker capability model, so threat-model coordinates do not gate the verdict.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RAAT: DPR-retrieved passages over NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ filtered for golden contexts, then perturbed into relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual; RGB: news-derived passages with search-engine retrievals and ChatGPT-assisted generation, manually adjusted, with controlled noise ratios in EN+ZH)
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT), evaluation artifact (RGB)
metric_target: answer correctness (both, F1/EM vs. accuracy), selective risk/coverage (RGB rejection rate), evidence support (RGB error detection/correction rate)
action_policy: answer (RAAT only), abstain + expose conflict (RGB negative rejection and counterfactual robustness)
breaking_coordinates: intervention point, metric target, action policy, evidence assumption
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness in RAG and both consider relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual-style retrieval noise, but they operate at fundamentally different levels of the stack. RAAT proposes a training-side intervention (adaptive adversarial training plus a noise-awareness auxiliary task on LLaMA-2 7B) and reports F1/EM under an answer-only action policy on its own RAG-Bench. RGB is a pure evaluation artifact that diagnoses four distinct abilities of off-the-shelf LLMs - noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness - and explicitly scores abstention and conflict exposure with rejection/error-correction rates over news-derived bilingual passages. Because the intervention point, action policy, evaluation metric family, and noise-construction pipeline all differ, they cannot share a leaderboard slot as substitutable methods, but they are clearly complementary (RAAT is a candidate method; RGB is a candidate benchmark).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run RAAT-trained and baseline models on all four RGB testbeds with matched noise ratios and report not only EM/F1 but also negative-rejection rate and counterfactual error-detection/correction rate; alternatively, harmonize RAG-Bench and RGB to a common (retriever, generator, document pool, noise ratio, metric family) tuple and require explicit action labels (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict) so both works contribute to the same scoreboard.
notes: Method-vs-benchmark mismatch is the dominant break; even if one ignores that, RGB's negative-rejection and counterfactual-robustness sub-abilities have no analogue in RAAT's evaluation.

failure_type: relevance/noise; CoN additionally addresses uncertainty/OOD (unknown questions)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (irrelevant/distracting passages from a standard ODQA retriever); not adversarial. No corpus write access, no attacker, no insertion budget; threat model is naturally noisy retrieval, so security coordinates are not applicable.
intervention_point: CoN: generator prompting/training (note-taking reasoning). Yoran: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator training (fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts).
metric_target: answer correctness (both); CoN additionally reports rejection rate / selective risk on unknown questions
action_policy: CoN: answer or abstain ('unknown'). Yoran: filter (drop non-entailing passages) then answer; no explicit abstention evaluated.
rationale: Both papers target the same failure mode—RALMs being distracted by irrelevant retrieved passages in open-domain QA under benign (non-adversarial) retrieval errors—and both report answer-correctness on overlapping benchmarks (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA). However, the intervention points differ: Yoran et al. act at context assembly (NLI-based passage filtering) plus generator fine-tuning on mixed-quality contexts, whereas Chain-of-Note acts purely at generator reasoning via per-document notes. The action policies are also materially different—CoN explicitly evaluates an 'unknown' abstention behavior and reports rejection rate on RealTimeQA, while Yoran's methods either drop a passage or answer, with no abstention metric. Because of these intervention and action-policy differences, plus an extra OOD/unknown metric that only one paper reports, the two cannot be ranked directly on a single leaderboard; they are best discussed as complementary distraction-robustness mechanisms (filter-then-answer vs. read-judge-answer-or-abstain).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on the same retriever and same base generator (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B with DPR top-k), over a shared evaluation suite that includes: (1) standard ODQA accuracy with retrieval, (2) a controlled distraction split with known irrelevant passages, (3) an unknown/OOD split with rejection-rate / selective-risk metrics, and (4) a common abstention contract (both systems must either be allowed to abstain or both forced to answer). Report accuracy, rejection rate, and coverage/risk curves under identical action-policy rules, plus an ablation that applies NLI filtering upstream of CoN to separate filtering effects from note-taking effects.
notes: Security-specific coordinates (write access, insertion budget, attacker objective) are not relevant: both papers assume benign retrieval noise rather than corpus poisoning.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error, naturally occurring conflict
intervention_point: generator prompting or training, verifier, system-control policy, retriever
metric_target: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: abstain (Sufficient Context, explicit selective generation); re-retrieve, filter (Self-RAG via reflection tokens); not aligned
rationale: Both papers target RAG quality issues from naturally noisy/insufficient retrieval and both add an introspective signal to control generation behavior. However, Sufficient Context intervenes post-hoc with an external autorater plus self-confidence to gate abstention, evaluated via selective-generation coverage/correctness curves, while Self-RAG fine-tunes the LM end-to-end with reflection tokens that mainly control on-demand retrieval and per-segment critique, evaluated via factuality and citation accuracy on long-form generation. Their action policies (explicit abstain vs adaptive retrieve + filter via reflection) and primary metric families (selective risk vs citation/factuality) do not align, and the intervention loci differ (inference-time verifier+policy vs trained generator with adaptive retriever). They should be discussed as complementary mechanisms—context-sufficiency-driven abstention vs self-reflective adaptive retrieval—rather than ranked head-to-head, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both methods on the same QA benchmarks with shared retriever and base LM; report a common selective-prediction protocol (e.g., accuracy at matched coverage with an explicit abstain option) so Self-RAG's no-retrieve/irrelevant signals are mapped to an abstain action; additionally report citation/support metrics for Sufficient Context to align with Self-RAG's evaluation; and fix the same noisy/insufficient context construction so both systems face identical evidence stressors.
notes: Sufficient Context's selective generation explicitly evaluates abstention; Self-RAG's reflection tokens are not framed as abstention but as retrieval/critique signals, so action policies are reported but not the same.

failure_type: uncertainty/OOD, relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: reranker, generator prompting or training, retriever
metric_target: calibration error, answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: answer (CalibRAG, confidence-augmented), re-retrieve/filter/verify (Self-RAG via reflection tokens)
rationale: Both papers aim to make RAG more reliable in a benign (non-adversarial) retrieval setting, but they target different failures and operate at different control points. CalibRAG addresses miscalibration in human-facing decision-making by training a forecasting function f(t,q,d) that reranks documents and produces calibrated confidence; its primary metric is calibration error (with answer accuracy as a secondary outcome) and its action is essentially 'answer with a confidence signal.' Self-RAG instead targets indiscriminate retrieval and unsupported generation by training reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval, passage filtering, and self-critique, with metrics centered on factuality, citation accuracy, and evidence support. Because the failure type, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all differ, ranking them on a single leaderboard would conflate calibration quality with factuality/adaptive-retrieval behavior; they are better framed as complementary control mechanisms, hence partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate both systems on a shared benchmark with (a) the same retriever and generator backbone, (b) joint metrics covering calibration (ECE/Brier), factuality/citation faithfulness, and downstream decision accuracy, (c) explicit action-policy labels (answer vs. abstain vs. re-retrieve) reported per instance, and (d) matched evidence-noise construction so that both 'when to retrieve' and 'how confident' can be compared apples-to-apples.
notes: Not a security pair; threat-model coordinates (corpus write access, attack budget, etc.) are not applicable to either work.

failure_type: consistency/conflict (FaithfulRAG) vs integrity/adversarial corruption (PoisonedRAG)
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric knowledge and benign retrieved context (no adversary). PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target question (query control via target selection), both black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, insertion budget = 5 malicious texts per target question, targeted attack objective (induce attacker-chosen answer).
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting + context assembly (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think). PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive injection, not a defense intervention).
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / evidence support (faithfulness). PoisonedRAG: attack success rate.
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (after reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action evaluated).
rationale: Both papers concern RAG behavior when retrieved context conflicts with expected answers, but the threat models are categorically different. FaithfulRAG addresses naturally occurring parametric-vs-context conflict from benign sources and intervenes at the generator with a self-think reconciliation module evaluated on answer correctness; it assumes no adversary and provides no defender action against crafted poison. PoisonedRAG defines an adversary with corpus write access, query control over target questions, and a ~5-text insertion budget, attacking the corpus-to-generation pathway and measured by ASR in black/white-box settings. The failure type, evidence assumption, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge, so a leaderboard ranking between an attack and a conflict-reconciliation defense would be category-incoherent and misleading.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG as a defense within the PoisonedRAG threat model (same retriever, generator, corpus, target questions, 5-text injection budget, black/white-box variants) and report ASR reduction alongside clean-task accuracy; conversely, evaluate a PoisonedRAG-related defense on FaithfulRAG's natural-conflict benchmarks. Align action policy (answer vs abstain/filter/quarantine under suspected poison) and use a shared metric family (accuracy under benign conflict AND ASR under adversarial conflict) so both methods sit on the same axis.
notes: Asymmetric attack-vs-defense pair with mismatched problem; could become a partial comparison only if FaithfulRAG were retargeted and stress-tested against poisoning.

failure_type: Paper A: consistency/conflict + relevance/noise; Paper B: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error + naturally occurring conflict + benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB worst-case); Paper B: attacker-created evidence. Threat model for B: corpus write access = yes (inject ~5 texts per target question), query control = yes (attacker-chosen target Q/A), retriever visibility = black-box and white-box, generator access = black-box, insertion budget = 5 malicious passages, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer. Paper A does not adopt or evaluate any of these attacker-capability assumptions.
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting + context assembly/compression (training-free source-aware consolidation); Paper B: corpus/index (poisoning the knowledge database)
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness (incl. worst-case accuracy under noisy retrieval); Paper B: attack success rate
action_policy: Paper A: answer (via consolidation/reliability selection), no abstain reported; Paper B: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy)
rationale: These papers are different artifact types competing on opposite sides of the security axis: Astute RAG is a training-free defense at the generator that consolidates internal and external knowledge to handle noisy/conflicting retrieval, evaluated on answer correctness (including RGB worst-case); PoisonedRAG is a corpus-poisoning attack that injects ~5 optimized malicious passages per target question to induce a chosen answer, evaluated on ASR. The threat models differ qualitatively (naturally noisy/conflicting evidence and benchmark-constructed stressors vs. an active attacker with corpus write access and query control), the intervention points are on opposite ends of the pipeline (generator vs. corpus), and the optimization targets are inverted (maximize accuracy vs. maximize ASR). A leaderboard-style ranking is therefore meaningless; the only sensible relationship is a future combined evaluation where Astute RAG is tested as a defense under PoisonedRAG attacks.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make these comparable, one would need a shared evaluation in which both works are instantiated as defense methods (or both as attacks) against a fixed threat model: same retriever, generator, corpus, target questions, attacker insertion budget, and visibility assumptions, then report ASR and clean accuracy plus an explicit action policy (answer/abstain) for each defender. Specifically, Astute RAG would need to be benchmarked against PoisonedRAG-style optimized injections (not only RGB noise), and PoisonedRAG would need a defender baseline (e.g., paraphrasing, perplexity filter) so that both are placed on the same attack-vs-defense matrix rather than ranked as substitutes.
notes: Attack-paper vs defense-paper pairs are categorically non-substitutable; the natural framing is complementary (combine for an attack/defense matrix), not leaderboard ranking.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; corpus write access = yes (both assume injection into knowledge base); query control = attacker chooses target question (PoisonedRAG explicit; RobustRAG threat model assumes adaptive attacker targeting queries); retriever visibility = black-box and white-box (PoisonedRAG); RobustRAG assumes adaptive attacker with full knowledge of defense; generator access = none/limited (PoisonedRAG); RobustRAG defends generator; insertion budget = small bounded number (PoisonedRAG ~5 texts/question; RobustRAG certifies up to k' bounded malicious passages); attack objective = targeted answer manipulation (PoisonedRAG); RobustRAG defends against arbitrary corruption including targeted attacks
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG, attacker side); context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG, defender side)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG); answer correctness with certified lower bound (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported for PoisonedRAG (attack paper, no defensive action); abstain ("I don't know"), filter, and answer via aggregation (RobustRAG)
breaking_coordinates: role (attack vs defense), intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy
rationale: Both papers operate in the same adversarial-corruption threat space (attacker injects bounded malicious passages into the RAG corpus to manipulate generation) and share the same failure type and evidence assumption. However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution measuring attack success rate against undefended RAG, while RobustRAG is a defensive contribution measuring certified response quality under corruption via an isolate-then-aggregate action policy. They occupy complementary roles in the same threat model rather than alternative solutions to one problem, so leaderboard-style ranking is incoherent (you cannot rank an attack against a defense), but they are clearly relatable as attack-defense pairs in a co-evaluation. Therefore the comparison is partial: useful as adversary/defense interaction but not as substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make direct comparison valid, both works would need to be reframed onto a shared evaluation axis: e.g., evaluate RobustRAG explicitly under PoisonedRAG attacks (same target questions, same insertion budget k', same retriever and generator) and report a common metric family such as attack success rate AND certified/empirical answer correctness, plus an explicit abstention/answer action policy. Even then, the appropriate framing is an attack-defense interaction matrix (rows = attacks including PoisonedRAG, columns = defenses including RobustRAG), not a single leaderboard ranking.
notes: Attack-vs-defense pairs are structurally partial by construction; the security threat models overlap substantially (corpus write access, bounded injection budget, targeted-answer objective), which is why this is partial rather than invalid or under-specified.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict (real LLM outputs in standard RAG); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactuals)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); but RAGTruth targets a downstream detector/verifier, RGB targets generator prompting behavior
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness via span-level hallucination detection; RGB: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (negative rejection rate), accuracy under counterfactuals
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (no generator action policy is evaluated; the dataset scores post-hoc detectors); RGB: explicitly evaluates answer vs. abstain (negative rejection) and partially expose conflict (counterfactual robustness)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation benchmarks concerned with faithfulness/robustness of LLM-RAG pipelines, and they share an interest in conflicts between generation and retrieved evidence. However, RAGTruth provides word-level hallucination annotations over naturally generated outputs (QA, summarization, data-to-text) and benchmarks span-level hallucination detectors, while RGB constructs four synthetic testbeds (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and scores end-to-end answer correctness plus an explicit abstention behavior. The metric targets (detector span-F1 vs. answer accuracy and rejection rate), evidence construction (natural vs. controlled stressor), and action policies (RGB scores abstain; RAGTruth does not score any generator action) all differ. They are complementary diagnostics of the same broad robustness/faithfulness concern, not substitutable entries on one leaderboard, so the verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To enable a valid head-to-head, one would need (a) a shared evaluation axis (e.g., both benchmarks scoring the same target such as answer-level faithfulness or detector span-F1 on a common task), (b) matched evidence construction so naturally occurring and synthetic stressors are aligned or separated, (c) a common action-policy definition (e.g., answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict) evaluated on both corpora, and (d) the same generator/retriever stack run across both, with results mapped to the same metric family. Without that, the two benchmarks should be reported as complementary modules rather than ranked against each other.
notes: Both are categorized as evaluation_benchmark, but they measure different objects (detector capability vs. system ability), which is the main reason direct ranking would mislead.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: deliberately noisy/counterfactual passages assembled into 4 testbeds) vs. benign retrieval error (Sufficient Context: analyzes naturally occurring (Q,C) sufficiency on standard QA datasets like NQ, HotPotQA, Musique)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); verifier + generator prompting (Sufficient Context only, via autorater + selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage, calibration error (Sufficient Context); answer correctness across 4 separate ability testbeds (RGB)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both papers explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via 'negative rejection' testbed; Sufficient Context via stratified hallucination/abstention rates and selective generation)
rationale: Both papers examine RAG behavior when retrieved context fails to support the query and both explicitly evaluate abstention as an action, so the failure type and action policy genuinely overlap. However, RGB is a pure evaluation benchmark using constructed stressors with discrete testbeds (noise ratio, all-noise, counterfactual, multi-doc integration), whereas Sufficient Context introduces an analytical lens (LLM autorater for sufficiency) plus an intervention (selective generation combining sufficiency with self-confidence) evaluated on natural QA datasets. RGB reports per-ability accuracy/rejection rates; Sufficient Context reports hallucination/abstention/correctness stratified by sufficiency and selective-risk curves. These differences in intervention point, evidence construction, and metric framing mean the two cannot be ranked head-to-head on the same leaderboard, but they are clearly complementary lenses on the same broad problem.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To enable direct comparison, one would need: (1) running Sufficient Context's autorater + selective generation on RGB's four testbeds and reporting RGB's accuracy/rejection metrics, OR (2) running RGB-style constructed noise/counterfactual stressors through Sufficient Context's sufficiency-stratified analysis with matched models, retrievers, and a shared abstention metric (e.g., selective accuracy at fixed coverage). Both papers would also need to agree on whether the unit of comparison is benchmark difficulty (RGB framing) or intervention efficacy (Sufficient Context framing).
notes: Treating these as 'alternative methods' would conflate a diagnostic benchmark with an analysis-plus-method paper; partial is correct because the shared abstention focus is real but the intervention/metric scopes are mismatched.

failure_type: RAGTruth: broad hallucination (relevance/noise, sufficiency, consistency/conflict); FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs. retrieved)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring conflict / benign retrieval error (responses from standard RAG pipelines); FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict but tested on conflict-stressed benchmarks. Not a security pair, so no attacker capability dimensions apply.
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (and verifier when fine-tuning detectors); FaithfulRAG: context assembly/compression + generator prompting (self-fact mining, alignment, self-think)
metric_target: RAGTruth: citation faithfulness / evidence support (span-level hallucination detection F1); FaithfulRAG: answer correctness under conflict
action_policy: unreported (both); RAGTruth as a corpus does not evaluate action policies; FaithfulRAG implicitly always answers after reconciliation without abstain/expose-conflict labels
rationale: Both papers address faithfulness failures in RAG generation, but they operate at fundamentally different levels: RAGTruth is an evaluation artifact (an 18K-response, word-level hallucination corpus and detector benchmark spanning QA, data-to-text, and summarization), while FaithfulRAG is a generation-time mitigation method targeting parametric/contextual knowledge conflicts via self-fact mining and self-think. Their intervention points (benchmark/detector vs. context+generator pipeline) and metric targets (span-level hallucination detection vs. answer correctness on conflict QA) do not overlap, and neither evaluates an explicit action policy such as abstain or expose-conflict. They are naturally complementary—RAGTruth could in principle be used to score FaithfulRAG's outputs—but they cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard as alternative robust-RAG methods. Hence the comparison is partial, not valid.
