what_valid_comparison_requires: To enable direct comparison, both works would need to be evaluated on the same task (e.g., conflict QA), with the same retriever, generator family, and a shared metric—either (a) score FaithfulRAG's generations using RAGTruth-style span-level hallucination annotation on a common test set, or (b) report both an end-to-end answer-correctness metric and a faithfulness/hallucination detection metric, plus explicit action-policy labels (answer/abstain/expose-conflict) so that mitigation and detection capabilities are measured under matched conditions.
notes: Category mismatch (benchmark/dataset vs. method) is the dominant source of incomparability; this is closer to 'invalid' than 'valid', but 'partial' fits because the two are genuinely complementary within the same faithfulness problem area.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers consistency/conflict via counterfactual passages
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (natural irrelevance from imperfect retrievers); Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (three-way noise typology curated in RAG-Bench, including counterfactual)
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (mixed-context fine-tuning); Paper B: generator prompting or training (adaptive adversarial training + auxiliary noise-aware multi-task head)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1 in both)
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (NLI explicitly decides whether to drop passages and fall back to no-context answering); Paper B: answer (multi-task noise classification is internal-only; no filter/abstain action reported)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA and share answer correctness as the metric, with clear overlap on the irrelevant-context failure mode. However, Paper A treats noise as benign retrieval error and pairs an explicit NLI-based filter action with mixed-context fine-tuning, while Paper B constructs a three-way noise typology (relevant, irrelevant, counterfactual) as a benchmark stressor and intervenes purely via adaptive adversarial training plus an internal noise-classification head, with no filter or abstain action exposed. These differences in failure-type scope (irrelevance only vs. irrelevance+conflict), evidence assumption (natural vs. curated), intervention point (filter+training vs. training-only), and action policy (filter+answer vs. answer-only) mean leaderboard-style ranking would conflate mechanisms operating on different stressor distributions. They should therefore be framed as complementary noise-robustness modules rather than direct alternatives.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-evaluate both methods on a single shared protocol: same retriever and corpus, identical noise-injection pipeline covering both naturally occurring irrelevance and the counterfactual category, the same base LM and fine-tuning data budget, evaluation on a common dataset set (e.g., NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ), and a harmonized action policy (either both filter-then-answer, or both answer-only with the filter ablated) so that EM/F1 differences are attributable to the intervention rather than to differing stressor distributions or action semantics.
notes: Paper B's noise-awareness classifier is auxiliary supervision, not an exposed abstain/filter action; Paper A's NLI filter is the only explicit action-policy step, which alone breaks symmetry for ranking.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (only B via counterfactual robustness testbed)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (A: real retriever output from 5 ODQA benchmarks); benchmark-constructed stressor (B: controlled noise ratios and synthetically inserted counterfactual docs)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression and generator prompting or training (A: NLI filter + fine-tuning); evaluation artifact (B: RGB benchmark, no proposed mitigation)
metric_target: answer correctness (both); selective risk/coverage (B only, via negative rejection rate)
action_policy: filter then answer (A, explicitly via NLI gating); answer and abstain explicitly evaluated (B, via negative rejection ability)
rationale: Both papers concern LLM behavior under noisy retrieved context, so the failure type overlaps on relevance/noise. However, Paper A is a method paper that proposes interventions (NLI-based passage filtering and robustness fine-tuning) and measures QA accuracy improvement, while Paper B is a benchmark paper contributing the RGB evaluation artifact across four distinct abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) without proposing any mitigation. The intervention points therefore live at different layers of the stack, the evidence assumptions differ (real retriever noise vs controlled noise-ratio and counterfactual injection), and Paper B explicitly scores abstention/negative rejection while Paper A's action policy is filter-then-answer without an abstention metric. They are complementary—Paper A's methods could be scored on Paper B's RGB—but they cannot be ranked as alternative methods on the same leaderboard, so the comparison is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and fine-tuned RALM on Paper B's RGB testbeds (matched LLM backbones, identical noise-ratio buckets, and the same counterfactual subset), and report both answer accuracy and an explicit abstention/negative-rejection rate. Conversely, Paper B's evaluated LLMs would need to be tested on Paper A's five ODQA distributions with retrieved (not constructed) noise. Only with shared retriever/corpus, matched action policy (answer vs abstain), and a common metric family (accuracy + selective risk) does direct ranking become meaningful.
notes: Method-paper vs benchmark-paper mismatch is the dominant structural break; even when failure types align, leaderboard ranking is not the intended use of either contribution.

failure_type: relevance/noise, consistency/conflict (counterfactual); RGB additionally probes sufficiency via negative rejection
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); RGB also mixes naturally occurring conflict via real search-engine documents over news; RAAT uses DPR over Wikipedia with constructed counterfactual perturbations
intervention_point: RAAT: generator prompting or training + evaluation artifact (RAG-Bench); RGB: evaluation artifact only
metric_target: RAAT: answer correctness (F1/EM); RGB: answer correctness + rejection/identification rates across four ability testbeds
action_policy: RAAT: answer (no abstain evaluated); RGB: answer + abstain (explicit negative rejection testbed)
rationale: Both papers target noise robustness of RAG over open-domain QA and construct noisy/counterfactual contexts, so the failure type substantially overlaps. However, RAAT is a training-time defense (adaptive adversarial fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B) evaluated on its own RAG-Bench built from NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ with DPR over Wikipedia, while RGB is purely an evaluation benchmark over news articles that decomposes RAG into four abilities (noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual robustness) and explicitly scores abstention. The intervention points differ (generator training vs. benchmark-only), the action policies differ (RAAT does not evaluate abstain whereas RGB does), and the metric families and evidence sources do not align (Wikipedia/DPR constructed noise vs. web-news mixed-source contexts). They are therefore complementary—RAAT could in principle be evaluated on RGB—rather than direct leaderboard substitutes, so the verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluate RAAT (and a non-RAAT baseline) on the RGB testbeds using RGB's exact corpus, noise-ratio protocol, and rejection/identification metrics; conversely report RGB-style abstention behavior for RAAT's adversarially trained model on RAG-Bench. Hold retriever, generator family, prompting template, and noise construction constant, and explicitly label the action policy (answer vs. abstain) so both papers report the same metric family on the same instances.
notes: Method paper vs. benchmark paper asymmetry is the main obstacle; once RAAT is run on RGB with rejection-aware metrics, a near-valid comparison becomes possible.

failure_type: relevance/noise; CoN additionally covers uncertainty/OOD (unknown handling)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both); DPR-retrieved noisy/irrelevant passages on ODQA benchmarks
intervention_point: CoN: generator prompting + training (read-judge-answer notes); Yoran et al.: context assembly/filter (NLI entailment filter) + generator training (mixed relevant/irrelevant fine-tuning)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1) on both; CoN additionally reports selective risk/coverage via rejection rate on RealTimeQA
action_policy: CoN: answer or abstain ('unknown') explicitly evaluated; Yoran et al.: answer with filter-triggered fallback to no-context LLM (abstention not explicitly evaluated)
rationale: Both papers target distraction by irrelevant retrieved context in ODQA under benign retrieval error, share answer-correctness metrics on overlapping benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA), and propose generator-side robustness fixes including fine-tuning. However, their intervention points and action policies diverge in load-bearing ways: Chain-of-Note rewrites generator reasoning via per-document notes and explicitly evaluates abstention ('unknown') plus a rejection-rate metric for OOD/unknown questions, while Yoran et al. insert an NLI filter before the generator and fall back to a no-context LLM rather than abstaining, evaluating only answer accuracy (with a multi-hop emphasis). A single leaderboard ranking on EM would conflate a calibration-aware abstention method with a filter-plus-robust-training pipeline that operates only on answer-mode behavior, so the comparison is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever and generator backbone; use identical noisy-context construction (and matched multi-hop vs. single-hop splits); evaluate both systems under the same action-policy contract (either both report answer-only accuracy on relevant/irrelevant splits, or both report joint correctness + abstain/rejection metrics with a shared coverage-risk curve); explicitly document filter/abstain thresholds; and align benchmark composition so OOD/unknown subsets are either both included with rejection-rate scoring or both excluded.
notes: Partial rather than under-specified because both papers do report enough about their actions (CoN abstains; Yoran filters+answers) for the coordinate break to be diagnosable.

failure_type: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: Sufficient Context: verifier (sufficiency autorater) + system-control policy (selective generation at inference); Self-RAG: generator training (reflection tokens) + retriever (on-demand) + verifier (critique tokens)
metric_target: Sufficient Context: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (hallucination rate among answered, abstention rate); Self-RAG: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: Sufficient Context: abstain, answer (selective generation explicitly evaluated); Self-RAG: re-retrieve, answer, filter (adaptive retrieval and passage filtering explicitly evaluated)
rationale: Both papers tackle the broader problem that retrieved evidence may be irrelevant/insufficient and that models should not blindly answer using it, and both explicitly evaluate a non-trivial action policy beyond pure QA. However, Sufficient Context intervenes at inference time via a sufficiency autorater plus self-confidence to drive selective answer/abstain decisions on a frozen generator, while Self-RAG intervenes at training time by teaching a generator to emit reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval, passage filtering, and critique. The action policies differ in kind (abstain vs. re-retrieve+filter+generate-with-critique), and the headline metric families differ (selective-risk/coverage and hallucination-conditional-on-answering vs. citation faithfulness and factuality on long-form). Hence they are complementary mechanisms in different operating regions, not interchangeable entries on a single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Fix retriever, corpus, generator backbone (or evaluate both methods on the same fixed-backbone variant), use a common set of QA + long-form benchmarks, and jointly report (a) selective-risk/coverage curves with explicit abstain option, (b) citation/evidence-support faithfulness, and (c) end-to-end correctness under a unified action-policy taxonomy that lets both abstain and re-retrieve be exercised. Without aligning intervention surface (train-time vs inference-time) and the action-policy space, any single-number ranking is misleading.
notes: Both papers do report explicit action policies, which keeps this above under-specified; the break is coordinate mismatch, not missing information.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD; Self-RAG: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (both); no adversarial threat model in either
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker (forecasting function over (t,q,d)) + generator confidence; Self-RAG: generator prompting/training (reflection tokens) + retriever (on-demand)
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error + answer correctness (decision accuracy); Self-RAG: answer correctness + citation faithfulness + evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence (no explicit abstain evaluated); Self-RAG: answer with embedded critique/re-retrieve signals via reflection tokens — both partially specified, neither evaluates a shared explicit action policy
rationale: Both papers address reliability concerns in RAG and modify behavior beyond a vanilla retrieve-then-generate pipeline, but they target distinct failure modes. CalibRAG addresses uncertainty/calibration so that confidence aligns with decision correctness, intervening at the reranker via a learned forecasting function and reporting ECE-style calibration alongside accuracy. Self-RAG addresses retrieval necessity and grounding/citation quality, intervening at generator training via reflection tokens and reporting factuality and citation accuracy. The metric families (calibration vs. citation faithfulness) and the action signals (calibrated confidence vs. on-demand retrieve/critique tokens) are not interchangeable, so leaderboard-style ranking would conflate orthogonal objectives. They are best framed as complementary modules rather than substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both systems on a common benchmark suite that reports a shared metric family (e.g., calibration metrics like ECE/Brier AND citation/faithfulness metrics) using the same retriever, generator backbone, and decision-task formulation. Additionally, evaluate an explicit, shared action policy (e.g., answer vs. abstain thresholded on each method's confidence/reflection signal) so that the same intervention surface is being measured. Without harmonized metrics and an evaluated action policy, the comparison remains partial.
notes: Neither paper is adversarial; the gap is methodological scope (calibration vs. self-reflective adaptive retrieval), not safety/threat-model mismatch.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict / benchmark-constructed stressor, no attacker assumed; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, known target question, black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, ~5 malicious texts per target question, objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attacker-side injection)
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / faithfulness; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (with reconciliation), no abstain/verify reported; PoisonedRAG: unreported (no defense action, this is an attack paper)
rationale: Both papers superficially touch situations where retrieved content disagrees with an expected answer, but they sit on opposite sides of the RAG security/robustness landscape. FaithfulRAG is a defender-side generator method that reconciles naturally occurring conflicts between an LLM's parametric knowledge and a benign retrieved context, reported via faithfulness/answer-correctness metrics with no attacker in the loop. PoisonedRAG is an offense paper that crafts ~5 adversarial passages per target question, injects them into the corpus, and measures attack success rate under explicit black-box/white-box threat models. Failure type, evidence assumption, intervention point, metric target, and action policy all diverge, and neither paper evaluates the other's setting. Placing them on the same leaderboard would conflate an attack with a defense for a different threat and would mislead readers.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Re-run FaithfulRAG (and matched baselines) under PoisonedRAG's threat model: same target questions, same retriever and generator, same insertion budget (e.g., 5 malicious passages), and report attack success rate plus clean answer correctness side-by-side. Alternatively, build a unified benchmark covering both natural parametric-vs-context conflicts and adversarial corpus poisoning, with explicit action-policy labels (answer/abstain/verify/quarantine) and a shared metric family so defenses and attacks can be co-evaluated.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense mismatch where the 'defense' targets a different failure mode than the attack; not rescuable to valid without new experiments.

failure_type: Astute RAG: relevance/noise and consistency/conflict; PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: Astute RAG: benign retrieval error plus benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB worst-case) and naturally occurring parametric-vs-retrieved conflict; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, attacker-chosen target question, both black-box and white-box retriever visibility, black-box generator, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective is to induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: Astute RAG: generator prompting (training-free iterative source-aware consolidation); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (malicious text injection)
metric_target: Astute RAG: answer correctness under imperfect/worst-case retrieval; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: Astute RAG: answer via reliability comparison between internal and external candidates; PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy evaluated)
rationale: Both papers concern robustness of RAG to problematic retrieved content, but they occupy opposite roles: PoisonedRAG is an attack that injects malicious passages into the corpus and reports attack success rate, while Astute RAG is a generator-side defense that consolidates internal and external knowledge and reports answer correctness, with adversarial content only loosely motivated rather than instantiated under PoisonedRAG's threat model. The intervention points (corpus vs generator), metric targets (ASR vs correctness), and evidence assumptions (attacker-crafted vs benchmark noise/conflict) differ, and Astute RAG does not evaluate against PoisonedRAG-style attacks while PoisonedRAG does not evaluate Astute RAG as a defense. They are complementary attack/defense artifacts rather than substitutable methods on a shared leaderboard, so the verdict is partial rather than valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Astute RAG (and baselines) as a defender against PoisonedRAG attacks on the same datasets (NQ/HotpotQA/MS-MARCO), with matched retriever, generator, corpus, target questions, and insertion budgets; report both ASR and answer correctness, and explicitly define the defender action policy (answer/abstain/quarantine). Symmetrically, PoisonedRAG should report attack success against Astute RAG to enable a shared attack-vs-defense leaderboard.
notes: Classic attack-paper vs defense-paper asymmetry; partial is appropriate because the failure-type families overlap conceptually but no shared evaluation axis exists.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence; PoisonedRAG assumes corpus write access with insertion budget of ~5 malicious texts per target question, query control over target Q/A pair, both black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer. RobustRAG assumes an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of the defense who can arbitrarily inject a bounded number of malicious passages into the retrieved set; threat model is structurally symmetric but the paper occupies the defender role.
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG, attacker side) vs context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG, isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success rate (PoisonedRAG) vs answer correctness with certified lower bound under bounded corruption (RobustRAG)
action_policy: unreported / not applicable for PoisonedRAG (attack has no defender action); RobustRAG explicitly evaluates answer + abstain ('I don't know') via secure keyword/decoding aggregation
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, action_policy, role (attack vs defense)
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat-model area—integrity attacks on RAG via injection of attacker-created passages into the retrieval pipeline—and even share compatible attacker-capability assumptions (corpus write access with a bounded insertion budget). However, PoisonedRAG is an offensive contribution whose metric target is attack success rate against an undefended RAG, while RobustRAG is a defensive contribution whose metric target is certified/empirical robust accuracy under bounded corruption with an explicit abstain action. The two artifacts intervene at opposite ends of the pipeline (corpus injection vs context aggregation/generator prompting), optimize antagonistic objectives, and cannot be placed on the same leaderboard as substitutable methods; doing so would be category-confused (ranking an attack against a defense). They are best framed as complementary—RobustRAG should be evaluated against PoisonedRAG-style attackers—rather than compared head-to-head.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct comparison is not recoverable because the papers play different roles. The appropriate comparability frame is a shared evaluation harness: fix the retriever, generator, corpus, query set, and insertion budget; instantiate PoisonedRAG (and other attacks) as the adversary; report RobustRAG's certified and empirical robust accuracy plus abstention rate against that adversary, alongside undefended baselines. Direct ranking on a single scalar only becomes meaningful within attack-only or defense-only leaderboards (e.g., PoisonedRAG vs other corpus-poisoning attacks on ASR, or RobustRAG vs other defenses on robust accuracy under a common attacker).
notes: Attack-vs-defense asymmetry is a structural break that no amount of extra reporting on either side can convert into a valid same-axis comparison.

failure_type: RAGTruth: consistency/conflict + sufficiency (word-level hallucination including unsupported and contradictory spans); RGB: relevance/noise + sufficiency + consistency/conflict (four separate abilities including counterfactual)
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring LLM-generated hallucinations on retrieved passages (benign retrieval setting, errors arise from generator); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents, fully-negative document sets)
intervention_point: Both: evaluation artifact (benchmark/corpus). RAGTruth additionally evaluates verifier/detector models fine-tuned on the corpus; RGB evaluates generator prompting behavior across testbeds.
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness measured as span-level hallucination detection (precision/recall on annotated spans); RGB: answer correctness, rejection rate, integration accuracy, counterfactual identification rate (case-level)
action_policy: RAGTruth: verify (post-hoc hallucination detection on generated answers); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection testbed explicitly evaluates whether model refuses) + expose conflict (counterfactual testbed)
breaking_coordinates: evidence_assumption, metric_target, action_policy, granularity (span vs case)
rationale: Both are RAG evaluation benchmarks broadly concerned with faithfulness/hallucination under retrieval, but the substrates and what is being scored are fundamentally different. RAGTruth scores word-level hallucination detectors on naturally produced LLM outputs (verify action, span-level faithfulness metric), while RGB scores generators on constructed stressor testbeds for four distinct abilities with case-level correctness/rejection metrics and explicit answer/abstain action policy. Because the evidence assumption (natural vs constructed), metric granularity (span vs case), and action policy (verify vs answer/abstain/expose-conflict) all diverge, the same system cannot be placed on a single leaderboard derived from both. They are best treated as complementary diagnostics of the RAG pipeline (detector quality vs generator behavior under stressors), supporting a partial rather than valid comparison.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, both benchmarks would need to (a) align on a common unit of evaluation (e.g., per-response faithfulness label or span-level annotations on the same generator outputs), (b) share an evidence-construction protocol (either both natural or both stressor-constructed with matched noise/counterfactual ratios), (c) report the same action-policy axis (e.g., both score abstention and answer faithfulness separately), and (d) use a shared generator + retriever stack so the measured failure is comparably attributable. Absent these, results can only be discussed as complementary.
notes: Both are benchmarks, so 'intervention point' largely coincides at evaluation artifact; the real breaks are in evidence assumption, metric granularity, and action policy.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: synthetic noise ratios over news plus counterfactual injections); benign retrieval error and naturally occurring (Sufficient Context: applies sufficiency autorater to standard QA datasets with retrieved contexts)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); generator prompting or training and verifier (Sufficient Context only, via selective generation plus autorater)
metric_target: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context), abstention/rejection rate (both)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both explicitly evaluate abstention: RGB via negative rejection ability; Sufficient Context via selective generation)
rationale: Both papers examine LLM behavior when retrieved context is imperfect, and both explicitly evaluate abstention vs. answering (RGB negative rejection; Sufficient Context selective generation), so the action policy is shared. However, RGB is a four-testbed bilingual benchmark using synthetically constructed stressors (controlled noise ratios, missing answers, integration across docs, counterfactual injections) built from news, while Sufficient Context introduces a (Q,C)-level property and autorater applied to existing QA datasets, plus a selective generation method combining sufficiency with self-confidence. The intervention scope differs (pure benchmark vs. analytical lens plus method plus verifier), evidence construction differs (synthetic stressors vs. naturally retrieved contexts), and metric stratification differs (four discrete abilities vs. sufficiency-conditioned correctness/hallucination/abstention). They are complementary diagnostic lenses rather than substitutable methods on a common leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's autorater and selective-generation method on RGB's four testbeds (or evaluate RGB's six LLMs on Sufficient Context's sufficiency-stratified datasets) using the same retriever, same context construction, and a unified metric set (correctness, hallucination rate, abstention rate, selective risk vs. coverage). Reporting both papers' abstention thresholds and the same answer/abstain policy under identical insufficient-context and conflict conditions would make leaderboard-style comparison meaningful.
notes: RGB is primarily a benchmark; Sufficient Context is a mixed analysis-plus-method contribution, which is the core reason direct ranking is partial rather than valid.

failure_type: RAGTruth: broad hallucination (sufficiency, consistency/conflict, evidence support); FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs retrieved). Partial overlap only.
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally occurring hallucinations from real LLM RAG outputs across QA/summarization/data-to-text. FaithfulRAG: benchmark-constructed knowledge-conflict pairs targeting parametric-vs-context disagreement. Different evidence regimes.
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (plus optional detector fine-tuning). FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training and context assembly (self-fact extraction, alignment, self-think).
metric_target: RAGTruth: hallucination detection accuracy and span-level F1 (and frequency benchmarking). FaithfulRAG: answer correctness on conflict QA benchmarks. Different metric families.
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (corpus does not prescribe a deployment action; detector outputs are not turned into answer/abstain/escalate). FaithfulRAG: answer (after self-think reconciliation). Action policies non-comparable.
rationale: RAGTruth is fundamentally an evaluation artifact, an ~18K-response hallucination corpus with word-level annotations across QA, summarization, and data-to-text, designed to benchmark and train hallucination detectors. FaithfulRAG is an intervention method that resolves parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflicts via self-fact mining, alignment to retrieved chunks, and a self-think module before generation. The two contributions live in different categories: a benchmark/measurement tool versus a generator-side mitigation method, with non-overlapping intervention points and metric targets (span-level detection F1 vs. conflict-QA answer correctness). They also differ in failure scope (broad RAG hallucination across three task families vs. narrowly scoped parametric-context conflict) and evidence regime (naturally generated hallucinations vs. constructed conflict pairs), so placing them on the same leaderboard would conflate a yardstick with one of the methods that could be measured on it.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make a direct comparison valid, FaithfulRAG would need to be evaluated as a hallucination-mitigation method on the RAGTruth corpus (or a comparable benchmark) using the same task families, the same generator backbones, the same evidence inputs, and matched metric definitions (e.g., span-level hallucination rate or answer faithfulness). Conversely, RAGTruth-trained detectors would need to be paired with an explicit action policy (answer/abstain/flag) and applied to FaithfulRAG's conflict QA benchmarks under identical retrievers and contexts. Only then could the two be ranked as substitutable approaches to the same operational task.
notes: Benchmark-vs-method asymmetry is the dominant break; even when both are framed as 'faithfulness' work, they are not substitutable on a single leaderboard.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); consistency/conflict (Paper B counterfactual noise)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error (Paper A, naturally retrieved irrelevant passages from real ODQA); benchmark-constructed stressor (Paper B, RAG-Bench mixes retrieved + injected counterfactual noise)
intervention_point: context assembly/compression + generator prompting or training (Paper A NLI filter + fine-tuning on mixed contexts); generator prompting or training (Paper B adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise-aware head)
metric_target: answer correctness (EM/F1 on ODQA)
action_policy: filter + answer (Paper A: NLI rejects non-entailing passages then answers with or without retrieval); answer (Paper B: no filter, model is trained to be robust); explicit noise-class prediction is auxiliary in Paper B but not a deployed action
rationale: Both papers tackle noise robustness of RALMs on open-domain QA and share the answer-correctness metric family (EM/F1), and Paper B explicitly builds on Yoran et al. as motivation. However, Paper A scopes 'noise' as irrelevant retrieved passages (a pure relevance/noise problem) and proposes either an NLI filter or training on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts, whereas Paper B expands the noise taxonomy to include counterfactual passages (a consistency/conflict failure type) and proposes adaptive adversarial training plus an auxiliary noise-classification objective with a new RAG-Bench. The action policies diverge (filter+answer vs. answer only), the evidence assumptions differ (naturally retrieved noise vs. benchmark-constructed counterfactual stressors), and the intervention points only partially overlap. The papers are best framed as complementary noise-robustness mechanisms operating in different regions of the noise space rather than as substitutable leaderboard entries, so the verdict is partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on a shared retriever (e.g., DPR over Wikipedia), shared generator backbone (e.g., LLaMA-2 7B), and a shared noise-injection protocol that separately reports performance on (a) naturally irrelevant retrievals, (b) constructed irrelevant distractors, and (c) counterfactual passages; report EM/F1 plus abstention/filter behavior on identical splits of NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ; and explicitly align action policies (whether the system is allowed to filter passages or must answer from given context) so the comparison isolates the training/intervention difference.
notes: Paper B cites Paper A, indicating recognized lineage; partial rather than valid because counterfactual noise and the filtering action are not jointly evaluated on a common harness.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); Paper B additionally covers sufficiency (negative rejection) and consistency/conflict (counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: Paper A: benign retrieval error (retrieved irrelevant passages from real ODQA retrieval). Paper B: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents).
intervention_point: Paper A: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting or training (fine-tuning on mixed contexts). Paper B: evaluation artifact only (no intervention proposed).
metric_target: Paper A: answer correctness on 5 ODQA benchmarks. Paper B: accuracy under varying noise ratios + rejection rate + integration accuracy + counterfactual error rate across 4 separate testbeds.
action_policy: Paper A: filter + answer (NLI-gated answering). Paper B: answer + abstain (explicitly evaluates negative rejection / 'I cannot answer').
rationale: Both papers explicitly address noise robustness in RAG and share the high-level concern that irrelevant retrieved context degrades LLM accuracy. However, Paper A is a method paper proposing NLI-based filtering and robustness fine-tuning evaluated on five ODQA datasets with naturally retrieved noisy passages, while Paper B is a diagnostic benchmark (RGB) that constructs four separate testbeds—including negative rejection and counterfactual robustness—and reports no intervention. The intervention point, action policy space (Paper B requires abstain; Paper A does not evaluate abstain), metric families, and evidence construction all differ, so they cannot be ranked head-to-head as alternative methods on the same leaderboard. They are complementary: Paper A's methods could in principle be evaluated on Paper B's benchmark, but neither paper performs that comparison, so the relationship is partial rather than valid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Paper A's NLI-filter and fine-tuned RALM on RGB's four testbeds (especially noise-ratio and negative-rejection subsets) using the same base LLMs, and conversely evaluate Paper B's tested LLMs on Paper A's ODQA benchmarks with matched retriever and prompt. Report a shared metric family (accuracy + rejection rate) and explicitly define the action policy (answer vs abstain vs filter) for both systems under identical retrieval conditions.
notes: Classic method-vs-benchmark mismatch; partial is appropriate because the failure-type overlap is real but action policy and intervention diverge.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); RGB additionally covers sufficiency (negative rejection) and consistency/conflict (counterfactual robustness)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (both); RAAT constructs relevant/irrelevant/counterfactual noise on DPR-retrieved Wikipedia passages; RGB constructs controlled noise ratios over news-corpus + search-engine documents
intervention_point: generator prompting or training (RAAT: adaptive adversarial training + multi-task noise classification on LLaMA-2 7B) vs. evaluation artifact (RGB: pure benchmark, no model intervention)
metric_target: answer correctness (RAAT: F1/EM); RGB also reports selective risk/coverage (rejection accuracy) and a counterfactual-handling metric
action_policy: RAAT: answer only (unreported abstain/conflict behavior); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection testbed) + expose conflict (counterfactual testbed)
rationale: Both papers center on noise robustness in RAG, but they occupy asymmetric roles: RAAT is a training-side method evaluated on its own RAG-Bench (NQ/TriviaQA/WebQ via DPR) with answer-only F1/EM, while RGB is a multi-ability evaluation artifact that probes noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness on a bilingual news corpus across 6 LLMs without proposing any intervention. The intervention points differ fundamentally (generator training vs. benchmark), the action policies diverge (RAAT does not evaluate abstain or conflict-exposure, both of which are first-class abilities in RGB), and metric families only partially overlap. They are best treated as complementary—one a method, one a yardstick—rather than directly rankable on the same leaderboard. Verdict is therefore partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run the RAAT-trained LLaMA-2 model (and the relevant baselines) on RGB's four testbeds using RGB's noise-ratio protocol, news corpus, and metrics (including rejection accuracy and counterfactual error/identification rates), or alternatively restrict comparison to a single matched noise-robustness subtest with identical retriever, corpus, noise-construction procedure, prompt template, metric definitions, and an explicitly evaluated action policy (answer vs. abstain vs. expose conflict).
notes: RGB is partly a benchmark paper; pairing a method with a benchmark almost always yields partial unless the method has been run on that benchmark.

failure_type: relevance/noise (both); uncertainty/OOD (Paper A only via RealTimeQA unknown scenarios)
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error and benchmark-constructed stressor (both papers use natural retriever errors plus controlled noisy/irrelevant context injections on ODQA benchmarks); not adversarial
intervention_point: Paper A: generator prompting/training (note-taking reasoning step). Paper B: context assembly/compression (NLI filter) + generator prompting/training (fine-tuning on mixed relevant/irrelevant contexts).
metric_target: answer correctness (both, EM/accuracy on ODQA); Paper A additionally reports rejection rate (selective risk/coverage); Paper B emphasizes accuracy on multi-hop.
action_policy: Paper A: answer + abstain ('unknown' when intrinsic and retrieved knowledge are insufficient), explicitly evaluated via rejection rate. Paper B: filter (NLI-based passage discarding, fallback to no-retrieval); abstention is not part of the evaluated action set.
rationale: Both papers target the same failure type—generator distraction by irrelevant retrieved passages on ODQA—and both report accuracy-style answer-correctness on overlapping benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA), so they are clearly in the same problem family. However, Paper A intervenes at generator reasoning (per-document reading notes) and explicitly evaluates an abstain action ('unknown' with a rejection-rate metric), pulling in an OOD/uncertainty dimension. Paper B intervenes either before the generator (NLI passage filter) or via fine-tuning on mixed contexts, evaluates only answer correctness, and treats irrelevance via filter-and-skip rather than abstention; it also adds a multi-hop emphasis. Because the action policies differ (abstain vs. filter), the intervention points only partly overlap, and the metric targets are not symmetric, a leaderboard-style ranking would conflate distraction robustness with abstention behavior. The comparison is therefore partial: they are complementary mitigations rather than directly substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Hold retriever, generator backbone, training/inference budget, and benchmark splits constant; evaluate both methods on (a) accuracy with relevant context, (b) accuracy with irrelevant/noisy context, (c) accuracy on multi-hop, and (d) rejection rate / selective risk on an unknown/OOD slice with a defined abstention action. Additionally, run each method's intervention component (CoN notes, NLI filter, robustness fine-tuning) under a shared action policy so that filter vs. abstain vs. answer can be compared on the same axes.
notes: Treating CoN's abstain capability and Paper B's NLI filter+fine-tune as substitutable would mask that one targets calibrated refusal while the other targets passage gating; reviewers should report both axes separately.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: benign retrieval error
intervention_point: verifier, context assembly/compression, generator prompting or training, retriever
metric_target: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, selective risk/coverage
action_policy: abstain, answer, re-retrieve
rationale: Both papers address the broad problem that retrieved context may be irrelevant or insufficient and that an RAG system should not blindly emit an answer, so they share the failure types of sufficiency and relevance/noise under benign retrieval errors. However, the intervention points are fundamentally different: Sufficient Context introduces a post-hoc autorater plus a self-confidence-gated selective generation layer, whereas Self-RAG retrains the generator end-to-end with reflection tokens that drive on-demand retrieval and self-critique. The action policies also differ in kind—Sufficient Context's evaluated policy is answer-vs-abstain (selective risk/coverage), while Self-RAG's evaluated policy is adaptive re-retrieve plus generation with citations and factuality scoring. Metric families overlap on answer correctness but Self-RAG centrally reports citation faithfulness on long-form tasks that Sufficient Context does not target, and Sufficient Context reports correctness-conditional-on-answering that Self-RAG does not. They are best framed as complementary modules (a verifier-style abstention layer vs. an adaptive retrieve-and-critique generator) rather than two methods on the same leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both systems on a common benchmark suite spanning short-form QA (e.g., PopQA, TriviaQA) and a hallucination/abstention-sensitive set (e.g., Musique or FActScore-style long-form), with the same retriever and generator base, and report a unified set of metrics: accuracy on answered subset, abstention rate, hallucination rate, citation precision/recall, and a coverage-risk curve. Both methods must be evaluated under a single explicit action policy (e.g., answer/abstain/re-retrieve with declared thresholds), so that one can be substituted for the other at the same operating point.
notes: Both action policies are explicit in the papers, so the break is in which policy is operationalized, not absence; this prevents direct leaderboard substitution.

failure_type: CalibRAG: uncertainty/OOD; Self-RAG: relevance/noise, sufficiency
evidence_assumption: Both assume benign retrieval (no adversarial corpus); standard open-domain QA / knowledge-intensive setting with no attacker model
intervention_point: CalibRAG: reranker (forecasting function over (t,q,d)) plus generator confidence calibration; Self-RAG: generator prompting/training (reflection tokens) plus on-demand retriever triggering
metric_target: CalibRAG: calibration error and answer/decision correctness; Self-RAG: answer correctness, citation faithfulness, evidence support
action_policy: CalibRAG: answer with calibrated confidence (no explicit abstain/re-retrieve policy reported); Self-RAG: adaptive re-retrieve plus verify via critique tokens
rationale: Both papers fall under 'controllability of RAG' and share a benign-retrieval evidence assumption, but they target fundamentally different control problems. CalibRAG addresses uncertainty/calibration: it trains a forecasting function to predict decision correctness and uses it for reranking + confidence calibration, with calibration error (ECE-style) as a primary metric. Self-RAG addresses adaptive retrieval and self-critique for factuality and citation faithfulness, intervening at the generator via reflection tokens. The failure type, primary metric, intervention point, and action policy all differ, so a leaderboard ranking would conflate calibration quality with adaptive-retrieval factuality. They are best framed as complementary modules (Self-RAG could in principle be calibrated by something like CalibRAG) rather than direct substitutes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark and protocol evaluating both calibration metrics (ECE, selective risk/coverage) and factuality/citation metrics on the same tasks, retriever, generator backbone, and decision elicitation procedure; an explicit, matched action policy (e.g., both methods either always answer with a confidence score or both perform adaptive retrieve/abstain), so that a single metric family decides the ranking rather than two different objectives.
notes: Both nominally 'control' coordinate of robust RAG, but CalibRAG = confidence/decision calibration, Self-RAG = adaptive retrieval + self-critique; overlap is structural (controlling RAG behavior), not operational.

failure_type: FaithfulRAG: consistency/conflict (parametric vs. retrieved); PoisonedRAG: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict / benchmark-constructed stressor, no adversary; PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, query control over target questions, black-box and white-box retriever/generator visibility, insertion budget ~5 malicious texts per target question, attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: FaithfulRAG: generator prompting (self-fact extraction, alignment, self-think); PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (offensive injection, no defense proposed)
metric_target: FaithfulRAG: answer correctness, evidence support, faithfulness; PoisonedRAG: attack success rate
action_policy: FaithfulRAG: answer (with reconciliation); PoisonedRAG: unreported (attack paper, no defender action policy evaluated)
rationale: Both papers concern RAG outputs being shaped by problematic retrieved context, but the overlap ends there. FaithfulRAG is a generator-side defense for naturally occurring or benchmark-induced conflicts between parametric and retrieved knowledge, with no adversary in the loop, measured by answer correctness and faithfulness. PoisonedRAG is an offensive paper that assumes an adversary with corpus write access and a ~5-passage insertion budget per target question, and measures attack success rate; it does not propose or evaluate a defense action policy. Failure type, evidence assumption, intervention role (defense vs. attack), and metric family all differ, so they cannot occupy the same leaderboard as alternative methods for one problem.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require either (a) evaluating FaithfulRAG as a defender against PoisonedRAG-style injections under a matched threat model (same retriever, generator, corpus, target questions, insertion budget) and reporting both clean accuracy and ASR reduction, or (b) reframing PoisonedRAG with an explicit defender-side action policy and shared faithfulness/correctness metrics. Without an attack-vs-defense pairing on common datasets, the two papers should be cited as complementary (threat surface vs. conflict mitigation), not ranked.
notes: Classic offense/defense category error; no shared metric target makes any direct ranking meaningless.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption (PoisonedRAG); relevance/noise + consistency/conflict + integrity/adversarial corruption (Astute RAG)
evidence_assumption: PoisonedRAG: attacker-created evidence with corpus write access, no retriever/generator access required (black-box variant), small insertion budget (~5 texts), attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer. Astute RAG: mixture of benign retrieval error, naturally occurring conflict, and benchmark-constructed stressors; no explicit threat model.
intervention_point: PoisonedRAG: corpus/index (attack-side injection). Astute RAG: generator prompting + context assembly/compression (defense-side consolidation).
metric_target: PoisonedRAG: attack success rate. Astute RAG: answer correctness (incl. worst-case accuracy on RGB).
action_policy: PoisonedRAG: unreported (no defender action policy is the contribution). Astute RAG: answer (with source-aware reliability comparison); no abstain/quarantine evaluated against an explicit adversary.
breaking_coordinates: intervention_point, metric_target, evidence_assumption, action_policy, role asymmetry (attack vs defense)
rationale: Both papers live in the broader robust/secure-RAG space and acknowledge that retrieved evidence can be misleading or malicious, but they occupy fundamentally asymmetric roles: PoisonedRAG is an attack that injects optimized malicious passages into the corpus and measures attack success rate, while Astute RAG is a generator-side defense that consolidates internal and external knowledge to maximize answer correctness under imperfect retrieval. Their intervention points (corpus injection vs. generator prompting), metric targets (ASR vs. accuracy), and evidence assumptions (explicit corpus write-access adversary with an attack objective vs. mostly natural/benchmark-constructed noise) do not align, and neither paper evaluates the other's setting (Astute RAG is not tested against PoisonedRAG-style optimized poisons, and PoisonedRAG does not evaluate Astute RAG as a defense). Putting them on the same leaderboard as alternative methods would be misleading, so the comparison is invalid rather than partial.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To enable a meaningful comparison, both works would need to share a common attack-defense evaluation: (1) instantiate PoisonedRAG (both black-box and white-box variants, with explicit insertion budgets, retriever/generator visibility, and target-answer objectives) as the threat model; (2) evaluate Astute RAG alongside other defenses (e.g., majority voting, filtering, RobustRAG) on the resulting poisoned corpora; (3) report a joint metric suite covering attack success rate, clean-task accuracy, abstention/coverage, and any verification/quarantine action policy; (4) hold retriever, generator, corpus, and queries constant across conditions. Without this, the two papers are complementary artifacts (attack benchmark vs. defense method), not substitutable methods.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense asymmetry; could become a valid comparison only if cast as defense-under-PoisonedRAG benchmark, which neither paper currently performs.

failure_type: integrity/adversarial corruption
evidence_assumption: attacker-created evidence (both); corpus write access = yes for both; query control = yes (attacker chooses target questions in PoisonedRAG; adaptive attacker in RobustRAG); retriever visibility = black-box and white-box variants in PoisonedRAG vs. assumed adaptive/full-knowledge in RobustRAG; generator access varies by threat-model variant; insertion budget = small bounded number (5 texts in PoisonedRAG; bounded k' in RobustRAG); attack objective = induce attacker-chosen target answer
intervention_point: corpus/index (PoisonedRAG injects malicious passages) vs. context assembly/compression + generator prompting (RobustRAG isolate-then-aggregate)
metric_target: attack success (PoisonedRAG ASR) vs. answer correctness with certified lower bound (RobustRAG certified accuracy)
action_policy: answer (PoisonedRAG, no defensive action) vs. answer + abstain ('I don't know' branch in RobustRAG keyword aggregation)
rationale: Both papers operate in the same threat model — an attacker with corpus write access who injects a small bounded number of malicious passages into a RAG knowledge base to corrupt downstream answers — so they share the failure type (integrity/adversarial corruption) and evidence assumption (attacker-created evidence). However, PoisonedRAG is an offense paper whose intervention is corpus injection and whose metric is ASR with no defended action policy, whereas RobustRAG is a defense paper whose intervention is context assembly/aggregation with an explicit abstain branch and whose metric is certified answer correctness. They are complementary halves of the attack/defense ecosystem (RobustRAG should be evaluated against PoisonedRAG-style attacks) but are not alternative methods to the same task; placing them on one leaderboard would conflate ASR-maximization with accuracy-defense and mislead readers. Hence partial, not valid; not invalid because the assumptions are coherent and a paired evaluation is natural.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Direct comparison would require both works to report the same outcome metric on the same side of the problem — e.g., both reporting defended accuracy and ASR under a shared attack (PoisonedRAG) and a shared defense suite (including RobustRAG) on the same retriever/generator/dataset, with explicit action-policy labels (answer vs. abstain) and a fixed insertion budget. Ranking would only be meaningful among alternative defenses (or alternative attacks), not across an attack and a defense.
notes: Classic attack-vs-defense pair; threat model alignment makes the relationship coherent (so not invalid) but the metric/action asymmetry blocks any leaderboard-style ranking.

failure_type: consistency/conflict, sufficiency, relevance/noise
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: benign retrieval error / naturally occurring conflict (naturally generated LLM responses under standard RAG); RGB: benchmark-constructed stressor (controlled noise ratios, injected counterfactual documents)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (both); RAGTruth additionally targets verifier (fine-tuned hallucination detector)
metric_target: RAGTruth: evidence support / citation faithfulness (span-level hallucination detection F1); RGB: answer correctness, selective risk/coverage (rejection rate), and counterfactual error identification
action_policy: RAGTruth: unreported (post-hoc detection only, no system action evaluated); RGB: answer + abstain (negative rejection is explicitly scored)
rationale: Both papers are RAG evaluation benchmarks broadly concerned with trustworthy generation, but they evaluate fundamentally different objects. RAGTruth is a span-level hallucination detection corpus over naturally generated LLM responses with word-level annotations, scoring detector precision/recall rather than generator behavior; RGB is a stressor-constructed multi-ability testbed measuring how LLMs answer or abstain under controlled noise, missing-evidence, integration, and counterfactual conditions. The evidence assumption (natural vs. injected), the metric family (span-level faithfulness detection vs. end-to-end accuracy/rejection), and the action policy (RGB explicitly evaluates abstention; RAGTruth does not evaluate any system action) all diverge. They should be discussed as complementary resources covering different slices of RAG trustworthiness, not as interchangeable leaderboards.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To make this comparison valid, one would need a shared evaluation surface: e.g., either (a) run RAGTruth-trained detectors on RGB's counterfactual/noise testbeds with the same span-level or response-level faithfulness metric and the same generator outputs, or (b) instrument RAGTruth responses with abstain/answer decisions and re-score using RGB's accuracy + rejection-rate protocol. At minimum the papers must agree on task formulation (detection vs. generation), fix retriever and generator, share noise/conflict construction (natural vs. injected), and report the same metric family with explicit action labels.
notes: Both are 'evaluation_benchmark' in spirit but with non-overlapping output spaces; treating one as a substitute for the other on a single leaderboard would mislead.

failure_type: sufficiency, relevance/noise, consistency/conflict (RGB only)
evidence_assumption: benchmark-constructed stressor (RGB: controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injections); benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor (Sufficient Context: autorater-labeled real (Q,C) pairs from existing QA datasets)
intervention_point: evaluation artifact (RGB); evaluation artifact + verifier + generator prompting/system-control policy (Sufficient Context's selective generation)
metric_target: answer correctness, abstention rate (both); selective risk/coverage (Sufficient Context only); per-ability accuracy/rejection/error-detection scores (RGB only)
action_policy: answer, abstain (both explicitly evaluate abstention; RGB tests negative rejection, Sufficient Context tests selective generation/guided abstention)
rationale: Both papers study RAG behavior when retrieved context is insufficient or noisy, and both explicitly evaluate abstention as an action policy, so they share the sufficiency failure type and the answer/abstain action space. However, RGB is a pure evaluation artifact built from constructed news-based testbeds with controlled noise ratios and counterfactual injections, scoring four discrete abilities (including counterfactual robustness, which is absent from Sufficient Context), whereas Sufficient Context introduces a sufficiency autorater and a selective generation method, evaluated via stratified hallucination/abstention rates and a selective risk–coverage style metric on standard QA datasets. The intervention point, metric framing, and evidence construction therefore differ enough that one cannot place results on a single leaderboard; they are complementary lenses on RAG abstention rather than substitutable methods.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run Sufficient Context's autorater and selective-generation pipeline on RGB's four testbeds (especially noise robustness and negative rejection) using RGB's metrics, and conversely apply RGB's per-ability scoring (including counterfactual robustness) to the models/datasets Sufficient Context studies; report a shared answer/abstain/hallucinate decomposition with a common selective-risk vs. coverage curve under identical retriever, generator, and noise-injection settings.
notes: RGB is fundamentally a benchmark/diagnostic and Sufficient Context is a framework+method; even where they overlap on abstention, the operationalizations (binary rejection vs. confidence-thresholded selective generation) are not directly rankable.

failure_type: consistency/conflict for FaithfulRAG; broader hallucination (relevance/noise + consistency/conflict + sufficiency) for RAGTruth
evidence_assumption: RAGTruth: naturally generated LLM outputs in standard RAG (benign retrieval error + benchmark-constructed stressor for annotation); FaithfulRAG: naturally occurring conflict between parametric and retrieved knowledge
intervention_point: RAGTruth: evaluation artifact (corpus + fine-tuned detector); FaithfulRAG: generator prompting/training (self-fact mining + self-think pre-generation reconciliation)
metric_target: RAGTruth: hallucination detection F1/precision/recall over annotated spans; FaithfulRAG: answer correctness / context faithfulness on QA benchmarks
action_policy: unreported (RAGTruth scores detector output, no downstream action; FaithfulRAG always answers after reconciliation, no abstain/escalate evaluated)
rationale: Both papers sit under the faithfulness umbrella for RAG, but they are categorically different artifacts: RAGTruth is an ~18K-response corpus with word-level hallucination annotations spanning QA, data-to-text, and summarization, used to benchmark and fine-tune hallucination detectors; FaithfulRAG is a generation-time framework that mines parametric self-facts and runs a self-think module to reconcile parametric-vs-retrieved knowledge conflict before answering. The intervention point differs categorically (evaluation artifact and post-hoc verifier vs. pre-generation generator intervention), the failure-type scope differs (broad hallucination taxonomy vs. specifically parametric-context conflict), and the metric targets are non-overlapping (span-level detection scores vs. end-to-end answer correctness on conflict-laden QA). A leaderboard-style ranking would mislead because RAGTruth does not propose a competing context-faithfulness generator and FaithfulRAG is not evaluated as a hallucination detector on annotated spans.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run FaithfulRAG end-to-end on the RAGTruth response distribution (or a held-out QA slice with knowledge-conflict annotation) and report span-level hallucination rates using RAGTruth's annotation schema; conversely, deploy the RAGTruth-fine-tuned detector as a verifier in a generate-then-check pipeline and compare its conflict-handling action policy against FaithfulRAG's self-think reconciliation under identical retriever, generator backbone, conflict distribution, and a shared metric family (both span-level hallucination and end-to-end answer correctness).
notes: Categorical artifact mismatch (benchmark/detector vs. generation-time conflict-resolution framework); even partial framing would overstate overlap because neither paper reports results in the other's evaluation regime.
